noticias.titulo: UK and allies call on Israel to allow rapid humanitarian access to Gaza
noticias.resumen: The UK, Australia, Canada and Italy say Israeli authorities are holding back vital supplies at the borders, including 150,00 tents.
noticias.texto:
UK and allies call on Israel to allow rapid humanitarian access to Gaza
- Published
The UK, Australia, Canada and Italy have issued a joint statement urging Israel to "allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza", where they say the situation on the ground is "dire".
The foreign ministers warn recent floods have brought "further suffering" to the war-torn territory, which recently had its first winter storm.
The statement says 150,000 tents and other vital supplies are being held at the border.
The Israeli military authority which controls the Gaza crossings has said it is co-ordinating with the US-led Board of Peace and the UN on a winter plan, and that 93,000 tents and 8,600 aid trucks with winter supplies had entered the territory.
It added that reconstruction "can only begin after Hamas fully disarms".
The UN Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs said the widespread flooding and a landslide led to a number of deaths, thousands of damaged shelters and the suspension of critical services.
The statement from the British, Australian, Canadian and Italian foreign ministers says, external: "This situation is entirely reversible - and there is still time to act before the winter fully sets in."
"The crossings must be opened, and the tents allowed in. Dual-use items necessary for humanitarian operations and early recovery must be granted entry before it is too late."
The European Union issued a similar statement on Saturday, external, reiterating its "grave concern" over what it called the "persistent and devastating humanitarian crisis".
The EU also urged Israel to comply with international law.
The war in Gaza was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Israel responded by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 74,690 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israeli air strikes and other attacks have continued to take place almost every day despite the ceasefire agreed in October last year.

- Published
South African police are investigating the murders of 17 people in two separate shootings on Sunday night.
Eight men were fatally shot in a minibus in KwaZulu-Natal province. Police declared them dead when they arrived at the scene. Hours later, nine people were found shot dead inside a shack in western Pretoria.
Police say the two incidents are unrelated. The motive for the shootings has not yet been established.
South Africa is struggling to contain violent crime, including gang-related killings. The country has one of the world's highest murder rates.
Police say they responded to reports of a shooting â outside Pietermaritzburg town in KwaZulu-Natal and found a white seven-seater vehicle riddled with bullet holes.
Inside were eight men with multiple gunshot wounds.
"It has not been established how the incident happened, and police are collecting pieces of evidence to determine the possible motive of the killings and the identity of the suspects," police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda said.
The police have launched a manhunt for the suspects.
In a separate shooting in the Jeffsville informal settlement in Atteridgeville, west of Pretoria, police found the bodies of six men and three women.
They are believed to have been killed inside a four-room shack between 22:00 and 23:00 on Sunday. The bodies were scattered across the rooms, with several spent cartridges discovered outside the shack.
Community members initially mistook the gunshots for thunder and lightning.
"The provincial commissioner of police in Gauteng [province, which includes Pretoria] has mobilized the necessary resources, including the crime intelligence and the deputy provincial commissioner tracking team to search for the suspect," police spokesperson Brigadier Brenda Muridili said.
It's not the first mass shooting in the area. In January, five men were shot dead outside a local shop in broad daylight.
Illegal firearms are widespread in South Africa, where gun violence remains a persistent problem, increasingly involving mass shootings.
In September, 28 people were killed in two separate cases.
Eighteen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar near Johannesburg and opened fire on 25 September. Fourteen others were injured.
In a separate shooting the following day, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town. A further 11 were injured.
Much of the violence has been linked to turf wars between gangs involved in drug trafficking and illegal mining.
In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa described organised crime as "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development".
Earlier this year, the military was deployed alongside police to five provinces with the highest murder rates, including Gauteng, in an effort to tackle armed violence.
According to the latest police statistics, 5,427 people were murdered nationwide between April and June 2026, an average of about 60 killings a day. This was a 6% decline compared with the same period a year earlier.

noticias.titulo: Australian MP 'full of gratitude' upon leaving hospital after alleged car attack
noticias.resumen: The MP lost both of her legs after the alleged attack outside her electorate office four weeks ago.
noticias.texto:
Australian MP 'full of gratitude' upon leaving hospital after alleged car attack
- Published
Australian politician Helen Haines has said she is "full of gratitude" upon being discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked with a car and left a double amputee.
The independent MP was struck outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on October 19, an incident which horrified Australia.
Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. He has yet to enter pleas.
In her first public comments since the attack, Haines, 65, said she had moved into the rehabilitation stage of her recovery.
"This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage," Haines said.
"I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing."
She added that she had been "overwhelmed" by the generosity of well wishers who had donated to Save the Children in her honour.
Haines, known for supporting stronger climate action and helping establish a national anti-corruption commission, entered parliament in 2019 as the Member for Indi after working as a nurse and midwife.
Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.
Nugent's father said he and his wife had been long-time friends of Haines, and Nugent's lawyer has said his client has mental health concerns.
The incident sparked a reckoning in the country more broadly over the tone of public debate.
Though a motive is still unclear, politicians, law enforcement, and experts have said heated public discourse is heightening the threat of political violence in the country.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had been in regular contact with Haines and her "extraordinary" family.
"All our thoughts and prayers continue to be with Helen for her recovery," he said in a statement.
"We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation."

noticias.titulo: US basketball player arrested with 34kg of cannabis at Nigerian airport
noticias.resumen: The anti-drugs agency says the American attempted to leave the airport, abandoning his luggage with the drugs.
noticias.texto:
US basketball player arrested with 34kg of cannabis at Nigerian airport
- Published
A basketball player from the US has been arrested in Nigeria with 33.95kg (75lbs) of cannabis in his luggage at the main airport in Lagos.
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) identified the player as Greene Da'monte Khiree, 28, from the US state of Georgia, who it said had arrived from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.
According to the agency, the suspect said he had been playing professional basketball in Thailand and was visiting to Nigeria to "build networks" for his career. He has not publicly commented on the allegations.
The agency said an examination of the suspect's phone had pointed "to his knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity".
In statement on Sunday, the agency said he was arrested on Wednesday after airport officials noticed him abandoning his two checked-in bags and attempting to leave with his carry-on bag.
The two bags, which bore his name, contained 32 packs of the drug known as "Loud", a potent strain of cannabis, the agency said.
A tracking device was also recovered from the bags, the agency added.
The International Basketball Federation (FIBA) lists a player by the name Damonte Greene, with the most recent appearance at the Phuket Elite Cup in Thailand, on 26 September.
Greene played with the Reinhardt University's basketball team in the US in the 2017-2018 season, before he went to play at the South Georgia Technical College.
He was the leading scorer with Georgia Bombers semi-professional basketball team during the 2023-24 season before he moved to Thailand.
Nigeria, once regarded primarily as a transit hub for drug trafficking, has increasingly become a producer, consumer, and distributor of illegal drugs, according to the UN.
Recent NDLEA operations have uncovered several industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratories, raising concerns about links between Nigerian drug producers and Mexican cartels seeking to manufacture and export the drug.
In September, the agency said it had dismantled a meth lab and arrested a Mexican suspected drug kingpin who was allegedly attempting to flee Nigeria through Lagos.
Methamphetamine, commonly known as meth, is a highly addictive synthetic drug that can cause severe psychosis, heart attacks or stroke.
In August, a social media influencer suspected of links to an international drug trafficking network was arrested after the authorities seized cocaine worth nearly $28m (Â£21m), which was destined for the UK.

noticias.titulo: Teenager Andreeva caps stunning week with WTA Finals title
noticias.resumen: French Open champion Mirra Andreeva caps her stellar season with a hard-fought victory over Elina Svitolina to win the WTA Finals.
noticias.texto:
Teenager Andreeva caps stunning week with WTA Finals title
- Published
For Mirra Andreeva, the thought of her first WTA Finals singles campaign was so stressful that it gave her "a little breakdown" in a practice session before the tournament.
The 19-year-old may have been nervous on arrival at Indian Wells, but she leaves California as the champion, having been the standout player of the week.
The French Open winner produced a hard-fought 7-5 6-3 victory over Elina Svitolina in Sunday's final to become the youngest champion of the event in 22 years.
The Russian has now risen to second in the world rankings - and she will start the 2027 season just 293 points behind top-ranked Elena Rybakina.
Andreeva did not drop a set on her way to the title and lost only 26 games across her five matches.
She raised her arms in celebration after beating Svitolina before racing to celebrate with her team, which includes 1994 Wimbledon champion Conchita Martinez.
"I am super thankful to my team for pushing me to my limits, for forcing me to do stuff when I don't want to do anything," Andreeva said.
"Thanks for fighting with me, thanks for forcing me to do everything that I have to do and not asking any questions!"
As well as Â£2.55m in prize money, Andreeva also won a custom purple Mercedes - and joked she was happy to remain a "passenger princess" until she passed her test.
Andreeva thanks herself again after stellar season
One of the most notable parts of Andreeva's performance has been her increased maturity.
In March, she swore at the Indian Wells crowd after suffering an early defeat in the venue's WTA Tour tournament, and she has struggled to control her emotions, external on court in the past.
However, she showed little sign of that during this tournament.
Against Svitolina, one of the grittiest players on the women's tour, she lost a break lead three times across the two sets. Each time, she reset admirably, upping her aggression on her backhand in particular to put pressure back on her opponent.
After losing serve in a mammoth nine-minute game in the second set, Andreeva marched back to her chair and then broke Svitolina from 40-0 down in the next game to stay in front.
While her serve was not at its best, Andreeva still saved nine of the 12 break points she faced and hit 19 winners to Svitolina's 10.
"This fighting mindset helped me to get more brave and aggressive in the important moments," Andreeva told Sky Sports.
"This is just a dream. I had a little breakdown in my practice just before Indian Wells because I was so stressed.
"I didn't want to lose a match in the group. It's amazing."
Andreeva had only won one of her six matches against top-10 players in 2026 coming into the tournament.
She has beaten three top-10 players en route to the title, including a demolition of four-time major champion Aryna Sabalenka on Wednesday.
She also laughed off an incident before the tournament where private comments Jessica Pegula made to her coach about Andreeva - including calling her a "diva" - were live-streamed.
Just as she did when she won the French Open, Andreeva ended her speech by thanking herself - a twist on a quote she "stole" from rapper Snoop Dogg.
"I want to thank myself for always doing the hard work and for never quitting," she said.
"For not taking the days off, for working every day and committing to what I have to do - just thanks to myself."
Ukraine's Svitolina was tearful after the defeat, but reaching this stage capped a fine turnaround after she lost 6-4 6-0 to Andreeva on the first day of the tournament.
She pushed Andreeva throughout, drawing her into lengthy baseline rallies before fatigue set in.
She will finish the year at six in the world rankings, having made it back into the top 10 for the first time since 2021.
Svitolina returned from maternity leave in 2022, and joked that daughter Skai would have some questions for her after the match.
"She's probably still awake and is going to ask me why I didn't win today," the 32-year-old said.
"I'm really happy to be in great form and coming back after pregnancy. Hopefully it inspires some ladies and athletes around the world to believe that it's possible.
"I also want to say thank you to people in Ukraine for supporting me and being on this journey with me."

noticias.titulo: 'You're going to win the war': Harry praises war veterans on surprise Ukraine visit
noticias.resumen: He has been showing support for injured veterans in Ukraine and praising the country's resilience.
noticias.texto:
'You're going to win the war': Harry praises war veterans on surprise Ukraine visit
- Published
The Duke of Sussex has received an enthusiastic welcome in a surprise visit to Ukraine to support injured war veterans, meeting Ukrainian competitors taking part in his Invictus Games.
There were emotional scenes as he was applauded by injured service men and women in Lviv, where he told his audience: "You're going to win the war."
Prince Harry spent two days at events for veterans, with a press blackout for security reasons until he had left Ukraine, as the country continues to face missile attacks from Russia.
Ukraine has more than 150,000 injured war veterans and the prince visited projects supporting their treatment and rehabilitation.
"Ukraine now is experiencing elements of war that no other country has experienced before," he said - with technology advancing in areas such as drone warfare, but also in protecting cities and providing treatment.
A mobile phone app is where Ukrainians look for air raid warnings, telling them the direction, timing and type of any incoming missiles.
At the Superhumans Center near Lviv, Harry was shown how growing numbers of injured veterans receive groundbreaking treatment.
International experts used to come to help Ukraine, he said, but "now that has flipped," with Ukraine having the greater expertise with trauma injuries to share with others.
That included an innovation for Mykhailo Damaskin, a Ukrainian air assault forces veteran, who was so seriously injured in fighting in Kherson he was never expected to walk again.
In an experimental treatment he had a spinal cord stimulator implanted in his back, which allows him to walk, but has to be re-charged every 12 hours. He cannot feel his feet and controls his steps using his eyes.
He needs to be plugged in and charged up to be able to move - and jokes that he is "like a demo model of a Tesla".
"My goal is to go to the Invictus Games. I promised my father before he was killed that I'd be part of the team to represent Ukraine internationally.
"I'll prove to every guy with spinal cord injuries that life goes on after injury," said Mykhailo.
At the Superhumans Center Prince Harry sat at the bedside of Konstiantyn Vlasenko, who was airlifted from the front line by a drone last month in a rescue that was a first of its kind.
He had been alone for more than 200 days and had stayed at his position, despite losing both his feet.
In a moving encounter, Prince Harry told him he represented the spirit of resilience of Ukraine.
And he described the injured veterans as "role models", promising his audience: "The rest of the world will continue to support you."
Along with all the determination, it was an inescapably poignant sight too, with so many families and children at the medical facility visiting the growing numbers of badly injured war casualties.
Olga Rudeva, chief executive of the SuperHumans Center, said it is seeing more injured civilians than ever because of "changes to the frontlines".
"The Russians are doing double taps, they are targeting civilian infrastructure," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
As a result, "it's not only about [an] increased number of patients, it's about increased complexity of new cases."
Russia has repeatedly denied it aims for civilian targets.
At a noisy sports centre in Lviv, Prince Harry arrived to watch a wheelchair rugby match taking place, with some thunderous collisions between the players.
He was welcomed by the competitors in what he has called his Invictus "family" and soon the visit turned into something approaching a group hug, with Harry disappearing into a sea of selfies and handshakes.
He was presented with a T-shirt remembering prisoners of war held by Russian forces.
And he later had a chance to play one of the events at the Invictus Games, a tennis-style competition called pickleball.
Watching was Ivan Voinov, who has lost a leg and suffered head injuries, but who is using sport to help his rehabilitation - including learning to dance again.
He said that dancing was his way to be together with his wife again, which meant so much to his recovery and recovering his identity.
At an Invictus awards ceremony during the visit, Prince Harry was greeted with choruses of "Harry, Harry, Harry", getting a rock star welcome.
"Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth, I feel encouragement," he said, having returned for a fourth trip here during wartime.
He promised that "when the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games".
There have been 400 wounded service men and women in Ukraine taking part in trials for next year's games, being hosted in Birmingham.
The sports events are an attempt to encourage rehabilitation and to recognise the resilience of people overcoming their challenges.
Prince Harry told a gathering of new Invictus members of a "cultural shift" from people being socially awkward about seeing injured veterans to wanting to show respect.
"These people have so much to offer," he said.
"Recovery cannot wait for the war to end, The scale of need in Ukraine is huge, and wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans need the chance to rebuild their lives now," said Rob Owen, chief executive officer of the Invictus Games Foundation.

noticias.titulo: Wife of assassinated ex-Haitian leader registers for presidential election
noticias.resumen: There has not been an election in Haiti since before the death of Jovenel Moise in 2021.
noticias.texto:
Wife of assassinated ex-Haitian leader registers for presidential election
- Published
The widow of assassinated former Haitian president Jovenel Moise has registered as a presidential candidate for next year's elections in the Caribbean nation.
Martine Moise was injured in the gun attack that killed her husband at their home in the capital, Port-au-Prince, in 2021.
Haiti, which last held an election in 2016, has been plagued with chronic instability and gang violence.
Elections were scheduled to be held in December but were postponed last month until July due to the country's insecurity.
Moise has to comment on her candidacy but the electoral council website showed her registration on Sunday.
Last week she said on X: "Haiti will rise again on its own two feet, because politics needs to be done differently."
A total of 33 candidates have registered for the elections, including former presidents Michel Martelly and Jocelerme Privert, former prime minister Claude Joseph and former foreign minister Dominique Dupuy.
Jovenel Moise, who led Haiti from 2017 until his death, was shot dead at his home in Port-au-Prince in July 2021, allegedly by a group of mainly Colombian mercenaries.
Martine Moise suffered serious gunshot wounds during the attack and was flown to a hospital in Florida.
She was charged in connection with the assassination in 2024, but the indictment was overturned last year.
The assassination shook the Caribbean nation to its core, with many Haitians shocked that the 53-year-old was killed with such apparent ease.
Thirty suspects have been indicted over the killing so far and in September 18 people were flown from Haiti to Florida to stand trial for their alleged involvement in the assassination.
Haiti has been engulfed in a wave of gang violence since the assassination of Moise.
At least 1,408 people were killed and 656 injured from April through to June this year, according to the UN Integrated Office in Haiti.

noticias.titulo: Canada bars Russia from Junior World Championships
noticias.resumen: Canada says it will not allow Russian athletes to compete in the Junior Ice Hockey World Championships because of the war in Ukraine.
noticias.texto:
Canada bars Russia from Junior World Championships
- Published
Russia's hopes of reintegration into international sport suffered a setback when it was barred from the upcoming Junior Ice Hockey World Championships in Canada.
It comes despite a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) last month ordering the country's return to the competition.
The hosts then said they would deny entry to Russian athletes as a result of the war in Ukraine.
"Due to the position and restrictions formally communicated by the Canadian government, the Russian Under-20 national team is unable to participate in the World Junior Championship," the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) said in a statement.
It added that "after carefully assessing the feasibility of alternative arrangements, the IIHF Council has determined that Canada will remain as host and the tournament will proceed from 26 December 2026 to 5 January 2027 in Edmonton and Red Deer."
The Russian Ice Hockey Federation called the IIHF's decision "unacceptable and unlawful" and said it would appeal to the International Olympic Committee (IOC).
"The IIHF's decision was made solely due to political reasons," it added.
"The exclusion of the Russian national team violates fundamental legal principles, Olympism, the principle of non-discrimination, equality among athletes and the integrity of international tournaments."
Russia had been suspended from competing in IIHF events since the country invaded Ukraine in 2022, but in October CAS overturned the ban.
It said that the IIHF's arguments citing safety and security were "not supported by sufficient evidence" and ordered it to allow Russia to participate in five of its events.
The move was welcomed by Russia but condemned by Ukraine, along with some sponsors of the Junior World Championships.
Six European ice hockey federations said they would refuse to play Russia if they were allowed to take part, appearing to leave the tournament in limbo.
On Wednesday the Canadian government said it would deny visas to any Russian athletes, effectively barring them from participating.
The IIHF's decision was welcomed by the head of Norway's Ice Hockey Federation (NIHF), who claimed the Cas ruling had meant the country would have lost its place to Russia.
"Norway's spot in the World Championship has been restored," said Petter Salsten, Secretary General of the NIHF.
"At the same time, it should be noted that this clarification regarding Russian participation applies only to this specific tournament and is due to the fact that they have been denied entry visas. The situation regarding Russia's participation in other upcoming championships this season remains unresolved."
This is the latest example of a wider backlash against efforts to allow Russia to return to international sport.
This week Norway, Finland and Estonia said they would block visas for Russian and Belarusian athletes.
Norway is preparing to host skiing's Cross-country World Cup next month, while Finland is due to stage the Figure Skating World Championships in March.
The International Skating Union (ISU) has said it "believes that athletes should not be punished for the actions of their governments in a world where, sadly, many conflicts are ongoing", and that it was "seeking clarifications" from officials in Finland.
In March several athletes from Russia and Belarus were allowed to compete under their national flags at the Winter Paralympics after partial suspensions by the International Paralympic Committee were lifted.
In July the IOC provisionally reinstated Russia to its competitions, saying a ban introduced in 2023 was "no longer applicable".
However, sports federations can enforce their own eligibility criteria.
While World Gymnastics, World Aquatics and World Boxing have removed restrictions on Russian athletes competing, a total ban has been maintained by World Athletics.
Last month it was announced that Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships, the first time an Olympic federation has chosen to stage a global event in Russia since the invasion of Ukraine.

noticias.titulo: Watch: New York teen reunites with cat missing after building collapse
noticias.resumen: Rescuers found the pet cat in the ruins of Zariah's apartment four days after she made an emotional plea to the public.
noticias.texto:
Watch: New York teen reunites with cat missing after building collapse
A teenage girl and her cat have been reunited four days after a building in the New York borough of Brooklyn collapsed.
Zariah Coleman, 13, made an emotional plea when her pet went missing after she and her family were forced to relocate when the side of their building was stripped off in the unexpected collapse.
City officials later found her cat, Isaac, in the debris of the their home and shared the reunion on Sunday afternoon.
Eight people died and 18 others were injured when the three-storey building collapsed in the Flatbush neighbourhood last Wednesday.

noticias.titulo: Libyan town rebuilt after devastating floods becomes showcase for strongman's rule
noticias.resumen: The remarkable reconstruction of Derna is being used as a showcase for the rest of Libya by Khalifa Haftar and his sons.
noticias.texto:
Libyan town rebuilt after devastating floods becomes showcase for strongman's rule
- Published
"It was joy when I moved in. I could finally relax," says Abdulwahab Damdoum, surveying his luxurious new apartment overlooking the Mediterranean Sea, in the eastern Libyan city of Derna.
Just three years ago he was clinging in terror to the roof of a house as the world's deadliest flood this century surged around him.
Now the 27-year-old port worker, his wife and two young daughters have been given a new, free, 300-sq-m home in a showcase development commissioned by a son of Khalifa Haftar, the warlord who controls eastern Libya.
It is part of a rapid $2bn (Â£1.5bn) rebuilding of Derna that the powerful Haftar family hope will serve as a model for development throughout Libya, increasing their influence across a country currently split between east and west, with rival governments in charge.
The money comes from the state coffers of the oil-rich country, allocated by its parliament. But there are no published records of how it has been spent, raising questions about accountability and possible corruption.
Damdoum, like many flood survivors, simply thanks the head of the Development and Reconstruction Fund, Belkacem Haftar, for what has been achieved since the early hours of 11 September 2023, when lashing rain from Storm Daniel burst two dams above Derna, sending a wall of water 7m (23 ft) high cascading down onto the sleeping city.
The exact death toll will probably never be known. Some estimates have been as high as 6,000, though 4,000 now seems a more likely figure. Many bodies are still unidentified.
In a city of about 100,000 people, that means almost everybody lost someone they loved. The 14 relatives and neighbours on the roof with Damdoum â including his father, brother and sister - all drowned.
He survived, but his home was destroyed, and he had to find temporary accommodation. "It was rent, rent, rent," he says. "Now, no-one can take this [new flat] from me. I thank Engineer Belkacem. God sent this person who picked the city up from disaster."
Portraits of Belkacem, widely known simply as "the Engineer", his younger brother Saddam, a military chief also involved in reconstruction, and their father Khalifa are on hoardings all over Derna and the region.
"Since 2011, Libya has not built big projects like this," says Hussein el-Mansory, project manager of the "2,000 Apartments" complex where Damdoum now lives. "I feel very happy and proud and I'll tell my children: 'I made this.'"
The complex includes a new mosque, hospital, shopping mall and schools. New roads, bridges have also been built in Derna. But while many survivors have been rehoused, some are still waiting.
Among them is Izz al-Nasr Ibzeou, a marine science lecturer at the university. His wife Salima, her mother Mouna, and all the couple's seven children, aged between one and 11, drowned.
His family home was ruined, but the authorities have not yet fully restored it because Ibzeou also has an undamaged apartment in another part of town.
He returns every day to his old house, now an empty shell, to see his children's possessions, which he has kept in dust-covered piles.
"This is my son Moez's bike. He played with it every day. And this is my daughter Fawzia's dress. She wore it whenever she went to a wedding," Ibzeou says. "Even if I decide not to come to remember them, my feet will bring me here of their own accord."
To this day, he has not found their bodies. In Derna's vast new flood cemetery, most graves are marked only by numbers, not names, because the process of matching survivors' DNA with corpses is still not completed.
"I go to the cemetery and try to guess where my family are," he says. "This has burned my heart too much. Thank God, I'm patient, but I'm still waiting just to read the Qur'an [at their graves] and say hello to them."
Belkacem Haftar has now extended the work of his reconstruction fund to Libya's second city, Benghazi, and other parts of Libya his father controls.
Libya's parliament, based in the east, last year allocated him a further sum of nearly $11bn, to be spent over three years, in addition to the $2bn it had already given him specifically for Derna.
Building in Benghazi has included new skyscrapers, hospitals, housing developments and a refurbished football stadium that last year hosted a friendly between Inter Milan and AtlÃ©tico Madrid. Officials have talked in the past about turning the city into a version of "Dubai on the Mediterranean."
Belkacem tells the BBC he has accomplished more than any previous Libyan administration.
"Libya went through the Gaddafi era, 40 years of neglect and poverty," he said. "The interim governments [post-Gaddafi, based in Tripoli] wasted a lot of money without providing anything the people could touch. I have never made promises to the people. But I have provided them with what they need."
International human rights organisations have repeatedly accused the authorities in eastern Libya and Libyan Arab Armed Forces headed by Khalifa Haftar of serious abuses, including secret executions, arbitrary detentions and forced disappearances.
The Haftars and the Benghazi-based government deny the allegations. Belkacem told the BBC there was complete freedom of speech in eastern Libya.
Critics also say the Haftars have a top-down approach to development, with little public participation in planning decisions, and no transparency.
"There is absolutely zero accountability. We've never seen any financial statements of the Reconstruction Fund, for even the legal on-the-table disbursements of funds," says Claudia Gazzini from the International Crisis Group (ICG) think-tank.
Belkacem says the fund is independently audited and that all contracts are drawn up to high international standards. Dismissing concerns about transparency, he says: "What we've done in Derna was almost impossible. What we care about is the reality, what we do on the ground."
He agreed to show the BBC the audits. But he has not provided them, despite repeated requests.
Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya expert affiliated to the Royal United Services Institute think-tank in London, who has talked to some of the foreign partners awarded construction contracts. He says they are usually obliged to work alongside a private Libyan company linked indirectly to the Haftar family or other powerful political figures.
He says: "What those foreign companies say off the record, is that they do the overwhelming majority of the work and the Libyan partner is often almost an empty shell, in a context where the money is split very often on a 50-50 basis, which indicates that a lot of those facilities and bridges and towers are overcharged, twice as expensive.
"It's a form of overpricing within a context that is utterly opaque, and this is not some fairy coming from the sky that funds these reconstruction efforts. Everything is funded using the public wealth of Libya."
Belkacem Haftar denies the suggestion of corruption in reconstruction projects.
He has said the reconstruction funding was processed through the Central Bank of Libya, which operates on behalf of both the UN-recognised government in the capital Tripoli, in the west of the country, and the government in the eastern city of Benghazi.
"The Haftar authorities used Derna as a showcase for what they were pitching to the rest of Libya," says Gazzini from the ICG.
International efforts to reunite the country have included a proposal by Donald Trump's envoy, Massad Boulos, for a power-sharing deal with Saddam Haftar as Libya's president.
In Derna, there is no plan to rebuild the broken dams, so another disaster on the same scale is unlikely. But there is still a possibility of future flooding.
Gazzini says the authorities failed to take up offers of advice from international experts on ways to reduce the risk, for example by creating flood plains along the river which flows through the town.
"I would have expected a holistic project about how you manage the water flow," Gazzini says.
"But that did not happen. The Libyan side responded more to people's needs, was more interested in having a quick solution to the destruction of the city."

noticias.titulo: Why Silicon Valley is backing Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang after his ouster
noticias.resumen: Huang's peers, including Elon Musk, have praised his business acumen and potential risks to the US's AI goals.
noticias.texto:
Why Silicon Valley is backing Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang after his ouster
Huang’s peers, including Elon Musk, have praised his business acumen and potential risks to the US’s AI goals.
Some of the biggest names in the United States tech sector have launched a campaign to back former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who stepped down last week after reports of an extramarital affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.
Billionaire Elon Musk and several others praised Huang on social media and urged the Nvidia board to consider reinstating him. Failing to do that, they warned, could hurt US aspirations and business deals within the burgeoning artificial intelligence (AI) sector.
Huang founded Nvidia, which manufactures advanced chips used to power AI, in 1993. The company has since become one of the most valuable in the world and is a cornerstone of the US push to secure AI dominance over China.
After Huang’s resignation, Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress stepped in as interim CEO. Since last week, Nvidia’s shares and those of some of its partners have suffered significant losses.
An online petition, meanwhile, gathered tens of thousands of signatures from Huang’s peers, former and current Nvidia employees, the company’s stakeholders and other supporters.
Here’s what we know:
Who said what?
Elon Musk, the world’s richest man and CEO of SpaceX, has been a vocal supporter. He praised Huang’s business acumen in a post on his X platform on Saturday, arguing that Nvidia could lose business without him.
“Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” he wrote. “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”
In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, the CEOs of investment firms Altimeter Capital Management and Atreides Management, said Huang was an “incredible leader” and deserved a measured investigation. The firms are shareholders in Nvidia.
“Given the extraordinary success of Jensen Huang’s leadership over a long period of time and given the massive uncertainty associated with recent events surrounding his departure, we believe it is in the best interest of all stakeholders and certainly the shareholders of Nvidia for the Board to pursue a slow, measured and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia that leaves all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang,” they wrote.
What is the ‘Stand with Jensen’ campaign?
Dozens of major tech leaders also signed an open letter titled “Stand With Jensen” calling for Huang’s return. They included Musk, Garry Tan, CEO of venture capital firm Y Combinator, and Steve Chen, cofounder of YouTube.
The letter, which has garnered more than 172,000 signatures, said Huang was “forced out without due process and without even a few days to make his case”. It asked the board to reinstate the CEO, investigate the allegations and then publicise its findings and decisions, including how it will weigh employees’ and shareholders’ interests when taking further action.
“We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process,” the letter read. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the centre of this controversy was a spy.”
“Thirty-three years of leadership do not place anyone above accountability. But accountability requires evidence, a fair hearing, and a reasoned decision. Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice,” the letter said.
Some Nvidia employees also showed solidarity with Huang who they said fostered a supportive company culture.
Darrell Dai, who identified himself as a robotics engineer, said in a LinkedIn post that he resigned in support, saying he was struggling to understand Huang’s departure “before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it”.
What has Huang done?
Huang is discussing a possible return with close confidants, according to the Financial Times.
But he faces hurdles. The US restricts Nvidia from selling chips to China, but lawmakers are now looking into whether Huang’s alleged affair may have affected the US’s own AI goals, and more seriously, whether the issue has national security implications.
At least two Congressional committees have asked Huang and senior White House officials to attend hearings in the coming weeks.
US President Donald Trump’s administration has faced criticism for allegedly failing to scrutinise Nvidia’s deals strongly enough, amid the AI race with China, with some pointing to a $25m Nvidia donation to Trump’s White House ballroom project.
The Financial Times newspaper reported that the board has already reached out to Rene Haas, CEO of British chipmaker Arm Holdings, as a potential successor. However, one of Huang’s supporters told the paper that his allies were nonetheless putting together a “war room” of tech executives to lobby for his return and were trying to gain support from the White House.
What does the scandal mean for tech founders?
The matter has rekindled a longstanding argument in Silicon Valley that founders are often unfairly treated by the very companies they founded.
Angel investor Elad Gil, who worked for Google and Twitter, said this was a good time for “founders to revisit their board” to avoid what he called a “coup”.
He cited the removal of OpenAI cofounder and CEO Sam Altman in 2023 over allegations that he was pushing profit over AI safety. Altman was reinstated a few days later after major figures such as Microsoft’s Satya Nadella offered him a position.
“Reset your board during good times to avoid sudden action during bad times,” Gil said.
Among those supporting Huang is Travis Kalanick, Uber’s cofounder and former CEO. The board asked him to resign in 2017 after allegations that he did not act on sexual harassment cases in the company. He has not returned.
Pavel Durov, founder of Telegram, warned founders not to have boards at all. In 2014, Durov was kicked off by the board of VK, his first platform, after several run-ins with Russian authorities, including for its refusal to submit protesters’ personal data to the government or to block late opposition leader Alexey Navalny from the site.
But Anthony Scaramucci, a former White House communications director and founder of investment firm SkyBridge Capital, dismissed the calls for Huang’s return.
“A suspected Chinese intelligence operative got close to the man running the most strategically important company in America,” he posted on X.
“Until every one of those probes closes, no director with a fiduciary duty can vote to bring him back. Genius doesn’t buy you an exemption from national security.”

noticias.titulo: Lebanon’s second airport could provide economic and political benefits
noticias.resumen: The establishment of a second airport in Lebanon gives the war-devastated country more options for air travel.
noticias.texto:
Lebanon’s second airport could provide economic and political benefits
The establishment of a second airport in Lebanon gives the war-devastated country more options for air travel.
Beirut, Lebanon – Lebanon’s second airport is scheduled to begin operating test flights on Independence Day, November 22, in what experts and analysts say could prove to be a boon to the country after years of war and an economic collapse.
In June, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and other officials took a test flight from Beirut to Rene Mouawad airport, located in the northern town of Qlayaat. Lebanese officials hope a new airport will stimulate growth in one of Lebanon’s poorest and most underserved regions.
Qlayaat airport was originally set to open mid-2026, but Israel’s war on Lebanon delayed it.
The beginning of commercial flights was deferred to November 22, but it was pushed further to mid-December, when many in the Lebanese diaspora return home for the winter holiday, due to construction delays. Commercial flights are now expected to start on December 14.
Chokepoint
Rafik Hariri international airport, Lebanon’s only functioning airport, located just south of the capital, Beirut, has been sensitive to political and regional disputes.
Supporters of Hezbollah, the Iranian-backed Shia armed group, have at times weaponised the vulnerabilities of Rafik Hariri airport’s location by blocking the road connecting it to the capital. In February 2025, Hezbollah supporters blocked the road when two Iranian planes were prohibited from landing in Beirut.
A new airport in the north, outside Hezbollah’s traditional zone of influence, could potentially weaken this logistical chokepoint, said Bassel Doueik, a Lebanese political analyst.
“Whenever tensions rise between them and the government, they [Hezbollah] tend to block the inbound and outbound [traffic] on the Beirut airport road through protests, and this is a strategic advantage for the group,” Doueik, a Lebanese political analyst, told Al Jazeera.
“I don’t think the new airport will remove this strategic advantage, but it will actually decrease it to a certain extent because the [Qlayaat] airport is small and it cannot substitute for the current airport.”
Hezbollah has been the strongest military and political actor in Lebanon in recent decades, but its role has come into open debate in the country following the 2024 ceasefire with Israel and the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in Syria, the group’s key regional ally.
The opening of a new airport is not expected to change internal political calculations, but analysts say it gives the state alternatives in the event of future conflicts.
“The state gains manoeuvrability and alternatives by opening a second airport. But in terms of Hezbollah’s arms or anything else, it doesn’t change much for the state,” Marcel Baloukji, a Lebanese political and security analyst, told Al Jazeera.
“This airport becomes a factor in any potential future war. Beirut airport could be shut down, but alternatives [to fly in and out] would still exist, especially for foreign nationals and diplomatic missions present in Lebanon.”
Economic troubles
But officials say the reason for opening a second airport is economic rather than political.
Lebanon’s economy has struggled to recover from the 2019 economic crash due to Israel’s ongoing assault on the country and the US-Israel war on Iran.
Inflation is expected to hit 17.5 percent this year, and the World Bank predicts Lebanon’s economy to contract by 6.4 percent in 2026. Previous estimates suggest Lebanon has suffered damage estimated at more than $14bn since 2023.
Still, Dania Arayssi, assistant director of the New Lines Institute for Strategy and Policy, told Al Jazeera that she believes there is a legislative angle for the establishment of a new airport as well.
“Successfully managing a facility that can generate significant public revenue could help rebuild citizens’ trust in state institutions,” Arayssi said.
“It would show that the government can enforce its authority, protect public assets from Hezbollah’s interference, and lead on delivering services that benefit the country as a whole.”
South Lebanon, where an Israeli invasion has turned into an occupation that analysts believe could last years, has been the worst-affected part of the country as a result of Israel’s war. But other parts of Lebanon are also struggling and have a history of state neglect.
Qlayaat, on the other hand, is located in the northern Akkar region, just 6km (3.7 miles) from the Syrian border. Officials believe the new facility would serve much of Lebanon’s north, as well as important Syrian cities like Homs, Latakia and Tartous, with the northern neighbour struggling to modernise its dilapidated airports.
Experts told Al Jazeera that the fall of President al-Assad in December 2024 partially paved the way for the airport project, as Syria’s former government had been opposed to the idea.
After Salam formed the government in early 2025, plans for the new airport became a priority.
Officials said Qlayaat airport is likely to receive low-cost airlines. In June, Turkiye’s Istanbul and Mersin airports and Dubai in the UAE had been confirmed as destinations for flights from Qlayaat, with new locations likely to be announced in the coming days. Officials said the airport could serve 115,000 passengers in the first year, reaching about 600,000 by the fourth year.
Baloukji said the airport would also have domestic benefits and be a more reassuring route for foreign tourists.
“From the perspective of employing workers, it keeps people in that area and enhances tourism because many people are avoiding Beirut airport due to Hezbollah’s influence,” he said.

noticias.titulo: USS Roosevelt arrives in Middle East: Is the US-Iran war about to resume?
noticias.resumen: The aircraft carrier joins two others operating in the US Central Command area of responsibility.
noticias.texto:
USS Roosevelt arrives in Middle East: Is the US-Iran war about to resume?
The aircraft carrier joins two others operating in the US Central Command area of responsibility.
The United States has deployed a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East as diplomatic efforts to permanently stop the US-Israel war on Iran and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remain stalled.
On Monday, a US official told Al Jazeera that the USS Theodore Roosevelt had arrived in the Middle East. The aircraft carrier joins two others operating in the US Central Command (CENTCOM) area of responsibility.
The United States and Iran entered into a two-week ceasefire in April and later announced a broader memorandum of understanding in June, which collapsed in early July.
Since then, mediators from Pakistan and Qatar have been trying to prevent a return to the full-scale exchange of attacks between the US and Iran that also badly affected the broader Gulf region in March.
Last week, US President Donald Trump stated that further military strikes against Iran are “quite unlikely” and said the military component of the war was “effectively over” following discussions with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani. But he noted the US military remains “locked and loaded” if conditions change.
Does the deployment of another aircraft carrier to the region mean the US-Israel war on Iran is going to resume?
Here’s what we know:
What is the USS Theodore Roosevelt?
Named after the 26th US president, Theodore Roosevelt, the vessel is a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier.
Commissioned by the US Navy in 1986, the ship carries more than 5,000 personnel and a full air wing of more than 60 aircraft, including F-18s, the twin-engine, supersonic, all-weather multirole fighter planes.
According to the US Navy, the warship is tasked with “conducting carrier air warfare operations and assisting in the planning, control, coordination and integration of air wing squadrons in support of carrier air warfare”.
Besides combat operations, the carrier also replenishes ships at sea and rescues people, including refugees, at sea.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt has performed combat and humanitarian missions since its commissioning. During the 1990-91 Gulf War, it was deployed to the Mediterranean and the Red Sea for combat operations. In 2003, it also supported US strikes during the Iraq War.
It was also deployed in the Asia Pacific region during 2020-21 for military exercises with India, Japan, Australia, South Korea and Malaysia.
In October, a US official told Al Jazeera that the USS Theodore Roosevelt left its San Diego base in September, bound for the Middle East. According to another official, it arrived in the Middle East on November 15.
But the Pentagon and CENTCOM, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, have not formally confirmed the carrier’s arrival in the region.
What is the state of US deployment in the region?
The arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt in the Middle East brings the total number of US aircraft carrier strike groups operating in the region to three. The USS George Washington and the USS George HW Bush are the other two aircraft carriers currently deployed in the region.
Last month, a US official told Al Jazeera that the Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group (ARG), carrying more than 2,000 Marines, has also followed the USS Theodore Roosevelt to the Middle East. The Wall Street Journal reported that the strike group and naval deployments could involve an additional 9,000 to 10,000 US soldiers in total, including sailors and Marines assigned to the carrier strike group and other ships. However, the US military is yet to confirm these deployments.
The US has had troops and military assets stationed at bases in the Middle East for decades. Of these, eight are permanent bases, located in Bahrain, Egypt, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. As of mid-2025, there were 40,000 to 50,000 US soldiers stationed in and around the Middle East, including personnel at large, permanent bases and smaller forward sites across the region.
According to open-source intelligence analysts and military flight-tracking data, the US has deployed more than 120 aircraft to the region since early February, before the war on Iran began. This is the biggest surge in US airpower in the Middle East since the Iraq War.
Reported deployments include E-3 Sentry Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) aircraft, F-35 stealth strike fighters and F-22 air superiority jets alongside F-15s and F-16s. In March, the Pentagon also ordered additional US forces to the Gulf.
The reinforcements consisted of three distinct formations.
The first was the Tripoli ARG, centred around the America-class assault ship USS Tripoli and the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit (MEU).
The second was the Boxer ARG, built around the Wasp-class assault ship USS Boxer and the 11th MEU, based in southern California in the US.
Together, these two Marine groups have added 4,500 Marines and sailors in the region.
The third was a contingent of about 2,000 soldiers from the 82nd Airborne Division’s Immediate Response Force, based at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. The airborne infantry division is focused on parachute assaults.
In total, nearly 7,000 additional soldiers have already been deployed to the Middle East since the US-Israel war on Iran began.
How has Iran responded?
Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister for legal and international affairs, has said the country “will not wait for the US to attack first”. He said, “The US may be seeking to buy time by abusing diplomacy, in order to prepare the ground for another attack.”
Speaking to state TV in a video released by Iran’s Fars news agency, Gharibabadi warned, “Iran is not Cuba that you can blockade, nor is it Venezuela that you can force to surrender.”
He said US forces “have had no success with either an air blockade or a land blockade” in Iran so far, while the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) is currently producing missiles with “new ranges”.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has called for stronger regional energy cooperation, warning US attacks threaten stability across the Middle East.
“Given the increasing impact of US and Israeli aggression on the region’s energy security, strengthening energy cooperation has become an urgent and strategic necessity,” Araghchi said at a meeting of foreign ministers of the Economic Cooperation Organization in Islamabad, Pakistan, on Monday.
“Our region needs not only an independent security framework but also a regional, reliable and sustainable energy mechanism to safeguard energy flows, ensure stable energy supplies, reduce vulnerabilities from external factors, and increase our collective resilience to geopolitical shocks and disruptions,” the IRNA news agency quoted him as saying.
What has the US government said on resuming the war?
The Trump administration has appeared increasingly divided on how to proceed with Iran, since the Republican Party suffered heavy losses in this month’s US midterm elections.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said Washington’s economic pressure campaign against Iran was proving effective, so a resumption of large-scale military operations was likely unnecessary. “The economic pressure on Iran is going to get even worse,” he added.
But Trump has given mixed messages about his plans for the war.
Last week, after a meeting at the White House’s Oval Office with Qatar’s prime minister, Trump stated on Truth Social and in a surprise briefing that there was “positive momentum” towards ending the conflict and that a resumption of strikes was “quite unlikely”, declaring the US-Israel war on Iran militarily “effectively over”.
Still, Trump insisted that the US economic pressure campaign against Iran would stay in place, including a naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz and a more recent task force aimed at cutting off Iran’s trade by land and through the Caspian Sea.
Meanwhile, Iran’s conditions to end the war include an end to the US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, the lifting of economic sanctions, the release of Iranian frozen funds, ending fighting on all fronts and an explicit announcement of an end to the war.
Iranian officials have in recent days underlined that Tehran will not accept the current status quo of “no war, no peace”.
Trump, on his part, has indicated that he is running out of patience with Iran as diplomacy stutters. Last week, Trump said he had told his country’s lead negotiator, Vice President JD Vance, “We don’t need a deal with Iran.”
“Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” he wrote on his Truth Social platform.
So can diplomacy work, or is the region on edge?
Ali Vaez, Crisis Group’s Deputy Program Director for the Middle East and North Africa told Al Jazeera that both sides are caught in a perilous game of chicken, convinced that striking first may be safer than waiting to be struck.
“The danger is that their efforts to deter another war could inadvertently ignite one that neither can win, contain or easily end,” he said.
Diplomatic efforts to stop attacks and reopen the Strait of Hormuz also remain stalled.
In an interview with Al Jazeera last week, Iran’s parliamentary speaker and chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, highlighted that Tehran wanted to move beyond a state of “no war, no peace”.
Ghalibaf said Iran has conveyed seven conditions for a deal through a Qatari mediator and was awaiting an official US response. The conditions he outlined included lifting the US naval blockade and sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian funds, ending hostilities on all fronts and formally declaring the war over.
Trump’s administration, meanwhile, has tightened sanctions and maintained the blockade on Iranian ports.
“Diplomacy still has a pulse, but it is suffocating under the weight of mutual mistrust and maximalist demands. Unless both sides find a face-saving exit, negotiations risk becoming little more than an intermission between successive rounds of warfare,” Vaez said.
The main issues in the US-Israel war on Iran now are those of sequencing and leverage, according to Rashid al-Mohanadi, vice president at the Center for International Policy Research. “Who does what, when, and how for a potential end of the conflict,” he told Al Jazeera on Sunday.
Al-Mohanadi added that it is clear that the region is against going back to full-scale war, which is obvious as “the whole region is leading on the mediation”.
However, he warned, the principal protagonists in the war appear to have divergent perceptions over their leverage.
“The Iranians perceive they have more leverage. The Americans perceive they have more,” al-Mohanadi said. “When you have a situation like that, reaching a diplomatic end is quite difficult.”

noticias.titulo: Jordan bans Telegram over national security concerns
noticias.resumen: The measure comes amid a security crackdown after last month's deadly attack on a Greek Orthodox church.
noticias.texto:
Jordan bans Telegram over national security concerns
Authorities say measure is part of ongoing efforts to reduce cybercrime and strengthen digital security.
Jordanian authorities have banned the Telegram messaging app, saying the move aims to curb the dissemination of illegal content and what they describe as “extremist material”.
The Public Security Directorate (PSD) announced the measure in a statement published on Monday amid a security crackdown after nine people were killed in an attack on a Greek Orthodox church last month.
The PSD urged citizens to “exercise caution when using social media applications, to avoid interacting with accounts, links, or entities of unknown origin, and to report any unlawful practices or content through official channels”.
The church shooting took place in the village of Hammoud in the west-central governorate of Karak. On Sunday, three men were sentenced to death by hanging over the attack.
The incident prompted Jordan to carry out air strikes on neighbouring Syria that Amman said killed 20 members of the ISIL (ISIS) armed group linked to the church attack.
Meanwhile, a security officer was killed and another wounded this month in Amman in what authorities described as another “terrorist attack”.
Telegram, founded by Russian entrepreneur Pavel Durov in 2013, is believed to be used by groups such as ISIL. In July, Russia issued an arrest warrant for Durov, accusing him of aiding “terrorism”.
The 42-year-old is currently believed to be in Dubai in the United Arab Emirates and faces up to life in a Russian prison if found guilty. He is also being investigated in several other countries.
Telegram supports end-to-end encrypted chats, but not all conversations are encrypted. The messaging app is popular in the Middle East and North Africa. The region accounts for about 8 percent of global users.

noticias.titulo: ‘NATO will collapse’: Russia stalls Ukraine talks, seeks to divide Europe
noticias.resumen: Russia has proposed nonaggression pacts with individual nations, which could shatter collective defence against Moscow.
noticias.texto:
‘NATO will collapse’: Russia stalls Ukraine talks, seeks to divide Europe
Russia has proposed nonaggression pacts with individual nations, which could shatter collective defence against Moscow.
Kyiv, Ukraine – A Russian drone struck a small house in the northern Ukrainian town of Hlukhiv, burying a nine-year-old boy and his grandmother under the debris.
Two Ukrainian police officers arrived on Saturday to dig them out, apply a tourniquet to the woman’s bleeding arm and take them away in their car.
But a second drone struck their vehicle, killing one of the officers, Mykola Savchenko, who covered the boy with his body, the Ministry of Internal Affairs said.
Such double-tap attacks are Ukraine’s daily reality as the war grinds on to its fifth anniversary. They’re also a metaphor for Russia’s latest attempts to target both Ukraine and those Kyiv has long hoped would help it survive Moscow’s onslaught – NATO and Europe.
On the surface, Russia is engaged in United States-mediated diplomacy. But Russian diplomats who met with US negotiators in Abu Dhabi for trilateral talks involving Moscow, Kyiv and Washington last week presented demands that go far beyond any peace settlement.
Moscow hasn’t agreed to Kyiv’s proposal to freeze the war along the current front lines as Ukraine lacks Western missile interceptors to shoot down Russian missiles and jet drones.
Instead, the Kremlin has shifted the focus of talks from a ceasefire and peace to demands that, if accepted, could dismantle Europe’s post-Cold War security architecture, analysts said.
Russia wants NATO to withdraw its troops from Central and Eastern Europe and ban the bloc’s further expansion, according to leaked documents obtained by The New York Times, The Economist and several Ukrainian media outlets.
Moscow also wants to ink nonaggression pacts with individual European nations, something that may sound alluring to Russia’s neighbours, such as Estonia or Finland.
“Agreements of this kind could be reached, among other things, with individual NATO member states, which would then receive, for instance, additional individual security guarantees” from Moscow, Russian negotiator Alexey Drobinin said at a news conference after the Abu Dhabi talks.
But a string of such agreements could in effect negate NATO’s cornerstone principle to regard any armed attack against one member state as an attack against all of its 32 members.
“NATO will collapse, and European nations will [individually] be face to face with Russia,” said Boris Bondarev, a former Russian diplomat who left his Ministry of Foreign Affairs job in protest against Moscow’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“Europe will surrender to Russia without firing a single shot in its defence, without losing a single soldier or spending a single shell,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Such individual deals are an absolutely blatant attempt to demolish Europe’s unity, which has already been bursting at the seams, and to undermine NATO’s unity,” said Bondarev, also the author of Time to Win the War, a book that tracks the potential steps needed to reach a peace agreement.
Any nonaggression pacts would most likely include conditions that bar a signatory nation from participating in a future conflict between Russia and another European nation, he said, destroying any potential for collective defence against Moscow.
Russia’s demands were presented to US special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff but not to European leaders.
“Russians want to talk to Americans. They don’t want to talk to Europe,” Maria Kucherenko, executive director at the Strategic Intelligence Institute, a think tank in Kyiv, told Al Jazeera.
To Kucherenko, who has for years scrutinised Moscow’s negotiating tactics, the “maximalist” demands continue the Kremlin’s habit of asking for everything.
Russia’s “demands will be maximalist, the way they used to be, and they will be deceptive about the subsequence of steps [towards a peace deal] in their interests. They’ll put politics ahead of security, the way they’ve done all these years,” she said.
Kushner, a real estate developer and son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, used the word “very” abundantly to describe the talks.
“These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex. It’s a very hot war,” Kushner said at a news conference.
To Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Russia’s demands sound otherworldly.
Russian President Vladimir Putin “lives in a different reality”, Zelenskyy wrote on X on Wednesday, adding, “I can draw a picture for him too where I fully occupy Russia. But it’s not true.”
“We are all very cautious with this topic because nobody really understands 100 percent what they want,” Zelenskyy said at a news conference hours later.
A top Ukrainian negotiator decried the “difficulty” of the Abu Dhabi talks.
“This round of talks was one of the most difficult ones. I believe the Russians came with very strict instructions, so it was really hard to ease the discussions,” Davyd Arakhamia, who has taken part in each round of talks since 2022, said on Wednesday.
Stalling the talks will not just weaken Kyiv and demoralise Ukrainians, it may also help Russia buy time until it is politically stronger in Europe’s key nations.
French far-right leader Marine Le Pen has pledged to phase out France’s military and financial aid to Ukraine within six months if she wins April’s presidential election. She is currently the frontrunner.
And if Germany’s ruling coalition falls apart amid debates over the budget, debt and economic stagnation, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is positioned to win a snap vote. It leads in national polls and is well ahead of the Christian Democratic Union of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
AfD also wants to terminate aid to Ukraine, push for immediate peace talks with Moscow and lift sanctions so Germany can once again buy Russian oil and gas.
If Le Pen and the AfD win, that would compound Ukraine’s struggles with its allies at a time when the Trump administration is already pressuring Kyiv to compromise on its sovereignty.
“We will not be able to withstand the joint position of the European Union and the United States, and a chance to manoeuvre between Washington and Brussels will be lost,” Kyiv-based analyst Aleksey Kusch told Al Jazeera.

noticias.titulo: Antimicrobial resistance could kill 39 million people over 25 years: WHO
noticias.resumen: UN's health agency says growing resistance to antibiotics and other medicines threatens 'future of modern medicine'.
noticias.texto:
Antimicrobial resistance could kill 39 million people over 25 years: WHO
UN’s health agency says growing resistance to antibiotics and other medicines are threatening the ‘future of modern medicine’.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has warned that growing antimicrobial resistance could cause 39 million deaths over the next 25 years as it threatens to make routine surgery and childbirth life-threatening.
Senior officials from the United Nations health agency said on Monday progress in prevention, diagnosis and the appropriate use of antibiotics remained too slow to meet global targets.
“Antibiotic resistance – but broadly, we are talking about antimicrobial resistance, or AMR – is widespread and threatening the future of modern medicine,” Jean-Pierre Nyemazi, acting director of the WHO’s AMR department, told a virtual conference of the 6th Annual Global Media Forum on AMR.
“Unlike COVID-19, which was very visible, drug-resistant infections have been taking people’s lives for years without us noticing it and raising the alarm as we should,” he said.
In 2021 alone, it was directly responsible for more than one million deaths and linked to about 4.7 million others, according to WHO figures.
National action plans
An investigation into the progress of the fight against antimicrobial resistance in 183 countries this year revealed that nearly nine in 10 countries had a national action plan against the phenomenon. In 2017, the figure was just about four in 10.
Pravasha Prakash, an AMR technical officer with the global health agency, said only 42 countries – less than one in five – had a plan that was financed, implemented and monitored.
“Countries are moving forward in every step, but progress still needs to be speeded up to reach the 2030 targets,” she added.
The latest global surveillance data show that, in 2023, one in every six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections flagged to the WHO was resistant to antibiotics used to treat it.
Sylvia Bertagnolo, head of surveillance for AMR at the WHO, said, “Without testing, clinicians must treat without knowing the cause of infection or which antibiotic will work.”
New diagnostic tools
The WHO announced the release of two new tools designed to help countries strengthen diagnostic capabilities.
The first defines the tests that should be available at every level of the healthcare system, from primary care centres to referral hospitals.
The second compiles 73 laboratory procedures, from sample collection to the identification of pathogens and antibiotic susceptibility testing.
The agency added that infection prevention, vaccination, improved access to water and sanitation, and the appropriate use of antimicrobials are the main levers to combat the issue.

noticias.titulo: Ahmad Tibi elected deputy speaker of Israel’s Knesset
noticias.resumen: Leader of alliance representing Palestinian citizens of Israel says election is 'rightful achievement' for Joint List.
noticias.texto:
Ahmad Tibi elected deputy speaker of Israel’s Knesset
Leader of alliance representing Palestinian citizens of Israel says his election is a ‘rightful achievement’ for the Joint List.
An Arab member of Israel’s parliament, Ahmad Tibi, the chairman of the Joint List alliance, has been elected deputy speaker of the Knesset.
“This is a rightful achievement for the Joint List, which secured 11 seats” in the October 27 elections, Tibi told Al Jazeera on Monday.
He added that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir “attempted to prevent my election, but they failed despite their reckless incitement. The Joint List will be represented in all committees.”
Tibi, who was elected by his fellow Knesset members on Monday, is the leader of the Ta’al party, which is part of the Joint List.
The groups representing Palestinian citizens of Israel – the Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra’am) – made historic electoral gains in last month’s elections, securing a cumulative 19 seats in the 120-member parliament.
The bloc endorsed Gadi Eisenkot after President Isaac Herzog tasked him this month with forming the next government.
Palestinian-led parties are now focused on using their increased representation to address discrimination and other issues facing their community.
Call for criminal investigation
Tibi on Sunday called for a criminal investigation into Netanyahu and his aides, accusing them of engaging in “Mafia-style conduct” after an investigative media report accused them of interference in the parliamentary elections.
According to Israel’s Channel 12 broadcaster, Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, contacted the police commissioner’s office before the Knesset elections, alleging that three activists from the Ra’am party in southern Israel were carrying large sums of cash and vouchers intended to sway voters.
Police relied on information from an intelligence source who was a former employee of the prime minister’s office to arrest the activists after raiding their homes without valid search or arrest warrants, the report said.
“No one is above the law, not even Netanyahu,” Tibi said on X.
Tibi was first elected to the Knesset in 1999 and previously served as its deputy speaker from 2006 to 2022.
Several Arabs have served as deputy speakers of the Knesset. Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, held the position between 2020 and 2022. Mohammad Barakeh, a former leader of the Hadash party, was appointed in 2003.
Other appointed Arab deputy speakers include Abdulmalik Dehamshe, a former Ra’am lawmaker, and Nawaf Massalha, the first Muslim to be appointed to the Knesset in 1988.
