noticias.titulo: Russia out of IIHF World Junior Ice Hockey as Canada refuses entry
noticias.resumen: Norway back in the tournament after being bumped to make room for Russia after a Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling.
noticias.texto:
Russia out of IIHF World Junior Ice Hockey as Canada refuses entry
Norway is back in the tournament after earlier being bumped to make room for Russia, following a Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling.
Russia will not compete at the World Junior Championship (WJC) following host Canada’s decision to bar Russian players, the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) has said.
The IIHF announcement on Sunday came after the Russian Ice Hockey Federation sought to have next month’s tournament either relocated or cancelled.
Canada took the position in response to a Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling late last month that reinstated Russia to international hockey.
Canada’s Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden said on Wednesday that Ottawa opposes Russian and Belarusian participation in international sport “as long as Russia continues its war of aggression against Ukraine with Belarus’s complicity”.
The minister for immigration, refugees and citizenship “will take measures to individually assess and prevent Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials from entering Canada to compete, regardless of whether they already hold valid visas”, van Koeverden said.
The tournament features top male players below the age of 20 and is being held in the province of Alberta beginning in late December.
“The IIHF confirms that due to the position and restrictions formally communicated by the Canadian Government, the Russian U20 national team is unable to participate in the World Junior Championship,” the IIHF said in a short statement on social media on Sunday.
“After carefully assessing the feasibility of alternative arrangements, the IIHF Council has determined that Canada will remain as host and the tournament will proceed from 26 December 2026 to 5 January 2027 in Edmonton and Red Deer.”
The CAS ruling overturned the IIHF’s ban, which was imposed after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The IIHF was vociferous in its disagreement over CAS’s decision, and its statement followed announcements from Norway, Denmark, Sweden and the Czech Republic that their national teams will refuse to play against Russia at next year’s men’s World Championships in Germany.
The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association said last weekend that it had been informed that it would be bumped from the tournament to make room for Russia. On Sunday, it said it would now be in the tournament.
Germany also welcomed the announcement.
“The Canadian government has taken a clear position, and many nations have also taken a stand in recent weeks,” German Ice Hockey Federation CEO Frank H Lutz said.
“We now need that same level of planning security for our home World Championship in May, for the teams, the fans and all our partners. We therefore call on the IIHF to provide clarification soon.”

noticias.titulo: Ecuador’s president denies existence of US military base
noticias.resumen: Daniel Noboa says US personnel in the country for 'temporary activities'.
noticias.texto:
Ecuador’s president denies existence of US military base
Daniel Noboa says US personnel in the country for ‘temporary activities’.
Ecuadoran President Daniel Noboa has denied that the United States has a military base in his country near the port city of Guayaquil after voters rejected a referendum to allow foreign military sites.
Noboa’s denial came on Sunday after the AFP news agency last month documented an unusual deployment of US aircraft at the Taura Air Base and the installation of dozens of tents and infrastructure work.
It also identified about 20 US military flights at the base from June to mid-October and obtained documents referring to the presence of US soldiers.
Noboa said US personnel were at the airbase solely for “temporary activities” as part of cooperation between the two countries.
“Sometimes there’s a specific mission. Sometimes there’s a specific operation,” he told the digital news outlet Altavoz. “We work together. It’s not an American base. It’s an Ecuadoran base.”
Noboa did not address the US aircraft and sidestepped the journalist’s request to visit the Taura base.
The US deployment raised questions about its legality, including among senior Ecuadoran military officials. The then-air force commander, General Mauricio Salazar, asked the armed forces to clarify the legality of the deployment, AFP said, citing a letter sent in September.
Salazar was subsequently removed from his post and reassigned to less senior duties.
The scope of the US military presence has not been disclosed, but Quito and Washington have been strengthening their cooperation in the fight against drug trafficking in the region.
The Pentagon, its Southern Command and Ecuador’s air force did not respond to requests for information when the AFP investigation was published in October.
Referendum against foreign bases
Noboa had campaigned to change the constitution and reverse a ban on foreign military bases, but Ecuadorans voted against it in a referendum in November last year.
According to Human Rights Watch, the US has arguably become Ecuador’s main partner in its crackdown on organised criminal groups in the region and has been providing equipment, training, intelligence and direct military support.
The New York-based rights watchdog has called the partnership “perilous” as “both governments have engaged in serious human rights violations fuelled by their insistence on framing their confrontations with organised crime groups as a kind of war”.
The administration of US President Donald Trump has struck boats it has alleged were transporting illegal drugs through international waters.
During Trump’s first term, he pondered bombing drug labs in Mexico. Since retaking office in January last year, he moved to formalise his rhetoric, designating several Latin America-based cartels as “foreign terrorist organisations”.

noticias.titulo: Why is China resisting a nuclear treaty with the US and Russia?
noticias.resumen: Beijing has a smaller arsenal than Washington and Moscow and worries that a pact could limit its nuclear capabilities.
noticias.texto:
Why is China resisting a nuclear treaty with the US and Russia?
Beijing has a smaller arsenal than Washington and Moscow and worries that any pact could limit its nuclear capabilities.
The world’s top nuclear-armed countries are slated to hold their first-ever trilateral meeting soon as United States President Donald Trump pushes for a new nuclear arms treaty among them.
Trump will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week in China’s Shenzhen, the White House confirmed.
Top of the agenda for Washington and Moscow is the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), which lapsed in February, marking the end of more than half a century of limits on US and Russian strategic nuclear weapons.
Trump previously rejected Russia’s proposal to extend the treaty, demanding instead a “new, improved and modernised” deal that includes Beijing.
But China has long signalled that it is not ready to join any nuclear arms control treaty.
So why is Beijing not eager?
What is the New START treaty, and why does it matter?
New START was a treaty signed in 2010 by then-US President Barack Obama and Dmitry Medvedev, a close ally of Vladimir Putin who served as Russia’s president from 2008 to 2012. It was extended in 2021 for an additional five years when Joe Biden was the US president.
Under the agreement, Russia and the US were permitted to deploy no more than 1,550 strategic nuclear warheads and a maximum of 700 long-range missiles and bombers, had to impose a limit of 800 intercontinental ballistic missiles in deployment and grant permission for up to 18 inspections of strategic nuclear weapons sites annually by the other party.
New START collapsed in February after the five-year extension lapsed. This key accord was in turn built from earlier arms control treaties signed between Washington and Moscow.
The first of those, START I, was signed in 1991 between the US and the Soviet Union in the dying days of the Cold War. It remained in place until 2009 with the aim of capping US and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals.
START II, its successor, aimed to further reduce the number of deployed strategic nuclear warheads in addition to removing multiwarhead intercontinental ballistic missiles altogether. It was signed in 1993 but never came into force. Russia formally withdrew from it in 2002.
The Strategic Offensive Reductions Treaty (SORT) from 2003 to 2011, meanwhile, had the same purpose as START I but included less monitoring.
The COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 ended on-site inspections between the two nations in recent years, leaving them dependent on their own intelligence to judge compliance by the other side.
Still, the treaty offered some checks and balances to the two biggest nuclear powers in the world. Together, they possess about 86 percent of all nuclear warheads.
Why does Trump want China included in a new nuclear arms deal?
Trump has long wanted China included in the treaty because Washington believes an arms treaty involving only it and Moscow would no longer reflect the global nuclear balance of power.
“Today, the United States faces threats from multiple nuclear powers. In short, a bilateral treaty with only one nuclear power is simply inappropriate in 2026 and going forward,” US Undersecretary of State for Arms Control Thomas DiNanno said in February.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that same month said Trump made it clear that “to have true arms control in the 21st century, it’s impossible to do something that doesn’t include China because of their vast and rapidly growing stockpile”.
Washington also wants a successor treaty to address weapons not covered by New START.
DiNanno has said a new agreement would have to “account [for] all Russian nuclear weapons, both novel and existing strategic systems and [address] the breakout growth of Chinese nuclear weapons stockpiles”.
Why is China reluctant to join a nuclear arms control treaty?
Beijing’s unwillingness is largely due to the sheer disparity of warheads it currently possesses when compared with the US and Russia.
It has an estimated 620 of them, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), well below the 800 cap each for Russia and the US under New START. Moscow and Washington now have more than 5,000 each, according to SIPRI data. While the US has retired a third of its nuclear warheads so far, Russia has retired less than a fourth.
China’s nuclear arsenal, however, is growing faster than any country’s – by about 100 new warheads a year since 2023, according to SIPRI.
In February, when New Start expired, Chinese officials explained their opposition to joining a nuclear weapons capping agreement.
“China’s nuclear forces are not on the same level as those of the United States and Russia, and China will not participate in disarmament negotiations at this stage,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Lin Jian said in a statement at the time.
This “structural asymmetry” explains China’s reluctance to join a nuclear arms control treaty with the US and Russia alongside its own domestic restraints, said Zhao Minghao, a professor at the Institute of International Studies at China’s Fudan University.
“China maintains a declared no-first-use policy and a ‘minimum deterrence’ posture – nuclear weapons as political instruments for assured retaliation, not warfighting,” Zhao told Al Jazeera.
“From Beijing’s perspective, its arsenal is already restrained by doctrine. The potential US-Russia-China treaty would cap its insurance while imposing intrusive verification on a comparatively small force.”
He also pointed to a “credibility problem”, given the US withdrawal from a number of related treaties, such as the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty and the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, which similarly seek to control missile numbers.
In China’s view, Washington has used arms control as a geopolitical instrument, Zhao said.
“Beijing’s strategic logic is that nuclear inferiority invites coercion – conventional or nuclear – while survivable second-strike capability neutralises it,” he said.
China’s smaller arsenal plays a role in its reluctance to join a nuclear arms treaty, but so does its ability to match US capabilities, said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing.
“Chinese assessments also consider US missile defences, precision-strike capabilities and emerging technologies that could weaken its retaliatory capability,” Sun told Al Jazeera.
“An agreement limiting China’s forces while leaving those concerns untouched would have limited appeal.”
According to William Yang, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst for Northeast Asia, there’s no clear advantage for Beijing and any treaty would be viewed “as a mechanism designed to limit its nuclear modernisation”.
“As a result, Beijing prefers to maintain strategic autonomy in expanding its nuclear arsenal and modernising relevant defence capabilities,” Yang told Al Jazeera.
At the same time, China’s rapid nuclear expansion raises “legitimate questions about where Beijing intends to stop”, said Alejandro Reyes, an Asia Pacific policy specialist and professor at the University of Hong Kong,
“It is difficult to assess China’s ultimate ambitions when it provides little transparency about its nuclear programme. We should not assume that China seeks parity, but neither should we assume that its declared commitment to minimum deterrence fully explains its current build-up,” Reyes told Al Jazeera.
Could the US, Russia and China ever agree on a nuclear arms deal?
According to the analysts, China would engage in a trilateral framework only when the US and Russia first reduce their arsenals towards “genuine” parity.
Zhao argued that such a path could be incremental.
It could appear as a “sustained US-China strategic stability dialogue with concrete reciprocity – test moratoria, data exchanges [and] notification of major exercises”, he explained.
The negotiations would also need to address missile defence, advanced conventional weapons and emerging technologies, Sun said.
“Differentiated obligations and phased verification would offer a more workable basis than identical reductions,” he added.
Sun said a practical starting point would be to combine US-Russian arms negotiations with “three-way discussions on crisis communication, nuclear doctrines and human control over AI-enabled nuclear systems”.
Reyes said an agreement would have to accommodate different levels of nuclear capability rather than insist on identical ceilings because all three countries have different arsenals, strategic doctrines and security concerns.
“The fundamental obstacle is political trust,” he said. “Each side regards its own nuclear capabilities as defensive while viewing the others’ modernisation programmes as potentially threatening. That dynamic encourages an arms race even when no side necessarily wants one.”
Still, such a result may not emerge anytime soon with the Ukraine war, tensions over Taiwan and US military deployments in the Asia Pacific still sources of simmering conflict between Washington and Beijing, Zhao argued.
“The likeliest near-term outcome is not a treaty but informal restraints while formal arms control waits for a geopolitical thaw that this decade is unlikely to deliver,” Zhao added.

noticias.titulo: At least 11 killed in blaze on Thailand’s Phuket island
noticias.resumen: Authorities are investigating the cause of the fire, which also injured 16, but have ruled out arson.
noticias.texto:
At least 11 killed in blaze on Thailand’s Phuket island
The fire is the second blaze in Thailand to cause mass casualties since July.
A fire in a commercial building on Thailand’s southern resort island of Phuket has killed at least 11 people and injured 16 others, according to police.
The blaze in the tourist hub of Patong started at about 3:17am on Monday (20:17 GMT on Sunday) in a building housing a restaurant, rented accommodation and a motorcycle rental shop, and later spread to several other buildings nearby.
Phuket police commander Surachai Sooksai said officers are still investigating the cause of the fire, but an initial investigation found that an electrical transformer near the building had exploded shortly before the fire started, ruling out arson.
Phuket Governor Chodnarin Koedsom said the rental shop had about 100 motorcycles, along with stored gas, engine oil, plastic materials and tyres. He said these combustible materials may have contributed to the rapid spread of the fire and the thick, toxic smoke.
Of the 16 people injured, the authorities said, 15 were Thai and one was a Myanmar national, adding that no tourists were among those injured or killed.
The injured were treated at a hospital for smoke inhalation and injuries from broken glass.
Thailand’s approach to health and safety regulations, especially in bars and nightclubs has long raised concerns.
In July, a crowded bar in the capital, Bangkok, was engulfed in flames and smoke, killing about 40 people after an electrical short circuit triggered the blaze, authorities said.
Four people were killed and many more injured in a fire that swept through a club popular with tourists on Phuket in 2012.
A fire tore through a Bangkok club during New Year celebrations in 2009, killing 67 people and injuring more than 200.

noticias.titulo: Russia’s Andreeva defeats Ukraine’s Svitolina 7-5, 6-3 to win WTA Finals
noticias.resumen: Mirra Andreeva won the final in straight sets to end her first Grand Slam-winning year as world number two.
noticias.texto:
Russia’s Andreeva defeats Ukraine’s Svitolina 7-5, 6-3 to win WTA Finals
Mirra Andreeva won the final in straight sets to end her first Grand Slam-winning year as world number two.
Russia’s teenage tennis star Mirra Andreeva has won her first WTA Finals crown without dropping a set against her Ukrainian rival Elina Svitolina, who did not shake hands with the champion at the end of a one-sided match in Indian Wells, California.
After her 7-5, 6-3 victory on Sunday, Andreeva, who turned 19 in April during a successful year that saw her win her first Grand Slam and ascend to number two in the world, took home $3.37m and a one-of-a-kind, ultraviolet purple Mercedes-Benz convertible car at the season-ending championships. Now, all she needs is a driver’s licence.
She happily got behind the wheel after the car was driven onto the court at the Indian Wells Tennis Garden.
“This is an amazing motivation for me to get my driver’s licence as fast as I can,” she said. “If not, then look, I have five people on my team. I’m going to be a passenger princess forever. That’s also an option for me.”
After match point, Andreeva ran to hug coach Conchita Martinez in the stands. Svitolina, a 32-year-old mother, sat down in her chair.
The players did not take part in the traditional post-match handshake or pose for photos together before the match. Svitolina and others from her country have refused to shake hands with players from Russia and Belarus since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 in line with a policy set by the Ukrainian Tennis Federation.
Svitolina didn’t mention Andreeva in her post-match comments to the crowd, which included several fans waving Ukrainian flags.
Later, she said, “I couldn’t thank the people of Ukraine enough for coming to watch my matches, to watch at home.”
Andreeva publicly congratulated Svitolina for what she called an “amazing” season.
“You’re an amazing mom to come back and do this. It’s super hard,” she said. “I just wish you the best of luck for the next season.”
Svitolina nodded without expression from her seat.
“I put everything out there, and she played incredible,” Svitolina said later.
Andreeva became the 11th player to win the finals without losing a set, joining, among others, Chris Evert, Martina Navratilova and Serena Williams, all of whom did it multiple times.
“I’m super privileged to put my name in that group,” she said.
She jumped in the air when Svitolina netted an easy smash on the second match point.
Andreeva is also the second youngest player to win the WTA Finals behind her compatriot Maria Sharapova, who won at 17.
During the awards presentation, she wore a jacket with the phrase “I want to thank myself” stamped on the front, and then she did just that.
“I want to thank myself for always doing the hard work, for never quitting, for always believing in myself, for not taking the days off, for working every day and for committing to what I have to do,” she said. “Just thanks to myself without any reason.”
In doubles, Katerina Siniakova and Taylor Townsend beat the Italian duo of Sara Errani and Jasmine Paolini 6-4, 6-3.
It was the sixth title of the year for the Czech-American team of Siniakova and Townsend, who also won the French Open and US Open.
Svitolina to return to a Ukraine at war
Svitolina said she would return to Ukraine next week, pledging to continue supporting her country through donations, her foundation and the platform she has built in tennis.
“It’s been almost five years. I’ve always been supportive of the army and the soldiers,” Svitolina told reporters. “They always support me by watching the matches, and I have lots of friends that are serving the country.”
Svitolina, the world number six, said sport could offer people a release from the strain and uncertainty of daily life during wartime.
“For me it’s all about the spirit, the spirit of the people,” she said. “I’m very happy that I can bring a little happiness to the people of Ukraine.”
“Sports in general and in Ukraine especially really unite people for one goal – to win.”

noticias.titulo: The Red Sea cannot be secured without restoring the Yemeni state
noticias.resumen: Deployment of naval forces to the region cannot restore maritime security. Reinstating the Yemeni government can.
noticias.texto:
The Red Sea cannot be secured without restoring the Yemeni state
Deployment of naval forces to the region cannot bring back maritime security. Reinstating the Yemeni government in Sanaa can.
For a decade, the Yemen civil war was treated as a regional issue, confined to the southern part of the Arabian Peninsula. But as escalations in 2024-2025 and this year have made clear, the conflict now directly affects the whole world, disrupting global trade and navigation and impacting the strategic interests of every major power.
The Houthis’ ability, with Iranian backing, to endanger maritime transit through the Bab al-Mandeb strait, one of the world’s most critical maritime corridors, is not an isolated military development.
It resulted directly from the collapse of Yemeni state institutions, the dwindling international support for the legitimate government, the proliferation of armed factions and the conflicting regional agendas.
As the past few months have demonstrated, the security of navigation cannot be restored with aircraft carriers and naval task forces alone. A long-term solution necessitates first recognising and then addressing the root causes of the Yemen crisis.
The international community, now facing the consequences of Houthi attacks on commercial vessels, did almost nothing to prevent Yemen’s disintegration. Some of its actions even contributed to the Houthis’ seizure of Sanaa in September 2014.
The Houthi coup marked a decisive turning point, ending the post-2011 transition and opening the way for a parallel armed authority with its own political project that controls strategic territory, including the approaches to Bab al-Mandeb and the highlands overlooking the Red Sea.
Most dangerously, the Houthis inherited the residual capabilities of a state whose military was once ranked the fifth most heavily armed in the Arab world.
This combination of territorial control, inherited state and military capacity, and external sponsorship has made the Houthi threat more serious and more durable than that ever posed by ISIS or al-Qaeda.
And yet, the international community has not treated the Houthis as seriously as it did ISIS and al-Qaeda, nor has it placed the restoration of Yemeni national institutions as top priority. It has approached the Houthis as a force that could be contained, negotiated with, or instrumentalised.
Instead of defending the Yemeni state, the international community settled for temporary understandings and political pressure. One example is the 2018 Stockholm Agreement on the strategic port city of Hodeidah, which secured a ceasefire, mutual redeployment, and UN-supervised security and financial arrangements directing port revenues to the Central Bank rather than to the Houthis. Yet, the deal entrenched the Houthis as the de facto authority over the port and the city as a whole, leaving the power imbalance tilted in their favour; it is highly unpopular among anti-Houthi forces.
In 2021, the Houthis managed to solidify their grip on Hodeidah governorate after the inexplicable withdrawal of the Joint Forces on the Western Coast, a coalition of forces fighting on the side of the internationally recognised Yemeni government.
Neither the Joint Forces nor the regional coalition supporting them had notified the Yemeni government or the UN of their movements; civilians in these areas were told 24 hours prior, which did not give them enough time to evacuate.
The episode exposed not just the failure of the Stockholm Agreement – something acknowledged by the UN Panel of Experts on Yemen – but also the failure of the anti-Houthi front, which faced multiple military decision-making centres, inadequate coordination with the government and growing contradictions within the regional coalition.
Rather than building a national army under the legitimate government through the defence ministry, the coalition allowed numerous local formations to emerge outside the state’s chain of command. This was reflected in the Emirati backing for the separatist Southern Transitional Council and Saudi Arabia’s divergent priorities.
By empowering armed formations that refuse to submit to the very state they claim to restore, Yemen’s backers left the anti-Houthi camp divided, allowing the Houthis to consolidate their gains and avoid a decisive confrontation with a united Yemeni army.
As a result, today, the region and the world face a militia that has captured a state and is armed with drones, ballistic and potentially hypersonic missiles. It is controlling coastline beside a major waterway and is using geography as an instrument of pressure and blackmail.
The international response has been a military deployment at sea. However sophisticated, naval deployments and maritime operations may intercept missiles but cannot deliver a lasting solution, since they leave untouched the conditions that allow an armed group to launch attacks from Yemeni territory.
Treating the Houthi threat as a discrete maritime problem addresses only its symptoms while leaving its causes in place. Red Sea security cannot be separated from the security of the states that border it.
Yemen has nearly 2,500km of coastline along the Arabian Sea, the Red Sea, and the Gulf of Aden, and overlooks Bab al-Mandeb. Any serious strategy must treat Yemen’s crisis as one of state, sovereignty and institutions rather than a contest between rival parties.
That requires restoring the primacy of the national-state project, supporting legitimate institutions, unifying military and security forces under a single national command, ending the multiplicity of power centres, and reaching a political settlement only after armed groups, represented by the Houthis, have been broken and defeated, so that a stable state becomes possible.
All Gulf states, including the UAE, must recognise that their own security and stability depend on restoring the Yemeni state and supporting its military and security institutions. Accommodating or empowering armed groups, such as the Houthis and the Southern Transitional Council, can only fuel instability.
The international community too must recognise that restoring the Yemeni state is not a purely Yemeni concern. It is in the strategic interest of the whole world.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

noticias.titulo: How Russia is preparing Iran for the next escalation
noticias.resumen: Russian space intelligence sharing can help Tehran get ready for an imminent US assault.
noticias.texto:
How Russia is preparing Iran for the next escalation
Russian space intelligence sharing can help Tehran get ready for an imminent US assault.
This week, there has been some cautious optimism about a de-escalation in the US-Israel war on Iran. Qatari and Pakistani mediators have intensified efforts to conclude a deal between the warring sides after a massive military build-up in the region raised fears of a renewed kinetic phase of the conflict.
There are various factors that have played into the decision of US President Donald Trump to hold off on new attacks for now. One of them is certainly Iran’s ability to see an assault coming and retaliate with precision – a capability that is likely made possible by Russian military-grade geospatial and signals intelligence.
For eight months now, Project AURORAH, which I founded, has followed the trajectories of Russian spy satellites. It has identified at least 20 Russian spacecraft in the Kosmos-2600 series, 18 of which can be tracked.
I focus on this group because it includes Russia’s newest and most manoeuvrable military reconnaissance satellites. They can provide military cartographic reconnaissance of installations and terrain, as well as optical imagery, radar observation, and signals intelligence collection, including radar and other radio frequency emissions and military communications activity.
The satellites I have followed cover an area that extends from Syria, Lebanon and Israel to Jordan, Saudi Arabia, the wider Arabian Peninsula, Iraq and Iran, including both Bab al-Mandeb and the Strait of Hormuz. They circle Earth approximately every 95 minutes, with roughly three to four relevant regional passes daily, depending on viewing geometry.
I observed how selected manoeuvrable satellites were repositioned so that they would pass directly or almost directly over military and infrastructure targets in the region. The entire constellation of satellites was not moved, just specific spacecraft, which would improve the timing and quality of coverage over relevant targets.
These Russian satellites could be observed passing over targets before they were struck and then again after they were struck, presumably to assess the damage. The same pattern occurred repeatedly before and after Iranian attacks.
Given the precision with which Iran was able to strike United States and Gulf military and civilian targets, my conclusion is that Russia provided the Iranian army with the geospatial intelligence it needed to carry out these attacks.
The problem for the US is that such intelligence capabilities can be used not just for target selection, but also for monitoring a military build-up.
As US aircraft are being repositioned, naval forces redistributed and military infrastructure reinforced in the region, Russian satellites can provide a clear picture of these movements and the intensity of military communications, including where the communications come from, when activity increases, and how the pattern changes.
It is possible that some spy satellites can also listen to military communications, although it is unlikely they can intercept every message.
The intelligence collected can be passed to Iranian intelligence to help Iranian leaders protect their forces, keep their command system operating, and prepare their response before fighting begins.
Therefore, Iranian access to Russian satellite data collection would complicate US efforts to combine offensive readiness with protection against retaliation. One solution is to move formations farther from Iranian weapons to reduce their immediate exposure, but also to alter the distribution of combat power Tehran is observing.
Russian assistance would also give Iran early warning capabilities for attacks originating from outside the region. During Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025, B-2 Spirit bombers flew from continental US to strike Iranian nuclear facilities. Tehran knows that there can be another such assault on deeply buried facilities and therefore can use Russian satellite capabilities to monitor for early signs of it.
Needless to say, apart from preparedness to receive an attack, access to Russian satellite intelligence is likely playing a central role in preparations for retaliation in the region. As Iranian leaders have warned, the danger extends to refineries, export terminals, desalination plants and power stations.
In other words, if Trump reverses his decision and decides to attack, Iran will not only be ready for what the US Army does, but it will also be able to exact a devastating blow to the region.
Damage would disrupt civilian water and electricity supplies and transmit the effects into international energy markets. Saudi Arabia’s position as the world’s largest crude-oil exporter gives its export infrastructure particular global significance. Neighbouring Arab Gulf countries would face these consequences regardless of their influence over the decision to resume war.
It is important to consider that by providing Iran with such space intelligence capabilities, Russia retains significant leverage. Moscow is able to strengthen or restrain Tehran by controlling intelligence access without entering the conflict directly.
Russia’s willingness to share satellite data collection will inevitably impact future US operations. The US Army must now assume that major force movements, military build-ups and electronic activity can be observed and rapidly relayed to an adversary. This reduces operational surprise and requires greater dispersion, emission control and rapid relocation.
The consequences also extend beyond this war. Last month, a Russian Kosmos-series satellite approached a Finnish commercial satellite, possibly rehearsing an attack. This incident indicates that conflict on the ground can expand into space, potentially disrupting civilian and military satellite infrastructure. In present and future wars, we may very well see an escalation into space.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

noticias.titulo: US and rivals spar over next UN boss as race lurches towards deadline
noticias.resumen: Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan is the current frontrunner, polls suggest, but the US and Russia could veto her bid.
noticias.texto:
US and rivals spar over next UN boss as race lurches towards deadline
Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan is the current frontrunner, polls suggest, but the US and Russia could veto her bid.
A tense race to replace outgoing United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres is heading into its final few weeks in advance of a deadline that has never been breached, as global powers spar over candidates in an opaque election process.
With eight candidates, secret polls and geopolitical rivalries at play, the choice of the UN’s next chief is still up in the air, even as Guterres must leave office on December 31.
Competing interests from the Americas to the Middle East have complicated the process, raising fears that, for the first time in history, the new year could begin without a leader at the helm of the world’s central diplomatic organisation. The late inclusion of two candidates — Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh and Turkish nominee Feridun Sinirlioglu — has further split the race wide open, with no name so far succeeding in overcoming opposition from all five permanent members of the UN Security Council (UNSC), who hold vetoes.
The protracted contest is part of a “struggle over who will exercise political influence within the UN at a time when multilateralism is under considerable pressure and attack”, Georgina Holmes, senior lecturer in politics and international studies at the Open University, United Kingdom, told Al Jazeera.
“P5 member states are not as politically aligned as they have been in previous eras, arguably even during the Cold War,” said Holmes, referring to the permanent members of the UNSC.
‘Most difficult job in the world’
The UN secretary-general has often been compared with a “secular pope” – a figure expected to unite countries and spearhead global diplomacy.
But the position is more than that of a figurehead. The secretary-general is also the UN’s top administrative official, responsible for tapping senior officials and supervising the UN Secretariat’s tens of thousands of staff.
“The secretary-general must be a skilled politician to navigate the geopolitics; a skilled diplomat and mediator to help settle disputes; a charismatic person in the public eye; and a solid and skilled administrator,” Jan Klabbers, professor of international law at the University of Cambridge, told Al Jazeera. “It has been called ‘the most difficult job in the world’ for a reason.”
This year’s race comes as the UN, under Guterres, is under heavy strain, having been sidelined from conflicts in Iran and Ukraine. It has faced blistering criticism from United States President Donald Trump and is suffering a financial crisis that has forced it to let go of thousands of staff.
It also comes as wider geopolitical rivalries extend to the pool of candidates to lead the organisation, who are being scrutinised over their nationalities and policy commitments.
Who is in the running?
Eight individuals who have been appointed by UN member states are currently in the running to replace Guterres. Most of them are from Latin America or the Caribbean, which is in line with representation according to informal UN protocol. Five of the eight are women, amid a push for the UN to select its first female secretary-general.
A leading contender, according to a series of anonymous straw polls the UNSC carries out to gauge support, is Costa Rican diplomat Rebeca Grynspan.
In the last poll on November 5, which does not show which UNSC members voted which way, Grynspan received 12 “encourage” votes and three “discourage” votes, according to PassBlue, a nonprofit that reports on UN affairs.
Grynspan, who heads the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), has been described as a “continuity candidate”, but there are concerns as to whether she would bring enough reform to an organisation facing huge political and financial pressures.
Richard Gowan, programme director of global issues and institutions at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera that Grynspan had “solidified her position as the frontrunner”, but still appears to face opposition from the US and Russia, which could veto her bid.
While she has avoided directly confronting any veto-wielding nation, some of her reports as UNCTAD head have voiced concerns over Israel’s actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, positions at odds with Washington’s more full-throated support for Israel. Grynspan has previously also disagreed with Russian justifications for suspending a deal to allow the transport of grain through the Black Sea.
At the same time, she — like other candidates — is believed to be lobbying with key member states to win their support. In April, she met Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov over her candidature.
“Grynspan’s team argue that they can still nudge Washington and Moscow to accept her, and US officials do seem to be leaving open the possibility of working with her in the end,” said Gowan.
To be elected, a candidate needs at least nine votes in favour in the 15-member UNSC, while avoiding any vetoes from its five permanent members – the US, the UK, France, Russia and China. The 193-member UN General Assembly (UNGA) then ultimately has to sign off.
Ben Donaldson, adviser to the 1 for 8 Billion campaign, a civil society campaign “advocating for a fair, open, inclusive way to select the next secretary-general”, stressed that opposition from P5 members in a straw poll does not necessarily equate to an eventual veto.
“It has been used in the past as a basis to extract a concession from a candidate, very often in the form of a backroom deal to get a P5 national appointed to a key role in the future UN boss’s cabinet,” he told Al Jazeera.
The Argentinian head of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Rafael Grossi, is also in the running. He finished second in the latest straw poll, with nine “encourage” and four “discourage” votes. However, his reputation for being closely aligned with Washington is expected to hurt him with some P5 members, especially China and Russia, though he has also had warm words for Beijing and Moscow in recent weeks.
The other candidates from Latin America or the Caribbean are Guyanese diplomat Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett, Antigua and Barbuda diplomat Maria Fernanda Espinosa and Ecuadorian diplomat Ivonne A-Baki.
Rodrigues Birkett, whose description of Israel’s actions in Gaza as “genocide” has drawn scrutiny in the US, received five “discourage” votes in the latest straw poll. Espinosa and A-Baki received 10 and 14 “discourage” votes, respectively, making their candidacies unlikely.
The UAE’s Lana Nusseibeh and Turkiye’s Feridun Sinirlioglu, nominated by their countries in recent weeks, have also shaken up the race but face significant opposition.
Nusseibeh is reportedly favoured by the US and Russia, but her candidacy has received pushback over her country’s alleged arming of paramilitary forces accused of atrocities in Sudan. The United Arab Emirates has denied the allegation. Nusseibeh received six “discourage” votes in the latest straw poll.
“Nusseibeh’s main challenge is to win over China, which has so far seemed sceptical about her candidacy,” said Gowan. “If she can get Beijing’s support, she could break through.”
Sinirlioglu’s candidature, which UNSC member Greece is expected to oppose, received eight “discourage” votes.
Ugandan politician Olara Otunnu, the only remaining African candidate, received nine “discourage” votes.
Far-right former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, though not an official candidate, has also been floated by the US as an outside choice, The Wall Street Journal has reported.
UN in ‘near-constant crisis’
Several analysts told Al Jazeera that Grynspan appears to be in the best position, though the influence of P5 countries could change the race.
Earlier this month, the US and Russia put their weight behind the UAE’s Nusseibeh, with France and the UK offering “little resistance”, according to diplomats cited by media platform Devex.
China, for its part, has signalled a preference for a Latin American candidate, reports The New York Times, although Beijing has not publicly endorsed anyone.
Ellen Ravndal, associate professor in political science at the University of Stavanger, Norway, told Al Jazeera the drawn-out selection process and struggle to reach consensus reflect an era of “more geopolitical tensions” and a UN that is in “near-constant crisis mode”.
Adam Day, head of the Geneva office of the United Nations University Centre for Policy Research, pointed out that while the leadership contest has been lengthier and more contested than in the previous cycles in which former Secretaries-General Guterres in 2016 and Ban Ki-moon in 2006 were elected, some earlier races stretched into December.
“In the broader scope of secretary-general races, this one is still within the range of what has been normal,” Day told Al Jazeera. “But the longer it takes, the less time the incoming secretary-general has to prepare a transition.”
If no successor to Guterres is selected by the end of the year, the UN Charter does not specify an automatic interim successor. Any gap in the post would therefore require the UNSC and other UN bodies to agree on how to manage organisational leadership and operations.
“There is widespread concern that the United States and possibly other influential states are running down the clock, potentially to increase pressure to settle for a less popular candidate or to leave the UN leaderless and weakened for a period,” said Donaldson.

noticias.titulo: Widow of Haiti’s slain leader Moise to contest presidential vote
noticias.resumen: Martine Moise is one of ​33 registered candidates running in Haiti's first presidential election in a decade.
noticias.texto:
Widow of Haiti’s slain leader Moise to contest presidential vote
Martine Moise is one of 33 registered candidates running in Haiti’s first presidential election in a decade.
The widow of Haiti’s slain President Jovenel Moise, whose 2021 assassination was a major turning point for the nation, has registered as a candidate for the first presidential election in a decade.
Martine Moise’s name appeared on the website of the Provisional Electoral Council (CEP) as a candidate on Sunday.
A first-round vote is set for July next year.
Haiti last held a presidential election in 2016. Successive leaders have repeatedly delayed elections, citing insecurity risks, amid the expanding influence of powerful and heavily armed gangs.
“Haiti will rise again on its own two feet, because politics needs to be done differently,” Moise, who has not publicly commented on the registration, said on X last week.
In the post, she also blamed “the opposition” for bringing the country “to its knees”. “They do not want the country to develop; they do not want the people to live well,” she said.
Three female candidates
Martine Moise is one of three women among 33 registered presidential candidates. Among other prominent candidates are Michel Martelly and Jocelerme Privert, both former presidents, former Prime Minister Claude Joseph and former Foreign Minister Dominique Dupuy.
Several candidates, including Martelly and Privert, have been sanctioned internationally over accusations, which they both deny, of supporting armed gangs.
Martine Moise has been a key witness in the Miami court case prosecuting dozens of suspects involved in the murder of her husband, who led Haiti from 2017 until his death in July 2021.
He was shot in his bedroom by Colombian mercenaries impersonating agents of the United States Drug Enforcement Administration. Martine Moise suffered serious gunshot wounds and was flown to a hospital in Florida.
A series of transitional governments followed, as armed gangs, widely believed to be aided by corrupt politicians, seized control of much of the capital, Port-au-Prince, and surrounding regions.
Tens of thousands killed
About 1.5 million people have been displaced and more than 22,000 have been killed, many by security personnel. Several international forces have been deployed to Haiti to help police fight the gangs; the most recent deployment, last month, involved soldiers from El Salvador.
Last week, Haitian security forces regained control of the country’s main stadium, which had been under gang control for two years, forcing the national football team to play elsewhere.
The operation was part of a deployment of about 2,000 soldiers ordered by El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele, who announced that the troops would set up an operational base in the stadium to push further into territory still controlled by the gangs.

noticias.titulo: Iraqi armed group denies involvement in oil smuggling, calls probe a ‘lie’
noticias.resumen: Iran-aligned Kataib Hezbollah says the group is subjected to 'blackmail' to force disarmament amid US pressure on Iraq.
noticias.texto:
Iraqi armed group denies involvement in oil smuggling, calls probe a ‘lie’
Iran-aligned Kataib Hezbollah says the group is subjected to ‘blackmail’ to force disarmament amid US pressure on Iraq.
The Iran-aligned Kataib Hezbollah group has denied its involvement in an oil smuggling operation in Iraq’s Jurf al-Nasr area after Iraqi authorities launched an anticorruption crackdown.
Kataib Hezbollah, one of Iraq’s most heavily armed factions, said in a statement on Sunday that the Iraqi prime minister’s office was “fabricating lies” and that the group was being subjected to “the largest blackmail operation” to force its disarmament.
The statement was issued a day after Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi sacked nine senior officials following an investigation into the allegations.
The Iraqi government said an investigation committee, chaired by al-Zaidi, confirmed oil smuggling based on “intelligence documents” containing satellite images showing operations being carried out in the armed faction’s stronghold.
The committee ordered those implicated, whom it did not identify, to be referred to the judiciary and dismissed nine officials, including security and intelligence officers in Babil province, an Interior Ministry commander and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the Ministry of Oil.
Responding to the committee’s findings, Kataib Hezbollah said the investigation “found no violations whatsoever of the oil pipelines” and that this “definitively proves that the smuggling allegations are false”.
The group said its members accompanied the committee’s visit to the Jurf al-Nasr area on Friday.
Baghdad has been under increasing pressure from Washington to rein in Iran-aligned groups and curb Tehran’s influence in Iraq, an ally of both the US and Iran.
Al-Zaidi has previously promised to ensure that non-state armed groups would hand over their weapons to the state.
However, Kataib Hezbollah has pledged to retain its weapons arsenal and accused al-Zaidi of caving to pressure from the US, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
Iran-aligned groups, including Kataib Hezbollah, have previously targeted US forces in Iraq and attacked Gulf states following the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in late February.
Washington accuses Tehran of using Iraq’s economy to evade sanctions and has previously sanctioned Iraqi individuals for blending Iraqi and Iranian oil.

noticias.titulo: Megaspeed, firm at centre of Nvidia scandal, says Alice Huang left in 2025
noticias.resumen: Chinese tech executive romantically linked to ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left in August 2025, Singapore-based firm says.
noticias.texto:
Megaspeed, firm at centre of Nvidia scandal, says Alice Huang left in 2025
Chinese tech executive romantically linked to ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left in August 2025, the Singapore-based firm says.
Megaspeed has confirmed that Alice Huang, the tech executive whose reported relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is at the centre of international spying claims, left the company last year.
The Singapore-based data centre company said in a statement on Sunday that Alice Huang left her executive role on August 30, 2025, and has held no position with the firm since.
“Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang’s personal and private matters,” the statement said.
Megaspeed also pushed back on media reports it said contained claims about its operations that “are not supported by verifiable evidence”.
“The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation,” it said.
Megaspeed, a major buyer of graphics processing units (GPUs) made by the California-based Nvidia, used to train and run frontier AI models, is facing scrutiny over its compliance with United States export controls intended to keep high-end chips out of China.
While data centres in Southeast Asian countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand can import high-end Nvidia chips legally, US authorities have long suspected the region is a hotbed of illicit smuggling on behalf of Chinese AI developers.
Megaspeed CEO and chairman Tan Yong Pong said on Thursday that the company had retained a top US law firm to lead a “comprehensive census” of its GPUs and verify its export control compliance practices.
Unnamed US officials have accused Alice Huang of working with China’s Ministry of State Security in an espionage operation targeting Jensen Huang, who stepped down as Nvidia CEO, president and board member on Thursday amid a board investigation.
Beijing has denied the allegations, describing them as “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.
Alice Huang has not publicly commented on the claims.
Singaporean authorities are investigating Megaspeed on suspicion of making false declarations in relation to its purchases of servers. They said last week they had previously confiscated Alice Huang’s passport for eight months as part of their inquiries.
Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said on Thursday that it barred Huang from re-entering the country after determining that she had provided inaccurate information to investigators to downplay her role at Megaspeed.
Police investigations into Megaspeed and six other individuals are ongoing, the ministry said in a statement.

noticias.titulo: Indonesian president apologises to Singapore, Malaysia for wildfire haze
noticias.resumen: Prabowo says his government has a 'zero-tolerance policy' for firms that contribute to blazes and pledges strict action.
noticias.texto:
Indonesian president apologises to Singapore, Malaysia for wildfire haze
Prabowo says his government has a ‘zero-tolerance policy’ for companies that contribute to blazes and promises strict action.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has apologised to Singapore and Malaysia for the transboundary haze due to months-long wildfires.
Prabowo conveyed the apology during a session at the ASEAN summit that kicked off on Sunday in the Philippine capital, Manila, according to a statement from the Indonesian presidential office.
“I would like to apologise to my neighbouring countries Malaysia and Singapore when we had a very big forest fire, which took nearly four months for us to control. The haze travelled to Malaysia and to Singapore. It is not our fault, but once again we apologise. But we have done our best,” he said.
Prabowo also said his government had and would continue to take firm action on companies involved in forest fires while also preparing to establish a new body to strengthen wildfire prevention.
Indonesia has a “zero-tolerance policy” for any company contributing to the blazes, the statement quoted him as saying.
“We’ve revoked 17 concessions [permits] from companies. [Meanwhile] 26 companies are currently under investigation and 11 others have been charged. Another 23 companies are on the list to be charged,” he said.
“In total, 104 companies are currently under investigation by our police.”
He also said Indonesia had deployed 71,000 forest firefighters, and 16 people died while battling the blazes.
Philippine Foreign Minister Theresa Lazaro told a news briefing later on Sunday that Jakarta was “very frank and candid in expressing the efforts they have been exerting in addressing the forest fires in Indonesia” during the plenary session.
Indonesia has been battling its most intense wildfires in 11 years, with large swaths of land scorched, mainly on the islands of Sumatra, Borneo and Papua.
Haze from the fires blanketed some of its nearest neighbours, primarily Singapore and Malaysia, over the past few months.
Malaysia and Singapore have refrained from criticising Indonesia, instead offering assistance to fight the fires.
Previously, an Indonesian official faced criticism after claiming the country’s forests supply oxygen to Malaysia and Singapore despite recurring haze from wildfires.
“We do not just send smoke, but when there is no smoke, we send oxygen,” Indonesian Government Communications Agency chief Syahganda Nainggolan said in October.
ASEAN agreement
On paper, Southeast Asian countries are committed to working together to prevent cross-border air pollution under the 2002 ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.
The legally binding treaty commits the 11 members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to tackle haze, a recurring issue for decades, through “concerted national efforts and intensified regional and international co-operation”.
However, the agreement does not contain provisions for enforcement by a judicial body such as the International Court of Justice. Disagreements over interpretation and application can only be settled through negotiation.
Implementation of the treaty has also moved at a snail’s pace. The treaty’s coordinating office in Jakarta only opened this April, nearly a quarter-century after it was envisioned.
Prabowo’s remarks came as the problem of transboundary haze has begun to disappear.
On Thursday, the ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC) issued a “no transboundary smoke haze” notice for southern parts of Southeast Asia, the Jakarta Post reported. The relief has been linked to recent downpours and fewer fire hotspots in Indonesia’s Sumatra and Kalimantan provinces.

noticias.titulo: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
noticias.resumen: Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city. The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.
The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.
The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. Some animal rights activists have compared authorities’ baboon management to apartheid.
During Friday’s relocation, outraged protesters tried to stop vehicles taking the baboons away. One person sprayed a fire extinguisher, according to the Daily Maverick, a local news outlet.
After the confrontation, the local Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals branch urged those opposed to the baboons’ capture not to try to stop the vehicles. “Capture and transport are already stressful for the baboons,” it said in a statement. “Delaying their arrival prolongs their time in crates and risks adding to that stress – this is not fair on the baboons.”
It said it remained opposed to the baboon’s relocation, adding: “Our presence did not imply support … our inspectors are present because the animals need someone looking out for them.”
On Sunday, dozens of people sat outside the wildlife centre in a silent protest, some tying flowers to the fence. Baboons from a different troop also gathered at the boundary, calling to the newly captive animals, the Daily Maverick reported.
“We stand together for the Seaforth and Waterfall troops, for their freedom, their dignity and their right to live as wild animals,” Mandy Neal, the administrator of the Save Kogelfontein Baboons Facebook group, posted on Monday, calling for weekly Sunday silent protests. “ Our message is simple: CAPTIVITY IS NOT CONSERVATION.”
The City of Cape Town said in a statement on Sunday that the relocation had been successful, with the baboons being monitored 24/7 after being checked by vets and the females receiving contraceptive implants.
It said: “The Waterfall troop has been relocated due to the severity and persistence of human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment, the limited available natural low-lying habitat, the increasing risk to the baboons’ welfare, and public safety concerns … [and] as a very last resort after other interventions were evaluated and deemed ineffective, and as an alternative to culling.”
Prof Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town, said the baboon management plan had undergone two years of public consultations. “It has thus been disappointing watching members of the public and select NGOs, many which did not engage in the stakeholder process, now compromising the safety and welfare of the baboons and people through violent actions directed at staff and baboons in transit.”
