noticias.texto:
The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989.
Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter). Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones.
India’s meteorological department has released an alert for a depression located in the Bay of Bengal with the potential to develop into a cyclone. A low-pressure system formed during the early hours of Friday before developing into a depression on Sunday. The department’s forecast is for the depression to intensify into a cyclonic storm by Tuesday before gradually drifting north-west towards eastern India, with the expectation it will make landfall on Thursday. If the storm were to develop it would become the third of the season and be named Akvan. There is a “watch” level warning for much of the eastern coast on Wednesday and Thursday, with parts of the Andhra Pradesh and Odisha states on an “alert” level.

noticias.titulo: ‘The blood of these brothers cries out’: Pope Leo demands justice for people killed protecting the Amazon
noticias.resumen: Pontiff delivers forceful speech in Peru as he travels from high in the Andes into the Amazon Pope Leo XIV has demanded justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon and backed efforts by Indigenous peoples to stop their lands from being ravaged by logging and illegal mining. On the penultimate day of his South American tour, Leo on Sunday travelled into the Peruvian Amazon and channelled one of Pope Francis’s core teachings that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God’s creation. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Pope Leo XIV has demanded justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon and backed efforts by Indigenous peoples to stop their lands from being ravaged by logging and illegal mining.
On the penultimate day of his South American tour, Leo on Sunday travelled into the Peruvian Amazon and channelled one of Pope Francis’s core teachings that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God’s creation.
“The cry of the Earth and the cry of the poor are inseparable,” Leo told Indigenous representatives and missionaries gathered along the Ucayali River in the north-eastern city of Pucallpa.
He said he came to Pucallpa to support them in their search for justice and peace and referred to what environmental groups estimate have been 57 murders of environmental defenders between 2010 and 2024.
“The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice,” Leo said to applause from the crowd, many of whom were wearing traditional feathered headwear and face markings of the region.
In addition to deforestation, illegal gold mining has become an increasingly lucrative business in the Amazon, devastating forests and polluting rivers. Illegal mining and coca production has also driven deforestation.
Leo addressed the combination of threats in one of his most forceful speeches to date, drawing on his years of experience as a Peruvian bishop and Francis’s constant preaching about the environment and the plight of Indigenous groups.
During the encounter and a subsequent mass in Pucallpa, he demanded a different model of economic development that respects the Earth and the Indigenous peoples who care for it, rather than the “irresponsible exploitation” by outside actors.
“Very little has been done – and very slowly at that – while the means to exploit and pollute creation have accelerated,” he said at mass. “In the face of these evils, let us not bury the Lord’s gifts, for he gives us the strength to repair and heal the suffering caused by an insatiable thirst for domination.”
In Peru, most murders of environmental defenders go unpunished; only a few have resulted in convictions.
The most recent conviction came in the case of Kichwa leader Quinto Inuma Alvarado, who was murdered in 2023 when he was ambushed by hitmen on a river in the San Martín region, the Amazonian territory he was defending.
Leo also referred to a notorious rise in sexual violence against Indigenous Awajún and Wampis schoolgirls in the northern Amazon, and blasted the “impunity” and “corruption” surrounding them.
The Awajún and Wampis Women’s Council has recorded 370 cases of sexual violence in the Condorcanqui province between January and July.
Julio Cusurichi, an Indigenous leader, handed Leo a letter during his visit to Pucallpa, asking him to help protect the rights of uncontacted Indigenous relatives.
“The Peruvian state is weakening the mechanisms that should safeguard their territories,” said the letter from the Indigenous rights organisation Aidesep, on which Cusurichi is a board member.
“We cannot allow economic interests to take precedence over the lives and rights of these vulnerable peoples. Therefore, we ask Pope Leo XIV to raise his voice and support this urgent call for their defence.”
Cardinal Pedro Barreto praised the pope’s decision to meet with Indigenous peoples. Barreto, a former Peruvian archbishop who helped win a multimillion-dollar pollution payout for an Andean town, said: “[Leo] is well aware of all the historical suffering … corruption, illegal mining, deforestation, and the contempt shown by politicians.”
Luis E Fernandez, co-founder of Cincia, a scientific research centre in Peru, also hailed the pontiff’s power to raise awareness. “Pope Leo’s recognition of pollution from illegal mining brings much-needed attention to a crisis affecting Indigenous and riverine communities across the Amazon,” he said.
Fernandez visited the Vatican in October and presented Leo with scientific evidence detailing the impact of illegal gold mining and associated mercury poisoning.
Leo’s last full day in Peru was also his most ambitious, crisscrossing the nation to minister to communities high in the Andes mountains. Peru’s air force released footage of the pope inside a helicopter and said it was “an unforgettable memory” to take Leo around the country.
His first stop was the mountain city of Cusco, where huge crowds greeted him.
“It is all worth it,” said Margarida Salomon, 63, who said she came from Sucre in Bolivia to see the pontiff, spending about $500 to take a bus and sleep in a tent. “I am still getting to know this pope, but the fact he is here in the Andes means a lot.”
The visit to Cusco, 3,400m (more than 11,000ft) above sea level, tested Leo’s stamina as he continues recovering from lung cancer surgery last month. Leo sat in the chair of his popemobile during part of the ride around Cusco, but it wasn’t clear if that was to preserve his energy or to steady himself on the uneven streets.
In general, the 71-year-old Leo has seemed unfazed by the toll of the three-nation South American trip, the longest of his pontificate.

noticias.titulo: Eurovision organisers criticise Malaysian removal of LGBT+ footage in first Asian contest
noticias.resumen: Broadcaster TV3 appears to cut footage of Thai drag performers and gay Philippine jury spokesperson Eurovision’s organisers have said they are “surprised and disappointed” that the first Eurovision Asia was altered when it was broadcast in Malaysia, apparently removing LGBTQ+ imagery and people from the show. The European Broadcasting Union (EBU), the alliance of public broadcasters that owns Eurovision, said it would write to Voxovation, the company producing the Asian contest under licence, and ask it to establish with the Malaysian broadcaster TV3 why it happened. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Eurovision’s organisers have said they are “surprised and disappointed” that the first Eurovision Asia was altered when it was broadcast in Malaysia, apparently removing LGBTQ+ imagery and people from the show.
The European Broadcasting Union (EBU), the alliance of public broadcasters that owns Eurovision, said it would write to Voxovation, the company producing the Asian contest under licence, and ask it to establish with the Malaysian broadcaster TV3 why it happened.
Footage circulating online of the contest, which was won by the Philippines’ Carmelle, showed the first of two cuts during the voting in Saturday’s final in Bangkok, when the Philippines’ spokesperson, Vice Ganda, awarded the Philippine jury’s points.
Vice Ganda is gay and identifies as non-binary. The comedian is among the biggest stars on Philippine television, has fronted the country’s most watched daytime show, and has campaigned for LGBTQ+ acceptance at home.
Announcing a national jury’s points is one of the most visible roles in a Eurovision final. Each country’s spokesperson appears in turn to reveal how their jury has ranked the other entries.
While the international feed showed Vice Ganda announcing that the Philippine jury had given its 12 points, the maximum, to the Malaysian entrant, Aina Abdul, TV3 viewers saw only the scoreboard.
Separate footage shows part of the show’s opening number showcasing Thai culture, in which drag performers appeared on street food carts, replaced with a wide shot taken from rehearsals.
Eurovision fans accused the channel of “censorship”. The Guardian has not been able to review TV3’s broadcast independently as its livestream is no longer available online.
Martin Green, the director of the Eurovision song contest, said: “We are surprised and disappointed to learn that the broadcast of Eurovision Song Contest Asia was altered in Malaysia.
“We take this matter seriously and will be writing to Voxovation, the producers of the show, to seek clarification and ask them to establish with Malaysian broadcaster TV3 why this happened.
“This appears to be isolated to the Malaysian broadcast of the show, and all other transmissions were not altered.”
Voxovation said in a statement that it was aware of the concerns raised and was “looking into the matter with the broadcaster to establish the circumstances … We are working with the Malaysian broadcaster to make sure this doesn’t happen again.”
Neither the EBU nor Voxovation said whether the contest’s participation agreement required broadcasters to carry the show unedited or what the consequences would be if one did not.
The Guardian has asked Media Prima, Malaysia’s largest media group and TV3’s owner, for comment.
This is not the first time the wider Eurovision song contest has faced allegations of censorship. In May 2018 the EBU terminated its partnership with the Chinese streaming service Mango TV after it dropped the Irish and Albanian entries and blurred a rainbow flag in the audience, saying such censorship was not in line with its “values of universality and inclusivity”.
Asked before Saturday’s final how the EBU’s commitment to its values squared with the laws in Malaysia and Bangladesh, the other competing country where same-sex relations are criminalised, the EBU’s head of communications, Dave Goodman, said the contest’s values were “non-negotiable”.
Malaysia has some of the harshest anti-LGBTQ+ laws in Asia, with oral and anal sex being punishable by up to 20 years in prison.
Rights groups have warned of a hardening climate. In November last year, authorities raided a men-only spa in Kuala Lumpur and detained more than 200 men, though no charges followed. And in 2022, police raided an LGBTQ+ Halloween party in the capital and arrested 20 people.
In 2023, a festival appearance by the British band the 1975, whose singer criticised the country’s homophobic laws and kissed a male bandmate on stage, led to the event being cancelled and prompted tighter entry rules for foreign performers.
TV3 has faced pressure over LGBTQ+ visibility before. In February 2025, it apologised after male guests arrived at a red carpet event in clothing resembling women’s dress.

noticias.titulo: Trump to embark on Asia trip in apparent foreign policy push before end of term
noticias.resumen: Experts say US president may lean toward global affairs after domestic influence curtailed in midterm elections Donald Trump is embarking on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters, in what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency. The US president will meet his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, for their first trilateral summit, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Before that, he will land in Manila in
noticias.texto:
Donald Trump is embarking on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters, in what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.
The US president will meet his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, for their first trilateral summit, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Before that, he will land in Manila in the Philippines on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit.
At the Asean summit, Trump is expected to sign a trade agreement with Thailand, push deals with other countries and lobby fellow leaders to favour the US over China on artificial intelligence.
He will also take part in the first leaders’ meeting of the Quad partnership – consisting of the US, Japan, India and Australia – since he returned to the White House in January 2025.
White House officials said the president would be accompanied to Apec by Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX entrepreneur who spent almost $500m (£380m) unsuccessfully supporting Republican candidates in this month’s midterms. The reason for Musk’s presence has not been explained.
The China leg of the trip will take place amid the continuing fallout from the Nvidia spying scandal, which prompted the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, to resign amid revelations he had had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Trump is under pressure to raise the matter with Xi when they hold a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of Apec.
The US president has said he does not plan to bring up the subject; administration officials insist he will not do so and that the meeting will be dedicated to implementing a trade agreement between the two superpowers.
Huang persuaded the Trump administration to lift restrictions on the sale of Nvidia’s AI chips to China that had been imposed during Joe Biden’s presidency.
Mao Ning, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, told reporters on Monday that at the trilateral summit, Xi, Trump and Putin “will exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance”.
Some analysts have characterised the meeting as a “big three” gathering echoing the 1945 Yalta meeting of Winston Churchill, Franklin D Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin that in effect carved up postwar Europe, between a communist-ruled east and a democratic, capitalist west.
Such a prospect has alarmed Ukraine, which fears that Putin – who initially suggested the trilateral meeting – will use it to persuade Trump and Xi to agree to a settlement of the war with Russia on Moscow’s terms.
However, Trump has said Ukraine will not be up for debate at the meeting and that its main purpose will be to discuss ending the US’s war with Iran and “denuclearisation” – shorthand for a deal among the three powers to limit nuclear arms.
That is believed to be unpalatable to China, which has been increasing its nuclear arsenal, and has signalled an unwillingness to enter into reduction agreements until it is closer to parity with the US and Russia.
Analysts say the main beneficiary of the three-way meeting is likely to be Putin, whose standing will be boosted by being treated on an equal footing by two other leaders whose countries are, in reality, much more powerful.
Expectations of a substantial agreement are low.
Lyle Goldstein, an international affairs fellow and China specialist at Brown University in the US, said the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting would not have a substantive result. “There will be no ‘Yalta’, as many have feared,” he said.
Jonathan Czin, the Michael Armacost chair in foreign policy studies at the Brookings Institution, said Trump’s lame duck status would deter Xi and Putin from trying to reach long-term arrangements with the US.
“Both men know Trump’s time is expiring even more quickly than his leverage – and that he will be irrelevant in a mere 26 months [when his term expires],” Czin told an online Brookings forum. “Why would either man make a deal with a leader whose time and leverage are waning? They will only do it if they think they can pilfer more from Trump diplomatically than they will be able to gain from the next American president.”
Nevertheless, Goldstein – who took soundings on Chinese expectations for the summit in a visit to Shenzhen last week – predicted Trump would follow the pattern of previous presidents by turning increasingly to global affairs while he faces the prospect of his influence on the domestic front being curtailed after the Democrats’ victories in the House of Representatives and the Senate.
“The president has been badly damaged by the election and will have limited prospects for the next two years,” he said. “That may cause him to be more active in foreign policy since he can act in that domain with fewer constraints. It would not surprise me if Trump is ready to go all-out to make some further splash in foreign policy.”
With the risks of reigniting the war with Iran high and the Russia-Ukraine war still resistant to a diplomatic resolution despite White House efforts, Goldstein suggested Trump could attempt “a dramatic foreign policy flourish in Asia”, such as an agreement with Kim Jong-un, the North Korean dictator with whom he has frequently boasted of having a close relationship. Kim is not expected to attend the Apec gathering, although there have been rumours he may appear.

noticias.titulo: Canada could work with Chinese automakers if US trade talks fail, says Carney
noticias.resumen: Ahead of Apec summit, PM says ‘Canada is going to move forward either way’ when asked if Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations The prime minister of Canada, Mark Carney, said the country could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with the US president, Donald Trump, failed to preserve an integrated North American auto industry. Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing t
noticias.texto:
The prime minister of Canada, Mark Carney, said the country could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with the US president, Donald Trump, failed to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.
Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.
“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of US trade actions.”
He said on Monday that negotiations with the US remained his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers. A day earlier in Manila, in the Philippines, Carney said any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry.
Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.
“If they [Canada’s auto workers] are not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”
The Detroit Three – Ford, General Motors and Stellantis – operate factories across Canada, the US and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the US from Canada.
Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would need proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.
“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”
Under a January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.
Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.
The deal drew criticism from Ontario premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the US market.
Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.
Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior US officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

noticias.titulo: Megaspeed, the company linked to the downfall of Nvidia boss, says it’s a ‘legitimate and lawful business’
noticias.resumen: Company insists Alice Huang, who is accused of being a Chinese spy, left business in late 2025 Elon Musk joins 165,000 others calling for Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang Business live – latest updates Megaspeed International, the company linked to the downfall of the Nvidia chief, Jensen Huang , says it is a “legitimate and lawful business” and has announced that its director, who allegedly had an affair with Jensen Huang, left the business in late 2025. The Singapore-based cloud computing company on the weekend said it was “aware of recent media reports containing assertions about our busin
noticias.texto:
Megaspeed International, the company linked to the downfall of the Nvidia chief, Jensen Huang, says it is a “legitimate and lawful business” and has announced that its director, who allegedly had an affair with Jensen Huang, left the business in late 2025.
The Singapore-based cloud computing company on the weekend said it was “aware of recent media reports containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence”.
Megaspeed said it had “retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation”.
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the chip manufacturer Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with Alice Huang and two company employees.
US intelligence agencies believe the tech chief, whose products have been crucial to the AI boom, had been targeted by Alice Huang, the former director of Megaspeed International.
US officials have alleged Alice Huang may have been acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times has reported.
In the past three years, Megaspeed has been one of Nvidia’s biggest foreign customers, buying nearly US$5bn (A$7.4bn, £3.8bn) in AI chips and advanced hardware.
A US senator asked the commerce department to investigate whether Megaspeed had diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Megaspeed said on Sunday it would not comment on Alice Huang’s “personal and private matters”.
“Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the company,” it said in a statement.
The global facades of Megaspeed International form a puzzling corporate picture, and involve a lottery retailer in rural Australia, a dilapidated storefront in Kuala Lumpur and a near-empty office in Singapore.
The company on Sunday said: “Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate.”
Short seller Culper Research in May quoted a Megaspeed employee as saying Alice Huang was “still our boss”, in a report accusing Nvidia of having a “China problem”.
On Thursday, Singaporean authorities said Alice Huang had been barred from re-entering the city state after a 2025 investigation into the company’s “suspected breaches of our domestic laws”.
The ministry of home affairs said it had held Alice Huang’s passport from June 2025 until February. Police believed she had given them “inaccurate” information, to downplay her role at the company, but released her due to insufficient evidence.
She was issued a stern warning and barred from re-entering the country. Taiwan has also barred her from re-entry, its authorities have said.
Singapore’s initial investigation related to Megaspeed’s potential “false declarations” over the purchase of computer servers.
On Friday, Malaysia said it was investigating a subsidiary of Megaspeed International over the possible diversion of advanced AI chips to other countries.
Megaspeed has previously said there was no evidence of illegal chip transfers.
Its registered Sydney office is home to numerous business and had no Megaspeed signage, mailbox or physical presence when the Guardian visited last week. No one had heard of Megaspeed Australia or its listed director, 29-year-old Kai Kang.
Reuters visited a news agency and lottery retailer, in Seymour, Victoria, an hour’s drive north of Melbourne, where a woman, who identified herself as Kang’s mother, said Kang was based in Shanghai and did not know anything about the Singaporean company.
Kang has not been accused of any wrongdoing. Attempts to contact him were unsuccessful.
The US attorney general, Todd Blanche, said last week that the Justice Department had not concluded whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy.
Asked whether she was a spy, the US president, Donald Trump, said: “I don’t know if that’s been determined yet.”
Beijing rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated. Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang for comment. The Guardian has sought comment from Alice Huang.
Megaspeed began as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer and was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International. It adopted its current name in March 2023, when all its shares were transferred to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company. Alice Huang is also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le.
By November 2023, she was no longer listed as a Megaspeed director, and all her shares had been transferred to an entity owned by Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan.
The company’s finances have also attracted attention. Singapore corporate records show its total assets rose roughly 90-fold from end-2023 to 2024, reaching almost US$3bn (A$4.4bn, £2.3bn).

noticias.titulo: Birth keeper told mother of baby who later died to ‘go home and rest’, NSW inquest hears
noticias.resumen: Sita Kali was involved in care for two of four babies who died between 2022 and 2024 in Lismore after free births or home births Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast A self-described birth keeper advised a pregnant woman whose baby later died to “go home and rest” after she was given urgent medical advice to present to an emergency department, the New South Wales coroner’s court has heard. Sita Tara Kali was involved in the care of two of four babies born in free births or home births who died in the northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024. An inquest into the deat
noticias.texto:
A self-described birth keeper advised a pregnant woman whose baby later died to “go home and rest” after she was given urgent medical advice to present to an emergency department, the New South Wales coroner’s court has heard.
Sita Tara Kali was involved in the care of two of four babies born in free births or home births who died in the northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024. An inquest into the deaths began in the Lismore local court on Monday. The families of the four babies were not present.
The inquest will examine whether the care was reasonable in the circumstances and whether care by an unregistered support worker was reasonable and appropriate before, during and after the birth.
Baby R’s mother had a distrust of hospitals in general, the court heard. She was aligned with and trusted Kali. She felt that having a home birth would give her a stronger connection to the baby. In a police statement she said she felt threatened by her experiences at the hospital.
At 43 weeks, an ultrasound confirmed that the baby was extremely compromised. The obstetric advice was urgent. She was urged to attend emergency and strongly advised against a home birth, the inquest heard.
She called Kali, who said in a police statement, “she was quite upset and anxious. I advised her to go home and rest. Calm yourself down and consider what you want to do.”
Baby R was born outside into his father’s hands at 9.51am. Two doulas were in attendance; neither had medical training. The baby was white in colour. He never latched on to feed.
About 14 hours later, the ambulance was called. The umbilical cord and placenta were still attached. Baby R died on the way to a waiting helicopter at 12.22am.
The cause of his death was determined to be unascertained. But an expert neonatologist surmised that it was caused by hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy resulting from severe post-maturity – being born at 43 weeks.
Prof Hannah Dahlen, a midwifery academic who has attended thousands of births, told the court that this was a baby “I would have been watching closely” as a midwife attending a birth.
She said the difference between a doula and a birthing midwife “is the theoretical knowledge that we add on to that clinical experience, which gives us an understanding and an ability to interpret signs and symptoms and to identify what pathology is going on, or what physiology is not actually working at this time and making a decision”.
The counsel assisting, Ragni Mathur, told the court women were choosing unregulated free birthing because of “traumatic or coercive experiences, fragmented care, lack of trust in clinicians, lack of available clinicians, lack of services in regional NSW, and including child protection notifications and regulatory actions against new lives”.

noticias.titulo: Albanese treads tightrope in upcoming Trump meeting, wanting Indo-Pacific engagement and end to Iran and Ukraine wars
noticias.resumen: Quad leaders’ summit in Philippines is Trump’s first, as Australia joins US and Japan to protect AI technologies in face of China efforts to dominate Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Anthony Albanese will attempt to walk a tightrope in his relationship with Donald Trump when the pair meets on Tuesday, arguing for a speedy resolution to the wars in Iran and Ukraine while urging the US to engage in the Indo-Pacific. The Quad leaders’ summit in the Philippines’ capital of Manila will be Trump’s first, in either of his presidencies. The US president, fresh from a crus
noticias.texto:
Anthony Albanese will attempt to walk a tightrope in his relationship with Donald Trump when the pair meets on Tuesday, arguing for a speedy resolution to the wars in Iran and Ukraine while urging the US to engage in the Indo-Pacific.
The Quad leaders’ summit in the Philippines’ capital of Manila will be Trump’s first, in either of his presidencies. The US president, fresh from a crushing midterms result, will take centre stage in gatherings of Asian leaders and prepare for historic three-way talks with Xi Jinping of China and Russia’s Vladimir Putin this week.
Underlying the diplomatic swing are efforts by the federal government to avoid angering China, as the Quad leaders gather for the first time since 2024 – and after Australia joined countries, including the US and Japan, in an agreement for new protections around key AI technologies.
Designed to firm up supply chains for chips and critical minerals components, the San Francisco Declaration was crafted to promote cooperation in the face of China’s efforts to control areas of AI development.
Part of the Pax Silica international accord, officials said the agreement would help ensure Trump worked with partners to set standards in AI, rather than relying on others for leadership. Signatories include the UK, India, Israel, South Korea and Singapore.
Albanese told the Asean-Australia summit on Monday that the region needed friendship, mutual trust, and optimism to prosper.
“At a time of global instability, the cooperation we demonstrate here will help us to confront the challenges we share at home and in our region,” he said.
Federal government sources told Guardian Australia the intense international efforts, including Albanese’s attendance at the Apec leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, China at the end of the week, was about maintaining engagement with Trump in the final two years of his presidency and stopping the US from withdrawing from global leadership.
Asia Society senior fellow Premesha Saha said the Quad talks would focus on critical minerals, maritime security and energy security.
“For Australia, keeping the United States engaged in the Indo-Pacific is a core strategic interest, and the Quad is one of the few settings where the president is tied into a regional agenda alongside three close partners,” Saha said.
“After a year in which Washington has been engaged elsewhere and has opened its own channel with Beijing, getting Trump to a Quad leaders’ meeting in the region matters to Australia.”
Saha said Albanese’s objectives included keeping Washington engaged in the region and building a Quad capable of delivering results, even during shifts in US policy and interest.
“Beijing will criticise it, as it always does, and will cast it as bloc politics. But I will be cautious about overstating how much this will anger China,” she said.
“The Quad isn’t a military alliance, and Washington has gone out of its way to say it isn’t an anti-China coalition.”
Jennifer Parker, a non-resident fellow at the Lowy Institute, said criticism of Albanese’s involvement in the annual international summit season was shortsighted.
“Our relationships in the region are essential to our security in an increasingly chaotic world, and our security is the backbone of our national prosperity,” she said.
“It is important for Australia to be seen on the international stage and advocate for our national interests.”
Parker disagreed that Australia was working to keep the US engaged in the Asia Pacific region.
“The US has enduring interests here, both economically and strategically. But sometimes it pays for Australia to remind them of that,” she said.
Albanese announced a new Asean-Australia digital economy program on Monday, to support AI safety and intelligence standards and digital trade standards.
He said humans must remain in control of AI, shaping the technology “rather than let it shape us”.
Albanese also held one-on-one talks with the Philippines president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
He told his Laos counterpart, Saleumxay Kommasith, that Australia remained very concerned about the deaths of backpackers Bianca Jones and Holly Morton-Bowles, who died after drinking methanol-laced alcohol at a hostel in Vientiane in 2024.
Albanese said Australia remained concerned about the seriousness of charges over the deaths. Investigators said they did not have enough evidence to do more because autopsies were not carried out.
Albanese called the case a “tragedy” and said it remained a serious issue in Australia.
Kommasith said the Laos government had attached importance to the case and officials were “trying our best to put an end to this by bringing those perpetrators into justice”.

noticias.titulo: NSW halts new law to crack down on underquoting by real estate agents at 11th hour
noticias.resumen: Backdown is one of several premier Chris Minns has announced in recent weeks as state prepares for election in March Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The Minns government has mothballed laws intended to protect homebuyers from underquoting after the premier said real estate agents in his Sydney electorate had raised concerns about their effect amid a housing market downturn. Changes due to come into effect on Tuesday would have banned agents in New South Wales from lowering the advertised price of a property beneath a written offer previously rejected by a seller, w
noticias.texto:
The Minns government has mothballed laws intended to protect homebuyers from underquoting after the premier said real estate agents in his Sydney electorate had raised concerns about their effect amid a housing market downturn.
Changes due to come into effect on Tuesday would have banned agents in New South Wales from lowering the advertised price of a property beneath a written offer previously rejected by a seller, with fines of up to $110,000 or three times an agent’s commission, whichever was greater.
But the laws and fines will be paused for up to a year after a last-minute intervention by the premier, Chris Minns, who flagged on Monday morning that concerns had been raised by agents in his south Sydney electorate of Kogarah.
“It has come across my desk from real estate agents in my electorate,” he told reporters, after he was asked about fears the laws could prevent sellers from advertising at a lower rate now that the market has fallen. Home values in Sydney have dropped by 10.1% from their 2026 peak, according to data from Cotality.
“I do think it’s [an] unforeseen [consequence], but it is something we’re going to have to deal with because it’s not the seller or the agent’s fault if the price of real estate is dropping, and the legislation at least intuitively believed that the prices would always rise,” said Minns.
The changes, which were passed in June, were modelled on laws already in effect in Victoria. Under additional transparency measures which came into effect in Victoria last month, sellers must reveal their reserve price at least one week before a sale, and agents must publish sale prices after a transaction is completed.
The decision is a potential embarrassment for NSW fair trading and corrections minister, Anoulack Chanthivong, who has previously been overruled by Minns on rental and prison reforms.
The minister faces a preselection battle in his seat of Macquarie Fields, but Minns would not say on Monday if he would intervene on Chanthivong’s behalf.
As recently as 1 November, Chanthivong had praised the laws as “important reforms to put the hammer down on underquoting and stop homebuyers being taken for a ride”.
On Monday afternoon, a spokesperson for the Minns government provided a statement from Chanthivong, who said the laws had been passed “at a different time and in a different economic and housing market”.
“We introduced these laws to crack down on underquoting, protect homebuyers from misleading practices and ensure a fair and transparent property market for buyers and sellers,” he said.
“People are already doing it tough, and the last thing we want is for laws designed to protect homebuyers to inadvertently make it harder for them to buy a home.
“That’s why the government has made the decision not to proceed with the implementation of these changes today.”
It is the latest of several reversals in recent weeks by the government, under pressure ahead of the March state election from One Nation and the Coalition, with the cost of living and pressures on small businesses among the key issues.
Last month, the government dropped parts of plastics legislation which would have required cafes to offer customers who dine in the option of mugs and glasses instead of takeaway cups.
Polling conducted internally by the Labor party has suggested that One Nation could win more than 20 seats in the lower house. The party was polling at 26% of the primary vote in NSW according to a Sydney Morning Herald Resolve poll in October, behind Labor on 30%, but ahead of the Coalition on 23%.
One Nation announced four more candidates on its six-person upper house ticket on Sunday, but has so far only announced one lower house candidate, NSW party leader Mike Newman.

noticias.titulo: MP Helen Haines’s first words since leaving hospital after alleged attack led to double amputation
noticias.resumen: Independent MP says she is ‘overwhelmed’ by thousands of warm wishes and thanks Australians for charity donations Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast The independent Australian MP Helen Haines has been discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked by a man outside her electorate office in Victoria resulting in the amputation of both her legs. In a statement, Haines said she had moved to the rehabilitation stage of her recovery, which would continue in Melbourne. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The independent Australian MP Helen Haines has been discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked by a man outside her electorate office in Victoria resulting in the amputation of both her legs.
In a statement, Haines said she had moved to the rehabilitation stage of her recovery, which would continue in Melbourne.
“This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred [hospital] and am receiving in this next stage,” Haines said.
“I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing.”
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said his thoughts were with Haines.
“We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation,” Albanese said in a statement.
Haines said she was “overwhelmed” by the many Australians who had donated to the Save the Children charity fundraiser.
Her husband, Phil Haines, had made the request to the public on her behalf to donate to the charity in lieu of flowers in the aftermath of the alleged attack.
As of Monday afternoon, more than $1.46m had been raised for the charity through Haines’s fundraising appeal.
“I am overwhelmed by the generosity of Australians in the form of donations to Save the Children and I look forward to working with them in due course on applying these funds to improve the lives of children.”
Haines, the federal member for the Victorian seat of Indi, had been in a critical but stable condition after she was repeatedly struck by a vehicle in Wangaratta on 19 October. Her condition was then downgraded to “serious but stable” on 24 October.
Police will allege the 65-year-old was standing by the boot of her car outside her electoral office when a car did a U-turn and struck her repeatedly.
Tarrawingee man Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged and the incident continues to be investigated. He is known to her family.
Police charged Nugent with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official.
Police have also charged him with two additional offences – cultivating and possessing cannabis – according to court documents.
The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, paid tribute to Haines in the Senate on Monday and on behalf of the parliament wished her strength through her challenging rehabilitation.
“It says a great deal about her character that even as she faces these challenges, in her statement she looks ahead to the work she wants to do to improve the lives of children following the donations to Save the Children that Australians made at her request. It is an example of her determination and her generosity that is so admired,” Wong said.
The leader of the opposition in the Senate, Michaelia Cash, added that Haines’s discharge from hospital was warmly welcomed across the parliament.
“She has demonstrated extraordinary courage and resilience. And on behalf, in particular, of my Coalition Senate colleagues, we wish Helen every strength during her continued recovery.”
Haines has been given leave of absence until 26 November, the last sitting day of the year.
MPs across parliament have expressed concern for their safety and that of their staff since the alleged attack, and prompted conversations about the temperature of political debate.
Albanese, during the last parliamentary sitting, warned against the rise in anger “that distorts and corrodes our public discourse”, and urged voters and politicians not to ignore it.
“Enabled by the anonymity and speed afforded by social media, we are seeing rage and aggression increasing, not just in politics, but towards workers in hospitality and retail, in schools and in hospitals, towards police, paramedics, and other officials, we are seeing a normalisation of the language of grievance and violence.”
The independent MP Allegra Spender said it was “wonderful” news that Haines was making good progress in her recovery.
“She is a remarkable person and her strength and positivity after everything that has happened inspires me.”

noticias.titulo: ‘It’s like the 16th-century version of doomscrolling’: the Book of Miracles may fetch £1m at auction
noticias.resumen: Exclusive: Public institutions get first chance to bid for rare ‘wonderbook’ of apocalyptic visions and extreme weather In one illustration, five suns blaze down on Leipzig in 1551. In another, blood rain falls on Rome in 1456. In a third scene, dated 1552, monstrous hailstones batter the Dutch city of Dordrecht during a storm so fierce people feared Judgment Day had come. Created during the mid-16th century, when earthquakes, storms, floods and other extreme weather events were often interpreted as ominous warnings from God, the Book of Miracles contains 167 paintings of apocalyptic visions,
noticias.texto:
In one illustration, five suns blaze down on Leipzig in 1551. In another, blood rain falls on Rome in 1456. In a third scene, dated 1552, monstrous hailstones batter the Dutch city of Dordrecht during a storm so fierce people feared Judgment Day had come.
Created during the mid-16th century, when earthquakes, storms, floods and other extreme weather events were often interpreted as ominous warnings from God, the Book of Miracles contains 167 paintings of apocalyptic visions, celestial wonders and meteorological phenomena.
It is the only known copy. To this day, no one is sure why it was created.
Now, public institutions will have their first chance to bid for the Book of Miracles since scholars learned it existed. It is expected to fetch between £700,000 and £1m when it is auctioned in London on 10 December, as the star lot of the Christie’s valuable books and manuscripts sale.
Members of the public will also have a rare opportunity to see it in person for six days before it goes under the hammer.
For nearly half a millennium, scholars were unaware of its existence. Found in the library of a small baroque castle in southern Germany nearly 20 years ago, the manuscript, which is from 1550s Augsburg, was put up for auction alongside the castle’s furniture, carpets and tankards in 2008 and sold for just over £100,000.
Shortly after the sale, the manuscript entered the private collection of Mickey Cartin, one of Connecticut’s biggest contemporary art collectors.
Eugenio Donadoni, Christie’s international specialist in medieval and Renaissance manuscripts, said the book was an “exceptionally rare” German wonderbook.
“German wonderbooks functioned as the sensationalist mass media of their day,” he said. “They were used by Lutheran theologians such as Martin Luther and Philip Melanchthon to further their Protestant eschatology, but crucially – with all the depictions of comets, cosmological events, natural disasters, all verified by witnesses, with exact dates and geographic coordinates – they laid early foundations for empirical observation and reporting. They mark a shift from medieval to Enlightenment.”
He expects the sale will attract collectors of both historic and modern art because some of the scenes, which are painted in watercolour and gouache, are “super surrealist … almost Dalí-esque”.
“If it weren’t for the little captions, which are obviously 16th-century German, some of them look so vividly modern … it’s really jaw-dropping,” Donadoni said.
The scenes depicted include a plague of locusts arriving in Poland on a “terrible wind” in 1527 and the North Sea flooding the coast of Frisia – in what is now the Netherlands and Germany – in 1230.
Other pictures are of fiery comets and eclipses, while scholars think an illustration of “wondrous dragons” flying across the sky over Bavaria in 1533 depicts the northern lights.
Underneath each scene, a German picture caption describes what is happening and where and when the event took place.
“All of these events are portentous,” said Donadoni. “The artists of the Book of Miracles, relying on contemporary broadsheets, chronicles and histories, have condensed into pictorial form the concerns of an age that was gripped by an anxiety – and learned curiosity – about the future.”
The book records how uneasy people felt about climatic anomalies at a time of doctrinal disunity, when there was growing interest in documenting and cataloguing visible, tangible scientific phenomena, he said.
“It’s really fascinating … it is a window into how Europeans were dealing with the impending end of the world, political uncertainty and extreme – and strange – weather events.”
The five suns over Leipzig, for example, is thought to depict the optical illusion of a parhelion, more commonly known as a sun dog. “You see in the sky various different rings of light and it looks like suns,” Donadoni said.
“Blood rain” occurs when high concentrations of red-coloured dust particles, usually from the Sahara, mix with water droplets in rain clouds. “Many of these things have actual rational scientific explanations to them,” Donadoni said.
He said he imagined that leafing through the pages of the book in the 1550s was similar to bingeing on bad news on social media today: “I think it could be a little like the 16th-century version of doomscrolling.”
In this way, the book straddles a momentous turning point in history. “We’re right at that period where the superstition of the middle ages turns into the age of scientific discovery,” Donadoni said.
Till-Holger Borchert, the director of the Suermondt Ludwig Museum in Aachen, has studied the manuscript and said the first time he saw it, his reaction was: “Wow”. “It’s one of a kind,” he said. “It grabs you by your heart or your soul or your belly.”
He said he thought £1m was a “very conservative estimate” of its value. “It [the final price] could possibly be much more,” he said.
A facsimile of the manuscript was published in 2013 that got people “really excited” about it, Borchert added, and since then the Book of Miracles has become “a kind of icon for people who are interested in apocalyptic things”. It would be wrong to value it merely as an historical document: “It’s more than that. It speaks to us, to our generation.”

noticias.titulo: Andy Burnham to say Brexit ‘has not worked’ and he will sign new deal with EU
noticias.resumen: Prime minister is to meet European leaders at summit this week and secure agreements that ‘could raise GDP by 0.4%’ Andy Burnham will say on Monday that Brexit “has not worked” and that he will sign a new deal with the EU. It is the latest in a string of comments by the prime minister criticising Brexit, after he told the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday that the UK has “lost more than we gained” through leaving the EU. Is consistent with the Labour manifesto and the government’s red lines. It improves the Brexit deal and brings it closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.
noticias.texto:
Andy Burnham will say on Monday that Brexit “has not worked” and that he will sign a new deal with the EU.
It is the latest in a string of comments by the prime minister criticising Brexit, after he told the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday that the UK has “lost more than we gained” through leaving the EU.
Burnham is due to meet European leaders at a summit this week and secure agreements that he says could raise GDP by 0.4% – about £17bn – including on food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.
Speaking at the lord mayor’s banquet in the City of London, Burnham is expected to argue that Boris Johnson’s promise to take back control was not delivered, and that the country was left with a needlessly hard Brexit that created barriers for businesses and damaged its economic potential.
“It’s like the Emperor’s New Clothes – where no one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on,” Burnham will say. “The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained.”
Burnham is to say he will sign an agreement with the EU, so long as it:
- Is consistent with the Labour manifesto and the government’s red lines.
- It improves the Brexit deal and brings it closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.
- And it passes the so-called “Makerfield test” by delivering real, tangible improvements in people’s everyday lives.
“This is a win-win,” Burnham is expected to say. “It illustrates our new approach. Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges – but being constructive and positive, showing that we can come together to confront shared challenges.”
However, the EU relations minister, Hamish Falconer, told the BBC on Sunday that the UK could have a “voice in the room” under a new deal with the bloc, but no vote on EU food policies.
He added there could well be an “exit clause” in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment, explaining that the EU was “worried” about the possibility of a future Reform or Conservative government undoing the agreement.
The exit clause, previously nicknamed the “Farage clause”, is designed to guard against any the cost of potentially reversing any reset on Friday should the UK’s political landscape change.
The cost of infrastructure at the borders has largely been paid for by private companies, including Eurotunnel, but French staff the food checks there, at Calais port and at Boulogne-sur-Mer, where all fish checks take place.
Meanwhile, Johnson, the former Conservative prime minister who resigned over Partygate in 2022, has said Britain would “absolutely” vote for Brexit again if Burnham forced another vote on the issue.
He told the Telegraph: “It is madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority. He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won’t win – because the reality is that people are not fools.”

noticias.titulo: Monday briefing: The many stages of the UK-EU relationship – and what’s next
noticias.resumen: In today’s newsletter: From situationship to a possible makeup, a look at the evolving relationship, and the bloc’s big feelings about the future Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated UK-EU summit this Friday, Andy Burnham is expected to make the reset of our relationship with Europe the pivotal theme of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet in London tonight.
