A project first conceived some 55 years ago has faced repeated delays because of lawsuits, environmental protection studies and onerous planning and permit procedures.
The bridge across the Angerbachtal (Angerbach Valley) should improve the road connection between the North Rhine-Westphalia state capital of Düsseldorf, the Bergisches Land mountain range and the industrial cities in the Ruhr Valley. It's also meant to help remove some strain from the perenially busy A3 highway and to improve the road connections to Düsseldorf International Airport.
The last stretch of highway is expected to cost around €200 million (roughly $220 million), or roughly the annual costs incurred each year by forcing traffic to divert around it, according to estimates from Düsseldorf's IHK industry and trade association.
Construction is expected to take several years, no formal end date has yet been set.
Merz heads to Munich for CSU meeting
Chancellor Friedrich Merz heads to Munich early on Monday, for a meeting with the leadership of the Bavarian Christian Social Democrats (CSU), the sister party to his conservative Christian Democrats(CDU).
No concrete details about the talks were made public ahead of time, except for the CSU saying it would serve as a general exchange that had been planned for some time.
The trip comes a week after Merz nominated Ilse Aigner as the next German president, likely paving the way for her to become the first woman and first CSU politician to assume the role.
It also follows soon after the 2027 federal budget cleared a marathon meeting of the parliamentary budget committee in Berlin. This serves as one of the more conspicuous examples of the frictions and difficulties in the grand coalition between the Christian Democrats and the center-left Social Democrats — with the compromises it contains a point of frustration among the CSU and for state premier Markus Söder.
Manuela Schwesig set for vote on new term as regional leader
The northeastern state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will likely vote in Social Democrat (SPD) Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier early in the afternoon.
The 52-year-old, who first stepped into the role in 2017, plans to lead a new coalition of the SPD, the environmentalist Greens and the socialist Left Party after state elections in September.
The right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) emerged as the largest single party in the sparsely populated state.
But still, the political calculus that emerged was arguably simpler than in Berlin — where the socialist Left Party is the largest party but could struggle to lead a coaltion — and in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD was by far the largest party but short of an outright majority.
Schwesig's SPD claimed 29 seats, with the Greens and the Left each taking 5, meaning that when combined, they hold a fairly clear majority over the AfD with its 32 seats.
The SPD's relatively successful performance in the state, at least compared to its national struggles, has also led to Schwesig being linked with a possible return to federal politics. The SPD plans to elect a new leadership duo early next year.
Schwesig has already had a spell in Berlin as the federal minsiter for families, pensioners and women, and briefly led the SPD on an interim basis in 2017, but after this she returned to her home state to seek the top regional job instead.
Welcome
Servus! Welcome to another Monday of news and analysis of matters making waves in German politics and society.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz is starting his week in Munich, at a meeting of the Bavarian CSU sister party to his conservative Christian Democrats (CDU).
This comes a few days after Merz naming CSU politician Ilse Aigner as candidate to be the next president, and days after the budget committee signed off on the federal government's spending plans for 2027. Merz is expected to appear with state premier Markus Söder in a joint press conference later.
Far to the north, in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Social Democrat Manuela Schwesig should be voted in for another term as state premier in the regional parliament later in the day. Schwesig emerged in pole position after state elections a few weeks ago; some suspect her regional success could translate into national ambitions within the struggling party.
And in the west, regional leaders are headed to a road to nowhere — literally, but also hopefully not for very much longer now.
The vast highway A44 bridge over the valley between Helsinghausen and Ratingen-Ost has been planned for decades, and was completed in 2022, but work to actually connect it to the road network will only start today.
Stay with us for more on these stories and whatever else develops around Germany on November 16.

noticias.titulo: Can a 'coalition of the willing' create momentum for a fossil fuel phaseout?
noticias.resumen: In April, about 60 countries held an unprecedented meeting in Colombia to work out a plan to slowly quit oil, coal and gas. How influential is this coalition at the COP31 climate summit?
noticias.texto:
Can a 'coalition of the willing' speed up a fossil fuel phaseout?
November 16, 2026
This time last year, as negotiations at the UN COP climate summit in Brazil entered crunch time, there was hope that governments would agree on a clear roadmap for phasing out oil, gas and coal. More than 80 countries backed the idea.
But instead, after opposition from oil-producing states such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, the conference wrapped up with a watered-down final agreement that did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.
As a compromise, summit host Brazil offered to produce a "voluntary" roadmap. At the same time, a group of 57 countries frustrated with the deadlock at the consensus-based UN talks decided to form a "coalition of the willing" to accelerate the fossil fuel exit outside the COP framework.
They held their own summit in April in Santa Marta, Colombia — the first such conference to specifically focus on implementing the transition away from fossil fuels (referred to as TAFF).
What happened in Santa Marta?
Co-hosted by Colombia and the Netherlands, the Santa Marta conference brought together countries including Canada, Norway, Brazil, Nigeria, Mexico, Australia and Germany, as well as highly climate-vulnerable states such as Vanuatu.
The idea was for governments to start developing national roadmaps and working out how to restructure their financial and trade systems to wean themselves off polluting energy sources — an incredibly complicated undertaking, particularly for developing countries dependent on revenue from fossil fuel exports.
Part of their discussions focused on cutting subsidies for oil, coal and gas, as well as supporting people whose livelihoods rely on the fossil fuel industry to find new forms of income.
What role will the 'coalition of the willing' play at COP?
A little over six months on from the Santa Marta meeting, representatives from almost 200 countries are holding talks in Antalya, Turkey, as part of the latest UN climate conference.
Countries agreed for the first time in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels — the main driver behind rising global temperatures. But summits since then have failed to pin down how to implement that pledge.
It's not yet clear whether the Santa Marta coalition will influence ambition at this year's COP.
"I think it's more of a long-term game," said Chetna Hareesh Kumar, a climate policy analyst at the Berlin-based research organization NewClimate Institute.
She says it's too soon to expect the coalition to have an influence on the negotiations but adds that that could change at future COPs. The grouping could bring more nations on board if, for example, it shows it can be truly inclusive, address the needs of different types of countries and show that a transition is feasible.
One role the group is playing, according to Alexandra Scott, a senior climate diplomacy adviser at Italian climate change think tank ECCO, is "keeping up the political momentum," and showing "that there is this huge group of countries who really want to accelerate this transition away from fossil fuels."
She says it's also building an invaluable "cadre of knowledge" on how to develop national TAFF plans and deal with barriers individual countries face — like how to secure funding for the infrastructure investments needed for the energy transition.
The Santa Marta group is "really answering a lot of the questions that countries have always had on how on earth do we even start to transition our whole economy off fossil fuels?" Scott said.
This expertise being shared and tested in practice can show what such a transformation could look like and the knowledge brought into COP, added Scott.
Few countries have announced national TAFF plans
Since the Santa Marta conference, Germany, France and the Netherlands have released national plans to phase out fossil fuels. While the plans contain no new commitments, experts see them as a positive first step.
Kumar says more countries could announce similar plans just ahead of the second TAFF summit in Tuvalu next year. Finland presented its TAFF roadmap in the first week of COP, but analysts do not expect many more countries to follow suit soon.
Another potential boost that could get momentum going is Brazil's recently published global roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, promised at last year's COP.
The nearly 200-page document seeks to serve as a toolkit for countries shifting from fossil fuels to renewable energy, such as wind and solar. It envisages countries making a phased transition between 2028 and 2033.
The aim, Ana Toni, CEO of last year's COP, told AP, is to break down the transition into "smaller actionable solutions" and help countries make practical progress.
The roadmap suggests measures tailored to each country's circumstances, including dependence on fossil fuel and financial capacities. "Levers" it proposes include reducing fossil fuel subsidies, expanding renewable energy and cutting methane emissions.
Kumar called it a "customizable" approach that allows every country to take action, regardless of its situation. "The question really is now what countries do with it and how much momentum they can generate," she added.
Focus on electrification
This year's climate change summit in Turkey — taking place after a series of deadly heat waves in Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people — isn't expected to result in any big announcements about fossil fuels.
Global renewable energy capacity has surged in recent years, making up a third of the world's power generation for the first time in 2025. But many countries still rely on coal, oil and gas.
A database compiled by the German environmental organization Urgewald shows that most oil and gas companies worldwide, among them QatarEnergy, Saudi Aramco and Russia's Gazprom, are exploring or developing new reserves.
Meanwhile, subsidies for fossil fuels amount to around $920 billion (around €830 billion) per year, according to data from the OECD, but that number is falling.
One issue Turkey is pushing at the COP conference is electrification. It's calling on countries to endorse the goal of 35% of final energy consumption coming from electricity by 2035 — up from around 20% today.
The pledge has drawn criticism from some circles, though, for leaving open whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources.
Ideally, Kumar said, electrification would be powered by renewables and tied to a goal of phasing out polluting fossil fuels.
"If something like that could make it to the final text, that would be a really good sign for momentum."

noticias.titulo: AI in German classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'
noticias.resumen: The research points in one direction: If students aren't careful about how they use AI-enabled tools, then academic performance can plummet. It's a huge challenge for teachers.
noticias.texto:
AI in the classroom: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'
November 16, 2026
Jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium. He and his classmates have already been using artificial intelligence-enabled tools, or AI, for the last two and a half years.
"I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW. Jakob isn't his real name, because he doesn't want to publicly admit he and many others of his age use AI to do their homework.
Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.
'Cognitive outsourcing'
In science, this is called "cognitive outsourcing." Basically, the required thinking is shifted to another device, whether that's a calculator, notepad or a large language model (LLM) like ChatGPT.
There's a difference with AI, though. A notepad or calculator can take over a step or two but rarely the whole thought process. That's not the same for an LLM, which can handle the entire problem-solving process.
Jakob admitted he's also had an AI help him with his homework. "But only when I was really stuck," he insisted. And he's also aware that it can become a problem when AI does all your homework. "The students who get good grades tend not to do that," he explained.
Franziska Müller has been a German teacher for several decades and is currently teaching senior classes at a gymnasium. Her name has also been changed for privacy reasons.
"They can't even think for themselves anymore," she told DW, complaining about some of her classes.
Even in ordinary classes, some of the students type their questions into their tablets or phones, asking for AI assistance. And should they be called upon in class, she knows that they're reading out the answers that the AI has prepared for them and hoping nobody notices.
Müller believes students these days are less able to comprehend text. "Because they read less and let AI summarize almost everything for them," she said.
Lower scores, thanks to AI
Several studies have reached very similar conclusions.
That includes the latest PISA (Program for International Student Assessment) study from September. PISA, which is run by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, regularly evaluates the abilities of 15-year-old students around the world.
"Students who report using AI chatbots get lower scores in science, on average, than those who don't use AI," Andreas Schleicher, the OECD director for education and skills, wrote in his report in October. "This includes using AI to summarize texts they had to read, conduct preliminary research on a new topic, or draft texts for writing assignments."
With participants from more than 90 countries, PISA is considered the largest international comparative study of 15-year-olds worldwide. This year, German 15-year-olds posted their lowest PISA scores in the 25-year history of the study.
"The connections are complex and depend heavily on how generative AI is used, but the central insight is simple: Just as we don't get fit by watching sports but by doing sports ourselves, learning doesn't come from consuming content, but from the mind's productive cognitive engagement with new material," Schleicher explained.
Put simply, those who don't exercise their brains risk becoming less intelligent.
How to deal with AI in class?
US think tank, the Brookings Institution, has already argued that the risks of using AI in education outweigh the benefits.
Its own research, which included young participants from around the world, speaks of students losing "fundamental cognitive and durable skills as they increasingly rely on AI to perform learning's intellectual work," as well as the decline of critical thinking, memory, perseverance and independent judgment.
But what can be done against the power of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and Meta AI?
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has banned the use of AI in public schools up to the eighth grade for the 2026 and 2027 school years — so that's up to about the age of 14 or 15.
Not everyone agrees this is the right thing to do. Julian Hinn, who teaches German to students aged between 15 and 18 in Germany, said class members can still use AI apps on their mobile phones. "And anyone who thinks they won't use it at home is ignoring reality," Hinn told DW.
Germany's annual JIM study, which tracks teenagers' media use and device ownership, supports that view.
Ninety-one percent of young people surveyed in Germany, between the ages of 12 and 19, stated that they use at least one AI application. The study also reports that 74% use AI for homework and learning.
The last JIM study actually dates back to 2024 so those percentages might be even higher now. Data on AI use in Asia, Latin America and the US from the Brookings study show similarly high figures.
German politicians have recognized the problem. Although education in Germany is the responsibility of the individual federal states, the so-called Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, or KMK, has been issuing statements on the use of AI since 2024.
The KMK's statements have been rather vague though, saying only that students should be enabled to engage with AI in a critical, reflective and responsible manner.
Students should question AI, too
Teachers and students alike are aware that AI can be a powerful support in the classroom.
"The AIs simply explain things much better than textbooks," said Jakob, adding that he'll often get an AI to explain basic concepts to him.
Sometimes teachers can't respond like an AI, Hinn conceded. "The AI can respond much better to the language and needs of the students."
That's why he thinks it's important to include AI in classes, starting from the 10th grade when students are around 15 or 16. Hinn doesn't think it should be introduced before that, when children's basic skills are still being developed.
In more senior classes, Hinn will encourage his students to question the AI critically. "We look at the quality of the solutions," he explained.
German teacher Müller has also integrated some use of AI into her lessons for older students. But in some aspects of the class, she also bans it altogether so that her students can focus on thinking for themselves.
"I understand very well that it's tempting to use AI," she said.
There are also other problems with AI in education. According to the Brookings study, students with basic skills can use AI to deepen their learning and progress faster.
But for children with gaps in their knowledge, they tend to adopt AI's errors, outsource their thinking and then fall even further behind. In this way, AI can exacerbate preexisting inequalities.
The PISA study notes that children from more affluent backgrounds often have a better start, and AI can widen that gap.
This is called the Matthew effect — the name comes from the biblical verse Matthew 25:29, "for unto everyone that hath shall be given." It basically means that early success in learning leads to better progress in the future, while early struggles equal a growing lag over time.
In the age of AI, teachers have become more motivated to challenge students to think independently and to consider their own personal autonomy.
Hinn, who also supervises the school newspaper, said: "I always tell everyone, you can use AI but the feeling of having written an article with your own pen is spectacular."
Both teachers also stress the idea of personal autonomy and responsibility. They believe this affects the students, especially because when they sit exams, they aren't allowed to use any aids or AI. And if they aren't able to solve their own problems, they will fail.
It's during exam time that the students really find out if they can solve those math, English or science problems by themselves.
Müller said one of her students recently confessed they were upset after a poor exam result. "He felt he simply couldn't think for himself anymore because of AI," she said.
This article was originally written in German.

noticias.titulo: Mozambique's justice under scrutiny as Venancio Mondlane faces trial
noticias.resumen: The trial of opposition politician Venancio Mondlane begins in Mozambique on Tuesday. The former presidential candidate is facing five charges, including incitement to terrorism.
noticias.texto:
Mozambique's justice under scrutiny as Venancio Mondlane faces trial
November 16, 2026
The trial of Venancio Mondlane will shape the political future of Mozambique, and influence how much trust citizens place in state institutions.
From November 17, the country will be watching the opposition politician and former presidential candidate as he faces five counts, including publicly advocating crimes and inciting collective disobedience and terrorism after the October 2024 elections.
If convicted, he could be sentenced to more than 20 years in jail.
'Nothing to do with violence'
Mondlane has denied all the charges, and said he never called for violence. In fact, he said, his public statements were meant to prevent violence.
"I have more than enough evidence that numerous statements I made went in exactly the opposite direction," he told DW during a Septembervisit to the European Parliament in Strasbourg. "I have more than sufficient evidence that numerous statements I made were in exactly the opposite direction."
The post-election protests had two main goals: To pressure authorities to investigate extrajudicial killings of members of Mondlane's political movement, and to find out the truth about election results.
"These were the fundamental issues of our entire protest," he said. "This has absolutely nothing to do with violence."
Where does criminal incitement begin?
In the October 2024 presidential and parliamentary elections, Mondlane ran as a presidential candidate with the support of the left-wing opposition party Podemos. Afterwards, he did not recognize the official election results.
The election saw Daniel Chapo of the Frelimo party declared winner. Frelimo has governed Mozambique since independence in 1975.
After the elections were called, Mondlane and his supporters protested. For months, there were demonstrations, strikes and road blockades as well as violent clashes with security forces nationwide. According to reports from civil society groups, more than 400 people died. Shops and public facilities were looted or destroyed.
The public prosecutor's office has alleged a connection between Mondlane's public calls to action and the violence. The indictment is based on his live broadcasts on social media, in which he called for protests, strikes and civil disobedience.
Albino Forquilha, who heads Podemos and is Mondlane's former political ally, is expected to testify at the trial. However, he told DW that he would not appear as a witness for the prosecution.
Forquilha said he would report his own observations of the protests and would only testify to what he personally experienced. He cannot predict whether his statements will benefit Mondlane or the state.
Prosecution overstating some aspects, says critic
Baltazar Fael, a prominent Mozambican lawyer, argues that the prosecution's case is problematic.
Speaking with DW, he warned against equating indictment with conviction. "What we currently have is an indictment by the public prosecutor," he argued. "And this does not mean that the accused has already been convicted."
The court will hear arguments from both sides and must decide whether what happened constitutes a criminal offense. Predicting the outcome is difficult.
Fael is particularly critical about the charge of incitement to terrorism. For this charge to be valid, a plausible connection between Mondlane's statements and specific acts must be proven. Acts of violence that occurred following his calls to action will not be enough to convict him on this charge, Fael said.
The question is whether Mondlane actually intended to incite terrorist acts. "What power did Venancio Mondlane actually have to incite people to commit all these crimes?" Fael asked, adding that, after reading the indictment, he believes the prosecution is overstating some aspects of its case.
Is the case politically motivated?
There are also questions as to whether the trial might be politically motivated in some way. For years, Mozambique's justice system has been criticized because of potential political interference.
Fael said several factors have raised doubts. "The timing of the trial and the circumstances that led to it — namely, a challenge to the election results — are clearly political in nature," he said.
Additionally, the speed at which the trial was prepared might also give the impression that there's some political pressure at work here, he added.
Adelino Muchanga, chief justice of Mozambique, has emphasized that his court will decide the case based on facts. But observers are still asking how independent the judiciary can be when the defendant is one of the most prominent critics of Mozambique's political leadership.
The Supreme Court's decision not to allow a live broadcast of the trial has drawn further criticism. Mondlane's defense requested a live broadcast but was denied by the court, which reasoned that such a broadcast could endanger the safety of those involved, influence or intimidate witnesses and disrupt proper conduct of the trial.
Critics see this refusal as a setback for transparency, especially since another recent, prominent trial, the so-called "hidden debt scandal" where state-owned companies secretly borrowed billions from international banks, got extensive media coverage.
Social unrest remains
Additionally, the causes of the protests that sparked this trial have not disappeared. DW's interviews with citizens in the northern Mozambican city of Nampula make this clear.
"The people still want the same thing," one resident told DW. "They wanted Venancio to become president."
Another Nampula resident pointed out that "the population protested against hunger and the lack of jobs for young people. And that's legitimate."
Still, some in Nampula just want to see closure, preferring to have peace and an end to the demonstrations. Even if the economic situation could be better, the country has to return to normality at some stage, they argued.
Additional reporting by Amos Fernando and Conceicao Matende in Maputo.
This article was originally written in German.

noticias.titulo: India news: Modi heads to ASEAN meet in Manila
noticias.resumen: Modi is also likely to attend the Quad leaders' summit involving the US, Japan and Australia on the sidelines of the ASEAN meeting. Meanwhile, the Sabarimala temple has opened for an annual pilgrimage. DW has more.
noticias.texto:
India news: Modi heads to ASEAN meet in Manila
Published November 16, 2026last updated November 16, 2026
What you need to know
- The three main issues on ASEAN's agenda include maritime security, economic cooperation and development partnership
- A building collapse in Delhi's Paharganj area has left eight people injured
Here is a roundup of headlines from India on Monday (November 16):
Thank you for reading
That is all for today. We will be back tomorrow with more news from India.
Stay tuned!
Bilkis Bano case: Supreme Court grants bail to two convicts
The Supreme Court of India suspended the life sentences and granted bail to two of the 11 convicts in the a 2002 gang rape and murder case on Monday.
The top court noted that the two convicts have already spent more than 17 years in jail and one of them is severely handicapped, Indian legal news outlet Live Law reported.
The two-judge bench passed the order against the Bombay High Court's May order, upholding their conviction and sentence.
Bipin Chandra Joshi and Pradeep Mordhiya are among the 11 convicts whose remission the Supreme Court quashed in 2024.
The Bilkis Bano case dates back to 2002, when the state of Gujarat was hit by communal riots during which some 2,000 people were killed — of whom most were Muslims, according to Human Rights Watch.
Bano was five months pregnant when she was gang-raped during the riots while her three-year-old daughter and six other family members were killed.
Devotees celebrate Chhath amid toxic froth in Yamuna river
Sabarimala temple in Kerala opens for annual pilgrimage
The Sabarimala temple in the southern state of Kerala will open at 5 p.m. local time on Monday ahead of the annual Mandala pilgrimage season, which begins on November 17.
The temple attracts millions of devotees during the two-month-long pilgrimage, which starts in November.
While the pilgrimage season, which marks the first day of the Malayalam calendar, begins on Tuesday, the temple doors will open to pilgrims on Monday evening.
Reportedly, cameras equipped with AI features have been installed as part of security and to improve crowd management.
In 2011, Sabarimala saw a stampede which killed more than 100 people. More than 30 million pilgrims had visited the temple during that year's pilgrimage season.
Delhi building collapse leaves eight injured
At least eight people were injured after part of an under-construction hotel collapsed in Old Delhi’s Paharganj area on Sunday, police said.
This is the second such incident in less than 10 days. Earlier this month, a building collapse in Old Delhi's Chawri Bazar claimed seven lives.
According to authorities, a call was received around 4:40 pm on Sunday, claiming that a house had collapsed in Paharganj.
When a team of firemen reached the spot, they found a two-storey structure collapsed in a narrow lane, Indian newspaper The Indian Express reported.
"A total of eight people sustained injuries and were shifted to Lady Hardinge Medical College and Hospital for treatment," Indian news channel NDTV reported, citing a senior police official.
Indian PM Modi to attend ASEAN summit in Manila today
Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to leave for Manila, in the Philippines, to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)-India summit and the 21st East Asia Summit.
The ASEAN meeting will focus on three main issues: maritime security, economic cooperation and development partnership.
According to the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), the Prime Minister will attend a dinner hosted by Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on November 16 before participating in the India-ASEAN Summit and the East Asia Summit process on November 17.
During his two-day visit to Manila, Modi is also likely to meet US President Donald Trump, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese as the leaders of the Quad group meet on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had indicated last month that the Quad meeting was planned alongside the wider meetings in the Philippines.
Announcing his visit to Manila, PM Modi said in a post on X, "Will be in Manila, Philippines later today and tomorrow to attend the following programmes: 23rd ASEAN-India Summit. 21st East Asia Summit."
Welcome to our coverage
Hello! This is Midhat from DW's New Delhi bureau, bringing you the latest news from across India.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is heading to the Philippines to attend the ASEAN summit, on the sidelines of which he will also attend a Quad leaders' summit.
In the Indian capital, a building collapse has left several people injured.
Meanwhile, in the south, the Sabarimala temple is opening for the annual Mandala pilgrimage season.
Stay tuned as we bring you more from India throughout the day!

noticias.titulo: Mexican drug lord Felix Gallardo dies at 80
noticias.resumen: Felix Gallardo was considered to be the architect of Mexico's modern drug-trafficking trade. He died of multiple organ failure at the age of 80.
noticias.texto:
Mexico's notorious 'godfather' Felix Gallardo dies at 80
November 16, 2026
Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo — known as the "godfather" of Mexico's modern drug trade and a notorious trafficker himself — died in a hospital on Sunday. He was 80.
"After remaining under observation with a guarded prognosis, he died on November 15 at the medical facility" after "he suffered multiple organ failure," said a statement from the security ministry of the state of Jalisco, where he was being held.
An inmate's death
Having founded the Guadalajara cartel, one of Mexico's first major drug syndicate which would later birth the Sinaloa cartel, Gallardo had been imprisoned since 1989 and was transferred to a private hospital two days ago.
He was arrested and sentenced to 40 years in prison on drug-trafficking and weapons charges tied to the cartel. While already behind bars, he faced a seperate prosecution for the kidnapping and murder of a US drug-enforcement agent. This earned him an addition 37-year prison sentence and his reputation as Mexico's most notorious trafficker.
Felix Gallardo had been an inmate in a maximum-security prison in western Jalisco state even after his lawyers repeatedly sought house arrest on the grounds of his deteriorating health.
The life of Felix Gallardo
Gallardo was born in 1946 in the Northwestern state of Sinaloa, which would later become synonymous with narco-trafficking.
He initially worked as a police officer and bodyguard for a local governer but soon transformed into a power criminal, known as the "boss of bosses."
Gallardo, along with others, set up the Guadalajara cartel becoming the first to move cocaine to the US on a massive scale. He was also the first to forge an alliance with Colombian drug cartels including Pablo Escobar's Medellin cartel.
In the 1970s, Gallardo rose to prominance as his narcotics empire expanded on the back of bribed law enforcers and the use of light aircrafts to move drugs across the continent.
His rise and fall as a Mexican drug lord was ortrayed on screen by Mexican actor Diego Luna in the 2018 Netflix hit series 'Narcos: Mexico.'
In his final years, Gallardo suffered poor health and was blind in one eye, practically deaf and unable to walk on his own. He maintained that he was innocent.

noticias.titulo: Rocket from Boeing-Lockheed firm fails mid-flight, destroys payload of Amazon satellites
noticias.resumen: A Vulcan rocket suffered an anomaly about 10 minutes after liftoff from Florida, failing to deliver 40 Amazon Leo satellites to orbit. It was the first total mission failure in the company's history.
noticias.texto:
Boeing-Lockheed rocket fails, 40 Amazon satellites lost
November 16, 2026
A Vulcan rocket operated by United Launch Alliance, a joint venture of Boeing and Lockheed Martin, failed about 10 minutes after liftoff from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Sunday. The incident resulted in the loss of all 40 AmazonLeo internet satellites aboard, marking the company's first mission failure.
"Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," ULA said in a statement.
The exact cause was not immediately clear.
"Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don't have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today," ULA added.
The failed launch marks a major setback for ULA's new flagship rocket. The two-decade-old company was set to begin a regular cadence of launches for Amazon's burgeoning satellite internet program.
Mission failure raises fresh concerns over US launch capacity
The failure is expected to trigger a lengthy technical investigation, potentially grounding the Vulcan rocket for months.
US companies could face reduced launch capacity amid other rocket failures, industry challenges and uncertainty over the future availability of SpaceX's Falcon 9, the world's most active rocket. SpaceX is no longer accepting bookings for the rocket.
"There is risk with any launch, and that's especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01," Amazon said in a statement, referring to Sunday's mission. "ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they'll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan."
Is ULA in trouble?
ULA was formed in 2006 through the merger of Boeing's Delta rocket program and Lockheed Martin's Atlas rocket program. The incident marked the first total mission failure in the company's history, ending its record of successful mission deliveries since its formation.
Sunday's launch was Vulcan's fifth since its debut in 2024 and its first in nine months. The gap followed separate technical investigations into its solid rocket boosters and core BE-4 engines, which are supplied by Blue Origin, the space company founded by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos.
The solid rocket boosters had come under scrutiny after anomalies on Vulcan's previous two flights, including a February 2026 mission for the US Space Force. Both missions successfully delivered their payloads into orbit despite the booster problems.
US national security clearance for Vulcan under scrutiny
The Space Force paused Vulcan's national security launches pending the outcome of an investigation and the implementation of corrective measures. Sunday's Amazon mission was expected to provide further data before the military decided whether to clear the rocket for those launches.
An investigation traced the problem to the engine's main oxygen valve. Blue Origin subsequently developed modifications for the BE-4 engines supplied to ULA, and the engines installed on Vulcan were retrofitted, ULA officials said.
It remains unclear whether the BE-4 engines played any role in Sunday's failure.
Nearly 400 satellites launched as Amazon challenges Starlink
Amazon relies on third-party launch providers to deploy satellites for its Leo internet network. Other launch providers have also faced technical problems and delays.
Blue Origin's New Glenn explosion in May occurred during a ground test, just days before the rocket was scheduled to launch Amazon Leo satellites.
Repeated launch setbacks have complicated Amazon's efforts to compete with SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet network, which has more than 11,000 satellites and millions of customers worldwide.
SpaceX's advantage over satellite internet rivals is partly due to its ability to use its own rockets to deploy satellites. Other companies rely on external launch providers, adding to the cost and complexity of building their constellations.
Before Sunday's failed mission, Amazon had launched 398 Leo satellites across 14 missions since 2025, according to Reuters. That represented about 12% of the 3,236 satellites the company needs for global coverage. Amazon had hoped to begin initial internet services this year.

noticias.titulo: Czechia: Thousands protest against public media reform
noticias.resumen: Hundreds of thousands of people gathered to protest against the government's plan to abolish broadcasting fees. Critics say the nationalist coalition would like to secure control over the media.
noticias.texto:
Czechia: Thousands protest against public media reform
November 15, 2026
A protest against plans to abolish broadcasting fees in Czechiadrew between 350,000 and 450,000 people in Prague, organizers said.
The amount of protesters resulted in overcrowded public transport, with many people traveling from other cities by bus and train.
According to protesters, the plan could bring public broadcasters under the control of the country's right-wing government under billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis.
The government would like public broadcasters to be financed by the state budget rather than through fees, arguing that while the plan will not affect editorial independence, broadcasters need to cut costs.
Critics accused the Czech government of wanting to secure more influence through the decision.
The suggested media reform would result in public media's budget being cut down by 15 percent.
Government denies takeover attempt
Babis himself defended the plan last week, saying that his government is not interested in controlling or nationalizing public media.
"None of what the people are protesting against… is true," Babi said.
Foreign Minister Petr Macinka also replied to the criticism by accusing the protest's organizers of turning demonstrations into a business model.
Since its introduction in April, the plan resulted in several large-scale protests, with Czech TV and radio going on a one-day strike in protest against it.
International groups have criticized the plan, including the European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists and Reporters Without Borders.
International criticism
The current coalition in Czechia is made of Babis's ANO party, the far-right SPD and the Eurosceptic Motorists.
While the protests also saw the current coalition being criticized, polls show ANO still enjoys some 30% of support.
Per the Reuters Institute Digital News Report for 2026, trust in the media in Czechia is low and stands between 30% and 33%, with public broadcasters still being considered "the most trusted brands."

noticias.titulo: Cape Verde election: Jose Maria Neves set to win second term
noticias.resumen: Nearly two-thirds of the voters in the West African nation voted to keep President Jose Maria Neves in office, according to provisional results.
noticias.texto:
Cape Verde election: Jose Maria Neves set to win second term
November 15, 2026
Cape Verde President Jose Maria Neves won re-election Sunday with 63.8% of the vote, according to provisional results from the country's electoral commission.
The 66-year-old Neves was seeking a second term as leader of the West African archipelago, which is known for its stable democracy.
His main challenger was 61-year-old Joana Rosa Amado, a former justice minister who secured around 31.6% of the vote.
Four other candidates also contested the election.
Some 420,000 people were eligible to vote in the west African archipelago, with the election being watched by about 150 observers from the Economic Community of West African States, the African Union and European Union.
Cape Verde among Africa's most democratic nations
Cape Verde is made of ten volcanic islands located in the Atlantic Ocean about 600 kilometers (375 miles) off the coast of Senegal.
The island nation is known for its democratic stability and good governance, and its economy has been showing strong growth. The Mo Ibrahim Foundation's 2026 index on global governance has the country in third place of Africa's 54 countries, with only Seychelles and Mauritius faring better.
According to the World Bank, Cape Verde is an upper-middle-income country due to its growing tourism industry.
The challenges it faces range from social inequality, the islands' geographic isolation and the lack of traveling options between islands.
The increased cost of living, energy prices and youth unemployment also play a role.

noticias.titulo: As millions lose food aid nationwide, this SNAP office is doubling up as a food pantry
noticias.resumen: The cuts and changes to SNAP have been difficult for government workers who take pride in helping others. In San Diego, workers said they couldn't sit back while their neighbors went hungry.
noticias.texto:
As millions lose food aid nationwide, this SNAP office is doubling up as a food pantry
SAN DIEGO, CALIF. — It should have been her day off. Instead, early Saturday morning, Rosa Rodarte was back at the social service office where she works, pushing carts of food and loading them into people's cars.
Rodarte's official job is to help people apply for programs like food assistance. But lately, she's been simply helping people get food.
"We have the same goal," she says. "We want to make sure everybody is being helped and not judged."
The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, better known as SNAP, has seen participation plummet over the past year. Some five million people nationwide have lost federal food benefits ever since the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill, a piece of sweeping tax and spending legislation that slashed SNAP funding, tightened eligibility, and prohibited food aid for most asylum seekers and refugees. It's considered the fastest decline in decades and far exceeding the federal government's own estimates of the impacts.
Not only has it been difficult for families facing food insecurity, but it's also taken a toll on the government workers who help administer SNAP. Over the past year, offices across the country have had to contend with new rules, heavier workloads and immense financial pressure to avoid errors. All the while, they've watched people lose food assistance en masse.
"The emotionally draining part is where you see someone that's telling you on the phone that they need your help and they need it today, and when you can't do something," says Nina Olivas, who oversees San Diego's Access Customer Service Call Center, where people inquire about assistance programs, such as SNAP or Medicaid.
There are 36,000 fewer people on San Diego County's SNAP program this September compared to July 2025, when Republicans' One Big Beautiful Bill was signed into law. In response, the county has been partnering with local food banks to hand out free groceries at their social service offices. It's not a long-term fix, but county officials say they couldn't sit back while their neighbors went hungry.
"We are not ending the call with nothing," Olivas says.
Inundated with paperwork
Olivas says she routinely reminds her staff of their impact: "There's not a lot of jobs that you can do where everyday you can come in and put food on someone's table."
Her office helps San Diego residents access government assistance. In a way, she says, they're frontline workers — sometimes meeting people at the lowest point of their life, such as losing a job or getting sick.
"You're helping someone put food on the table. You're helping someone pay rent. You're helping someone buy diapers," Olivas says. "Those are things that are just so rewarding when you're able to do it. But when you're not, or when you can't do it right now, that can be really difficult."
Among the challenges has been grappling with new work requirements imposed on homeless people, former foster youth, veterans, parents with a child older than 14 and able-bodied adults aged 55 to 64. Supporters of the policy change argue it's bringing back the dignity of work.
"For many, welfare is no longer a lifeline to self-sufficiency but a lifelong trap of dependency," U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins and other Trump officials wrote in a New York Times op-ed piece last year.
But for social service employees on the ground, these requirements have mostly meant more paperwork to process, on top of the wide swath of documents already required to receive food aid.
"Many of them already work," Olivas says of SNAP recipients. "So really what it is, is just that extra burden of having to really quantify how many hours they're working."
San Diego processed over 830,000 more documents between January and October, compared to the same time last year, according to the county. That accounts for mailed documents alone, which make up only about a third of all incoming paperwork.
What's happening in other states
Over the summer, the San Diego County Board of Supervisors chose to get ahead of the federal changes by securing $15.8 million to offset the loss in federal funding. They also approved the hiring of 122 new social service workers. These efforts helped keep call wait times relatively low and a majority of paperwork processed on time.
Other local and state governments are stepping up to fill the gaps. Illinois sent out a one-time $400 benefit for individuals who were kicked off SNAP. Similarly, Phoenix, Ariz. offered a similar $600 payment toward utility bills for those who lost federal food aid. Maine created a state-funded food assistance program for certain noncitizens.
Meanwhile, some states are showing just how severe the fallout from the federal policy changes can be. Texas' SNAP application backlog ballooned from 3,700 pending in January to 175,000 in September, according to a recent letter of concern penned by several members of Congress from Texas. Over 700,000 Texans have lost food aid since July 2025, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities.
During the same time frame, Arizona's SNAP rolls shrunk by nearly half — the steepest decline in the nation. State officials attributed the decline to a staffing shortage that left them ill-equipped to handle a surge in paperwork, member station KJZZ reported. They also pointed to the state's efforts to more closely scrutinize SNAP applications in order to reduce the its payment error rate and avoid federal penalties.
And in Louisiana, SNAP enrollment fell by 154,000 between July 2025 and this September, according to state data. Three-quarters of removals stemmed from procedural issues such as missing forms or missed interviews, according to an analysis by the think tank Invest in Louisiana.
"We have to do something"
The idea to hold food distribution events outside San Diego's social service offices came from a restless night.
Monica Montgomery Steppe, vice chair of the County Board of Supervisors, was shaken by how many people in the area were projected to lose food benefits. Having relied on the assistance when she was younger, this felt personal, she says.
"So one night, ideas just started coming to me, so I took my phone and just started writing them in a Google Doc," she says. "And I gave them to my staff and said, 'We have to do something.'"
The food distribution events began in August. Between then and September, nearly 70,000 pounds of food have been distributed to over 5,200 people in partnership with Feeding San Diego and the San Diego Food Bank, according to the county.
Earlier this month, the line started to form about 90 minutes before the event officially began. Among those waiting were young families, seniors and some wearing hats that read "veteran."
As social service workers guided people to the food line, they also fielded questions about the federal changes and addressed any issues that SNAP recipients may be experiencing with their food aid. Their goal: making sure no one is falling through the cracks.
Ambar Santiago was one of those people. She came needing help with groceries after her benefits didn't arrive that month. There was a hiccup in her case regarding her paperwork. After loading free vegetables, canned goods and diapers into her car, Santiago sat with a worker and explained her situation. The employee listened carefully, then offered Santiago a sense of relief.
"Let's look," the worker said. "We can do that."
Back home, Santiago prepared dinner with the very ingredients she received that day: tomato sauce, potatoes, onions. She whipped up her mother's carne guisada, a Puerto Rican beef stew that can stretch for days.
As she stirred, she told her husband that she felt grateful. Santiago had lived in different parts of the country and, not long ago, experienced homelessness. She knew getting help the way she did on Saturday wasn't the norm.
" I feel like the assistance that I would've gotten in the hood or in the Southeast or anywhere else is completely different from my ZIP code that I give them now," she says. "It's just a blessing."

noticias.titulo: Trump heads to Asia to meet with Xi and Putin amid Nvidia fallout
noticias.resumen: The trip to China marks Trump's second time this year, and comes as the president and his party faced widespread backlash from voters in the recent midterm elections.
noticias.texto:
Trump heads to Asia to meet with Xi and Putin amid Nvidia fallout
President Trump heads to Asia this week where he's set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin for a high-stakes trilateral summit.
The trip to China marks Trump's second visit this year, and comes as the president and his party face widespread backlash from voters in the recent midterm elections, potentially weakening his bargaining position across the Pacific.
The president and administration officials – including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick – are also under scrutiny after the recent resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believe was recruited by China's top spy agency, according to The New York Times. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.
Huang traveled to China with Trump earlier this year – this time, tech billionaire Elon Musk is joining Trump in Shenzhen.
The expectation for major deals or pronouncements coming out of the meetings this week are low – but the meeting is still expected to make waves over the imagery of the trilateral summit.
Before China, Trump will first travel to the Philippines where he'll meet with allies at the ASEAN summit in Manila.
The president is expected to be in the region for just about three days.
Trilateral meeting
For weeks the president has said he's keen to discuss the Iran war and denuclearization with Putin and Xi. But Edgard Kagan, the former ambassador to Malaysia and a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said it's a topic that Xi likely won't want to get into. The White House confirmed Friday that Trump is expected to meet with Xi and Putin together.
"The Chinese strongly disagree with the idea that they should be involved in any kind of trilateral discussions with the United States and Russia on nuclear weapons," Kagan said.
"China wants to avoid this because they don't want to be locked into a subservient position. And they also don't want to create a precedent. I think the main thing for the Chinese is they know if they do a meeting and nuclear issues are discussed, it becomes much harder for them to refuse to do it in the future," he said.
A White House official said they do not expect any agreement to come out of the meeting on denuclearization.
"We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement," the official said, calling the trilateral an "entry point" for the three countries to talk about reducing nuclear weapons stock.
Another U.S. official not authorized to speak on the record acknowledged that denuclearization is a "difficult" topic for China.
"But we do think it's time for China to sort of step up to the adult table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things," the official said.
Putin, for his part, stands to benefit from a meeting with Trump and Xi, as Russia's war with Ukraine nears its five-year mark. Trump has made friendlier moves toward Russia in recent months, siding with Putin and striking a deal to release more Russian oil into the market ahead of the midterm elections.
Trump said last month that he was fine with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy not being present at a potential meeting with Putin about the war.
"Anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not," Trump said.
A White House official said Ukraine is not intended to come up in the meeting with Xi and Putin. And there is no plan for Putin and Trump to have a separate meeting.
Kagan said the meeting with Xi, Trump and Putin could end up being on the shorter side if there isn't much all parties are willing to discuss. But at the same time, "I could see this going longer because President Trump likes dealing with Putin and Xi. He sees them as his peers. He sees them as important world leaders," Kagan said.
Either way, a photo of the three leaders meeting together is enough to make headlines.
"That picture alone is going to be worth well over a thousand words," Kagan said.
Busan Agreement
This is the second time Trump and Xi are meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit – but this year's meeting is notably different from last year's in Busan, South Korea, when tensions between the US and China were fraught amid the escalating trade war.
The meeting in Busan established a sort-of truce between the two countries. The U.S. immediately lowered some tariffs on Chinese goods and China agreed to loosen exports on rare earths. But the execution of the agreement has been spotty.
"There's friction in this truce. It's not smooth, but it's basically functional," Kurt Tong, Managing Partner at The Asia Group, said.
A White House official said the U.S. isn't getting rare earths from China at the pace or level they'd like.
"We really want to focus minds among our counterparts in China on compliance with this," they said.
Still, Tong expects the agreement to be renewed past its January expiration. The two sides will likely agree to the renewal either in Shenzhen or later this year at the G20 summit Trump is hosting in Miami, according to Tong.
Meetings in Manila
Before the president arrives in China, he's holding meetings with several allies in Manila, including a meeting with the other leaders of the Quad nations: India, Japan and Australia.
"I think it's quite significant symbolically and politically that the U.S., Australia, Japan and India, the major democracies of Asia and the Pacific, get together… it's especially significant that they're doing it just before the meetings in China," Tong said.
The White House said Trump will also sign a trade deal with Thailand while in the Philippines.
The opportunity in Manila for Trump is to repair and reinforce relationships with countries like Japan and India, and the host country the Philippines. The ASEAN summit is also the region's first look at the president since his party lost control of Congress and on a global stage, a chance to see what the last two years of Trump's presidency may look like.
"I think the real thing that people will be looking at first is, how does he present himself?" Kagan said. "How does his behaviour towards Modi and towards India change? Those are things people will be looking at very, very closely for clues for what the next two years are likely to be like."
Nvidia fallout
A White House official said they don't expect Trump to raise the issue of Huang's affair and resignation with Xi. The focus of the meeting is about trade, the official said.
Huang resigned last week after admitting the extramarital affair with Alice Huang. Trump administration officials are now facing scrutiny and questions about how much they knew about Huang's affair and how much Huang had access to Trump and his orbit.
"I think the main impact is here in the United States, where there are calls for accountability with respect to Mr. Huang's activities with the U.S. government and questions about what happened… the net result of that is to provide a tailwind to persons who are interested in tightening up the technology denial regime toward China," Tong said.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick agreed last week to appear in front of the Senate Banking Committee to answer further questions. Trump, for his part, has continued to defend Huang and called him an honorable person.

noticias.titulo: These birds fly 17,000 miles every year. Climate change could make it harder
noticias.resumen: Migratory birds cross the entire globe, carefully timing their journeys with the seasons. In a hotter climate, that timing is increasingly out of sync.
noticias.texto:
These birds fly 17,000 miles every year. Climate change could make it harder
Pectoral sandpipers are ultra-marathoners. They fly more than 17,000 miles a year, crossing entire continents on their migration from Alaska to Argentina and back again. They don't soar or coast on the wind – they flap the entire way. And these elite athletes are only the size of a robin, weighing around three ounces.
The sandpipers are among more than 12 million shorebirds that migrate to Alaska every year to breed, spending the short summer season in open lands near water. For years, scientists have been trying to understand how these unassuming birds accomplish such monumental journeys from places like New Zealand, Asia, South America.
"Shorebirds are not these little brown birds on the beach, but they're miraculous migrants that travel these huge distances by these crazy adaptations," says Rick Lanctot, a wildlife biologist with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.
For 24 years, Lanctot and other researchers have tracked the return of shorebirds to northern Alaska. The data shows a concerning trend. Overall, almost half of the 41 shorebird species that breed in Alaska are declining. Some have lost more than half of their population over the last 30 years.
Migration, like any kind of travel, requires careful timing. Birds orchestrate their journeys to take advantage of the seasons, arriving when food is ample and the weather is ideal. But for many species, their itineraries are going increasingly awry. Habitats they count on, such as wetlands and grasslands, are disappearing. In a hotter climate, spring is arriving earlier, which affects when their food is available. It's like making a pit stop on a road trip and finding all the restaurants are closed.
The question is whether long-distance migrators, which already push the limits of survival, can adapt to a rapidly warming world.
"Shorebirds truly are sentinels about what is happening to the planet, because they're touching down in so many of the places across that planet," says Nathan Senner, who studies shorebirds at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. "If we can't listen to what they're telling us about the unpredictability of what we're currently doing to the planet, then we're not going to be able to respond to a lot of changes."
Tiny trackers
Lanctot gently holds a brown and white pectoral sandpiper in his hands as field technician Braden Meyer attaches what looks like a tiny backpack. This tracking tag will log the bird's locations as it flies thousands of miles.
Nearby, male pectoral sandpipers call out, searching for females and attempting to ward off other males. Some have already found places to nest, spread out among the low-lying plants of the Arctic tundra. The sun is still well above the horizon at midnight, since summer days last for 24 hours in Utqiaġvik, the northernmost city in the U.S., formerly known as Barrow.
The female Lanctot holds recently arrived from Argentina, after a pit stop in the Central U.S. to eat. Flying here used all her energy reserves.
Loading...
"When we catch birds when they first show up, they're really skinny," Lanctot says. "You can feel the keel or the breastbone really prominently. They have hardly any fat on them."
His team secures the backpack tracking tag with stretchy loops around the bird's legs. It will collect her GPS position every 15 minutes, storing the data until the bird flies by any cell tower on her journey, where it's uploaded. Lanctot's team also uses tiny tags that attach to a bird's leg like an anklet, which weigh about as much as a grain of rice and were originally designed for butterflies.
Tracking technology has revealed that shorebirds undertake far more arduous journeys than once thought. While scientists have studied the migrations of larger animals for decades, tracking tags have only become light and compact enough for small birds in the last 15 years. Since then, new migratory records have been broken.
One bird, a bar-tailed godwit, flew more than 8,000 miles for 11 days straight without stopping from Alaska to Australia. Researchers are still figuring out how these birds navigate an entire ocean. They also seem to take advantage of weather patterns, waiting for the optimal winds.
"That's why I still haven't retired, frankly," Lanctot says. "Because there's always a new tag or something coming out that lets you learn things you couldn't learn otherwise."
Disappearing shorebirds
To fly thousands of miles, shorebirds must drastically reshape their body. Some double their body weight to store enough fat to fuel them on the journey. Some internal organs, like the digestive system, even shrink before takeoff, since they're not needed during a nonstop flight.
It's why the roughly six weeks pectoral sandpipers spend in the Arctic are crucial. The birds must eat enough to build their fat reserves for the next migration, while laying eggs and raising chicks. Those chicks only have about a month after hatching to eat and grow large enough to join that migration.
The numbers of shorebirds, like pectoral sandpipers, migrating to the Arctic have been declining over the last few decades. It's noticeable around Utqiaġvik, including within the community that's lived with them for centuries.
"Birds have always been very special to the Inupiat people," Robin Mongoyak says, walking on the coastline where the Chukchi Sea meets the Beaufort Sea. "They give us something to always look forward to after a long, cold winter. The Inupiat people have always thought of it as a quvianaq time – a very wonderful time when the birds start flocking in."
Mongoyak is a wildlife guide who grew up in Utqiaġvik. He says each bird species has a different cultural meaning, telling a story of the world around them. That environment is shifting rapidly. Mongoyak remembers when sea ice lasted multiple years. Now, he says that's becoming rare and the ice is breaking up earlier in the spring. Temperatures in the Arctic have risen four times faster than the rest of the globe.
"The climate is getting warmer," Mongoyak says. "I don't see as many birds as I used to like seeing. It's really changed a lot in the last 35 years, at least."
Birds out of sync
To understand the decline in Arctic birds, researchers are studying how warmer temperatures affect their food – insects.
"Whenever there's a sunny day, there's going to be clouds of non-biting midges," says Julia Berliner, a graduate student at the University of Texas at Austin, looking across the tundra. She holds up a bug vacuum, a modified leaf vacuum from the hardware store, that sucks insects into a net to collect a sample.
These small flying insects only emerge briefly during the short Arctic summer. Normally, the ground is frozen solid, but as the weather warms up, the top few inches of permafrost thaws, and flies and spiders emerge for their short life cycles.
Loading...
"Insects and spiders are really tied to the weather," says Amanda Koltz, an assistant professor of integrative biology at the University of Texas at Austin. "So it could be that one week, there aren't any prey flying around, and then next week, there might be tons of flies flying around. And so that really changes the menu from week to week."
Shorebirds time their trip to this buffet of bugs, ideally hatching their chicks when the insect population peaks. But when spring arrives earlier with warming temperatures, the insects also emerge earlier. That puts the shorebirds out of sync with insects, which means the birds could miss their peak food supply, what's known as mismatch.
Missing the peak food supply seems to have the biggest impact on shorebird chicks. Research shows that when chicks hatch late, fewer of them survive. Koltz says because different insects emerge at different times, what the birds can eat also matters.
"We need to know how much food they have available, but also what's the quality of that food?" she says. "If they eat a spider and beetle, the spider and the beetle have different nutrients in them, just the same as if you ate a pepper or a banana versus a potato chip."
Koltz and Berliner are sampling insects to measure crucial nutrients like calcium, which birds need to produce eggs. If insect populations shift their timing, it could also shift the nutritional menu, another way climate change could impact Arctic bird populations.
Shifting migrations
Researchers are trying to figure out whether migratory birds have the ability to adapt to a warming Arctic. When spring arrives early, some shorebirds can speed up their nesting and lay eggs slightly earlier than normal, but not enough to keep up with the changes.
Birds that migrate long distances can also shift the timing of their migrations by a few days, but scientists are still studying how birds make those decisions, whether they use environmental cues or learned behaviors. Some cues may not help them adapt. They may be relying on signs in environments thousands of miles away from the Arctic, or in some cases, on signals that don't change, like when days get longer in the spring.
Habitat loss, largely from development, is also driving the decline of many shorebirds, particularly the wetlands and grasslands they use as rest stops along their journey. Drought is also affecting these places and is only intensifying with climate change.
Many migratory birds in the U.S. use agricultural fields and ponds instead, which may be useful habitat for only short periods of time. In a handful of places, conservation efforts are underway to boost that habitat, such as paying farmers in California to keep their rice fields flooded for longer periods so birds can use them while migrating.
"Shorebirds are actually frequently quite well-adapted to finding where patches of habitat are, but our current environmental state is that we've really messed with the predictability of a lot of landscapes," Senner says. "That's what starts to make it really difficult for some of these species."
Senner says if shorebirds keep declining, extinction is a possibility for many species. Now, the race is on to understand how much these birds can adapt to a changing world.
"We need to figure out: what are those tactics and then can we manage environments to maximize the likelihood that those tactics will be successful?" Senner says. "Because no one species can be ready for all of the types of changes that could possibly come their way."
Reporting for this story was supported by a Braided River Overlooked and Untold Alaska Journalism Grant.

noticias.titulo: NPR's Student Podcast Challenge is back for 2027
noticias.resumen: The annual audio competition for grades four through 12 returns in January. Now in its ninth year, the contest has involved more than 90,000 students around the country.
noticias.texto:
NPR's Student Podcast Challenge is back for 2027
Students and teachers, it's time to turn on your microphones and start recording – in January, the NPR Student Podcast Challenge returns for its ninth year.
Since its launch in 2018, our annual audio storytelling competition for students in grades four through 12 has introduced more than 90,000 students to the world of podcasting.
During that time we've heard from students, teachers, parents and educators around the country about how they've enjoyed participating – and how much they've learned along the way.
"I can't tell you how many of my students come back to tell me this project was the most meaningful thing they did while in middle school," says Laura Frisbie, an advanced learning teacher at Minnetonka Middle School West, in Excelsior, Minn. "What a powerful way for students to use their voices in an authentic way and share a message that is important to them."
For teachers coming to the competition for the first time, maybe looking to shake things up in your classroom and try something new, we've got tons of resources available to help you get started. And for our returning educators, there's plenty there to draw on to help your students get better.
How it will work
The 2027 competition will open Jan. 4, to students in grades four through 12. You'll have until May 30 to submit. Grand prize winners will be announced after summer break in September.
Getting started?
Check out these resources!
Our NPR education team will listen to every single one (more than 22,000 podcasts so far!) and narrow them down to a list of finalists and honorable mentions.
From those entries, our judges will select the grand-prize winners: one for grades five through eight, and another in grades nine through 12. Since 2024, we've also opened our contest to fourth-graders, and we choose winners and honorable mentions from that category as well.
"The Student Podcast Challenge gives kids an opportunity to shine and tell their own stories," says Ameya Desai, a middle school student in San Jose, Calif., who was our first-ever two-time winner. "Every kid should podcast about something they feel strongly about, something that's personal to them, something they have ties to."
Over the years, we've found that the best podcasts are the ones where students bring a particular passion for the story they want to tell.
For example, here are some of our favorite entries from last year:
These fifth graders in Hewlett, N.Y., for the celebration of the USA's 250th birthday, asked each other: "What do you really know about our country?"
An Iowa middle schooler told the story of her grandfather's dementia, and her struggle to understand how the disease took him from her.
A group of high school students explored a scientific mystery linked to a gas leak in their town of Glasford, Ill. And a student in Los Altos, Calif., told the story of how a football coach's courage and dedication defied the odds and changed the lives of students.
Resources
To learn more about making a podcast, you can start by reading the rest of this announcement post, and check out our student podcasting resources page. And subscribe to our newsletter for updates from the contest team.
It's worth noting that several of our finalists and past winners (including this year's middle school and high school grand prize winners) were first-time podcasters, so you can do it too!
And here are two important rules to keep in mind:
- Podcasts must be between three and eight minutes. We're pretty strict about this so make sure your story falls within that range.
- Because of legal considerations, we have specific rules about what music you can, and can't, use in your podcast.
A special note here: Parents and educators, step away from the microphone! Please, no podcasts produced or edited by adults. The entries should be original work by students (see FAQ section below). Each year, we've had to disqualify some entries for clearly breaking this rule.
And, students, please keep it clean! No offensive language will be allowed.
As noted above, students do need to work with a teacher, educator or family member — who is 18 years or older — to fill out the submission form to enter the contest.
Other important stuff
Our judges will select a middle school and high school grand prize winner. The grand prize includes a certificate, a trophy and a visit from the NPR education team. The team will interview the winner and their teacher for a story to appear on an NPR program, such as Morning Edition or All Things Considered.
In previous years, many podcasts created by our other finalists and honorable mention recipients, including some of our fourth graders, have aired on various NPR programs and podcasts. They've also received additional recognition from their schools or school districts, and many winners have been interviewed by local media.
In other words, it's a great opportunity to share your story and get a lot of people to listen to it.
Some "Sound Advice" from the contest team
Before you hit the record button, check out our podcasting resources. We have a starting out guide for student podcasters and a curriculum guide for educators.
In them, we cover everything from how to tell a good story, how to sound like yourself on mic to how to use music in your podcast, among other topics. Even, and we're serious about this: how making a pillow fort can make you sound better!
There are other good resources out there too: Check out this audio storytelling toolkit and recording tutorial from PBS News Student Reporting Labs. Or The Student Podcast Playbook, a four-week podcasting curriculum created by our friends at The Bell.
You can find more tips and tricks on The Students' Podcast, which our team created to help you make a good podcast. We also encourage you to get a feel for what we're looking for by listening to last year's high school winner and middle school winner, and previous years' winning entries.
Quick FAQ
Here are a few questions we get over and over again each year. For any other questions, don't hesitate to reach out to us at studentpodcastchallenge@npr.org.
What's an appropriate way teachers and adults can be involved?
All eligible contest entries must be written, recorded and produced by students. We welcome teachers and educators to incorporate podcasting into their class curriculum and walk students through the basics of audio recording and editing. And as a part of this process, we understand that students may be getting feedback from the adults involved. Bottom line, we ask the adults to provide coaching and guidance, but to make sure that the podcasts submitted are original work by the students.
And, of course, that goes for the use of AI in your podcasts as well! Here's NPR's policy on the use of artificial intelligence for our journalists. While students these days may be using AI tools in gathering information or conducting research, we've added a box on our application asking you to acknowledge that you didn't use AI in the writing or performance of your podcast.
Am I allowed to use this song or sound effect in my podcast?
Here's an excerpt from our rules page that discusses music and copyrighted audio:
"Pre-recorded music may not be used. Entrants may include live performances of public domain songs or non-copyrightable rhythm elements if it is relevant to the story. For avoidance of doubt, for the purposes of these Official Rules, "public domain" does not mean "publicly available"; it means that copyright has expired and the material is no longer under copyright protection. We encourage Entrants to err on the side of excluding music if the Entrant is not sure whether the music is copyrighted or not."
You can use your own audio, interviews, field recordings or natural sound, music or sound effects you recorded for the podcast. We advise not using audio if the student isn't sure about copyright.
On our entry form, we ask you to confirm that any music in your podcast is either copyright free, or self-produced.
Can I submit more than one podcast?
Yes! You can submit as many entries as you'd like. Just make sure that each of your podcast entries are (1) between three and eight minutes in length and (2) don't use copyrighted audio. We wouldn't want any of your work to be disqualified.
And we really do listen to every single entry. So whether it's you and your friend's podcast, a class assignment or a passion project you're finally putting together, we're excited to hear from you and listen to whatever you got for us.
And, as we said above, for more tips, advice and the latest updates on this year's contest, make sure to sign up for our newsletter. Students, we can't wait to hear your stories. Good luck!

noticias.titulo: Why sleep matters when it comes to weight gain and loss
noticias.resumen: Sleep can have a powerful impact on weight. Research shows it can affect appetite. There is also a two-way relationship between sleep quality and diet.
noticias.texto:
Why sleep matters when it comes to weight gain and loss
If you want to maintain a healthy weight, you probably know you should watch what you eat and get some exercise, maybe hit the gym. But what about hitting the hay?
There is a lot of evidence linking lack of sleep to overeating and an increased body weight. But does that mean that getting more sleep could also boost efforts to lose weight?
"That's a good question," says Seth Creasy, an associate professor of medicine at the University of Colorado Anschutz who studies the interplay between weight management and lifestyle behaviors like sleep, diet and physical activity. "It's actually still an active area of research."
