Creasy says the best evidence so far comes from a randomized clinical trial involving 80 overweight adults who were chronically short on sleep. Researchers randomly assigned half of them to get counseling on how to extend their snooze time.
"They got them to sleep a little over an hour more per night," Creasy says. "And they saw that, without intervening on food, these people started to eat less by about 270 calories per day. So once they were getting adequate sleep, they ate less."
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Other research has found associations between better sleep and weight loss. For example, one study found that people enrolled in a year-long weight loss intervention program who had good sleep health lost more weight and more fat mass compared to poor sleepers.
The poor sleepers in that study were also much more likely to report having trouble sticking to their diet and exercise goals, says Christopher Kline, the study's lead author and an associate professor of health and human development at the University of Pittsburgh.
And good sleep health doesn't just mean how long you sleep, Kline says. He says that factors like sleep timing, regularity and satisfaction also play a role.
"A good analogy I like to make is if you get your eight hours of sleep, but those eight hours are between 4 a.m. and noon, that might not be as healthy as someone who regularly obtains their sleep between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.," says Kline, whose research focuses on how physical activity, sleep and cardiometabolic risks are related.
The links between sleep loss and weight gain
Researchers say right now, the evidence that more sleep can boost weight loss efforts is still scant, but the science is much more consistent when it comes to linking insufficient sleep to weight gain.
When researchers restrict people's sleep, they eat more — by an average of around 300 calories a day if you look across studies, says Creasy, who recently published a review of the research on sleep and weight management.
Most of those studies required participants to severely curtail their sleep, usually to around four or five hours a night. That's much less than the seven to nine hours of sleep that adults are supposed to get.
But Creasy worked on a recent study that found even milder sleep loss can result in weight gain. In that study, people who were assigned to sleep just 90 minutes less than usual gained an average of one pound over six weeks. While that may not sound like much, "over time, it adds up," says Marie-Pierre St-Onge, the study's senior author and a sleep and nutrition scientist at Columbia University.
Imaging studies from St-Onge and other researchers have found that, when we're short on sleep, activity ramps up in areas of the brain involved in pleasure and reward. In other words, it becomes harder to make good food choices.
"Our brain is less able to inhibit our desires for those sweet and salty foods" — especially later in the day, Kline says. The result is we end up overeating when short on sleep.
Kline says he experienced this phenomenon first-hand when he was still a doctoral student working the overnight shift in a sleep study lab. Once a week, every week, one of his fellow lab workers would bring in glazed donuts from Krispy Kreme.
"I can tell you there was no chance I was going to end a shift without having at least one or two of those donuts. And I don't even really like glazed donuts," Kline says ruefully.
Skimping on sleep can also disrupt our circadian rhythms and impair our sensitivity to insulin, which may promote fat storage and make it easier to gain weight.
Creasy says early studies suggested poor sleep also affects hormones that regulate appetite, but newer research hasn't always borne that out. "Some studies have shown an effect on them and some have not. So it's just been inconsistent," he says.
Better sleep through food?
St-Onge says the relationship between sleep and food goes both ways. "As we find that how we sleep influences our food intake, we also find that what we eat during the day also influences our sleep at night," she says.
Research from her team and others has linked eating added sugars and saturated fat to more sleep disturbances and less deep slumber. Meanwhile, fruits, vegetables and fiber were associated with better sleep and fewer awakenings at night, she says.
If you want to eat better to sleep better, St-Onge says you can start with small, easy changes. "As a first step, cut out foods that are higher in added sugars and sweetened beverages," she says.
Switching to whole grains instead of refined carbohydrates is also a good idea. Her research has linked added sugars and refined carbs to a greater risk of insomnia.
And she says look for opportunities to eat more fruits and vegetables throughout the day.
"I always put a ton of leafy vegetables in my dishes, like stews and soups and stir fries," St-Onge says.
And of course, don't forget good sleep hygiene, says Philip Cheng, a sleep and circadian rhythms researcher and professor of medicine at Henry Ford Health in Michigan. That means things like keeping your bedroom cool and dark, and sticking to a regular schedule for going to bed and waking up as best as you can.
"That's going to stabilize your sleep in the long run," Cheng says.
But if your poor sleep lasts months or even years, he says it's time to see a medical provider for help.

noticias.titulo: Flight disruptions expected to last into Monday
noticias.resumen: Congress recently gave the Department of Transportation $12.5 billion to upgrade the aging air traffic control system. President Trump wants more.
noticias.texto:
Flight disruptions expected to last into Monday
Thousands of travelers are still waiting on airlines to reschedule cancelled flights after Friday's nationwide ground stop.
More than 2,300 flights have been cancelled and more than 8,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. are delayed as of Sunday evening, according to FlightAware.com. Airports in Dallas-Fort Worth and Atlanta were experiencing the largest number of delays, with more than 250 flights each.
U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that "by the end of today, end of tomorrow, I think we will be back to normal."
"What happens when you have a ground stop like what happened on Friday is we have airplanes and air crews that are out of position," Duffy said during an interview with NBC's Meet The Press. "It takes some time for the airlines to re-choreograph all of their crews and aircraft."
Duffy on Saturday blamed faulty maintenance by L3Harris Technologies Inc., a federal contractor, for the nationwide ground stop.
L3Harris was working on replacing two sections of old copper wire with new fiber-optic cables, Duffy said. At some point, the FAA's legacy equipment became overloaded and disrupted communications.
"The initial investigation indicates that two potential locations as the reason for the excessive data flooding the systems: a radar site in Amarillo, Texas and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas."
L3Harris on Saturday said it takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on the nation "seriously."
"With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3 Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system," the company said in a statement. "We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel."
President Trump on Sunday called on Congress to approve more funding for air traffic control to update its aging systems.
"We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs. Congress must approve," Trump said in a post on social media.
In 2025, under Trump, Congress approved $12.5 billion for air traffic control safety system upgrades. But on Friday, Duffy and the White House requested $50 billion in emergency funding.
"We have to make investments into a network that has been neglected for decades," Duffy said on the Sunday news program. "We need to put money into it to make sure that it's still resilient for the future."
But two Democrats, Rep. André Carson of Indiana and Rep. Rick Larsen of Washington state, members of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, said billions have been appropriated but only a portion has been spent.
"Congress approved $12.5 billion for the Department of Transportation to make necessary safety upgrades to our air traffic control system," Larsen and Carson said in a statement on Saturday. "Fifteen months later, the administration's obligated $4.3 billion but only spent $1 billion, leaving $8 billion unobligated and $11 billion unspent. Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money?"
Nick Daniels, president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, told NPR on Sunday that he encourages every effort to understand what led to Friday's ground stop, and ensure that policies, practices and mitigation plans were followed.
But the ultimate credit goes to the air traffic controllers, he said.
"It's one of those moments that nobody can be prepared for, nobody can plan for," Daniels told NPR. But it shows what air traffic controllers can do when an entire national airspace system is shut down while working on unreliable equipment, he said.

noticias.titulo: EU ministers demand united response as Russian attacks spill beyond Ukraine
noticias.resumen: Romania, Estonia and Sweden have called for a united European response to mounting Russian threats, from drone attacks in the Black Sea to suspected sabotage, as the EU weighs its role in future Ukraine peace talks.
noticias.texto:
Romania, Estonia and Sweden have called for a united European response to mounting Russian threats, from drone attacks in the Black Sea to suspected sabotage, as the EU weighs its role in future Ukraine peace talks.
The foreign ministers of Romania, Estonia and Sweden have called for a strong, united European response to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, now approaching its fifth anniversary, as Moscow’s hostile activities increasingly spill over into European territory.
Romanian Foreign Minister Dan Neculăescu said he would seek closer coordination between NATO and the European Union over the “unacceptable” escalation of hostilities off Romania’s Black Sea coast.
“We have had four alerts in 24 hours, and we have had three ships hit over the weekend. This is unacceptable,” he said on his way into Monday’s meeting, which would formally touch on support for Ukraine and the evolving situation in the Middle East as well as the increasingly dangerous situation in the Black Sea.
“I’m going to ask our colleagues and our fellow ministers to continue contributing with capabilities in Romania,” Neculăescu said.
Drones struck three vessels on Sunday near Romania’s Sulina Canal, a key shipping route linking the Danube to the Black Sea and used by Ukraine to export goods. No injuries were reported, and crews extinguished fires that broke out on board, Romanian Defence Minister Stefan Radu Oprea said on Sunday.
Neculăescu said he would also brief his counterparts on the Black Sea Maritime Security Hub, which is being fast-tracked for development by 2027. The hub is intended to identify maritime threats, including drones and attacks on undersea cables.
The ministerial is also expected to continue conversations occurring over last week regarding the substance of what the European envoy at Russia-Ukraine ceasefire negotiations would argue for, and what their mandate could be.
Representatives from five countries – the UK, France, Germany, Italy and Poland – alongside officials from the European Council and NATO, will speak on Europe’s behalf in any future talks, leaders agreed following an informal meeting in Dublin on Friday.
Estonia’s Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna wrote on social media platform X that the recent attempted sabotage incident against Threod Systems, attributed by Estonia’s security authorities to Russia’s GRU intelligence services, “is yet another reminder that Russia’s hostile activities extend far beyond Ukraine”.
“Estonia is preparing to close its road border crossings with Russia in response,” he added. “Hostile actions must have consequences.”
Mounting a European response to hybrid warfare should follow the same priciples applied to the European envoy, Tsahkna said.
“Nearly five years on, Putin is still making the demands he made in 2021, seeking to dictate Europe’s security arrangements. We cannot allow him to gain through peace negotiations what he has failed to achieve on the battlefield," he said.
Sweden’s Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard told Euronews that these increased hybrid warfare incidents reflect the Kremlin’s frustration that they are “not winning in Ukraine”.
“They've been trying for almost five years to invade Ukraine now. They have failed,” she said, adding that what is needed now is for Europe to be “united” and for its citizens to be resilient.
“Sweden has spent a lot more money on civil defence to make sure that people are prepared and aware,” Stenergard added.

noticias.titulo: Millions of red crabs begin annual migration on Australia’s Christmas Island
noticias.resumen: Millions of red crabs have begun their annual journey from Christmas Island’s forests to the coast, crossing roads and specially built bridges to reach the sea and breed.
noticias.texto:
Tens of millions of red crabs have begun their annual migration on Australia's Christmas Island, turning roads and specially built crossings into streams of red on 14 and 15 November 2026.
Following heavy wet-season rains, the crabs are making their way from the island's forests to the coast to breed. Images show large numbers crossing roads, climbing overpasses and following barriers designed to guide them safely along their route. Road closure signs have also been installed to protect the migrating animals.
According to Parks Australia, which oversees the event, preparations begin months in advance. Workers clear underpasses, build special bridges and install kilometres of roadside barriers to keep the crabs away from traffic.
The migration is closely linked to both rainfall and the lunar cycle, with the animals timing their journey to release their eggs into the ocean before dawn, as the high tide recedes during the moon's last quarter.
This mass movement takes place every year, as millions of crabs travel from the forests to the shoreline.

noticias.titulo: French actor Gerard Depardieu drops appeal for sexual assault conviction
noticias.resumen: Depardieu, who has acted in more than 200 films and television series, is the highest-profile figure caught up in France's response to the #MeToo movement.
noticias.texto:
Depardieu, who has acted in more than 200 films and television series, is the highest-profile figure caught up in France's response to the #MeToo movement.
French actor Gerard Depardieu formally dropped his appeal on Monday against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women during the filming of a movie in 2021.
A court last year handed the 77-year-old an 18-month suspended sentence and ordered him to register as a sex offender, marking a spectacular fall from grace for an actor who dominated French cinema for half a century.
Depardieu, who has acted in more than 200 films and television series, is the highest-profile figure caught up in France's response to the #MeToo movement.
The trial related to charges of sexual assault during the filming in 2021 of "Les Volets Verts" ("The Green Shutters") by director Jean Becker.
Depardieu's withdrawal was lodged at the start of the appeal trial on Monday, bringing it to an end and rendering the original judgement final.
"Justice has spoken. I was found guilty. I hear it and I accept this conviction," Depardieu said in a statement sent to the AFP news agency shortly before the hearing began.
At the start of the hearing, the prosecutor and the civil parties also withdrew their appeals.
"For a long time on film sets, I hid behind provocation and ribald humour," Depardieu said, acknowledging that his remarks and "some of my gestures" were not "without consequences."
He offered his "deep and sincere apologies" to those who "may have suffered as a result."
The actor said he had never intended to hurt the women he encountered, but added that he had "come to understand that intention changes nothing about the harm caused."
"Court proceedings damage us," added the actor.
The plaintiffs were a set dresser and an assistant director. Depardieu has denied the allegations.
In another case, a French investigating judge in 2025 ordered Depardieu to stand trial on charges of raping actor Charlotte Arnould in 2018.
He has denied those charges and is appealing.

noticias.titulo: EU clears UniCredit takeover of Germany's Commerzbank
noticias.resumen: The EU has approved UniCredit’s takeover of Germany’s Commerzbank, a cross-border deal aimed at strengthening Europe’s banking sector.
noticias.texto:
The EU has approved UniCredit’s takeover of Germany’s Commerzbank, a cross-border deal aimed at strengthening Europe’s banking sector.
The EU on Monday approved Italian bank UniCredit's takeover of Germany's Commerzbank as Europe seeks to reinforce the bloc's banking sector.
With the acquisition of Commerzbank, UniCredit plans to cement its status as a European heavyweight, a goal shared by the European Union.
The EU believes better integration of the bloc's banking sector will help it keep up with US lenders and boost its competitiveness.
"Europe needs stronger banks that can compete, grow and support our businesses and families," EU competition chief Teresa Ribera said in a statement.
"Cross-border mergers can help make this happen, allowing banks to operate more efficiently and better withstand economic shocks," she said.
The European Commission, the EU's powerful competition regulator, approved the acquisition after determining the deal would not raise competition concerns.
"Our approval of UniCredit's acquisition of Commerzbank shows that it is possible to support a stronger European banking sector while safeguarding competition and choice," Ribera said.
The EU this year announced plans to overhaul the rulebook on company mergers as Brussels seeks to forge what it calls "European champions".
The European Central Bank had already approved UniCredit's hostile takeover.
The bank has pursued Commerzbank for the past two years, raising alarm in Germany where the bank is a key financing source for small and midsize industrial companies.
Despite fierce resistance from Berlin and the German lender, UniCredit had built up a stake of nearly 50% in Commerzbank.

noticias.titulo: Fewer students are traveling from abroad to study at US universities, new report shows
noticias.resumen: US campuses saw a 9% decrease in international enrolment this autumn compared to last year, according to a survey from the Institute of International Education.
noticias.texto:
US campuses saw a 9% decrease in international enrolment this autumn compared to last year, according to a survey from the Institute of International Education.
Fewer international students are studying at US universities as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration and reshapes higher education, data released on Monday shows.
Overall, US campuses saw a 9% decrease in international enrolment this autumn compared to last year, according to a survey from the Institute of International Education.
And the number of new students entering the United States for the first time fell by 15%.
“No one aspires to send their kids to get educated in the US,” said Veena Dubal, general counsel for the American Association of University Professors, whose father travelled from India to attend Tuskegee University, then the Tuskegee Institute, in the late 1960s on a student visa.
"It feels like an unsafe place. That’s the message that the Trump administration has been sending to families all over the world and they’re listening.”
Last year, the enrolment decreases were partially offset by large numbers of students who stayed in the US for temporary work after graduating.
But after months of speculation, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposed requiring schools to pay a $70,000 (€63,583) fee for every student who participates in the optional practice training programme.
Although the rule hasn't been finalised, participation in the programme, known as OPT, dropped 6% this fall, according the survey.
International students facing political headwinds
The proposed rule, which is expected to face legal challenges, is part of wider DHS efforts that include terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, along with detaining and deporting many of them.
And this summer, the administration finalised a rule that will prevent international students from staying in the US for more than four years without approval from the federal government, although a judge has temporarily blocked it.
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said the changes were intended to crack down on loopholes that international students were exploiting by extending their studies.
Although the US remains the top destination for international students globally, the changes are having an effect, college leaders told the IIE.
Among more than 800 US colleges and universities surveyed, 88% blamed the visa application process and 70% blamed travel restrictions for the enrolment drops.
And if OPT options are limited, 95% of schools predicted that international students would likely look to another country, according to the survey, which offers an early look at trends before full data is released next year.
Politics aren't the only reason students are looking elsewhere, said Mirka Martel, head of research, evaluation and learning for the institute. Its survey found more global competition for international students and the rising cost of a US degree also contributed.
Fanta Aw, the executive director and CEO of NAFSA, an association that represents international education, said students also are worried about research funding.
Last year, the Trump administration began dismantling the federal grant-giving process and attempting to exert more political influence over which projects get funded.
“They’re saying to themselves, ‘Too much uncertainty in the United States. It’s too difficult, and you know, more importantly, we have many more choices today than we did 10 years ago. Why subject ourselves to this?’” Aw said, noting that students are going to places like China.
NAFSA, in partnership with the international education technology company JB International, found that amid the enrolment decline, international students’ contributions to the US economy dropped by $2.4 billion (€2.1 billion) this autumn.
Colleges see budgets squeezed
US colleges and universities heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue. So the drops have punched big holes in tuition revenue at some schools.
At Cleveland State University, international enrolment has dropped by 46% in two years, from 1,542 in fall 2025 to 828 this fall.
And fewer than 50 new international students started this year, said Provost Nigamanth Sridhar, who estimated that the budgetary impact ranges from $2-4 million (€1-3 million).
Decades ago, he arrived in the US on an F1 student visa and participated in OPT. Eventually, he went through the process to became a naturalised citizen.
“I am here in this position, in this job, because I had the opportunity to come to the United States as an international graduate student and then decided to stay here and build a career," said Sridhar, who is from India. "So international education is personal to me."
The biggest drops were at the graduate level. This autumn's data shows a 15% drop in international graduate enrolment, compared to a 3% decrease at the undergraduate level.
The report also found declines in international students from India, which sends more students to the US to study than any other country.

noticias.titulo: Italy fines Meta €805m for accessing Facebook Android photos and videos without consent
noticias.resumen: The social media company has 60 days to disable the ‘Get tips from your gallery while browsing Facebook’ feature and introduce explicit consent.
noticias.texto:
The social media company has 60 days to disable the ‘Get tips from your gallery while browsing Facebook’ feature and introduce explicit consent.
Italy has fined Meta €805 million for using photos and videos from Android users’ galleries on Facebook without specific consent or adequate disclosure.
The Italian Data Protection Authority said the feature, called “Get tips from gallery when browsing Facebook”, violated the European privacy directive known as the ePrivacy directive.
The directive protects smartphones as part of a person’s private sphere and requires “free and informed consent” for such access, the authority said.
Investigators found that the feature was enabled by default and that Facebook requested gallery access through a single permission covering multiple app functions with different purposes.
The authority gave Meta 60 days to disable the feature and seek separate consent for its use. Italy has about 20 million Android users, the agency said.
The fine was imposed on Meta Platforms Ireland Limited, which challenged Italy’s jurisdiction, according to the statement.
The authority said Meta’s “lack of cooperation” with the investigation factored into the penalty, which amounts to approximately 0.47% of the group’s global turnover.
The proceedings did not look at the possible use of user content to train AI models, something Meta also denies doing.
Meta said it would appeal the decision. A Meta spokesperson said the company “strongly disagrees” with the regulator’s assessment, its interpretation of the law and the “disproportionate level of the fine”.
“This is a simple feature that helps people share photos and videos on Facebook,” Meta said in a statement.
“Users must grant permission on their device before the feature can operate, and they can change that permission at any time in their settings," Meta added.
The investigation was launched in July 2025 following a complaint by the Bolzano Consumer Protection Centre and was based on a technical analysis conducted by Italian authorities.

noticias.titulo: 'Temu Harry Potter': New clip of HBO's series gets panned online
noticias.resumen: A new clip of the upcoming Harry Potter TV reboot has been released, and the internet is unanimous. "As a millennial who spent hours upon hours reading Harry Potter growing up, I’m insulted by this."
noticias.texto:
A new clip of the upcoming Harry Potter TV reboot has been released, and the internet is unanimous. "As a millennial who spent hours upon hours reading Harry Potter growing up, I’m insulted by this."
The upcoming HBO adaptation of JK Rowling’s Harry Potter has already courted controversy, with many questioning what the point of a new series is and whether watching it would be lending support to Rowling's anti-trans views.
Fans already reacted negatively to the first trailer released in March, criticising a lack of magic.
Now, a new scene from the series has been shared online, showing the Hogwarts students in the Great Hall, as John Lithgow's Dumbledore makes his big entrance.
The clip, intended to drum up enthusiasm, has backfired massively, with the internet reacting in unison.
It's “absolute slop that should not exist”; “I’m insulted by this”; “Why’s it filmed like an SNL skit?”; a “*profound* sense of ‘why are we doing this’ that permeates every frame”...
Check out some other overwhelmingly negative reactions to the clip:
"This new Harry Potter looks so lifeless man in all aspects."
"It’s actually so funny they spent millions of dollars to make Temu Harry Potter."
"The best way to describe the new Harry Potter series is that they all look like they're fully aware that they're in a Harry Potter series."
"Why’s it filmed like an snl skit?"
"This is going to be the HP version of “Rings of Power”. Absolute slop that should not exist."
"It looks very cold. I like the organic warmth of the original's grading."
"Absolute cinema."
"As a millennial who spent hours upon hours reading Harry Potter growing up, I’m insulted by this."
"There is *profound * sense of “why are we doing this” that permeates every frame."
The first episode of the Harry Potter TV series is out on 25 December 2026.

noticias.titulo: Carney says US tariffs could push Canadian carmakers towards China
noticias.resumen: Mark Carney has warned that US tariffs could push Canadian carmakers towards China, as Ottawa weighs alternatives to an increasingly strained North American auto market.
noticias.texto:
Mark Carney has warned that US tariffs could push Canadian carmakers towards China, as Ottawa weighs alternatives to an increasingly strained North American auto market.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Monday his country's carmakers could turn to China if the North American auto industry becomes less integrated due to US President Donald Trump's tariff hikes.
"We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed... in an integrated North American market," Carney told reporters ahead of a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at this week's APEC summit in southern China.
"That market has become less integrated because of US trade actions."
Carney said at a summit of French-speaking nations in Cambodia the current system was "the best result for Canadian workers, for Canadian business, and for US consumers".
"It's part of the trade negotiations, as you know - depending on where that settles, there'll be other options, European options, Asian options, of course, Chinese, Japanese," he added.
Trump imposed punishing tariffs on Canada's auto sector last year, and has repeatedly said he wants autos sold in the United States to be made exclusively by American workers.
Carney walked away from trade talks with Trump in August, but Ottawa and Washington have sounded optimistic about prospects for a deal in recent weeks.
Carney said looking to China was "not leverage, but action, reaction".

noticias.titulo: Take That and 'You Can See Everything': The best things to do, hear, see or watch in Europe this week
noticias.resumen: An exhibition exploring the history of drugs, the return of boy band Take That, and this year's most anticipated documentary — here's what to look out for this week.
noticias.texto:
An exhibition exploring the history of drugs, the return of boy band Take That, and this year's most anticipated documentary — here's what to look out for this week.
It's finally here — the week where You Can See Everything.
And by that we of course mean Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's highly-anticipated documentary about convicted American fraudster, Elizabeth Holmes.
Its teaser trailer has already spawned a thousand memes and the delayed European release dates have made it near-impossible to avoid any spoilers; whispers from the hallowed halls of Letterboxd hinting at a three-hour runtime full of unexpected twists and turns.
While it comes out on the 20 November in the United Kingdom and Ireland, those in France and other European territories will unfortunately have to wait until the end of December. But hey, you can still take a peek at our film critic David Mouriquand's (spoiler-free) review this Friday.
Another upcoming highlight is the opening of an exhibition on mind-altering substances at Paris' Musée de l'Homme. Through delving into the origins, mechanisms and historical context of various drugs, it de-stigmatises and re-evaluates their meaning within culture and society.
Keep scrolling to find out more about what else is coming up.
Exhibitions
Cosimo I de' Medici: Art and Dynasty
When: 18 November 2026 - 21 March 2027
Where: The Wallace Collection (London, United Kingdom)
Centred around five key historical objects, The Wallace Collection's latest exhibition dives into the world of Cosimo I de' Medici — the first Grand Duke of Tuscany. From expanding the Palazzo Pitti in Florence, to commissioning masterful Mannerist painters like Agnolo Bronzino, Cosimo I became a key figure within Italian culture for using art and craftsmanship to secure his political powers. The works on display demonstrate this, including a 70 centimetre-long Maiolica wine cooler from 1574 and lion-headed ceremonial short sword. Find out more here.
Drugs
When: 18 November 2026 - 6 June 2027
Where: Musée de l'Homme (Paris, France)
The word drugs has become synonymous with taboo, often conjuring stigmatised pre-conceptions about those that use them recreationally. But the truth behind psychoactive substances is far more nuanced and complex than that — something the Musée de l'Homme untangles in its fascinating and mind-altering new exhibition. From the everyday drugs we consume like caffeine, to vintage vials of opium and botanical specimens, the displays collectively explore the sociological, psychological and economic impact of drugs throughout history, re-evaluating and re-educating in the process.
Bonus highlight: Hosted by Institut Lumière director Thierry Frémaux, 'Un Soir au Temps des Lumières' is a live event celebrating the invention of Cinématographe in Lyon, France. It takes place on the 19 November at 8pm at the Théâtre Antoine Riboud.
Movies
You Can See Everything
Where: Cinemas
When: 20 November
Few documentaries have generated as much buzz as You Can See Everything, which premiered at the Telluride Film Festival in September and is finally getting its release across Europe. And phew! Because avoiding spoilers has not been easy.
Directed by Lance Oppenheim (Primetime) and comedy genius Nathan Fielder (The Curse, The Rehearsal), it's an almost 3 hour-long deep dive into the world of Elizabeth Holmes, filmed in the weeks leading up to her prison sentence for defrauding investors in her blood-testing stat-up, Theranos. But it's also so much more than that — a psychologically tense and darkly comic exploration of perception, performance, media and truth that cleverly subverts your expectations.
Bonus highlight: Mahershala Ali stars as a devoutly religious hitman on a mission to protect his family in Your Mother Your Mother your Mother, released in the UK on 20 November.
TV series
Yellowjackets (Season 4)
Where: Paramount+
When: 20 November
The Emmy-nominated thriller about a high school girls’ soccer team that survived a 1996 plane crash is back for a fourth and final series. Alternating between past and present, and featuring an all-star cast including Juliette Lewis, Melanie Lynskey and Christina Ricci, the upcoming episodes will conclude the teenager's rescue and difficult reintegration into society. Meanwhile, the horrifying impact of their shared ordeal continues to stir conflict 25 years later, as the return of an old flame sparks even more paranoia. New cast members include Molly Ringwald and Eric Stoltz.
Bonus highlight: The Altruists, Netflix's new biographical drama about the rise and fall of cryptocurrency exchange FTX, premieres on 19 November.
Music
Take That: Dreamers
When: 20 November
While we can't confirm that they're back for good, they are back for now! Indeed, British boy band Take That are releasing their 10th studio album this week, 'Dreamers'. Recorded by three of the original five-piece, Gary Barlow, Mark Owen and Howard Donald, it's a return to the band's infectious brand of fizzy, feel-good pop. Covering themes of love and hope, it's exactly the kind of live, laugh, love sounds needed for combatting end-of-year comparisons and burn out.
Bonus highlight: For a uniquely diverse and cinematically retro sound, look no further than London-based band Los Bitchos, whose third album 'Los Bitchos & Friends Vol 1' is out now.

noticias.titulo: Exclusive: EU countries weigh shorter probation period for newcomers
noticias.resumen: The Irish EU presidency proposes cutting the probation period for newcomers from 15 to 10 years, extendable by five. Member states remain split on suspending voting rights, how to trigger measures and pre-accession monitoring, ahead of a key discussion at EU ambassadors' level.
noticias.texto:
The Irish EU presidency proposes cutting the probation period for newcomers from 15 to 10 years, extendable by five. Member states remain split on suspending voting rights, how to trigger measures and pre-accession monitoring, ahead of a key discussion at EU ambassadors' level.
The Irish presidency of the EU Council is proposing to cut the probation period for new member states from 15 to 10 years, extendable by five more, as governments prepare to finalise their position on the new safeguards.
In recent weeks, EU countries have been discussing how to implement the stronger safeguards the European Commission proposed in early October, including a probation period during which newcomers could see their voting rights suspended.
The Irish government, which chairs the talks, has circulated a draft paper compiling member states’ initial positions. Ambassadors will discuss it on Wednesday as input for Montenegro’s accession treaty.
“The presidency proposed a duration of ten years with the possibility of a five year extension. While there is broad support for this proposal, a number of member states still seek a longer duration of 15 years citing the need to provide an effective deterrence or response to possible backsliding for a longer period post accession,” reads the paper, seen by Euronews.
The Irish admit that member states remain divided on core elements of the scope. Some governments object to triggering the institutional safeguards over a violation of the principle of sincere cooperation, which may be hard to assess objectively.
“Member states have indicated the importance of having suspension of voting rights as a potential measure under this safeguard for particularly serious breaches. However, a small number of member states oppose such an option,” the document continues.
Five founding member states, led by the Netherlands, have been pushing for tighter safeguards to react more swiftly to the emergence of a new Viktor Orbán. The Friends of the Western Balkans, including Italy, want a more tailored approach that avoids putting newcomers on an unequal footing.
“Should the duration of the postponement be tailored depending on an assessment of the acceding State’s readiness at the time of accession or should the postponement be for an initial period of a year, with a possible extension (by QMV) for additional period(s) of one year and until the situation is remedied?” the document asks.
The presidency also concedes that governance needs further discussion. The Commission proposed that the process be triggered unless a qualified majority (QMV) of member states opposes it.
Some countries back this so-called reverse qualified majority, while others argue the gravity of the measure demands unanimity. As a compromise, the presidency proposes using simple QMV.
Pre-accession monitoring
The Commission also proposed a monitoring mechanism to ensure candidate countries honour their commitments before formally joining the bloc, with the option of postponing accession in the most serious cases.
The paper notes broad support for pre-accession monitoring of the so-called fundamentals, such as EU values, the rule of law and judicial independence.
The presidency acknowledged that several member states also want alignment with the EU’s common foreign and security policy (CFSP) added to the monitoring. Such alignment has become a key tool for keeping candidates from drifting into the orbit of foreign powers.
According to the paper, there appears to be general support for a new paragraph to facilitate engagement with acceding states where measures are proposed, and for linking pre-accession monitoring to the postponement clause, with monitoring continuing in the event of postponement.
Several member states also asked for a monitoring mechanism after accession. The presidency left the idea out of the legal text: despite some openness, there are concerns it could duplicate existing measures.
On how to trigger postponement, the document describes a “clear divergence” among member states, split between QMV and unanimity as the basis for decision-making.
As a possible solution, the presidency proposed an optional clause enabling postponement by qualified majority in areas of specific concern, though this raised questions over whether it would also apply to violations of EU values.
“The duration of a postponement remains a divisive matter. Some member states have called for a maximum duration of between 1 - 3 years. Others have requested that postponement continue until such a time as the situation has been remedied,” the paper states.
Sector-specific safeguards
On sector-specific safeguards, the document sees significant support for the presidency’s compromise of 10 years with a possible five-year extension. Stark divisions remain, however, between those pushing for 15 years and those wanting a shorter period of three to five.
“Most member states have supported the presidency proposal to strengthen an extension clause so that it would be invoked where measures have been taken in the first nine years and where sufficient grounds are demonstrated,” it adds.

noticias.titulo: Japan’s economy stalls as inflation weighs on growth
noticias.resumen: Japan’s economy stalled in the third quarter as Iran war-fuelled inflation, bad weather and an earthquake weighed on growth. Analysts still expect the Bank of Japan to raise interest rates again in December.
noticias.texto:
Japan’s economy stalled in the third quarter as Iran war-fuelled inflation, bad weather and an earthquake weighed on growth. Analysts still expect the Bank of Japan to raise interest rates again in December.
Japan’s real gross domestic product was virtually flat from July to September compared with the previous quarter, according to preliminary data released on Monday by the Cabinet Office.
This came in below forecasts for a 0.1% expansion and was well down from the 0.4% recorded in the previous three months.
On an annualised basis, the economy shrank by 0.1%, against expectations of 0.2% growth.
Higher oil prices pushed up costs for businesses and households. Japan, which imports virtually all its oil, has been hit hard by the surge in prices caused by the Iran war. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a major route for oil shipments, has been severely disrupted since the outbreak of the war.
Meanwhile, the weak yen is adding to the problem of rising energy prices, making imports more expensive. The US dollar has recently traded at about 160 yen, up from below 115 yen five years ago.
Inflation, excluding fresh food, rose to 2.1% in September, up from 1.7% in August and above the Bank of Japan’s 2% target.
Real private consumption fell by 0.3% quarter on quarter, matching the decline in the previous three months. Bad weather likely also played a part, “as typhoons and heavy rain kept consumers away from shops”, according to Taro Kimura of Bloomberg Economics.
Net exports knocked 0.6 percentage points off growth as imports rose 2.5% and exports fell 0.2%. A July earthquake on the southwestern island of Kyushu disrupted factory operations. Business investment rebounded by 1.6%, or 6.8% on an annualised basis, helped by strong demand for digital technology. A build-up in public inventories also supported growth.
Marcel Thieliant of Capital Economics said the GDP reading was slightly weaker than economists had expected and described the details as “rather discouraging”.
Before the data release, Shumpei Fujita, chief researcher at Mitsubishi UFJ Research and Consulting, said that “considering the headwinds from the worsening situation in Iran, the domestic economy is maintaining its resilience”.
The government of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is trying to pass legislation to cut the tax on food. The plan faces uncertainty over rising public debt and how the cut would be funded.
Another rate hike in December?
The latest growth figure is unlikely to dissuade the Bank of Japan from raising interest rates again in December as inflationary pressure builds, analysts say.
“In fact, it looks increasingly likely that the Bank will have to tighten policy more aggressively than we’ve been anticipating as inflation is about to surge,” Thieliant said.
Last month, the central bank said underlying inflation was broadly in line with its 2% target, which it adopted in 2013 to pull the economy out of deflation.
The International Monetary Fund projects that Japan will fall from fourth place in 2026 to sixth in 2027 among the world’s largest economies by nominal GDP in US dollars, with India and the UK overtaking it.

noticias.titulo: Prince Harry says 'you're going to win' on surprise weekend visit to Ukraine
noticias.resumen: The British royal took to the stage at a conference for medics organised by Superhumans, a clinic in the city that specialises in the rehabilitation of wounded soldiers.
noticias.texto:
The British royal took to the stage at a conference for medics organised by Superhumans, a clinic in the city that specialises in the rehabilitation of wounded soldiers.
Britain's Prince Harry made a surprise visit to Ukraine at the weekend, meeting wounded veterans and medics specialising in war injuries and telling them: "You're going to win the war."
Making his fourth visit to Ukraine since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion, Prince Harry told the wounded soldiers that "the world will continue to support" Kyiv and expressed hope that the lengthy war would end.
He took part in events Saturday and Sunday in the western city of Lviv, with the trip kept secret for security reasons.
The British royal took to the stage at a conference for medics organised by Superhumans, a clinic in the city that specialises in the rehabilitation of wounded soldiers.
"You're going to win the war and then you're going to be set up for success," Prince Harry told listeners, including Health Minister Viktor Liashko.
The prince, a former British army officer and founder of the Invictus Games, also met athletes hoping to represent Ukraine at next year's games in the British city of Birmingham.
His trip took place as Russia has pounded Ukraine in the run-up to winter.
The 42-year-old prince was dressed casually in a dark hooded puffer jacket and brown desert boots as he attended a series of events.
In a school sports hall, he watched wheelchair rugby players zooming around as they vied for a place in Ukraine's team at the next Invictus Games, an international sports contest for veterans and serving military personnel founded by the prince.
Ukraine plans to send its largest ever team, 60 competitors, to the games next year.
The Russia-Ukraine war has killed hundreds of thousands, displaced millions and left a large number of Ukrainians with disabilities and missing limbs.
The country has around 1.4 million combat veterans, over 10% of whom have disabilities.
On Sunday, the prince called the veterans "role models" for society and for Western support for Kyiv's army to be extended to veterans.
"We've invested in them before they put the uniform on, we must invest in them once the uniform comes off."
Invictus Games
Among those attending Saturday's event was Illia Pylypenko, 33, from Odesa, who suffered severe burns and lost a lung when the tank he was driving struck a mine.
Adaptive sport "really supported me mentally, I found a new stimulus," he said.
His dream was for every wounded veteran in Ukraine to be able to take part in such games.
Prince Harry told the veterans joining the movement: "When the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games."
At a rugby game, he hugged a player he recognised: Valeriy Odainyk, a former contestant at the Invictus Games in Canada in 2025 who has an amputated leg.
The 41-year-old with a large tattoo on one arm explained to the prince that he was "still an active serviceman".
"So when do you find time to train?" Harry asked.
Odainyk said afterwards he told the prince that his involvement in such sport "all started and continues with the Invictus Games".
The British prince, a former soldier, has spoken of being profoundly moved by witnessing death and life-changing injuries while on deployment in Afghanistan.
He launched the Invictus Games in 2014 while still serving in the British army.
"Every single person in Ukraine is playing their part in this war," he said on Sunday.
"In my mind you've already won, I hope the war is going to come to an end."

noticias.titulo: Travelling in 2027? Here are the new European flight routes to know about
noticias.resumen: In 2027, there will be many new flight routes to and from Europe, including a historic inaugural link between Belize and Frankfurt, as well as between Geneva and Latin America.
noticias.texto:
In 2027, there will be many new flight routes to and from Europe, including a historic inaugural link between Belize and Frankfurt, as well as between Geneva and Latin America.
Do you already have a spreadsheet mapped out with your 2027 travel plans?
Luckily enough, many airlines have already published scheduled updates and new routes for travel to and from Europe for next year.
For instance, Mexican carrier Aeroméxico is set to add Milan to its network from 28 March with four weekly flights from Mexico City, launching its second connection with Italy alongside Rome. From 13 April, Aeroméxico will also operate a new route between Guadalajara and Paris Charles de Gaulle with three weekly flights.
Ryanair recently announced its new flights for summer 2027, including routes from Alicante to Tangier, Krakow to Tangier and Palermo to Marrakesh and Tirana.
EasyJet has also earmarked 18 new routes from 10 UK airports, including Aberdeen gaining flights to Barcelona and Majorca, while Edinburgh will add Bilbao alongside Rome, Hamburg and Tivat.
Here’s some of the new European flight routes to keep on your radar for travel in 2027.
New flights in March 2027
Norwegian will connect Norway and Denmark with Spanish destinations. Starting from 24 March, the carrier will launch its Oslo to Seville route with two weekly flights. The seasonal service will operate until 16 June, before resuming from 18 August to 30 October. Norwegian will also link Copenhagen and Santiago de Compostela in the summer.
On 29 March, Brussels Airlines will launch its first flight between Brussels and Cairo, which will run five times a week. The Belgian carrier said it intends to initially operate the route seasonally during the summer, but "has the ambition to expand it to a year-round service".
Wizz Air will also launch new routes from Naples to Palermo, Nice, Basel and Genoa starting in March.
Other new routes launching in March 2027:
- American: Chicago-Tokyo, from 19 March
- Delta: Austin-Paris, daily from 27 March
- United: Austin-Paris, daily from 27 March
- Aeroméxico: Mexico City-Milan-Malpensa, from 28 March
- American Airlines: New York JFK-Amsterdam, from 28 March
- American Airlines: New York JFK-London Heathrow, from 28 March
- American Airlines: Philadelphia-Porto, from 28 March
- Eurowings: Stuttgart-Copenhagen, from 28 March
- Eurowings: Stuttgart-Madrid, from 28 March
- Eurowings: Hanover-Venice, from 28 March
- Lufthansa: Frankfurt-Tokyo (Narita), daily from 28 March
- Ryanair: Shannon-Milan Bergamo, from 28 March
- ITA Airways: Rome Fiumicino-Caracas, three weekly flights from 30 March
New flights in April 2027
April will mark the first direct airlink between Geneva and Latin America, with the launch of LATAM Airlines Brasil’s São Paulo-Geneva-São Paulo route three times a week.
"By launching the first direct service between Geneva and Latin America, LATAM Airlines is making history and significantly enhancing the international connectivity of our region," Jean-François de Saussure, CEO of Geneva Airport, said.
Sky Alps will operate new weekly routes every Thursday from 29 April, connecting holidaymakers from Groningen Airport Eelde in the Netherlands to Kerry Airport in Ireland.
In the largest expansion in its history, US airline United will add 10 cities to its international network in 2027. This includes daily flights from Newark to Luxembourg starting 2 April and from Washington Dulles to Toulouse from 26 April.
Another new addition is Delta's nonstop service from Boston to Reykjavik, starting 12 April through to 30 October.
Other new routes launching in April 2027:
- KM Malta Airlines: Malta-Bordeuax, from 1 April
- Aeroméxico: Guadalajara-Paris, from 13 April
- British Airways: London Heathrow-Bergen, from 15 April
- easyJet: Southend-Rhodes, from 27 April
New flights in May 2027
Starting from 29 May, British Airways will add Kilimanjaro, home to Africa’s tallest mountain, and Zanzibar to its network. These flights will operate three times a week from London Gatwick and will run until 31 October.
BA will also make changes to its London network, replacing flights from London City Airport. From 1 May, flights to Perugia, Italy, will be from London Heathrow Terminal 5 instead. For travellers with their sights set on Greece, the London Heathrow-Skiathos route starts later on 20 May.
Starting from 15 May, Cityflyer, a BA subsidiary, will connect travellers in Glasgow to Nice. While travellers in Edinburgh will be able to enjoy direct flights to Split in Croatia once a week starting from 15 May to 17 June, which will later resume from 4 September to 2 October.
“From Norway's spectacular fjords and the beaches of Skiathos to the rolling countryside of Umbria, the glamour of the French Riviera and Croatia's stunning Adriatic coast, these additions provide greater choice and connectivity for customers planning their next summer trip," Neil Chernoff, British Airways’ Chief Planning and Strategy Officer, said.
Also launching is Lufthansa’s Frankfurt to Columbus, Ohio, route. Starting from 5 May, this will make Lufthansa the first European carrier to operate a nonstop connection to the American state.
Other new routes launching in May 2027:
- Eurowings: Hanover-Dublin, from 3 May
- American: New York JFK-Nice, from 6 May
- American: Philadelphia-Vienna, from 6 May
- Azerbaijan Airlines: Baku-Brussels, from 8 May
- Air Canada: Montréal-Dubrovnik, from 11 May
- United: Newark-Ljubljana, four times weekly from 12 May
- American: Charlotte-Barcelona, from 27 May
- American: Philadelphia-Reykjavik, from 27 May
- United: Newark-Olbia, three times weekly from 27 May
- United: Newark-Catania, four times weekly from 28 May
- United: Newark-Ibiza, four times weekly from 31 May
New flights in June 2027
Launching on 1 June, Discover Airlines will fly from Frankfurt to Edmonton in Canada. The upcoming three weekly flights will make it the only nonstop service between Germany and the Canadian city.
Switzerland’s flag carrier will add a southern French destination to its network. Starting from 25 June until 23 August, SWISS will connect travellers from Zürich to Toulouse twice a week.
Also in June, Austrian Airlines will launch its Vienna to Beirut route, which will run until September.
Canadian airline Air Transat will launch a weekly service from Québec City to Lyon, France, starting from 8 June until 26 October. Then on 14 June, the carrier will launch the first non-stop route between Québec City and Barcelona, Spain, which will run until 25 October.
Other new routes launching in June 2027:
- Air Canada: Toronto-Oslo, four times weekly from 2 June
- United: Newark-Valencia, three times weekly from 2 June
- Eurowings: Berlin-Verona, from 4 June
- United: Newark-Marseille, daily from 4 June
- United: Newark-Terceira, three times weekly from 9 June
- Air Canada: Toronto-Shannon, three times weekly from 10 June
- Air Canada: Toronto-Nice, twice weekly from 16 June
- Air Canada: Montréal-Basel-Mulhouse, four times weekly from 16 June
- Norwegian: Copenhagen-Santiago de Compostela from 19 June
New flights in August 2027
Lufthansa’s new Munich to Phoenix, Arizona, route will start from 3 August. The flights will operate three times a week on Tuesdays, Fridays and Sundays.
New flights in October 2027
Qantas’s long-awaited ‘Project Sunrise’ will see the world's longest non-stop passenger flight cover more than 16,000 kilometres, with flights between Sydney and London expected to range between 19 and 22 hours. This connection between the two cities is set to launch in October next year.
Vanessa Hudson, CEO at Qantas Group, said: "We made a commitment in 2017 that Qantas would conquer the final frontier of long-haul aviation and connect Australia's east coast directly to London, something that has never before been possible. From October 2027, that promise becomes reality."
New flights in December 2027
Discover Airlines will begin flights from Frankfurt to Belize City’s Philip S.W. Goldson International Airport on 16 December 2027. Flights will operate twice weekly on Thursdays and Sundays until mid-April 2028. This will mark the first time a European carrier is flying directly to the Central American country.
Anthony Mahler, Minister of Tourism of Belize, said that strengthening the country’s presence in Europe is a “key priority”, that will increase opportunities for visitors to experience Belize for its “world-renowned Barrier Reef and pristine islands" to its "lush rainforests, ancient Maya sites, and rich cultural heritage”.

noticias.titulo: Israeli opposition chiefs denounce Netanyahu over 'attempted coup'
noticias.resumen: Netanyahu's main rival, former army chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, wrote on Sunday that the caretaker prime minister "cannot remain at the head of the government for a minute longer".
noticias.texto:
Netanyahu's main rival, former army chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, wrote on Sunday that the caretaker prime minister "cannot remain at the head of the government for a minute longer".
Two Israeli opposition leaders denounced an "attempted coup" on Monday following press reports that outgoing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office tried to frame members of an Arab-Israeli party ahead of last month's election.
"As more and more details come to light, it becomes clear: This wasn't an attempt to disrupt the elections. It was an attempted coup," Yair Lapid, who headed the opposition in the previous legislature and co-chairs the Beyachad list, wrote on X.
Israel's Channel 12 television reported on Sunday that on the eve of the 27 October election, Netanyahu's chief of staff Ido Norden had phoned in a complaint to the police about members of the Arab-Israeli Raam party.
Norden reportedly pointed the police to a purported intelligence source, a former employee of Netanyahu's office, who provided information that led to the arrest of three Raam members.
The three men were later released when the police determined that the information was unfounded.
Netanyahu subsequently accused Arab parties of electoral fraud after they gained a record number of seats. His Likud party issued a statement denying the latest allegations.
The Israeli newspaper Haaretz also reported that David Zini, head of the Shin Bet domestic security service, sought to wiretap leaders of the other Arab slate, the Joint List, but the attorney general turned down his request due to lack of evidence.
Following the report, Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen also denounced an "attempted coup by Netanyahu".
"If the findings are confirmed, this is a criminal mechanism that operated from the heart of government to rig the election results. Everyone found responsible must be held accountable, including Netanyahu," he wrote on X.
Raam's number two, former police chief Yoav Segalovitz, called for an urgent investigation.
"These suspicions require an immediate, independent and thorough criminal investigation that reaches everyone involved, at every level and in every role," he wrote on X.
"Netanyahu cried out that his election was being stolen, while he himself tried to steal the country and is still trying to do so now," he added.
Netanyahu's main rival, former army chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, wrote on Sunday that the caretaker prime minister "cannot remain at the head of the government for a minute longer".
Neither Netanyahu's bloc nor Eisenkot's opposition secured the 61 seats required to form a government following last month's election.
The two Arab parties, the Joint List and Raam, have indicated support for Eisenkot who was tasked by President Isaac Herzog with forming a government.

noticias.titulo: Peruvians honour Pope Leo XIV with procession through Lima
noticias.resumen: In Peru, crowds escort the Lord of Miracles through Lima while Catholics camp outside Las Palmas Air Base ahead of Pope Leo XIV's final Mass.
noticias.texto:
Crowds lined the streets of Lima, Peru, on Sunday, 15 November, as the revered Lord of Miracles icon was carried by truck to Las Palmas Air Base, where Pope Leo XIV was due to celebrate Mass the following day. Worshippers waved papal flags and held portraits of the pontiff as the procession made its way through the capital.
One woman scattered flower petals as the icon passed. One of Peru's most cherished religious symbols, the Lord of Miracles was set to be present at the largest gathering of the Pope's visit to the country, on the final day of his 12-day Latin American tour.
Outside the air base, hundreds of Catholics had already begun queuing, prepared to spend the night waiting for a chance to get close to the Pope. Some sang and prayed, while others shared food they had brought with them. Street vendors sold rosaries, T-shirts, portraits and even plush toys depicting Leo XIV.
Some devotees described the overnight wait as a sacrifice worth making, while others expressed hopes that his visit would bring peace and unity. Meanwhile, volunteers entered the air base to prepare for Monday's Mass.

noticias.titulo: Elon Musk joins calls to bring back Jensen Huang as allies build 'war room' to lobby his return
noticias.resumen: Silicon Valley is supporting the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO, while Elon Musk joins a petition demanding that the company "Bring Jensen Back".
noticias.texto:
Silicon Valley is supporting the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO, while Elon Musk joins a petition demanding that the company "Bring Jensen Back".
Nvidia's co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week after multiple extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy, is eyeing a comeback, with tech executives calling for his reinstatement.
Huang, a long-admired figure in artificial intelligence who rose to international stardom, discussed with confidants the possibility of returning to his post, according to a report by the Financial Times.
A Huang ally also told the publication they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return.
It comes as tech executives, including Elon Musk, have called for Huang's reinstatement in an online petition, which has gained more than 160,000 signatures.
The petition also counts Epic Games boss Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator chief executive Garry Tan among its signatories. More than 7,500 signatories were also identified as Nvidia employees.
But in the United States, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said on Sunday that Nvidia should look “outside” the company for its next leader. “They need a dramatic shake-up,” Bessent said on Fox News.
The treasury secretary also urged Nvidia to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced semiconductors to reach China.
The US bans the sale of the most advanced chips to China as part of its strategy to stay ahead of Beijing in the race to lead AI. This measure came under former President Joe Biden, who signed the CHIPS Act into law.
This was bad for Nvidia, as China was one of its largest markets for GPU chips. Then, under the Trump administration, Huang lobbied the US to relax its export controls on chips to China, with several meetings with President Donald Trump.
Trump eventually allowed the export of its H200 chips, which are more powerful, to China in exchange for 25% of the revenue.

noticias.titulo: Dreaming of visiting the Taj Mahal? Getting a visa to visit India is about to get easier
noticias.resumen: The required fields for all e-visa applications are set to be reduced by between 65% and 70% by the end of the year.
noticias.texto:
The required fields for all e-visa applications are set to be reduced by between 65% and 70% by the end of the year.
Anyone who has applied for a visa for India can back me up on this: It's not the easiest of processes.
The form is long and unwieldy, asking for details like your father and mother’s nationality (and previous nationality), every country you’ve visited in the past 10 years (which is capped at 250 characters, meaning those who travel frequently won’t be able to list them all), and for a reference in India.
Well, that will soon be a thing of the past as the Ministry of Home Affairs has just announced the required fields for all visas will be reduced by between 65% and 70%, depending on the category.
The exact details around what will be taken out of the visa application forms is yet to be announced. The updated forms are expected to be introduced by the end of the year.
The ministry has said that the move will “reduce time and effort required to complete application by the applicant” while “enhancing administrative efficiency by facilitating more focused scrutiny and processing”.
Other changes include the reduction of the number of main visa categories from 13 to nine, and the number of sub-categories from 49 to 23.
The main visa categories are now: Business, diplomatic, work, journalist, medical, official, student, visitor, and miscellaneous.
The tourist visa was given its new moniker “to reflect a broader range of permitted purposes beyond conventional tourism”.
Visitor visas have two sub-categories. The V-1, which is valid for 30 days with multiple entries, covers regular tourism as well as business meetings, medical consultations, wellness retreats, short-duration medical treatment and short-term courses in Indian languages, music, art and craft.
The V-2, which can have a validity of one, five or 10 years, covers all of the above as well as mountaineering. Those looking to climb India’s peaks will be given a multiple-entry visa of six months.
India’s tourism ambitions
India received around 9.15 million foreign arrivals in 2025, down from a peak of 10.93 million in 2019.
The country is aiming to attract 100 million tourists annually by 2047, and streamlining the visa process will no doubt be part of the plan to bring in more visitors.
According to WTTC’s Economic Impact Research (EIR) released earlier this year, the travel and tourism sector now contributes 6.6% of India’s GDP and supports one in 10 jobs in the country.
The sector is set to increase dramatically in the coming years, with WTTC predicting the country will be the fourth largest travel and tourism economy by 2036, up from 10th currently.

noticias.titulo: Are European households prepared for a crisis? Take our poll
noticias.resumen: The EU is asking citizens to become more self-sufficient in a crisis. The European Commission has advised households to stock up on emergency supplies, to last at least 72 hours.
noticias.texto:
The EU is asking citizens to become more self-sufficient in a crisis. The European Commission has advised households to stock up on emergency supplies, to last at least 72 hours.
Under the new crisis-preparedness guidelines, presented last week, the European Commission recommended citizens prepare emergency supplies, evacuation bags, and family plans. People should keep sufficient drinking water, stockpile non-perishable food and essential medicines, and keep first-aid supplies, flashlights, batteries, a radio, power banks, cash and important documents.
The first 72 hours are considered critical because emergency services may be overwhelmed. During a large-scale flood, blackout, cyberattack or armed conflict, rescue teams must prioritise immediate life-threatening situations and may not be able to assist every household simultaneously. Essential services such as electricity, drinking water, heating, transport, telecommunications and electronic payments can be interrupted, making access to necessities increasingly difficult.
This initiative is part of the EU Preparedness Union Strategy launched in March 2025, which aims to shift Europe from reacting to disasters to anticipating and preparing for them.
The EU faces several threats, including Russia's war against Ukraine, potential sabotage of critical infrastructure, cyberattacks, disinformation, extreme weather, floods, wildfires and major power outages. However, European countries have very different levels and traditions of preparedness; several northern European countries already operate established national preparedness systems, but Southern states are trailing behind.
Can these guidelines help protect Europeans in an emergency? Or are they taking the responsibility away from public services? Our poll is anonymous and takes only a few seconds to complete. The results will be featured across XL's EU-wide coverage, including videos, articles and newsletters, and will help shape our reporting as we examine how Europe can secure its position in the age of artificial intelligence.

noticias.titulo: European Film Awards: 'Fatherland', 'La Bola Negra' and 'Fjord' lead the nominations
noticias.resumen: Paweł Pawlikowski’s 'Fatherland' and Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo's 'La Bola Negra' lead the EFA nominations with 11 and 10 noms respectively, while Cristian Mungiu's Palme d'Or winner 'Fjord' follows with five nods. Check out the full list of nominees for the 39th European Film Awards.
noticias.texto:
Paweł Pawlikowski’s 'Fatherland' and Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo's 'La Bola Negra' lead the EFA nominations with 11 and 10 noms respectively, while Cristian Mungiu's Palme d'Or winner 'Fjord' follows with five nods. Check out the full list of nominees for the 39th European Film Awards.
The European Film Academy has revealed the nominees for the 39th European Film Awards.
The announcement took place in front of a live audience at the Pavlos Zannas Theatre located in the iconic Olympion building in Thessaloniki, as part of the Thessaloniki International Film Festival.
Leading the charge are Paweł Pawlikowski’s German period drama Fatherland and the Spanish epic La Bola Negra by directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo, with 11 and 10 nominations respectively.
Both Fatherland and La Bola Negra picked up EFA nominations in the Best European Film, European Director, European Screenwriter and European Cinematographer categories, with Fatherland also receiving European Actress and European Actor noms for Hanns Zischler and Sandra Hüller.
Hüller scored a dual best actress nom this year, nominated for her starring role in Markus Schleinzer's Rose, with the likes of Penelope Cruz, Javier Bardem, Andrew Scott, Renate Reinsve and Sebastian Stan among the acting nominees. Both Reinsve and Stan are nominated for this year's Palme d'Or winner Fjord, which picked up five nominations in total.
Scroll down for the full list of nominees.
Elsewhere, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s NAZA scored a nomination for Best Documentary. The exposé which Israel is treating as a national security crisis has become one of 2026's most watched documentaries.
NAZA shows “in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” and features interviews with 24 Israeli military intelligence officers, soldiers and whistleblowers. They describe how Palestinians are targeted and how strikes are carried out using AI and automated surveillance in military targeting systems - despite Israel being aware that civilians are present in targeted areas.
The 80-minute hot-button doc builds on reporting between 2023 and 2025 published by the Israeli-Palestinian +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call, and The Guardian. It left this year's Venice Film Festival with the Special Jury Prize, received a record-breaking 25-minute standing ovation at the festival, and has led Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to attack the makers of NAZA, accusing the film of contributing to “global antisemitic incitement”.
As reported by the Guardian, Ricardo Gutiérrez, the general secretary of the European Federation of Journalists, said: “These threats constitute a blatant act of intimidation against journalists who have simply been doing their job, in strict accordance with ethical standards and in the public interest.” Regarding Netanyahu’s threats, he added: “I am not surprised by this outburst, which confirms that this regime is prepared to do anything to cover up its crimes against humanity and the ongoing genocide in Gaza.
All of the Best Documentary and Best Animation nominees are also nominated in the Best European Film category.
The 39th European Film Awards will be held in Athens, Greece, on 16 January 2027.
