noticias.titulo: Listen: Is Europe ready to defend itself against cyberattacks?
noticias.resumen: Bomb threats, election interference, espionage, and sabotage. Cyberattacks are becoming an increasingly serious threat across Europe, affecting everything from public services to critical infrastructure. So, how prepared is Europe to deal with them?
noticias.texto: Production: By Europod , in co-production with Sphera Network . EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms . Find the full transcript below : Bomb threats, election interference, espionage, and sabotage. Cyberattacks are becoming an increasingly serious threat across Europe, affecting everything from public services to critical infrastructure. So, how prepared is Europe to deal with them? Let’s start with the scale of the threat. What’s been happening recently? Just last week, we’ve seen a wave of bomb threats across Europe. The latest target was Eurostar , which received a bomb threat on Thursday. Before that, schools in Italy , Ireland and Scotland had also been targeted. And we’ve seen attacks affecting all sorts of things, from aircraft to refrigerators. Now, these incidents don’t all have the same consequences. Some cause economic disruption, while others turn out to be hoaxes. But cyberattacks can also be used for election interference. Read more EU Commission to host security talks after week of bomb hoaxes that hit 20 airports and dozens of European flights Are we as vulnerable as it sometimes seems? Well, the EU has developed a number of tools to tackle cyber threats. But there are still some significant weaknesses. Take cooperation, for example. The EU has established several mechanisms to help countries and institutions share information and coordinate their responses. Because this is crucial when it comes to such coordinated attacks. But in September , the European Court of Auditors published a rather critical assessment. It concluded that EU action only partially facilitates the detection of and response to major cybersecurity incidents. Information sharing is still limited, reporting procedures have weaknesses, and there are considerable delays in putting some of the mechanisms into operation. Even within a single country, several different authorities may be responsible for cybersecurity. So the challenge is to make sure they all follow compatible procedures and can communicate as smoothly as possible. Before coordinating anything, you need to focus on preventing attacks. Here the idea is to make systems as secure as possible, so that attacks can be prevented or their impact limited. This is an ongoing effort, at every level. The EU Agency for Cybersecurity, ENISA , plays an important role here. It provides guidance to public authorities and businesses, helps identify emerging threats and supports the development of more secure digital products and services. The EU has also introduced legislation to set minimum cybersecurity requirements. One of the main pieces of legislation is the NIS 2 Directive , which has been in force since October 2024. It requires organisations operating in critical sectors, such as energy, transport, healthcare and digital infrastructure, to put security measures and procedures in place to manage cyber risks and respond to incidents. Read more Divided EU cyber defence faces real-life Russian and Chinese threats And is it working? Are these sectors actually becoming better protected? Well, there are signs of progress, but the picture is uneven. ENISA regularly assesses the cybersecurity maturity of Europe’s critical sectors. In its latest assessment, it found that sectors such as electricity, telecommunications and banking are relatively well prepared. But it also identified significant weaknesses in other areas, including healthcare, gas, maritime transport, public administration, space and information and communication technologies. So the level of protection still varies considerably depending on the sector. Beyond prevention, there’s the question of responding to an attack. Have Europeans learned to react quickly enough? Here again, they’re working on it. Every year, EU member states and the European Commission take part in large-scale cybersecurity exercises. These simulations are designed to test how authorities respond to major incidents and identify weaknesses in their coordination. But in real life, response times can vary enormously, depending on the type of attack and how sophisticated it is. And sometimes, simply identifying who’s behind an attack can take a long time. Take the incidents involving the manipulation of the temperatures in refrigerators in France, for example. It took around a month to identify the suspected perpetrators, in this case a group linked to the Iranian regime. Read more Listen: When does a hybrid attack become an attack on Nato? And there’s another figure worth keeping in mind. According to Google’s Mandiant cybersecurity research, the median time an attacker remained inside a compromised system before being detected was 14 days worldwide in the latest figures cited here. All in all, despite the growing number of agencies, regulations and initiatives dedicated to cybersecurity, the threat keeps evolving. And the biggest challenge isn’t necessarily a lack of tools or money. The EU is investing heavily in cybersecurity, including around €1.4bn through its Digital Europe programme over the current budget period. The real challenge is making sure all these tools work together.

noticias.titulo: THIS WEEK: EU piles on more Russia sanctions, a crunch UK-EU summit, and budget wrangles
noticias.resumen: The draft new sanctions list includes Russia's richest woman, Tatyana Kim, as well as dozens of Russian banks and propagandists, with both France and Germany saying that the extra sanctions were already a done deal.
noticias.texto:
The EU aims to blacklist Russia’s richest woman on Monday (16 November) despite the US push for a Ukraine peace deal, while also inking a new post-Brexit accord with the UK later in the week.
Foreign ministers meeting in Brussels on Monday will impose visa bans and asset freezes on 137 Russian individuals and entities, according to internal proposals seen by EUobserver on Friday.
The list includes Russia’s richest woman, Tatyana Kim, who is the CEO of online retailer Wildberries, as well as dozens of Russian banks and propagandists, with both France and Germany saying on Friday that the extra sanctions were already a done deal.

noticias.titulo: Romania regrets failure of Francophonie chief election
noticias.resumen: Romania has expressed regret after the 20th Summit of the International Organisation of La Francophonie ...
noticias.texto: Romania has expressed regret after the 20th Summit of the International Organisation of La Francophonie in Phnom Penh failed to elect a new Secretary-General, postponing the decision by one year amid an inability to reach consensus among member states. The closed-door session of the 53 full members on 16 November 2026 ended without selecting a successor for the 2027–2030 term. Instead, the mandate of the incumbent, Louise Mushikiwabo of Rwanda, was extended for one year. She will not be eligible to stand again, and an extraordinary summit is to be convened by the end of 2027. Other existing candidacies remain valid, and new ones may be submitted. Four candidates had been in the race: Mushikiwabo (seeking a third term), Dacian Cioloș (Romania’s official candidate and a former prime minister and European Commissioner), Juliana Lumumba (Democratic Republic of the Congo), and Coumba Ba (Mauritania). Under the organisation’s 2022 rules, the process prioritises consensus among full members; failing that, a simple majority vote applies. Formal candidacy files and ministerial hearings had already taken place earlier in the year. Cioloș, whose candidacy was backed by Romanian President Nicușor Dan, who attended the summit to promote it as a boost to Romania’s international profile, described the outcome as “a very sad day for our organisation” that risks leaving deep traces. He argued that the absolute priority must be rebuilding trust among member states, warning that the Francophonie cannot function effectively if candidates are rejected on regional grounds or if states refuse to accept the prospect of defeat. He also called for limiting the Secretary-General’s terms to a maximum of two and introducing greater geographic rotation. African deadlock The deadlock was widely linked to tensions between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo over the conflict in eastern Congo. Kinshasa accuses Kigali of supporting the M23 armed group operating in the mineral-rich east, an allegation also made by the United States and United Nations experts; Rwanda denies the claims and has pointed instead to security threats from other armed groups. The DRC had previously signalled willingness to withdraw its own candidate in favour of a consensus figure, with some reports indicating openness to supporting Cioloș. Mediation efforts, including by France, did not produce an agreement that would allow a choice to be made at the summit. Romanian officials and media have framed the result as a diplomatic disappointment rather than a direct electoral defeat of Cioloș. His candidacy remains open for the postponed process in 2027. The episode has highlighted the difficulty of insulating the organisation’s leadership selection from broader African geopolitical rivalries. Caption: From left to right: Romanian President Nicușor Dan , Swiss Confederation Vice President Ignazio Cassis, Dacian Cioloș , Romania’s official candidate for Francophonie chief and a former prime minister and European Commissioner . [Dacian Cioloș on X]

noticias.titulo: The EU landmark plan for more sustainable and competitive tourism explained
noticias.resumen: European Commission presented in early November the first comprehensive EU Strategy for Sustainable Tourism, setting ...
noticias.texto: European Commission presented in early November the first comprehensive EU Strategy for Sustainable Tourism, setting out a coordinated framework to reinforce the competitiveness, sustainability and green transition of one of Europe’s most economically and culturally significant sectors. The strategy responds to mounting pressures that can no longer be managed through promotion alone, including demographic change, climate impacts, geopolitical uncertainty near the Union’s borders and the uneven distribution of visitors that leaves some destinations overcrowded while others remain underused. Tourism generates roughly 10 per cent of the European Union’s gross domestic product and supports more than 20 million jobs. Nearly all of the five million tourism enterprises in the bloc are small and medium-sized businesses. In 2025 the sector contributed 4.1 per cent of the EU’s gross value added; when its effects on related industries are included the figure rises to 10.1 per cent. Europe continues to attract about 40 per cent of the world’s international tourists, a position the Commission describes as both an economic asset and a source of soft power that shapes the Union’s global image. Yet the same success has exposed structural vulnerabilities. Forty-two per cent of all overnight stays still occur in the three peak summer months, concentrating pressure on a limited number of popular sites while other regions struggle to attract year-round demand. Climate-related events, labour shortages and disruptions linked to conflicts have further tested the sector’s capacity to adapt. Although tourism policy remains primarily a national competence, the Commission argues that the single market and climate frameworks give the Union both the responsibility and the tools to coordinate action. The new strategy therefore focuses on supporting national and regional authorities and destination management organisations, which stand on the front line of daily management. It also seeks to reduce administrative burdens on businesses, improve access to skills and data, and create mechanisms for more balanced visitor flows. Balancing flows and building shared data infrastructure A central pillar of the strategy is the more even distribution of tourists across seasons and territories. The Commission plans to table a proposal for a unified EU model for tourism management in the second half of 2027, accompanied by a draft Council Recommendation on balanced tourism management and a practical toolkit for destinations. These instruments are intended to help authorities spread demand beyond traditional hotspots and peak months. Parallel work is under way to complete the European Tourism Data Space, a shared digital platform that will allow the exchange of visitor numbers, accommodation data and trend indicators among member states. Officials stress that high-quality, timely information is essential if local decision-makers are to manage capacity effectively and communicate the benefits of data sharing to businesses. Eastern Member States, including Bulgaria and Romania, have drawn particular attention to the need for the forthcoming Multiannual Financial Framework 2028–2034 to reflect the specific challenges faced by destinations whose tourism economies have been affected by the war in Ukraine. The current MFF already contains instruments that can support tourism infrastructure, digitalisation, innovation and skills; the Commission is urging governments to make fuller use of them while preparing for expanded opportunities under the next budget cycle. Modernisation of VAT rules for the tourism sector and measures to ease administrative requirements on destinations are also envisaged, with a clear emphasis on strengthening the competitiveness of the SMEs that dominate the industry. Sustainability, skills and crisis readiness Environmental sustainability forms a second major strand. The Commission intends to encourage businesses and destinations to reduce their climate footprint through circular practices that cut waste of food, water and energy, and through wider adoption of environmental, social and governance principles. Island and mountain regions, which often face acute pressure on resources during peak periods, are expected to benefit especially. Sustainable transport receives specific attention. Earlier proposals to facilitate multi-operator rail journeys have met resistance from carriers and some national parliaments, yet the Commission still plans to revise passenger rights by 2028 with the aim of improving accessibility. Cultural and natural assets are presented not as obstacles to growth but as assets that can reinforce it, illustrated by existing networks of mountain trails and huts that already combine heritage, public health, conservation and rural development. Workforce challenges are addressed through the planned European Tourism Academy, scheduled to open by 2027 and designed to deliver training leading to micro-credentials. A study on working conditions is due in the second half of 2028, while the broader Quality Jobs Act, expected before the end of 2026, is intended to raise standards across the labour market. Member states are also encouraged to use existing tools such as the Seasonal Workers Directive and the forthcoming EU Talent Pool to attract skilled labour from outside the Union. To improve preparedness for crises – whether drones near eastern borders, airspace disruptions linked to conflict in the Middle East, or climate events such as forest fires – the Commission is establishing a European Tourism Crisis Coordination Network. The network will bring together the Commission, national governments and regions to share information rapidly; private operators may contribute by designating “safe havens” for travellers in emergencies. Industry representatives have broadly welcomed the strategy. The European Travel Agents’ and Tour Operators’ Associations described it as a vision for balanced, connected and resilient travel, while the International Road Transport Union highlighted the first explicit recognition of the difficulties coach operators face with fragmented urban vehicle access rules. The European Travel Commission called the plan a positive step toward multi-level governance. Within the European Committee of the Regions, rapporteur Marga Prohens noted that the voice of island and tourism-dependent territories had been heard. The strategy’s ultimate aim is to keep Europe the world’s leading destination while ensuring that tourism delivers lasting benefits for residents as well as visitors. Sources: The European Regions Research and Innovation Network (ERRIN), European Commission announcements, Update EU Caption: People walk along a street lined with bistros and souvenir shops, in Montmartre, Paris, France, 1 August 2025. The Montmartre district in northern Paris welcomes about 11 million visitors each year, with local residents raising concerns about ‘overtourism’ fueled by the popularity of films and TV series such as Amelie and Emily in Paris, among others. EPA/TERESA SUAREZ

noticias.titulo: Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan advance the “Caspian Bridge” as core upgrade to the Middle Corridor
noticias.resumen: In early November 2026, Kazakhstan’s Samruk-Kazyna and Azerbaijan’s AZCON Holding signed a cooperation agreement to ...
noticias.texto: In early November 2026, Kazakhstan’s Samruk-Kazyna and Azerbaijan’s AZCON Holding signed a cooperation agreement to prepare and implement the Caspian Bridge system. Separately, Kazakhstan Temir Zholy and Azerbaijan Railways signed a term sheet for a joint intermodal cargo terminal at Azerbaijan’s Port of Alat. These steps address one of the Middle Corridor’s main bottlenecks: the Caspian Sea segment, where ferry capacity, reliability, and handling efficiency have constrained growth. The core purpose of the Caspian Bridge is to act as an integrated sea-ferry and terminal network across the Caspian Sea connecting Kazakh ports (such as Aktau and Kuryk) with Azerbaijani infrastructure (such as Baku and Alat). The ferry concept envisions modern, high-capacity vessels running regular services between Kazakhstan’s Kuryk port and Alat, with specialized terminals and integrated logistics so that the Caspian crossing functions more like an extension of the rail network – reducing the need to unload and reload cargo. Project targets call for guaranteed annual cargo volumes of 8 million tonnes, with capacity expected to rise to 10–12 million tonnes. Discussions around the agreements also covered joint terminal infrastructure, industrial cooperation in locomotives and shipbuilding, tariff policy, and measures to shorten transit times toward Europe. This bilateral work supports broader trilateral coordination. Georgia’s Deputy Prime Minister Mariam Kvrivishvili has noted that Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Kazakhstan have developed a joint plan aimed at scaling freight through the Middle Corridor, including a target of 30 million tonnes by 2029 through coordinated regional measures. The Middle Corridor (Trans-Caspian International Transport Route) links China and Central Asia through Kazakhstan, across the Caspian to Azerbaijan, then via Georgia (including the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars railway) and Turkey or Black Sea ports toward Europe. Opinion: Kazakhstan needs to turn Middle Corridor into economic growth It has seen rising demand as an alternative to northern routes. Container volumes have grown substantially, with transit times from China to Georgia or Turkey ports often in the 13–17-day range and ambitions for more predictable 10–12-day services. A September 2026 World Bank report estimates that coordinated infrastructure investment and operational reforms could more than triple trade volumes along the corridor and cut travel times by half by 2040 (or more with stronger efficiency gains), while raising regional GDP and creating jobs. The Bank highlights the need for over $25 billion in physical infrastructure through 2040, focused on rail, ports, and connections, with many priority projects already underway. The Caspian Bridge agreements, combined with ongoing rail, port, and coordination efforts by the three countries (including the Middle Corridor Multimodal joint structure), aim to make the route more reliable and competitive for Asia-Europe trade. In terms of broader connectivity, the Caspian Bridge ties into broader regional efforts like the Aral–Caspian Highway project and digital/energy corridor developments in Central Asia and the South Caucasus. In her 2026 State of the European Union address, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced that Bulgaria would host a major Regional Connectivity Summit in spring 2027, focused on strengthening links along routes such as the Middle Corridor. Caption: Ferry terminal at the Kazakh port of Aktau [The Astana Times]

noticias.titulo: The Cyprus issue: the grand bargain with Turkey, GSI, gas and Eastern Mediterranean balances
noticias.resumen: António Guterres’ effort to hand over an active Cyprus process to his successor, the European ...
noticias.texto: António Guterres’ effort to hand over an active Cyprus process to his successor, the European proposal on Turkey’s Customs Union and the possibility of extending Maria Angela Holguin’s mandate are shaping a new diplomatic landscape, with 2027 on the horizon, writes Dionysis Dionysiou. Dionysis Dionysiou is chief editor of EUalive’s partner Politis. The diplomatic activity surrounding the Cyprus issue is now taking on dimensions that go beyond efforts to restart negotiations. If it is true that the search for a settlement is linked to EU-Turkey relations, Greek-Turkish ties, energy planning in the Eastern Mediterranean and the new security balances taking shape in the region, then developments cannot be ruled out. In recent years, Turkey has shown little meaningful willingness to treat the Cyprus issue as a standalone priority. Instead, it appears to assess any restart through the prism of its broader strategic and economic interests. This is precisely what Nicosia and Brussels are seeking to leverage by linking progress on Cyprus to the prospect of upgrading the EU-Turkey Customs Union. The visit of European Commission Special Representative Raffaele Fitto to Ankara on 20 November forms part of this approach. According to Greek Cypriot sources, the proposal he is expected to convey to Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan concerns the launch of discussions on modernising the Customs Union, provided there is a substantive resumption of Cyprus negotiations. This is not a pre-emptive concession to Turkey, the same sources say, but a process of reciprocal moves in which European benefits would be linked to concrete progress. The five-party conference passes through the crossing points At the diplomatic level, the 9 November agreement on the simultaneous opening of two new crossing points, Louroudjina and Lympia, as well as Kampos and Karavostasi, enabled the UN Secretary-General’s Personal Envoy, María Ángela Holguín, to keep the process alive, even though the results were more than modest. According to a United Nations source, it would be particularly important at the forthcoming trilateral meeting between Guterres, Cyprus President Nikos Christodoulides and Turkish Cypriot leader Tufan Erhürman to reach agreement on the two other main crossing points, Mia Milia and Athienou via Pyroi to Aglandjia. Such a development would significantly strengthen the prospects of convening an informal five-party conference before the end of 2026, providing Guterres with tangible evidence that the two sides can overcome their differences. The outgoing Secretary-General is seeking to hand over an active process to his successor, potentially with an agreed roadmap, timetable and methodology for restarting talks in 2027. In that scenario, an extension of Holguín’s mandate could also be considered. Her continued presence would ensure continuity of contacts during the transition to new UN leadership, particularly if talks advance in parallel with a European process of engagement with Turkey. GSI changes the landscape Meanwhile, another development is attracting considerable geopolitical interest. The resumption of surveys for construction of the Great Sea Interconnector (GSI), the subsea electricity cable linking Greece and Cyprus, appears to be taking place under conditions of temporary Turkish tolerance. The departure of the French survey vessel Abeille Marengo and the associated NAVTEX notices signal the resumption of the necessary technical work, although they do not yet indicate the start of cable laying. Despite its initial objections, Ankara appears, for the time being, to have chosen not to obstruct the surveys while maintaining its claims regarding maritime jurisdictions. French firm Meridiam takes majority control of Great Sea Interconnector The significance of this development extends beyond the electricity interconnection itself. Greece, leveraging both French participation and European support, is contributing to the creation of a broader framework of economic and energy cooperation in the Eastern Mediterranean. The electricity link between Greece and Cyprus, with the prospect of extension to Israel, together with the development of Cypriot natural gas through Egypt, could become complementary infrastructure within a regional energy market. Over time, should the Cyprus issue be resolved and Greek-Turkish relations normalised, even Turkey could participate in this framework of cooperation. Instead of a region characterised by competing energy strategies, a network of interdependencies linking Europe with the Eastern Mediterranean could emerge. Natural gas and Turkey’s interests The energy dimension provides Ankara with an additional potential incentive. Estimates for the natural gas potential of Cyprus’ exclusive economic zone stand at around 20 trillion cubic feet. These volumes do not correspond entirely to proven commercially recoverable reserves. At present, Egypt is the principal destination in plans for the utilisation of Cypriot natural gas, either for domestic consumption or for re-export to European markets. Cypriot offshore gas to be sent to European markets using Egyptian infrastructure An agreed Cyprus settlement, combined with the new drilling programme Exxon is preparing for 2027, could allow the Turkish Cypriot community to participate in the management of the natural resources of a unified federal state. By extension, it would also create prospects for Turkey on energy cooperation that currently remain politically constrained. Ankara’s interest is not merely theoretical. It is already advancing plans for energy links with the northern part of Cyprus, including the prospect of wider regional utilisation. The Israel relationship and the security dimension There is, however, a second strategic reason why a settlement could serve Turkey’s long-term interests. It relates to preventing further military polarisation in the Eastern Mediterranean. Cooperation among Cyprus, Greece and Israel has already expanded beyond economics and energy. It includes joint exercises, defence planning, infrastructure protection and the exploration of cooperation in the defence industry. For Ankara, this relationship is seen as the emergence of a strategic axis that limits Turkish influence in the region. Some Turkish analysts even speak of encirclement and, by extension, a direct threat. The possibility that trilateral cooperation could evolve into a more structured military arrangement would intensify mistrust and competition. Such a development would not inevitably lead to conflict. However, when combined with existing disputes over maritime zones, it could increase the risk of military incidents or uncontrolled escalation, with serious consequences for the entire region. A Cyprus settlement could act as a de-escalation factor, reducing the need for competing regional military alignments and strengthening the economic content of Cyprus-Israel cooperation. This does not mean that defence cooperation among the three countries would come to an end. It could, however, create a different environment in which Turkey would no longer view every regional initiative as a potential threat but would itself have an interest in participating in a system of economic and energy interdependence. A political race against time For the Republic of Cyprus, the resumption of substantive negotiations inevitably entails a significant reshaping of domestic political discourse. Discussion of governance, security, guarantees, territorial adjustment and property issues will require repositioning by all political forces, particularly in view of the 2028 presidential elections. The cost of negotiation, however, must be weighed against the consequences of continued stagnation. In the northern part of Cyprus, realities are becoming entrenched that make the prospect of reunification increasingly difficult. Growing economic dependence on Turkey, demographic changes and the strengthening of Turkish influence over institutions and daily life are gradually limiting the political and economic autonomy of the Turkish Cypriot community. Extending the current status quo does not preserve unchanged the conditions for a future settlement. On the contrary, it allows new faits accomplis to become entrenched, making an agreement progressively more difficult. Nicosia therefore faces a moment that requires political preparation and strategic thinking, without underestimating the substantial challenges of negotiation. The major challenge for 2027 is whether Turkey will conclude that the economic, energy and geopolitical benefits of a credible settlement process outweigh those of its current policy. If that happens, the five-party conference and any accompanying roadmap could become the starting point of a different course. Ultimately, the real stake is not only the future of the Cyprus issue. It is whether the Eastern Mediterranean will evolve into a region of economic cooperation and interdependence or remain an arena of competing strategies and growing military tension. Caption: Visit of Raffaele Fitto, Executive Vice-President of the European Commission for Cohesion and Reforms, to Cyprus, 25 June 2026. With Cyprus President Nikos Christodoulides and UN special envoy for Cyprus Maria Angela Holguin. [Europe by Satellite]

noticias.titulo: Strong backlash after Serbian nationalist song at EU enlargement forum
noticias.resumen: Kosovo officials and European Parliament members have sharply criticised the European Commission after a Serbian ...
noticias.texto: Kosovo officials and European Parliament members have sharply criticised the European Commission after a Serbian patriotic song was performed on Sunday at the opening of the EU Enlargement Forum in Brussels, demanding explanations from Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos and the Commission. Kosovo’s chief negotiator Jeton Zulfaj and Ambassador Agron Bajrami described the performance as scandalous and unacceptable, arguing that a song linked to Serbian historical claims over Kosovo had no place at an EU event dedicated to enlargement, reconciliation and good-neighbourly relations. Estonian MEP Riho Terras (EPP Group), the Parliament’s rapporteur for Kosovo, called the choice either a deliberate provocation or sheer ignorance and said the Commission and Kos owed Kosovo an explanation. The song in question, “Oj Kosovo, Kosovo”, was performed instrumentally on 15 November 2026 by the Slovenian ensemble Marko Hatlak & Kapobanda during the invitation-only opening concert titled “Melodies of Unity”. The concert formed part of the official programme of the European Commission-hosted Enlargement Forum, which was opened by Commissioner Kos. Kosovo itself was not represented at the main Forum the following day. Scandalous: Serbian nationalist song against Kosovo performed on the eve of the EU Enlargement Forum, led by Marta Kos pic.twitter.com/WyChQI8Gg8 — Muhamet Hajrullahu (@MetiHajrullahu) November 15, 2026 The episode has drawn additional attention because of longstanding allegations against Kos that continue to be pressed by figures linked to the European People’s Party. Slovenian historian Igor Omerza has published archival documents he interprets as showing that Kos collaborated with the Yugoslav State Security Service (UDBA/SDV) in the late 1980s under the codenames Tara and Blanka. Either a deliberate provocation or sheer ignorance. Performing a Serbian nationalist song asserting claims over Kosovo at an EU enlargement event is an extraordinarily tactless and tasteless blunder. @EU_Commission and @MartaKosEU owe Kosovo an explanation❗️ pic.twitter.com/yyMg3Ptfxs — Riho Terras (@RihoTerras) November 15, 2026 Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Janša (SDS/EPP) and EPP MEP Romana Tomc have repeatedly raised these claims, with Tomc previously calling for a special European Parliament hearing and further investigation. Kos has consistently denied ever being a collaborator or informant of the Yugoslav services, describing the allegations as lies and noting that she passed the Commission’s full vetting process. It is not yet clear who selected the specific song or whether the Commission pre-approved the repertoire. The shared Slovenian background of Kos and the performing band does not, on current evidence, establish a direct link. The incident nonetheless highlights both the sensitivity of cultural programming in the Western Balkans context and the unresolved questions about the Commissioner’s past that EPP-affiliated politicians continue to pursue. EPP secures special hearing to grill Marta Kos over alleged Yugoslav secret police ties Caption: Marta Kos, European Commissioner for Enlargement attends a press conference on the Enlargement package following the read-out of the College meeting in Brussels, Belgium, 4 November 2026. EPA/OLIVIER MATTHYS

noticias.titulo: Moldova’s restive Gagauzia heads to runoff after low-turnout vote
noticias.resumen: Voters in Moldova’s restive, pro-Russian autonomous region of Gagauzia went to the polls on Sunday ...
noticias.texto: Voters in Moldova’s restive, pro-Russian autonomous region of Gagauzia went to the polls on Sunday to elect a new bashkan (governor) and members of the People’s Assembly. Eight candidates vied for the position of bashkan of Gagauzia, a region in Moldova’s south inhabited mainly by Turkic-speaking Orthodox Christians who generally favour close ties with Russia. With all 67 protocols counted, no candidate secured the absolute majority needed to win outright, sending the contest to a second round expected on 29 November between independent candidate Alexandr Stoianoglo and Fiodor Gagauz of the Party of Socialists (PSRM). According to the Central Electoral Commission and multiple Moldovan outlets, Stoianoglo (a former Prosecutor General and current MP) took 38.44% (18,136 votes). Fiodor Gagauz followed with 24.22% (11,426 votes). Independent Cornel Dudnic placed third on 15.59% (7,354), followed by Ivanna Koksal (11.05%), Serghei Anastasov (4.72%), Oleg Garizan (3.18%), Petru Vlah (1.98%) and Ivan Cîlcic (0.83%). Turnout stood at 37.60% (around 48,749 voters), above the 25% threshold for validity but well below typical levels and reflecting apparent voter fatigue or disillusionment. One local race (Baurci) was declared invalid due to sub-25% turnout. Background and candidates The bashkan post has been vacant since Evghenia Guțul (Gutsul) was sentenced to seven years in prison on charges of illegally channeling Russian funds to finance the Shor party. The Șor (Shor) Party was a pro-Russian populist party in Moldova, founded in 1998 and later led by fugitive oligarch Ilan Shor (convicted in the 2014 “theft of the century” bank fraud), which Moldova’s Constitutional Court banned as unconstitutional in June 2023 after it organized anti-government protests accused of seeking to destabilize the country. Guțul denied the charges and accused the pro-European authorities of political persecution; Moscow has repeatedly condemned her imprisonment. The People’s Assembly’s term had also expired, contributing to prolonged deadlock. Elections were held under national rules after Constitutional Court rulings curbed aspects of the region’s control over electoral bodies. Stoianoglo, born in Comrat, previously served as Gagauzia’s prosecutor and Moldova’s Prosecutor General before entering politics. He ran (with Socialist backing) against President Maia Sandu in the 2024 presidential runoff, taking roughly 44–45% nationally and dominating Gagauzia. He has run for bashkan before without success. Fiodor Gagauz is the candidate of the main pro-Russian opposition party. Both frontrunners are widely viewed as critical of Sandu’s government and its strong pro-EU, anti-Russian orientation. Gagauzia’s roughly 150,000 residents (predominantly ethnic Gagauz—Turkic-speaking Orthodox Christians) have long favored closer ties with Russia and largely rejected Moldova’s pro-EU referendum. Police recorded a limited number of violations (illegal campaigning, organized voter transport, one case of aggressive behavior). Independent observers from Promo-LEX reported dozens of incidents involving ballot secrecy, mobile voting procedures, unauthorized persons near stations, and campaigning. Pre-election monitoring had also flagged misuse of administrative resources and online advertising surges. Parallel developments and Russian designs The same day, Transnistrian leader Vadim Krasnoselski returned to Chișinău after receiving Russia’s Order of Honour from Vladimir Putin in Moscow. He was observed at the airport and reportedly escorted for procedures; the government confirmed his arrival and announced a five-year exit ban linked to the Moscow visit and his statements framing Transnistria as part of the “Russian world.” Promo-LEX has questioned the legal basis for the ban. Transnistria’s own “presidential” vote is scheduled for mid-December. These events unfold against a broader backdrop reported by the German outlet BILD just days earlier. According to the report, drawing on unofficial negotiation channels linked to efforts to end the war in Ukraine, Russia has floated transforming Moldova into a federal state comprising the territory controlled by Chișinău, Transnistria and Gagauzia. If Moldova joined the EU, the two pro-Russian regions would gain the right to hold independence referendums. In exchange, Moscow would reportedly withdraw its troops from Transnistria, pull nuclear weapons from Belarus and drop intermediate-range missile deployment plans there. BILD stressed that the ideas remain among several circulating proposals and it is unclear whether Putin has endorsed them. Moldovan government spokesperson Dumitru Ciorici dismissed such reports as “scare tactics and provocations” from Moscow aimed at derailing the country’s European path, stating that Chișinău remains focused on reforms and EU accession. Gagauzia and Transnistria have long been the two main vectors of Russian influence inside Moldova. The former is an internationally recognized autonomy within the unitary state; the latter is a de facto breakaway entity hosting Russian forces. A runoff between two candidates generally aligned with the opposition and skeptical of Sandu’s course keeps the region’s leadership outside the ruling party’s orbit, even as central authorities have tightened electoral and institutional oversight. Full results for the 35-seat People’s Assembly (majoritarian, 132 candidates) were still emerging, with one district requiring a re-run. This article draws on reporting by EUalive’s partners Nordnews and European Pravda . Caption: Fiodor Gagauz of the Party of Socialists (PSRM) casts his vote [@erKnoncn on X]

noticias.titulo: Iran renews attacks on Bahrain as prospects for U.S. peace deal fade
noticias.resumen: Iran launched a new drone attack against a U.S. military facility in Bahrain on Sunday, ...
noticias.texto: Iran launched a new drone attack against a U.S. military facility in Bahrain on Sunday, renewing its strikes against Gulf states and further dimming prospects for a diplomatic breakthrough with Washington. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it had targeted a U.S. air defence radar facility at the Riffa helicopter base with six drones, in retaliation for American strikes on Iranian territory. Bahrain’s military said its air defence systems had intercepted and destroyed the drones before they could reach their targets. U.S. Central Command spokesman Tim Hawkins said there had been no impact on American forces. Sunday’s attack was Iran’s second attempt to strike Bahrain in three days, following a period of relative calm since September. It came as the confrontation between Tehran and Washington remained deadlocked, with the U.S. maintaining a naval blockade of Iranian ports and Iran restricting shipping through the strategically important Strait of Hormuz. Sirens sounded across Bahrain on Sunday, prompting the country’s Interior Ministry to urge residents to remain calm and seek shelter at the nearest safe location. Bahrain’s Foreign Ministry condemned the renewed attacks as “heinous aggression” and a flagrant violation of international law, holding Tehran fully responsible for their consequences. “The kingdom also rejects the transformation of its territory into an arena for settling scores,” it said in a statement, dismissing Iran’s justifications for targeting the country as “flimsy pretexts and baseless claims”. Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Qatar also condemned the attacks and expressed solidarity with Bahrain. Tit-for-tat strikes deepen the stalemate Bahrain hosts a significant U.S. military presence, including the U.S. Fifth Fleet and U.S. Naval Forces Central Command, which serve as a key support hub for American military operations in the Middle East. The kingdom was repeatedly targeted by Iranian drones and missiles during the first months of the war, but had experienced a relative lull in attacks before Tehran resumed strikes on Friday. On that occasion, the IRGC claimed to have hit an American early-warning radar system in Bahrain. U.S. Central Command denied that the radar had been destroyed, saying American forces had shot down two Iranian one-way attack drones. It reported no injuries or damage. Tehran described Sunday’s operation as the second phase of a “decisive and crushing response” to U.S. military actions. In a statement carried by Iranian state media, the IRGC warned that the Strait of Hormuz remained closed and that any further American aggression would be met with an even stronger response. At a press conference in Tehran, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Iran would continue to respond to any military aggression by the U.S. or other countries. Asked whether the latest attacks signalled a change in Tehran’s approach as negotiations with Washington stalled, Baghaei said Iran was “not waiting for anyone” and was focused on its security. The renewed attacks follow a series of U.S. strikes against Iranian targets in recent weeks, including on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. officials described the strikes on Qeshm as limited and defensive, saying they were carried out in response to an attack by the IRGC on an American aircraft. Iranian state media subsequently reported explosions on the island. President Donald Trump has played down the scale of the latest American operations, describing them as minor strikes and saying Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states had cautioned him against launching large-scale combat operations. At the same time, Trump has said Washington is no longer interested in a deal to end the war with Iran. He has instructed Vice-President JD Vance, who had been involved in efforts to restart negotiations, to turn his attention to alleged corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states. Vance had requested a personal meeting with Iranian negotiators to discuss possible peace terms. He had also blamed the Republicans’ loss of Congress in the midterm elections on the war with Iran. The two sides had reached a preliminary understanding in June to end the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, but the arrangement collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and Washington reinstated its naval blockade of Iranian ports. Iranian negotiators had subsequently discussed a proposal with mediators to reopen the waterway within two days if the U.S. met seven conditions, reportedly including lifting the blockade and releasing frozen Iranian assets. However, diplomatic efforts have made little progress, leaving the two countries locked in a confrontation over control of the vital shipping route. About a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supplies normally pass through the Strait of Hormuz. Since the outbreak of the war in February, shipping has been severely restricted. Iran insists it should control the waterway and has attacked vessels it considers unauthorised, while the U.S. military has sought to protect tankers carrying oil from Gulf Arab states. U.S. and Iran exchange attacks as lull in war appears over Sources: The Guardian, BBC, The Washington Post Caption: People drive past a political billboard at Valiasr Square in central Tehran, Iran, 6 August 2026. According to Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei, Iran and Oman have been holding talks for the past two months to establish a safe navigation corridor for commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. EPA/ABEDIN TAHERKENAREH

noticias.titulo: Elecciones generales colegio
noticias.texto:
Elecciones generales 2026: cómo sé en qué colegio tengo que votar y cuándo me informan
- El próximo 29 de noviembre casi 39 millones de españoles están llamados a votar a las urnas
- Se puede consultar por internet la información; en RTVE Noticias te contamos como hacerlo
Los españoles acuden a las urnas este próximo 29 de noviembre. Ese domingo, cerca de 39 millones de electores están llamados a votar en todo el país en las elecciones generales.
El próximo 29 de noviembre casi 39 millones de españoles están llamados a votar a las urnas en las elecciones generales.
De cara a los comicios, las tres principales fuerzas parlamentarias han decidido mantener a sus candidatos actuales. Repiten Alberto Núñez Feijóo en el PP, Pedro Sánchez en el PSOE y Santiago Abascal en Vox. El cambio en el otro gran partido, el Frente Amplio, llega de la mano de Ada Colau, como cabeza de lista.
En los partidos soberanistas también se opta por la continuidad en líneas generales. Desde el espacio independentista en Cataluña, Gabriel Rufián, repite por ERC. Al igual que Míriam Nogueras en Junts. En el País Vasco, el PNV apuesta por Maribel Vaquero y EH Bildu opta por Oskar Matute. En Galicia y Canarias también deciden por mantener a sus candidatos. Por parte del BNG, Néstor Rego vuelve a ser el cabeza de lista de la formación y en Coalición Canaria repite Cristina Valido.
¿Cómo sé en qué colegio electoral tengo que votar y cuál es mi mesa electoral?
De cara al domingo electoral los votantes suelen recibir una carta en su domicilio con documentación y su tarjeta censal. Ahí se indica la mesa electoral y el colegio asignado al que tiene que acudir.
Sin embargo, si por algún motivo se ha extraviado, la has perdido o estás fuera de España y de tu domicilio habitual, se puede consultar por internet la información. El Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE) ha puesto a disposición de los electores un buscador para localizar tanto el colegio como la mesa en la que votar. Puedes consultarlo en ese enlace.
¿Cómo me identifico ante la mesa?
El día de las elecciones, el elector puede identificarse ante la mesa de diferentes maneras. Por un lado, con el DNI, aunque no sirve el resguardo de que está pedida la cita, porque no aparece fotografía del votante. También se pueden utilizar el pasaporte o el carné de conducir, ambos con fotografía. No importa que estos documentos estén caducados, pero deben ser los originales, no valen fotocopias.
¿A qué hora cierran los colegios electorales?
El 29 de noviembre la votación comenzará a las 9 horas, aunque los locales están abiertos antes para que puedan presentarse los miembros de las Mesas electorales y constituyan las mismas, verifiquen que no hay problemas con el material electoral (urnas, cabinas, mesas, soportes señalizadores, sobres, papeletas, impresos…), acrediten a los interventores, etc.
La votación terminará a las 20 horas. Sin embargo, si aún queda alguien dentro del local electoral, el presidente de la mesa le permitirá votar o si se ha abierto más tarde el centro electoral se podría ampliar el horario por circunstancias excepcionales.
