noticias.titulo: Nationwide ground stop could cost US airlines hundreds of millions
noticias.resumen: Airline executives support modernising FAA systems as US Transportation Secretary Duffy seeks $50bn from Congress.
noticias.texto:
Nationwide ground stop could cost US airlines hundreds of millions
Airline executives support modernising FAA systems as US Transportation Secretary Duffy seeks $50bn from Congress for FAA overhaul.
Following the nationwide ground stop last week, United States airlines could face a financial hit of hundreds of millions of dollars even as airline executives press for increased investment in ageing air traffic control infrastructure.
The four largest US airlines – American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Southwest Airlines – could face a combined hit of $345m to pretax earnings, according to brokerage firm Bernstein.
The effects of Friday’s ground stop continued to ripple through airline schedules on Monday, with more than 18,500 flights within, into or out of the US cancelled since the disruption began, according to FlightAware data.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CNBC on Monday that the wider impact of the disruption could run into the “billions of dollars”. No official estimate of the total economic cost has been released yet.
Flights were grounded across the country for more than four hours on Friday, and the disruption continued to affect airline schedules over the weekend.
Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian also said the financial impact could run into the “billions”, telling Fortune on Monday that the disruption underscored the need for greater investment in the country’s air traffic control infrastructure.
Bastian pointed to the vast sums investors are putting into artificial intelligence and data centres, adding that the US should also be investing in its aviation system.
“We can’t even get $50bn to fix our skies,” he said.
United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby agreed that the disruption should be a “call to action”, saying the air traffic control system needed greater investment in modern technology to improve its reliability.
Transportation Secretary Duffy has asked US Congress for $50bn for air traffic control and airport infrastructure upgrades, an addition to the $12.5bn lawmakers approved for air traffic control modernisation last year.
The existing system relies on outdated equipment and needs a comprehensive overhaul, he said.
But Democrats have questioned the request, saying only about $1bn of the $12.5bn already approved has been spent so far.
On Sunday, US President Donald Trump called on Congress to approve the funding, arguing that the upgrades should be carried out all at once rather than in stages.
“We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs. Congress must approve,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
The funding debate is moving into a narrow window for congressional action. The House and Senate are scheduled to convene once more before the end of the year.
Speaker Mike Johnson has said lawmakers will take up the administration’s funding request during the current Congress’s lame-duck session, but Democrats have demanded more information on how the money will be spent.
The precise cause of Friday’s failure remains under investigation. Duffy has said the problem began at a remote Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) site in Arkansas where workers from defence contractor L3Harris were replacing ageing copper wiring with fibre-optic cables.
The Government Accountability Office, the congressional watchdog, raised concerns about the FAA’s management of its modernisation programme in a September report. It found that the agency had not developed an integrated schedule for the first phase of upgrades, and warned that poor planning increased the risk of disrupting air traffic control operations.

noticias.titulo: Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of attempted ‘coup’
noticias.resumen: Rivals call for investigation into reports that PM's office tried to frame Arab parties.
noticias.texto:
Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of attempted ‘coup’
Political rivals call for investigation regarding media reports that Netanyahu’s office tried to frame Arab party members ahead of the elections.
Israeli opposition leaders have denounced an “attempted coup” by outgoing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The accusations on Monday came in response to media reports that Netanyahu’s office tried to falsely incriminate members of an Arab-led party before last month’s election, in which the premier’s Likud party was voted out of office.
“As more and more details come to light, it becomes clear: This wasn’t an attempt to disrupt the elections. It was an attempted coup,” opposition leader Yair Lapid said on social media.
Israel’s Channel 12 reported on Sunday that on the eve of the election, Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, called police with a complaint about members of the Ra’am party.
Norden reportedly pointed officers to a purported intelligence source – a former employee of Netanyahu’s office – who provided information that led to the arrest of three Ra’am members. They were later released after police determined the allegations were unfounded.
Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported on Sunday that the head of the Shin Bet domestic security service tried to wiretap leaders of the Arab-led Joint List, but the attorney general refused due to a lack of evidence.
Israeli police said in response that they will “review the decision-making and information-transmission process”. Likud has issued a statement denying the reports.
Following the vote, Netanyahu accused Arab parties of electoral fraud after they gained a record 19 seats in the Knesset.
‘Dark regime’
Yousef Jabareen, the leader of Joint List also decried “an attempted coup by Netanyahu,” and labelled the allegations regarding Shin Bet as “conduct characteristic of dark regimes”.
Ra’am deputy and former police chief Yoav Segalovitz called for an urgent investigation.
“Netanyahu cried out that his election was being stolen, while he himself tried to steal the country and is still trying to do so now,” he wrote on social media.
Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, wrote that departing prime minister was “a concrete, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy”.
Neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor Eisenkot’s opposition grouping secured the 61 seats required to form a government. However, Joint List and Raam have indicated they support Eisenkot to lead a coalition.

noticias.titulo: Five EU countries announce plan to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda
noticias.resumen: In a joint statement, 47 aid, trade union and rights groups urged ‌the five countries to ​abandon the Rwanda plan.
noticias.texto:
Five EU countries announce plan to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda
In a joint statement, 47 aid, trade union and rights groups urged the five countries to abandon the Rwanda plan.
Five European countries have announced a plan to send rejected asylum seekers to a processing centre in Rwanda as early as next year, drawing condemnation from rights groups who said it would leave vulnerable people at risk of abuse.
The planned scheme, which is still being negotiated with Rwanda, would send people to a centre where the migrants could choose to return home, settle or go somewhere else where they had a right to stay, Kigali said on Monday.
Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands said that the plan aimed to deter more people from migrating to Europe. The European Union has worked for years to tighten migration rules, reduce the number of asylum seekers arriving and increase deportations of migrants who are not entitled to stay.
“I think this will be a game changer, making us able to confront the massive challenges with illegal migration,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said. “We will break down the business model of human smugglers. We will take back control of our borders and we will remove the incentives for illegal migration.”
Rwanda’s interior minister, Vincent Biruta, said his country would give a “second chance” to people who have no right to stay in Europe.
He added that arrivals would be able “to voluntarily return to the countries of origin, integrate into Rwandan society or relocate to another destination where they have the legal right to reside, according to their preference”.
When asked how Kigali would ensure refugees’ human rights, Biruta said, “There will be an independent monitoring mechanism” and that it would cooperate with the United Nations’ refugee agency.
Human rights groups criticised the plans, saying that EU countries could not guarantee their rights would be respected there.
In a joint statement, 47 aid, trade union and rights groups urged the five countries to abandon the Rwanda plan — echoing criticisms of a different migration settlement plan between Britain and Rwanda in the early 2020s.
The plan “signals that Member States accept the risk of serious human rights violations against one of the most marginalized groups in society, in return for a deterrence goal that evidence clearly suggests they will not reach,” read the statement from the International Rescue Committee, the Dutch Council for Refugees and other groups.
A Human Rights Watch researcher said the deal “would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad”.
Germany’s interior minister said the European plan was not comparable to a scrapped 2022 deal with the United Kingdom because only those whose asylum claims are rejected will be sent to Rwanda.
The UK’s Supreme Court ruled that the 2022 deal was unlawful because Rwanda was not considered a safe third country to which migrants could be sent.

noticias.titulo: Saudi Arabia dismisses commander of coalition forces fighting Houthis
noticias.resumen: Move comes as government forces withdraw from Red Sea coast to halt Houthi approach to interim capital Aden.
noticias.texto:
Saudi Arabia dismisses commander of coalition forces fighting Houthis
Move comes as government forces withdraw from Red Sea coast to halt Houthi approach to interim capital Aden.
Saudi Arabia has replaced the commander overseeing its coalition forces as they battle the Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen.
King Salman issued a decree on Monday assigning General Fayyad al-Ruwaili to the command, according to Saudi state media. The removal of Lieutenant General Fahd bin Hamad al-Salman came as coalition forces were forced to abandon their recent push to recapture regions along the Red Sea coast in order to reinforce the Yemeni government’s interim capital, Aden.
Al-Salman was appointed as a military adviser to the Saudi defence minister a day after coalition forces were forced to withdraw.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government said on Sunday that coalition forces were withdrawing from areas near the key Bab al-Mandeb strait – via which Saudi oil exports have been flowing while the United States-Iran war stifles traffic through the Strait of Hormuz – to focus on defending Aden.
The retreat marked a major setback for the Saudi-backed campaign against the Houthis, who have been firing ballistic missiles at Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil facilities since Yemen’s civil war restarted in July.
A Houthi offensive in September saw the government lose control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the key port city of Mocha. Later Houthi advances also saw Taiz completely besieged by the Houthis.
Government forces – backed by the Saudi-led coalition – quickly retook key positions near Bab al-Mandeb after the Houthi advance on the strait and the Red Sea coast this summer, but have been unable to retake Mocha.
They have said they killed or wounded 173 Houthi fighters as part of Operation Dawn of Yemen and engaged the Houthis in Marib, Lahij and in al-Jawf.
However, they are now retreating from theterritory they held near the Bab al-Mandeb strait and preparing to fortify defences around Aden, after the Houthis advanced to an area 60 kilometres (37 miles) north of the city.
Yemeni Armed Forces spokesperson Majed al-Nuzaili defended the retreat, saying it was part of a wider tactical manoeuvre.
“[The redeployment] is an extension of the heroic positions of the popular resistance and the southern forces in protecting the temporary capital Aden,” he said on X.
As the fighting continues, civilians remain exposed. Houthi-affiliated media reported coalition air strikes on the capital Sanaa, which the Iran-backed group took in 2014, and said one person was killed in an attack on a school in Taiz.
Authorities in the besieged city of Taiz have called for humanitarian corridors to allow civilians to evacuate, as medical officials warned hospitals could be forced to end operations within two days due to a lack of fuel and oxygen.
Earlier on Monday, Saudi Arabia said it had shot down two Houthi drones targeting the Mecca and Riyadh regions.

noticias.titulo: Thousands report difficulties accessing accounts online at major US banks
noticias.resumen: Customers report online access issues at major US banks, including Chase, Wells Fargo, and Bank of America.
noticias.texto:
Thousands report difficulties accessing accounts online at major US banks
Customers report online access issues at major US banks, including Chase, Wells Fargo, and Bank of America.
Customers at five major banks in the United States are reporting outages, according to Downdetector, which tracks service disruptions online.
The impacted institutions include US Bank, Wells Fargo, Zelle, JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America, according to reports on Monday.
At Wells Fargo, for example, more than 800 customers reported issues, including problems with logins, account balances and fund transfers. At Chase, nearly 5,000 customers reported issues, 50 percent of which involved account balances and transactions.
“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” a Chase spokesperson said in a statement. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”
JPMorgan Chase says “bad actors” do not appear to be involved in the disruption, according to CNBC, which cited an unnamed source.
Al Jazeera reached out to all the major impacted banks but they did not respond to our request for comment.

noticias.titulo: Is Israel’s Eisenkot bloc less right wing than Netanyahu?
noticias.resumen: An Israeli government without PM Netanyahu may be close, but a government without his politics is far less certain.
noticias.texto:
Is Israel’s Eisenkot bloc less right wing than Netanyahu?
An Israeli government without caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may be close, but a government without his politics is far less certain.
As the long and complex negotiations to form Israel’s next government drag on, hopes are high that former military chief Gadi Eisenkot will be able to form a coalition that marks a break from the far-right and divisive politics of the previous administration.
The coalition brought together by the now-caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu brought figures from Israel’s far right into government. Beyond the genocidal war on Gaza following the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel, and repeated military strikes against neighbouring countries, the government sought to weaken judicial oversight and pursued an aggressive policy of illegal settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. There, settler pogroms against Palestinian communities have continued with near impunity.
“Likud sits further to the right than most conservative parties in Europe. Although historically it was thought of as something like the Conservative Party, today it looks like something of a far-right party,” said Roi Zur, an Israeli academic at the University of Essex, who has researched the comparison between Israeli parties and their international equivalents.
In contrast, Eisenkot and his opposition bloc have said that they will repeal the judicial overhaul legislation introduced by Netanyahu, establishing a state commission of inquiry into the security failings ahead of the October 7 attack, and ending the draft exemption offered to many ultra-Orthodox youth in defiance of a 2024 ruling by the Supreme Court.
But will a new government under Eisenkot – made up of a number of right-wing figures – really be any different from what has come before?
Here’s what we know.
What parties and politicians are likely to sit in government with Eisenkot?
As it stands, before any fresh alliances are brokered, there are five main political leaders of the opposition bloc.
Its leader, Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar Party, is generally regarded as a centrist security hawk.
Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid of the B’Yachad Party are considered right-wing and centre-liberal, respectively.
Avigdor Lieberman, the head of Yisrael Beiteinu, is secular and right-wing, while Yair Golan of the Democrats sits as the sole outlier on the left.
What do we know about Eisenkot’s politics?
Many observers regard Eisenkot’s politics as difficult to read.
While he has been broadly supportive of the genocidal war on Gaza, in which more than 74,600 Palestinians have been killed, and attacks on countries across the region, including the current war on Iran, little is known of his domestic politics.
His Yashar Party’s economic platform points towards a broadly pro-market approach, prioritising tax cuts over wealth redistribution.
On security, there is less ambiguity. Eisenkot is the architect of the Dahiya doctrine, an Israeli military strategy that calls for overwhelming force against areas from which Israel comes under attack.
Eisenkot warned in 2008 that Israel’s destruction of large parts of southern Beirut’s Dahiya area during the 2006 war on Lebanon “will happen in every village from which fire is launched toward Israel”. In March, he said the doctrine should again be used in Lebanon, noting it had “never been more relevant”.
Eisenkot has also firmly rejected the establishment of a Palestinian state, and supports the continued existence of illegal settlements in the West Bank, even though he has pledged to tackle settler violence.
How about the others in Eisenkot’s bloc?
The bloc may be viewed internationally as more moderate than Netanyahu, but its members also largely adopt right-wing positions towards Palestinians.
Bennett, a former settler council chief, opposes Palestinian statehood and has previously said that he favours annexing 60 percent of the West Bank. His political partner, Lapid, backs a two-state solution, but without any firm details, and then only in the long term.
Netanyahu’s former ally and now one of his fiercest critics, Lieberman has been vocal in his support of the expansion of illegal settlements.
Both Bennett and Lieberman have made incendiary comments about Palestinians. Bennett defended cutting off water and electricity to Palestinians in Gaza in October 2023, while Lieberman said in December 2023 that there were “no innocents in Gaza”.
Bennett and Lapid have led a government in the past: their 2021 coalition included the United Arab List (Ra’am), a party representing Palestinian citizens of Israel. But it eventually collapsed the next year, partly because it was split over privileges settlers received in the West Bank.
However, while something can be gleaned from Bennett and Lapid’s time in office, how the contrasting visions of the left-wing Golan and the right-wing Lieberman will work in the same coalition remains to be seen.
“Golan and the party he is heading, the Democrats, are a merger of two Zionist left-wing parties, the centre-left Labour and the harder-left Meretz,” said Or Tuttnauer, interim professor at the University of Mannheim, who has studied the Israeli opposition. “The party holds liberal, progressive, dovish, secular positions.”
In contrast, Tuttnauer said, Lieberman and his right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu party sought to define themselves against others holding similar positions through both his emphasis on secularism and fierce opposition to Netanyahu.
Can the potential new coalition be considered more liberal in any way?
Any country that depends on the military occupation of roughly 7,252 square kilometres (2,800 square miles) of Palestinian and Syrian territory, and rules over some 5.5 million Palestinians who have no vote in the state that controls them, is unlikely to be considered progressive or liberal.
Beyond its foreign policy, however, Israel’s society has been shifting steadily to the right, a trend that polling suggests accelerated sharply following the October 7, 2023 attack.
“Many people have pinned their hopes on Netanyahu leaving, imagining that a moderate or even progressive government would follow,” HA Hellyer of the Royal United Services Institute said. “But the problem was never just Netanyahu. His absence would only expose how far the rest of the Israeli political spectrum, including much of the opposition, shares the same positions on occupation and Palestinian rights.”
“It will take years before Israelis, the public and not just their leaders, accept the case for withdrawing from Gaza, the occupied West Bank, or even Syria and southern Lebanon,” Hellyer said. “Ending the occupation and dismantling apartheid all entail recognising that these things have happened first.”

noticias.titulo: Abdul El-Sayed’s victory is a blow to the politics of Islamophobia
noticias.resumen: He embraced his Muslim identity, put Gaza on the ballot and showed Democrats a different way forward.
noticias.texto:
Abdul El-Sayed’s victory is a blow to the politics of Islamophobia
He embraced his Muslim identity, put Gaza on the ballot and showed Democrats a different way forward.
The blue wave that swept Republicans from their congressional majorities and brought Democrats back into the spotlight was called everything from a flood to a political earthquake. In a montage on The Daily Show, TV anchors reduced the night to a gleeful succession of words and phrases like “rout” and “shellacking”. On Zeteo’s election-night coverage with Mehdi Hasan, Prem Thakker coined the term “Tsunamanani”, a brief injection of comic irony amid serious news and analysis. The night was all those things.
Arguably the most significant victory of the congressional sweep was Abdul El-Sayed’s win over Trump-backed extremist Mike Rogers, whose candidacy was propped up by roughly $169 million in outside spending benefiting him, including spending by Republican super PACs tied to Donald Trump and Elon Musk. El-Sayed will be the first Muslim ever to grace the floor of the US Senate.
It was hard to look away from the joy on El-Sayed’s face as he shared the win. His words were just as striking, offering a vision of how American politics could be redirected towards peace and humanity. He told the crowd:“Michiganders, we want our taxes spent here, for schools here and healthcare here, and infrastructure here. We don’t want our money sent to do apartheid or genocide or war.”
When he said, “My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, and I am so proud and honored to stand here as your senator elect,” the crowd roared. Throughout the campaign, right-wing enthusiasts had used his whole name to brand him a “terrorist”, a “jihadist” and “a danger to the American public”. By pronouncing that name, complete with its Arabic intonation, he reclaimed what pundits and politicians, including Donald Trump, had spent months mocking. Later in the speech, El-Sayed joked, “Donald, look, I know you struggled with my name, so after JD swears me in in January, you could just go on and call me Senator.” The crowd roared again.
He also said, “You might have noticed, I always say Inshallah, or God willing, whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned. But today, tonight, we can turn that Inshallah into a…”
One minute and twenty seconds into his speech, the crowd shouted the answer together: “Alhamdulillah!” Then the hall filled with chants of “Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul!”
Still smiling, El-Sayed added, “For the right-wing ops, that just means praise be to God.”
When we heard the thunderous applause for his name and for “Alhamdulillah”, one of the most common yet sacred expressions in Islam, it felt as though a deeply entrenched stereotype about Islam and Muslims was being shattered, undermining the Islamophobia that has been used to stir fear and hatred in American politics.
With no meaningful policy accomplishments to point to and a wildly unpopular Donald Trump, Republicans resorted to a relentlessly bigoted smear campaign against El-Sayed.
The attacks he faced were part of a broader pattern of organised anti-Muslim prejudice, extending beyond bots and social media influencers into Republican politics and policymaking. As documented by the Center for the Study of Organized Hate, this hostility was being promoted through social media, legislation and a congressional caucus. According to the CSOH, 89 Republican elected officials took part in a coordinated anti-Muslim campaign over thirteen months: 46 of them published 1,111 social media posts, eight Sharia-related bills were introduced, and the Sharia-Free America Caucus grew to 62 members by April 2026.
Political advisers told El-Sayed that “someone with a name and my story, a Muslim, was unelectable”, as if anti-Muslim prejudice were an immovable grassroots bias. In reality, it was a prejudice deliberately cultivated and promoted with millions of dollars from billionaire funders, most of them Zionists.
When he entered the race for the US Senate, El-Sayed accepted the challenge of confronting the toxic Islamophobia built on the othering of Muslims and Islam. He refused to be demonised or to accept the artificial divide between “us” and “them”, responding with skilful verbal panache, always in his own words. At his final campaign rally, his wife, Dr Sarah Jukaku, introduced him with the words, “With Abdul, what you see is what you get … No corporation, no billionaire, no special interest. No one tells him what to do or what to say.” He offered voters an alternative, one notably humanistic and built on the promise of diversity, unity and a community of care. He put Gaza on the ballot as part of his vision.
Abdul El-Sayed is an American, a Midwesterner, a doctor and a husband who talks to his mother on a swing and pops up behind his grandparents on a video tape as a way to affirm his midwestern values. He worked in public health to help provide glasses to 16,000 children from low-income families in Detroit and Wayne County.
He is also a Muslim man with a long Middle Eastern name who speaks Arabic. As an American and a Muslim, he lays bare the lies that have dehumanised Muslims for so long. He visits farmers and residents across Michigan, including rural conservatives in the Upper Peninsula. When media pundits present his religion as a threat to Americans, he doesn’t back down. He talks openly about Islam and his identity, rejecting the narrow mindset of those who would brand him “foreign”. He places his religion in the context of Judaism and Christianity. In one video filmed at a Rosh Hashanah dinner, he talks with his Jewish hostesses, who recite a prayer before they share home-cooked kugel.
He invented new ways to talk about religion. In one campaign ad, he looks into the camera and says he prays, and that we all “need faith and hope that we can fix things”. The ad ends with, “I’m Abdul El-Sayed, a man of faith. That’s a good thing.”
In his speech on election night, he returned to the connection between war and the economy, which helps explain the blowback that cost Republicans control of Congress. He said, “It just shouldn’t be this hard to buy a second bag of groceries or fill your tank. It shouldn’t be this hard to see a doctor in the richest, most powerful country in the world. It shouldn’t be this hard to pay your taxes and know that that money’s going to be spent on you and your kids instead of dropping bombs on somebody else and their kids.” His words bring together the suffering of those caught in wars funded by our tax dollars and those deprived of their basic needs at home.
He used his voice to broaden the horizons of American politics, offering a vision that could reshape how we imagine America: a more expansive country where we all fit, embracing its diversity and rejecting the violence, hate and exclusion of the shrinking Trumpian world. He closed his speech with the call, “We deserve an America for all her kids. So Michigan, let’s go build it.”
Abdul El-Sayed’s accomplishment was a major blow to a world built on Arab and Muslim hate. He embodies, by contrast, a politics of joy, care, concern, justice and equality, and the possibility of an America so often lost to our imaginations in a world at war.
Now the so-called “centrist” or “moderate” Democrats must decide whether to champion a new anti-Islamophobic politics or keep taking money from hate mongers and mass murderers, and face the consequences of the same political blowback that cost Republicans their majorities.
A version of this article first appeared on Al Jazeera Arabic.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

noticias.titulo: British actor Robert Pattinson named as new James Bond
noticias.resumen: The actor called the studio's decision a 'dream come true'.
noticias.texto:
British actor Robert Pattinson named as new James Bond
The actor, who shot to fame in the Twilight series, called the studio’s decision to make him the new 007 ‘a dream come true’.
Robert Pattinson has been named the new James Bond, becoming the seventh actor to assume the role of the iconic British secret agent.
Amazon MGM Studios released a photo of Pattinson in Bond’s signature tuxedo on Monday, confirming the much-anticipated news of who will succeed Daniel Craig. “Identity confirmed,” read a statement posted on Instagram.
Pattinson expressed his gratitude to those at the studio, describing the role as a “dream come true” in a statement.
“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” he added.
The prolonged casting process to replace Craig, who starred as the super-suave spy in five films since 2006, included British actors Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor and Jack Lowden.
Pattinson shot to international fame playing Edward Cullen in the Twilight series. Since then, he has taken on more independent and fringe roles, most recently in Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime, which starred Pattinson as Chris Hansen from the reality television series To Catch a Predator.
Pattinson has also starred alongside Hollywood superstars Matt Damon and Anne Hathaway in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, as well as Matt Reeves’s The Batman. His film, The Drama, alongside co-star Zendaya, was also released this year.
Pattinson’s debut as Bond, currently untitled but widely referred to as “Bond 26,” will be the first 007 film since long-term producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael Wilson stepped back and Amazon took creative control of the franchise, after acquiring the series’ parent company MGM.
Reports have suggested that Pattinson has signed a commitment to make three Bond films.

noticias.titulo: Cargo ship capsizes off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast
noticias.resumen: Bulgaria's Transport Ministry says that all 12 of the ship's crew members were saved in a rescue operation.
noticias.texto:
Cargo ship capsizes off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast
Bulgaria’s Transport Ministry says that all 12 of the ship’s crew members were saved in a rescue operation.
A cargo ship has capsized off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, the country’s Transport Ministry has said.
The ship’s crew, eight Turkish citizens and four Azerbaijani nationals, were rescued from the Somali-flagged Betul 8 in an operation on Monday that involved four ships, two from Bulgaria, one from Romania and one from Turkiye.
Bulgaria’s Transport Ministry confirmed that one of its helicopters repatriated them to shore and that the crew was in good health.
Speaking to journalists after being brought to the port city of Varna, crew members said their ship had been hit by two sea drones.
The incident comes after three ships were hit off Romania over the weekend, according to authorities in Bucharest, though no casualties were reported.
Romanian Foreign Minister Dan Neculaescu said on Monday the latest incidents were “unacceptable”.
The ship was carrying 3,000 metric tons of wheat and was headed to Egypt from Romania. Bulgaria received a distress signal early on Monday that the ship was sinking approximately 40 nautical miles (74km) southeast of Cape Kaliakra.
Black Sea attacks
Betul 8 is the 17th vessel to be attacked off the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania since mid-July, according to Diaplous, a maritime security firm.
The waters off the coasts of the two countries, both of them NATO members, have become the primary route for shipments from Ukraine, one of the world’s largest grain exporters, whose own Black Sea ports have come under fire since Russia’s full-scale invasion more than four years ago. Ukraine has also been accused of targeting Russian vessels in other areas of the Black Sea.
Romanian and Bulgarian officials have both pointed the finger at Russia over the attacks, though Bulgaria has underlined that there is no proof of who was behind them. Russia has previously denied it was responsible for deadly drone attacks in the region.

noticias.titulo: Israeli court upholds detention of Palestinian land activist Ghassan Najjar
noticias.resumen: Occupied West Bank land defender is set to remain in detention until at least February 26 next year.
noticias.texto:
Israeli court upholds detention of Palestinian land activist Ghassan Najjar
Occupied West Bank land defender is set to remain in detention until at least February 26 next year, with the possibility that the term could be extended.
An Israeli military court has upheld a four–month administrative detention order against Palestinian land activist and farmer Ghassan Najjar.
Najjar appeared at Ofer Military Court on Monday. He was arrested during a pre–dawn raid on Burin village, south of Nablus, in the occupied West Bank on October 27, and has been held in administrative detention since.
The Israeli authorities have not given a reason for Najjar’s arrest, as administrative detention allows them. The Palestinian human rights defender, farmer and veteran grassroots organiser has a long history of arrest, having spent nearly a decade in Israeli prisons, much of it under administrative detention. He has been subjected to a travel ban since 2011.
The Institute for Middle East Understanding (IMEU) told Al Jazeera that Najjar was arrested because he intended to harvest olives on his land and planned to help other Palestinian farmers do the same. Israel’s security agency Shin Bet reportedly warned Najjar, cofounder of Burin’s Land and Farming Agricultural Cooperative, that he would be arrested if he did not stop organising with grassroots groups and Western activists.
The olive harvest in the occupied West Bank is a key target of pogroms by Israeli settlers. The attacks have surged during this year’s harvest and have already surpassed last year’s figures.
The United Nations and international voices have long urged Israel to guarantee Palestinian farmers’ protection and safe access to their land.
‘Helpless’
Administrative detention allows Israel to detain people without charge or trial, notes B’Tselem, an Israeli human rights group. It adds that the absence of legal proceedings leaves detainees “helpless”.
Following the court’s confirmation of the detention order, Najjar will remain in Ofer Prison until at least 26 February, his sister, Suha Najjar, told Al Jazeera. However, in the meantime, an Israeli military court will review his case and decide whether to extend the term.
“It is an unjust decision, and it is deeply upsetting that my brother has been subjected to such a great injustice,” Suha said.
“He has been placed under administrative detention for four months, without any charges [lodged] against him. Even more concerning is that this detention could be renewed when the four months come to an end.”
Earlier this month, Amnesty International demanded Israeli authorities release Najjar immediately. The rights group accused Israel of detaining him “solely because of his peaceful activism to protect the olive harvest season in Burin”.
“I am extremely worried, especially because we are not allowed to visit him or even see him. This makes our anxiety as a family even greater, as we have no way of knowing how he is doing, either physically or psychologically,” Suha said.
“We are aware of the cruel methods used by the Israeli occupation to torture Palestinian prisoners, both physically and psychologically, and this makes us even more fearful for his safety and wellbeing.”
In a statement released earlier this month, Amnesty called on states with leverage to pressure Israel to release Najjar.
“Like Palestinian human rights defender Ayman Bani Owda and countless other Palestinians, Ghassan Najjar is being hounded by a discriminatory justice system that has played a key role in legitimising and maintaining Israel’s system of apartheid and unlawful occupation,” it said.
“States with influence on Israel must use their leverage to pressure Israeli authorities into releasing all arbitrarily detained Palestinians, including Ghassan Najjar, and finally end their use of administrative detention.”

noticias.titulo: Musk, Silicon Valley insiders urge Nvidia to restore Jensen Huang as CEO
noticias.resumen: Nvidia faces a potential 30 percent value loss in value without Jensen Huang, market analysts say, amid a stock downturn.
noticias.texto:
Musk, Silicon Valley insiders urge Nvidia to restore Jensen Huang as CEO
Nvidia faces potential 30 percent value loss without Jensen Huang, say market analysts amid stock downturn.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and other Silicon Valley insiders are calling on chipmaker Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang, who resigned last week from the company he cofounded.
Musk is one of the 177,000 signatories to a petition titled “Stand With Jensen”, calling for the reinstatement of the executive, who resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
“We are current and former NVIDIA employees, partners, shareholders, and supporters. We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the Board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA’s best interests,” the letter published on the petition’s website said.
More privately, a group of Silicon Valley insiders is pushing to get Huang back in the role, with the Financial Times reporting that Huang is considering a comeback. The paper reported that an unnamed group of Silicon Valley insiders has put together a so-called war room and is lobbying the White House for support which is a move that may have been successful.
“A lot of people are asking Jensen, they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” United States President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday.
Trump’s reported trades this year suggest he held between $13m and $62m in Nvidia stock as of the end of August, the Washington Post reported on Monday, citing a review of his financial disclosures.
But Nvidia’s board is not considering bringing Jensen back, the Reuters news agency reported citing three unnamed people.
Much of Nvidia’s value is tied to Huang, with analysts estimating that the company could lose as much as 25 to 30 percent of its value without him.
Nvidia’s stock was trending downward in early trading on Wall Street, with US markets opening down 2.3 percent on the day. Over the last five days, the stock has dropped 8.5 percent and is down more than 25.7 percent over the last month.
AI constraints
The developments come as the White House moves to designate Nvidia, along with more than two dozen other companies, as “national champions” in the artificial intelligence industry, a new initiative intended to help the company secure more business overseas, according to reporting by The Wall Street Journal.
They also come as the Trump administration issued a rule on Monday that it would restrict China’s access to chips made by companies including Nvidia, as Trump begins a trip to China where he will meet with President Xi Jinping.
The restrictions are aimed at preventing Chinese companies from “circumventing” existing limits by using data centres in Southeast Asian countries such as Malaysia and Thailand to train their AI models.
“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centres in third countries,” the Department of Commerce said in a statement.
The new rule comes as the Commerce Department is scrambling to demonstrate that it is cracking down on Chinese access to sensitive US technology, following reports that the agency under Secretary Howard Lutnick turned a blind eye to the smuggling of advanced Nvidia AI chips into China.

noticias.titulo: Iraq deploys army to stronghold of Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah
noticias.resumen: US pressure on Iraq to curb Tehran's influence leaves potential for direct confrontation with Iran-linked armed group.
noticias.texto:
Iraq deploys army to stronghold of Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah
US pressure on Iraq to curb Tehran’s influence leaves potential for direct confrontation with Iran-linked armed group around the town of Jurf al-Nasr.
Iraq has ordered its armed forces to move into a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah group, amid an investigation into suspected oil smuggling.
Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has ordered the military to enter the town of Jurf al-Nasr, government spokesman Haidar al-Aboudi said on Monday, according to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA). The Iraqi leader has also set a deadline for the armed faction, which has been implicated in the oil probe, to leave the area.
The order comes amid pressure on Baghdad from the United States and some of its Gulf-state allies to counter Tehran’s influence in Iraq.
Al-Aboudi told local media the “deadline is not far off”. A senior Iraqi official told Al Jazeera Arabic that Kataib Hezbollah has until Friday to leave Jurf al-Nasr, which sits south of Baghdad in the centre of the country and was previously known as Jurf al-Sakhar.
Al-Zaidi told military and security commanders to deploy additional forces around the town and to prepare for government troops to enter. The order would potentially bring the government and its troops into direct confrontation with the armed group.
Security agencies have also been instructed to prevent tankers carrying oil or petroleum products from leaving the area.
Iraq recently launched a sweeping anticorruption crackdown centred on the town, which allegedly harbours illicit oil refineries.
Kataib Hezbollah, one of dozens of heavily armed pro-Iranian groups that have semi-official status in Iraq, denied the allegations on Sunday, saying that an inspection found no interference with pipelines.
“We are therefore being subjected to the greatest campaign of blackmail aimed at forcing us to relinquish the weapons of dignity that have upheld sovereignty and protected the rights of Iraqis at multiple stages,” the group said in a statement.
The campaign to stamp out the oil smuggling trade has seen the dismissal and judicial referral of nine senior officials accused of corruption. It has also led to the sacking of senior government officials and security directors.
Al-Aboudi said an investigative committee, following an intelligence agency report, had “detected clear tampering with pipelines passing through the area, as well as attempts to bury and conceal traces of that tampering”.
Sources told the Reuters news agency that the smuggling, carried out with accomplices among some security and oil officials, has robbed the government of hundreds of millions of dollars since 2021.
While officially framed as an initiative to protect public funds, analysts believe the oil probe is a calculated strategy to sever the financial arteries of armed factions that refuse to integrate into Iraq’s state apparatus.
Iranian-backed armed groups, including Kataib Hezbollah, have resisted repeated calls by both al-Zaidi and his ally, US President Donald Trump, to disarm.
They have struck US troops and targets in Saudi Arabia and the UAE in solidarity with Tehran since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in February.

noticias.titulo: Iran braces for natural gas shortages during winter energy imbalance
noticias.resumen: The gas infrastructure in Iran has suffered from underdevelopment and sanctions, and now damage from the war.
noticias.texto:
Iran braces for natural gas shortages during winter energy imbalance
The gas infrastructure in Iran has suffered from underdevelopment and sanctions, and now damage from the war.
Tehran, Iran – Iran is heading into winter with warnings of natural gas shortages, as damage from strikes by the United States and Israel deepens an energy imbalance that has plagued the resource-rich country for years.
Iran holds the second-largest proven natural gas reserves in the world, only behind Russia, but its government last week forecast a peak-demand deficit of about 430 million cubic metres per day for winter that could impact both households and industries.
The country’s ageing energy infrastructure has long suffered from underinvestment and international sanctions that have restricted finances and equipment. Authorities say that inefficient consumption and limited storage capacity are also to blame, in addition to the damage from the ongoing war.
Saeed Tavakoli, head of the National Iranian Gas Company, told local media last week that 26 projectiles struck six refineries on March 18, knocking out 28 percent of Iran’s gas production capacity in the immediate aftermath of the strikes.
According to the government, about 100 million cubic metres per day of processing capacity has since been restored, but fully bringing back the additional 130 million cubic metres lost in the US and Israeli attacks could extend into 2028.
Hashem Oraee, head of the Iranian Energy Associations Union, told local media last week that Iran was not able to rely on any gas imports to plug the gap.
Gas shortages could also lead to electricity blackouts if the gas feeding some power plants goes out, something that has repeatedly happened in recent years. To avoid electricity shortages, those power plants resort to burning cheap fuel, predominantly a heavy oil alternative called mazut, which significantly pollutes the air.
Despite that, Mostafa Rajabi Mashhadi, a deputy energy minister, told the state-linked ILNA outlet on Saturday that mazut burning would continue this year.
Umud Shokri, energy strategist and senior visiting fellow at George Mason University, said that if the problems facing Iran’s gas industry remain unresolved over the coming years, the consequences would extend beyond the energy sector, affecting industrial production, employment, inflation, and living standards.
“In my view, Iran’s biggest challenge is not a lack of energy resources, but its inability to turn those resources into reliable supplies for its people and economy,” Shokri told Al Jazeera. “Without serious reforms, sustained investment, and better energy management, what is now largely a seasonal crisis could gradually become a year-round problem.”
Shortages possible across Iran
Gas accounts for 73 percent of Iran’s energy mix, the gas company’s Tavakoli said last week, adding that household consumption had reached 480 million cubic metres per day and was expected to sharply rise as the cold season approaches.
Last winter’s peak consumption for households, businesses and small industries was recorded at 737 million.
The National Iranian Gas Company identifies 11 of Iran’s 31 provinces as considerably vulnerable to shortages this winter, particularly some provinces to the north of the country, including Mazandaran, Golestan and North Khorasan. High consumption due to cold temperatures, as well as locations near the ends of transmission lines, increase gas pressure problems in those provinces.
Government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani explicitly warned during a press conference last week that if consumption grows, gas might be cut off across the country, including Tehran.
“Unlike electricity, which can be reconnected quickly after being cut off, bringing back gas after cutoff is a time-consuming process,” she said. “So, network stability is of utmost importance and we must work to prevent any disruptions.”
The government has said it will do its best not to let households or industries go offline due to gas shortages. But on Saturday, the Zagros Petrochemical Company, operating in southern Iran’s energy production hub of Asaluyeh, notified its shareholders that it shut down a methanol production unit until further notice in line with directives from the National Iranian Gas Company
David Jalilvand, managing director at Orient Matters, a geopolitical research consultancy in Germany, said the industrial sector would bear the brunt of the shortages as the authorities prioritise households, which rely on gas for heating.
“Prioritising households, however, does not guarantee that residential supplies will remain uninterrupted if shortages become severe,” he told Al Jazeera.
To help save on gas, the government has tasked its affiliated executive bodies with reducing their gas consumption by 20 percent. It has also said offices are obligated to keep their temperatures at around 18 degrees Celsius (64 degrees Fahrenheit), while homes are advised to maintain 18-21C (64-70F). Offices must also switch heating off on holidays.
The government said inspections last week led to disconnections at the Education Ministry building and five other government buildings in Tehran that were not complying with the energy-saving directives.
The government has also been struggling with a lingering petrol supply imbalance, and imposed sporadic power blackouts to cover electricity production shortfalls during summer and early autumn. In addition to raising the price of petrol twice in less than a year, the government has also significantly limited monthly petrol quotas allocated to personal vehicles.
Authorities have repeatedly asked Iranians to help offset the shortages by consuming less, while saying more price hikes are possible over the coming months.
An October directive also required eligible civil servants to work from home at least two days a week and encourage commuting without private cars on one day a week, as part of efforts to reduce fuel consumption.
“We must speak to the people honestly and explain we are facing gas shortages due to previous years’ imbalances and also damages from the war, so we need to save on gas,” First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said last week.
High-consuming users have also been told their gas prices will increase exponentially if they do not reduce consumption.
Jalilvand, from Orient Matters, said developing the South Pars gasfield, the world’s largest offshore natural gasfield shared between Iran and Qatar, has been cruicial in addressing the key challenge of keeping the supply of gas growing in line with domestic demand.
But he said sustaining production growth increasingly depends on addressing technical challenges that require foreign investment and technology.
“An equally important challenge lies on the demand side. Iran has enormous potential to improve energy efficiency, but realising it requires investment, technology and domestic policy reforms, particularly to address heavily subsidised energy prices.
“Reintegration into the global economy would make it considerably easier to finance and implement these improvements.”
Hamed, who runs a small apartment hotel in the northern province of Mazandaran, said his business experienced a drop in gas pressure last year, depsite not being a heavy consumer. But there were no total cutoffs.
He told Al Jazeera that lower-pressure gas can impact his business by affecting heating in guest rooms, disrupting the boiler for hot water used for showers and sanitation, and most of the hotel’s kitchen operations.
“It’s basically everything; I really hope it doesn’t come to that this year,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
noticias.resumen: Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’ Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”. The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe t
noticias.texto:
Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.
Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.
In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.
Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.
The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.
The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.
Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.
The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”
Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.
The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”
Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.
“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.
Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.
Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.

noticias.texto:
An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country.
Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said a 28-year-old player named as Greene Da’monte Khiree from the state of Georgia was arrested at Lagos’s main airport last Wednesday after he arrived on a flight from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.
The NDLEA said the player told them he had come to Nigeria to “build networks” for his basketball career. The agency said evidence on his phone suggested he had “knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity”. The NDLEA said it detained the player when he attempted to leave the airport with his hand luggage after abandoning two checked-in bags. The agency said those two bags were found to contain 32 parcels of marijuana, and a tracking device.
Nigeria has strict drug laws, and trafficking carries a sentence of life in prison.
A basketball player by the name of Damonte Greene is listed on the roster of the Pattani Raptors in the Thai Premier Men’s League. Greene, a Georgia native, played college basketball for Reinhardt University and South Georgia Technical College. He played semi-professional basketball in the US before representing a number of teams in Thailand.
WNBA star Brittney Griner and former Utah State player Jarred Shaw were imprisoned in Russia and Indonesia respectively for marijuana offenses. Griner was released in December 2022, while Shaw remains in prison.

noticias.resumen: Many countries surprised to see first version delivered with more than four days of negotiation remaining A draft text of a possible final outcome from the Cop31 UN climate summit is an attempt to “draw out parties” on their areas of agreement and disagreement, Australia’s president of the talks has said.
