Infantino, who was first elected as president in 2016, came under huge pressure in the summer after FIFA announced a highly controversial private investment plan that would have seen third-party investors invited to take stakes in a commercial subsidiary dubbed the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE).
The proposal, which was later scrapped, drew fierce pushback from across the football community, with some accusing the world governing body of looking to "sell" the sport.
"Against the backdrop of serious concerns over the direction of FIFA, the national associations called for renewed unity and trust within the global football community," UEFA said on Monday.
"They expressed their full confidence in Philippe Diallo to provide the leadership needed to achieve this ambition," it added.
FIFA confirmed in September that Infantino, who has also faced questions over his relationship with US President Donald Trump, would stand for re-election.
"The FIFA President announced in April that he will stand for re-election in 2027. Of course, nothing has changed. Mr Infantino will be standing for re-election," a spokesperson said.
The presidential election is due to take place at the 77th FIFA Congress on Thursday, 18 March 2027 in Rabat, Morocco.

noticias.titulo: Serbia to accelerate work on EU accession, Student List representative says
noticias.resumen: Serbia’s Student List will speed up rule-of-law reforms needed for EU accession, MP Aleksandar Baucal said in the movement’s first international appearance.
noticias.texto:
Serbia’s Student List will speed up rule-of-law reforms needed for EU accession, MP Aleksandar Baucal said in the movement’s first international appearance.
The Student List will speed up work on meeting the EU’s interim accession benchmarks on the rule of law, professor and newly elected MP Aleksandar Baucal said in the much-awaited first international public appearance of Serbia's new main political force.
“The next question is whether Serbia will remain on the European path. For us, the European path is one of reforms: strengthening European values, building functional institutions and a genuine rule-of-law system, developing a sustainable economy integrated in the European market,” Baucal said on Monday.
Baucal spoke at the EU Enlargement Forum in Brussels, the first time a Student List representative has addressed an international audience. Most of the room gave him a standing ovation after the speech.
For the professor, the EU accession path is not only key for good neighbourly relations, but, more broadly, for building a more democratic society.
“One of Serbia’s strategic objectives will be to accelerate the fulfilment of the interim benchmarks under chapters 23 and 24, as well. We want Serbia to be a reliable partner to the European Union and to its members,” he continued.
The party’s historic electoral victory last month raised hopes of a reset in Serbia’s troubled relations with the EU. The movement, born of nearly two years of mass protests, ousted Aleksandar Vučić’s party after 14 years in power.
Two weeks ago, Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos met a Student List delegation in Brussels, their first formal exchange with a senior EU official. The delegates said the incoming government would focus on restoring the rule of law, judicial independence and media freedom, not only for the sake of accession but above all for the Serbian people.
Baucal returned to those themes, pledging to advance on the “fundamentals” of EU accession. The professor-turned-MP said the new government would stay open to dialogue and seek to solve concrete problems rather than create new ones.
“This is not only about the European Union helping Serbia protect democracy. It is also about a democratic Serbia contributing to a stronger and more resilient Europe,” he said.
Yet prominent figures in the Student List remain cautious about aligning with EU foreign policy, notably on sanctions against Russia. These are deeply unpopular in Serbia, where memories of the Western sanctions that hit the population under the Milošević regime still run deep.
Recognition of Kosovo could also prove a sticking point with EU countries. Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama warned that the new government is unlikely to change Serbia’s stance.
The Student List grew as a heterogeneous movement without a clearly defined leadership. Belgrade’s position on accession and foreign policy may become clearer once its MPs settle on the make-up of the new government.
For now, Baucal sees the party’s next challenge as turning the solidarity forged in the struggle into lasting trust in institutions.
“Citizens were able to set many differences aside. But in a democratic society, these interests and opinions will once again come to the fore. We believe that thanks to our differences, we will build a better system for our citizens,” he said.

noticias.titulo: All the ladies in the house: RAYE and Rosalía lead the way for 2027 Grammy nominations
noticias.resumen: Europe's leading songstresses are frontrunners for top awards at the 2027 Grammys. With 11 nominations, British singer RAYE has equalled Beyoncé's 2025 record number of nods while the American star has now become the most-nominated Grammy artist in history with 100 nods.
noticias.texto:
Europe's leading songstresses are frontrunners for top awards at the 2027 Grammys. With 11 nominations, British singer RAYE has equalled Beyoncé's 2025 record number of nods while the American star has now become the most-nominated Grammy artist in history with 100 nods.
British jazz and soul sensation RAYE has written herself into the record books with a whopping 11 nominations for the 2027 Grammy Awards.
The singer-songwriter is a contender in all the major categories, including record, song and album of the year for her 2026 Mercury's Prize winning work 'This Music May Contain Hope.'
Her haul of 11 nominations equals that of Beyoncé who notched up the single year nods record in 2025 with her groundbreaking album Cowboy Carter. And she's still very much in the race to extend her reign as the most-nominated artist in Grammy history after notching up her 100th nod for 'Morning Dew (Donk)' in the R&B solo performance category.
Sisters doing it themselves
Rosalía joins RAYE and Beyoncé in bringing up an impressive line-up of female artists receiving recognition.
The Spanish singer has nine nods for her sumptuous album 'LUX' and is a first-time nominee in all the categories she's competiting for, including pop solo performance, song, record and album of the year.
Her nomination also comes days after she swept the board at the Latin Grammys taking home five out of seven awards she was up for.
Following her are Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo, Phoebe Bridgers and first-time nominee Ella Langley, who are tied with seven nods each.
The album of the year category is rounded out by Bridgers' 'Lost Weekend,' Dean's 'The Art of Loving,' Langley's “Dandelion,' Bruno Mars' 'The Romantic,' Rodrigo's 'You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love' and Taylor Swift's 'The Life of a Showgirl.”
Swift's nomination is her fifth consecutive studio album to be nominated for album of the year, something only one other artist has ever done: Kendrick Lamar.
Bruno Mars, Leon Thomas and 2026's best new artist winner Olivia Dean have six nominations each.
The 2027 Grammy Awards will take place on Sunday 7 February, live on ABC for the first time since 1972, from the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. It will also stream on Disney+ and Hulu.

noticias.titulo: Prince William and Princess Catherine play street cricket with locals in Mumbai
noticias.resumen: Prince William and Princess Catherine play street cricket with local players in Mumbai, India, during a three-day visit for the Earthshot Prize.
noticias.texto:
Britain's Prince William and Princess Catherine joined local players for a game of street cricket in Mumbai, India, on Monday, 16 November 2026.
The couple took turns playing "gully cricket", a popular informal version of the sport played in streets and open spaces across the country. William was seen batting before Catherine took her turn. The princess then greeted young cricketers, and the couple posed for photographs with the players.
The game was part of a three-day visit to India, where William is hosting the Earthshot Prize, his environmental initiative.
The trip also includes a planned meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi. Cricket, one of India's most popular sports, gave the royal couple a chance to join local players during their visit to Mumbai, the country's financial capital.

noticias.titulo: Trump says he could meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un in China
noticias.resumen: Trump is planning to discuss nuclear disarmament when he meets with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China this week.
noticias.texto:
Trump is planning to discuss nuclear disarmament when he meets with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China this week.
US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he may meet with North Korean Supreme Leader Kim Jong-un in China this week.
Trump made the comments while speaking to reporters as he departed the White House to begin his trip to Asia, which will see him arrive in the Philippines early on Tuesday.
The president is then set to travel on to China, where he is scheduled to take part in trilateral talks with his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping.
"We may meet with Kim Jong-un also," Trump told the media. "So that would be good. We have the chance to accomplish a lot."
Trump is planning to discuss nuclear disarmament when he meets with Putin and Xi in Shenzhen in southeastern China this week, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
"We're going to talk about denuclearisation. Tough subject because it's very hard for any of us say we'll get rid of our nukes," Trump said on Monday. "Especially since you do have other countries."
He added that the wars in Iran and Ukraine would also come up, as well as "economics and trade."
In August, Trump talked up his relationship with Kim and said the pair would meet at some point in the year, although he gave no further details.
"The fact that I get along with him, that's a good thing not a bad thing. He has 57 very powerful nuclear weapons. Should have never allowed it to happen," the president said at the time, adding: "If I were president, I wouldn't have allowed it. But he's got them."
The director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Rafael Grossi, said in September that the reported expansion of North Korea's production of weapons-grade nuclear material was a "cause for serious concern."

noticias.titulo: Five EU countries unveil Rwanda deportation plan in migration crackdown
noticias.resumen: Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece aim to begin deporting rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda in 2027, despite concerns over human rights and potential legal challenges.
noticias.texto:
Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece aim to begin deporting rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda in 2027, despite concerns over human rights and potential legal challenges.
Five EU countries announced a partnership with Rwanda on Monday to establish the first EU return hub outside the bloc, marking a radical hardening of European migration policy.
Although the details of the agreement are still being negotiated, Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece say they are confident of reaching a deal and beginning deportations of irregular migrants in 2027.
The first facility is expected to accommodate around 100 people at a time. Those sent there will be free to move around Rwanda and are expected to integrate into local society and the labour market, according to people familiar with the negotiations.
“I think this [agreement] is a game changer. We will take back control and remove the incentive for illegal migration,” said Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, during the announcement in Vienna, along with Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker and the interior ministers of other countries involved, including Rwanda’s Vincent Biruta.
The initial hub will be a small-scale pilot project, with plans to expand the scheme once it is operational and the risk of deportations being blocked by legal challenges has diminished.
Who will be sent to the return hubs?
The five countries will deport only rejected asylum seekers who are subject to enforceable return decisions.
Minors will be excluded, while each country will apply its own criteria for selecting those to be deported.
The Netherlands will focus on adult men from countries in Rwanda’s region, while Germany will target migrants who refuse to cooperate with efforts to establish their identity and come from countries reluctant to readmit their own nationals, according to people familiar with the negotiations.
After a period at the facility, the length of which has yet to be determined, migrants will be expected to rebuild their lives in Rwanda or voluntarily return to their countries of origin or another country where they have the right to reside.
The EU border agency Frontex will not have a role in deportations in the initial stages, despite a reform of its mandate recently proposed by the European Commission, which would allow it to do so.
Costs remain unclear
The five EU countries will bear the full cost of deporting migrants and accommodating them in Rwanda. However, no estimate for the initial facility was provided at the press conference, as negotiations are still ongoing.
According to people familiar with the negotiations, services in Rwanda will be considerably cheaper than equivalent services in Europe.
What Rwanda will get in return is also unclear at this stage. Kigali is, however, set to sign a partnership agreement with Denmark next week, related to cooperation on migration.
“The agreement is a shame”
Return hubs have raised concerns over their compatibility with EU law and the protection of human rights.
Critics warn they could lead to human rights violations, particularly when established in countries with limited democratic standards.
“The agreement is a shame,” said French lawmaker Mélissa Camara, of the Greens/EFA group, considering the countries involved are “crossing another disgraceful moral line by reaching an agreement with an authoritarian regime.”
The group of five countries said that all procedures will be carried out in line with international human rights standards.
However, legal complications may arise when deportations to Rwanda begin next year, as the European Court of Human Rights prohibits countries from transferring individuals to states or situations where they may be subjected to violations of fundamental rights.
The United Nations has raised concerns about Rwanda's human rights record.
A similar agreement between Rwanda and the United Kingdom, under which Britain planned to send asylum seekers to the African country, was ruled unlawful by the UK Supreme Court in 2023 because of the risk that those transferred could subsequently be sent to countries where they faced persecution.
According to the law enabling EU states to set up return hubs outside the bloc, only non-EU countries — “where international human rights standards and principles in accordance with international law are respected” — are eligible.

noticias.titulo: Countries to decide future of 'killer robots' at UN conference
noticias.resumen: UN Secretary General and Pope Leo XIV have urged countries to agree stricter rules for autonomous weapon systems, to stop them from being given the ability to make life and death decisions without human intervention.
noticias.texto:
UN Secretary General and Pope Leo XIV have urged countries to agree stricter rules for autonomous weapon systems, to stop them from being given the ability to make life and death decisions without human intervention.
Killer robots and drones are coming up for a reckoning this week as government envoys on Monday revved up a discussion and could decide this week whether to launch negotiations toward setting rules for use of the deadly machines — or not.
Pope Leo XIV, the UN chief and advocacy groups have framed the issue as an existential debate: Whether robots can be allowed to kill and whether humans must maintain some control of and accountability for use of lethal autonomous weapon systems.
Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones like Ukraine and the Middle East, but widespread rollout hasn’t happened.
Scary would-be scenarios, like armed drones flying amok and gunning down civilians with pinpoint precision, have peppered years of discussions about killer robots. But those talks haven't produced any international restrictions.
The United States and Russia, longtime rivals, want to limit any curbs on their ability to develop and deploy powerful new tools in the high-tech arms race — just as AI is gaining steam and changing battle plans.
Proponents of an AI weaponry rulebook say time is of the essence.
"We’re at a pivotal point now, where it’s an experimentation phase. We’re seeing some cases here, some cases there, but not full operationalisation," said Anna Hehir, head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute, an advocacy group.
"It will be a lot harder to regulate and create rules when these systems have already been in use for many years."
UN meeting comes after seven countries seek negotiations
The issue comes to a head at UN offices in Geneva, where the seventh review conference, about the awkwardly named Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, will consider whether to start talks on regulation of killer robots.
Supporters of an accord acknowledge powerful forces are in the way, but point to precedent: governments have already struck a deal to regulate blinding lasers.
Most countries support reining them in. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ deadline this year for the launch of talks toward regulation has given the issue urgency, but some top military powers are hesitant.
Last month, seven countries — Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama — submitted a proposal to launch negotiations of a new legally binding agreement on autonomous weapons at the conference.
The various sides have been gearing up for the diplomatic standoff.
On Friday, International Committee of the Red Cross President Mirjana Spoljaric said in a statement: "States must act to ensure the future of warfare is not handed over to machines."
Stop Killer Robots, an advocacy group, says 130 countries support new international rules on the weapons systems.
Activists began running advertisements on the streets and in the subways of Berlin, London and Paris touting public support for reining in killer robots.
Russia: talks on restrictions are 'premature'
In his first encyclical in May, the pope denounced a "culture of power" driving the AI race, especially in developing ever more sophisticated methods of remote warfare, and said it's not permissible to entrust decisions about life and death to remote AI systems.
Under the convention’s rules, decisions must be made by consensus. That means that any single country can thwart an agreement, and that any such deal is likely to be based on a low common denominator. Another sticking point is how long negotiators might be given to try to agree on language.
In the run-up to the conference, humanitarians and activist groups said Russia looked ready to deploy tactics to slow or even stall progress toward launching formal negotiations.
"Russia attaches great importance to the successful outcome of the conference and to reaching mutually acceptable agreements that will help strengthen the Inhumane Weapons Convention and further its universalization," Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told reporters on Wednesday.
Moscow wants "organisational matters” to be ironed out first and see a process “free from politicization," she said.
Most tellingly, Zakharova said: "We consider it premature to argue that the time has supposedly come to develop restrictive or prohibitive measures concerning such systems."

noticias.titulo: Meet the new James Bond: It's Pattinson, Robert Pattinson
noticias.resumen: Daniel Craig’s successor has been confirmed after a long casting process, making Pattinson the seventh actor to play the role of 007.
noticias.texto:
Daniel Craig’s successor has been confirmed after a long casting process, making Pattinson the seventh actor to play the role of 007.
After years of rumours and speculation, arguably the most coveted role in cinema has been cast for the seventh time.
The (00)7th actor to portray legendary cinematic spy James Bond will be Robert Pattinson.
The 40-year-old actor will replace Daniel Craig as 007 and has beaten other frontrunners Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O'Connor and Nicholas Hoult to the coveted role.
"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," said Pattinson in an official statement. "I'm deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya, and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."
He becomes the most established actor to be cast as Bond.
Indeed, the actor needs little introduction. Following his star-making turn in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire and the Twilight franchise, he has gone from strength to strength with roles in The Lost City of Z, High Life, The Lighthouse and Tenet. He is also the current Batman, having debuted as the Caped Crusader in Matt Reeves' The Batman in 2022. He is currently filming the sequel.
This year has been a particularly busy (and productive) year for Pattinson, as he starred alongside Zendaya in The Drama, played Antinous in Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, and portrayed American TV presenter Chris Hansen inPrimetime. He will next star in Dune: Part Three, which is directed by none other than Canadian filmmaker and four-time Oscar nominee Denis Villeneuve – the director of the upcoming James Bond film.
“Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond as we proudly introduce Robert Pattinson as the next 007,” said Mike Hopkins, Head of Prime Video & Amazon MGM Studios. “This iconic character has captivated audiences around the world for more than six decades, and there’s no doubt that Robert’s remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice to carry that legacy forward. With Denis Villeneuve at the helm, Amy Pascal and David Heyman producing, Tanya Lapointe executive producing, and a brilliant script from Steven Knight, we have a world-class creative team in place to usher in a new era of Bond, and we couldn’t be more excited about the journey ahead.”
“Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin,” said director Denis Villeneuve.
“James Bond is one of the most beloved, inspiring, iconic, and yet enigmatic characters in literature and movies. The legacy of this character is in great hands with Robert Pattinson. His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times,” said producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman.
Pattinson was rumoured to be Amazon's favourite following a secret audition and reports from Puck News that he had been given favourable contract terms: playing Bond in three films, one less than other contenders.
“O'Connor and Lowden, for instance, were required to sign up for four Bonds, if chosen,” the outlet reported. “Pattinson, on the other hand, was able to lower that commitment to three (plus a whole lot more money than the others), given his stardom."
As of writing, no official statement has been made regarding his contractual obligations.
Bond 26 will be directed by Denis Villeneuve and written by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight. It will be the first Bond film since Amazon took full creative control over the franchise from longtime 007 custodians Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson.
Only six actors have ever played Ian Fleming's British Secret Service agent 007 in the official film series: Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig.
Production on the next Bond film is expected to kick off in 2027, with a release planned for 2028 at the earliest.

noticias.titulo: ECB warns AI share boom could end in 'abrupt repricing'
noticias.resumen: Eurozone funds have bought heavily into the technology, leaving European savers exposed if the boom turns to bust in the US.
noticias.texto:
Eurozone funds have bought heavily into the technology, leaving European savers exposed if the boom turns to bust in the US.
The European Central Bank (ECB) has warned that investors could suffer heavy losses if confidence in artificial intelligence falters.
Speaking in Frankfurt, Germany, on Monday, ECB vice-president Boris Vujčić said the “rapid expansion of AI is creating new challenges for financial stability” in the 21-country eurozone.
"A reassessment of the AI narrative may trigger an abrupt repricing in markets and significant valuation losses," he said.
Vujčić noted that the amount raised through new stock market listings, measured against the size of the US economy, is on track to exceed the peak of the dot-com boom of the late 1990s. "Historically, such surges have often coincided with market peaks, pointing to the risk of excessive investor optimism," he said.
His warning comes days before the AI company Anthropic makes its stock market debut. Shares in the Claude maker are expected to start trading on Nasdaq on Thursday. The listing could be the second-largest in history, raising about $61bn (€55bn) and valuing the company at about $1.2 trillion (€1.1 trillion).
Markets have already been unsettled by the resignation of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang after a scandal, and by the US midterm elections. Vujčić said the market falls after the elections, in which Democrats won both chambers of Congress, were a reminder to be cautious about AI valuations.
Major US tech companies are projected to spend a combined $5.5 trillion (€5 trillion) on capital investments by 2030. Vujčić said a sharp fall in AI valuations would hit the eurozone hard because the region’s investment funds have become more exposed to the sector.
Government debt
The ECB also pointed to high public debt and weak public finances in some eurozone countries. With long-term borrowing costs already rising, investors could suddenly demand much more to lend to those governments. Hedge funds help keep government bonds trading smoothly but can quickly unwind their positions when markets are under stress.
Non-bank lenders
The third risk comes from the fast growth of private lenders and investment funds. Some can borrow heavily, be hard to monitor and have close ties to the rest of the financial system, all of which can amplify shocks.
The ECB wants funds’ rules on withdrawals to better reflect how quickly they can sell their assets. It also wants regulators to consider limits on how much hedge funds can borrow.
Vujčić warned that all three risks could hit at the same time. Eurozone banks, by contrast, have strong capital and liquidity positions, he said.

noticias.titulo: President Trump says he 'wouldn't mind' Jensen Huang being reinstated as Nvidia CEO
noticias.resumen: The comments come as a petition calls on Nvidia to reinstate Huang.
noticias.texto:
The comments come as a petition calls on Nvidia to reinstate Huang.
US President Donald Trump said he “wouldn’t mind” seeing Jensen Huang being reinstated as Nvidia CEO following his resignation last week amid reports of extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy.
"I would not mind that," he told reporters on Monday.
"I think he learned a big lesson," he added.
The comments come as tech executives, including Elon Musk, have called for Huang's reinstatement in an online petition, which has gained more than 160,000 signatures.
Asked if he trusts US intelligence that Huang was having an affair with a Chinese spy, Trump replied, "Well, I don’t know that she’s a Chinese spy."
"Any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China they say she’s a spy," he said. "I don’t know that she was a spy at all," he added.
Huang and Trump had formed a close relationship, with Huang becoming a key voice for the US on artificial intelligence while he also lobbied for allowing chip exports to China.
Trump left on Monday for a trip to Asia that includes a stop in China and the Philippines.
The trip will discuss economics, among other topics and include a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Huang is not scheduled to join the trip but Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk will join some of the voyage.

noticias.titulo: 12 crew members rescued after cargo ship capsizes off Bulgaria following suspected drone strike
noticias.resumen: All 12 crew members working on board the vessel were rescued and were being flown by helicopter to Bulgaria's Chaika air base, according to authorities.
noticias.texto:
All 12 crew members working on board the vessel were rescued and were being flown by helicopter to Bulgaria's Chaika air base, according to authorities.
A cargo ship capsized off the coast of Bulgaria in the Black Sea on Monday following a suspected drone strike.
Maritime authorities received a distress call from the Somali-flagged Betul 8 ship in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone at around 9:15 am, reporting that the vessel was sinking, according to Bulgaria's transport ministry.
Four vessels from the Black Sea Mine Countermeasures Group were deployed to the scene of the incident, the ministry said. Two Cougar helicopters and an Su-25 jet were also mobilised to carry out surveillance.
"An aerial survey of the area has established that the vessel has capsized. A naval vessel has been dispatched to the scene of the incident to check for any marine pollution," the transport ministry said in a later update.
Video footage circulating on social media appears to show the vessel as it goes down.
The Betul 8 was travelling from Tulcea in Romania to Egypt and was carrying almost 3,000 tonnes of bulk wheat, the ministry added.
All 12 crew members working on board the vessel were rescued and were being flown by helicopter to the Chaika air base, according to authorities. They were said to be in "good overall condition" but were suffering from the cold.
The crew reportedly told journalists that their ship had been struck by sea drones.
If confirmed, it would mark the latest in a wave of drone attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea in recent months. Russia is suspected of being behind the strikes.
The European Union has pledged €50 million for a Black Sea Maritime Security Hub hosted by Bulgaria and Romania to help combat security threats in the region.

noticias.titulo: US clamps down on chip 'loophole' in foreign access to advanced AI chips
noticias.resumen: A new US Commerce Department rule targets foreign remote access to chips like Nvidia's Blackwell.
noticias.texto:
A new US Commerce Department rule targets foreign remote access to chips like Nvidia's Blackwell.
The United States is moving forward on a rule that will make it harder for some countries, such as China, Russia and Iran, to access the most advanced artificial intelligence chips through data centres located in other countries.
On Monday, the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule to address remote access to advanced computing and superintelligence (SI) chips and servers.
"Rapid advancement in cloud computing and super intelligence infrastructure have made it increasingly possible to access advanced American computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers located outside countries subject to US export restrictions," the statement reads.
The US bans the sale of the most advanced chips to China as part of its strategy to stay ahead of Beijing in the AI race. This measure came under former President Joe Biden, who signed the CHIPS Act into law.
Countries have been able to sidestep the US ban, which prevents Chinese companies from buying the most advanced chips from firms such as Nvidia, by renting them from data centres in Southeast Asian countries.
The new rule means overseas data centres will be required to do due diligence on their customers. It will "undermine" the ability of companies in those countries to use US chips to train advanced AI models.
It will also put restrictions on overseas data centres that supply "significant volumes of computing power" to companies with headquarters in high-risk countries, which include China, Russia and Iran.
The provision, which goes into effect in 90 days, will require a license to export advanced chips to companies with headquarters in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, which have a higher than normal risk of smuggling, the administration said.
The rule comes in the wake of alleged spying connected to Nvidia. US investigators looked into whether Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company, helped Chinese clients obtain export-controlled Nvidia chips.
Jensen Huang, the Nvidia co-founder who stepped down as CEO last week after he admitted to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive suspected of spying for China, whom Huang is not related to.
Megaspeed rejected allegations that it sent chips to China.
The move by the US comes just days before President Donald Trump will travel to China for an economic summit where he will meet with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping.

noticias.titulo: Revolut's Italian unit put under judicial administration after anti-money laundering failures
noticias.resumen: The measure against the digital bank was requested by the Milan Public Prosecutor's Office as part of a Guardia di Finanza investigation. According to investigators, shortcomings in control systems facilitated the concealment and transfer of €76.5 million.
noticias.texto:
The measure against the digital bank was requested by the Milan Public Prosecutor's Office as part of a Guardia di Finanza investigation. According to investigators, shortcomings in control systems facilitated the concealment and transfer of €76.5 million.
For one year the Italian branch of Revolut will be placed under judicial administration.
The Milan court decided this at the request of public prosecutor Paolo Storari, following investigations that revealed serious weaknesses in the digital bank's anti-money laundering system, including "relationships between the credit institution and persons under investigation or convicted of offences of money laundering and fraudulent transfer of assets, including those aggravated by mafia methods or facilitation", wrote Milan chief prosecutor Marcello Viola.
According to the prosecutor's office, by allowing access to the financial system to people who in many cases were also "subject to personal or asset-based preventive measures", this would have facilitated "the execution of transactions to transfer, conceal or divert capital" with a total value of 76.5 million euro.
A spokesperson for the UK-based digital bank said that Revolut will cooperate with the authorities. Within 60 days the bank will have to draw up a plan of action to address the problems identified. The next hearing has been scheduled by the court for 25 February 2027.
The checks that led to Revolut being placed under administration
The need for a "remediation programme" with judicial administration also stems from the fact that Revolut's problems span "a time frame extending from 2021 to 2026" and "concern different sectors, clients and schemes".
The failure to carry out mandatory anti-money laundering checks turned into a "stable management model", according to the prosecutor's office, which led to the concealment of financial flows worth almost 42 million euro between 2021 and this year. The financial anomalies are described as having a "repetitive and combined nature", with "incoming payments of significant amounts, immediate splitting and transferring, use of cash, currency conversion, sending funds to foreign accounts or crypto assets". These activities triggered alarms at several other institutions but not at Revolut.
The investigations by the Anti-mafia district directorate (Dda) follow two separate checks by the economic police unit of the Guardia di Finanza, Ansa reports.
The first concerns a 2024 anti-money laundering inspection of a Revolut virtual asset service provider, during which numerous irregularities emerged in identifying and verifying clients – more than one million breaches were alleged – and in applying control procedures, as well as failures to report suspicious transactions.
Among the client names are people investigated in the "Hydra" and "Equalize" cases
The second investigation concerns tax fraud proceedings in Milan in 2025, where the use of Revolut accounts to carry out transactions linked to tax offences and money laundering reportedly emerged; 24 people are under investigation. For these individuals, taken as a "sample", several other institutions had filed hundreds of suspicious transaction reports.
Through an order to produce documents, the prosecutor's office requested paperwork from Revolut but received only partial answers.
According to Ansa, among the names of Italian clients of the bank is Maurizio Ponzoni, who according to another investigation is allegedly in "business relations" with the Calabrian mafia boss in Lombardy, Vincenzo Rispoli. The files also contain the name of Saverio Pintaudi, involved in the "Hydra" case, and that of Nunzio Samuele Calamucci, an IT expert arrested in 2024 in the "Equalize" case over alleged unauthorised access to strategic databases.
The investigations led to the reconstruction of flows in "a circuit of Italian and foreign companies" that are allegedly linked to the "Greco clan", known for arms and drugs trafficking. The name of Pasquale Puglia also appears, linked to the Molluso clan and convicted of mafia association. In his case, diversions of sums "subject to seizure" are also believed to have occurred.
However, there is no evidence to link Revolut directly "to the persons who benefited" or that its corporate bodies "knowingly agreed to the individual criminal schemes", according to the documents.
What will happen to Revolut
The administrators' mandate is limited to the areas in which problems have been identified and, under the decision of the preventive measures section of the Milan court, there will be no general intervention affecting all of the bank's activities.
Working alongside the bank's management as court-appointed administrators will be lawyer Ilaria Ramoni and professional consultant Piero Antonio Capitini.
Judicial administration does not, under the decision, entail a general intervention across all the institution's activities. The administrators' mandate is confined to the areas where problems have been identified.
The task will be carried out by lawyer Ilaria Ramoni and professional consultant Piero Antonio Capitini, who have been called in to work with the bank's management to reconstruct how internal responsibilities for anti-money laundering prevention are allocated.
Checks will also be carried out on the IT tools used to monitor financial movements, to determine what information is collected, how alert thresholds are set and whether the anomalies identified are actually subjected to further investigation.
The procedures for opening online accounts and for linking payment cards to their respective holders will also be examined, with particular attention to user identification, authentication, identity fraud prevention and the handling of complaints from people who claim they did not request a card or open an account.

noticias.titulo: Moulin Rouge dancers kick off Paris Christmas celebrations
noticias.resumen: Moulin Rouge dancers and Republican Guard musicians launch Christmas lights in Paris, France, with a French cancan performance near the Madeleine church.
noticias.texto:
Moulin Rouge dancers performed the French cancan alongside Republican Guard musicians in Paris, France, on Sunday, 15 November 2026, to mark the launch of the Christmas lights on Faubourg Saint-Honoré.
In front of the Madeleine church, the dancers kicked their legs to the sound of brass instruments as spectators watched, filmed and applauded. The show ended with the trees along the street lighting up for Christmas.
Organised by the local merchants' association, the event aimed to bring festive cheer to the capital and improve its image following recent protests.
The association's chair said he wanted to show a more positive side of Paris, while a Moulin Rouge dancer described the occasion as special and welcomed the chance to bring some joy ahead of the festive season.

noticias.titulo: Can we trust AI to guide climate policy? New report warns against glaring ‘design flaw’
noticias.resumen: AI models answer about 90 per cent of climate questions accurately in English, but quickly give in to pushback, according to a report showcased at COP31.
noticias.texto:
AI models answer about 90 per cent of climate questions accurately in English, but quickly give in to pushback, according to a report showcased at COP31.
The desire to please is baked into AI chatbots, which are designed to keep users engaged in conversation for as long as possible.
This often means predicting and modelling what you want to hear – even if it means bending the facts.
While it might be harmless for certain tasks – and can even be helpful for things like overcoming self doubt – it could be far more damaging if its influence seeps into high-stakes realms like government climate policy.
AI chatbots can explain climate science well, but they quickly abandon the facts when users push back, according to a new report by UNESCO and University College London (UCL) presented at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.
Researchers found that AI models answered around 90 per cent of neutral climate questions correctly. But when users challenged those answers, or asserted plausible-sounding fabrications, the models rapidly gave way.
In eight out of 10 cases, they changed course at the first sign of mild disagreement, including by confirming false claims such as that CO2 is not the main driver of climate change.
‘Sycophantic by design’: A design flaw that could skew climate policy
The report says sycophantic behaviour is built in during training. Models are rewarded for polite, non-confrontational and validating answers, because humans prefer them.
“AI has extraordinary potential to make complex climate science accessible to all,” says Leona Verdadero, UNESCO’s lead author of the report. But “models have a design flaw – they are incentivised to agree with their user”, she says.
Senior author Dr Maria Perez-Ortiz of UCL adds that AI models’ fluency with existing knowledge can give “a false sense of their capabilities”.
Despite having impressive factual recall, the models were found to be an unreliable tool for building robust climate policies.
When they were given a new piece of evidence and asked whether it supported or contradicted accepted climate science, even the strongest ones were only 75 per cent accurate on average.
Their performance was even worse when they were asked to assess how well policies work together – an important part of designing effective climate strategies. The models scored just 33.8 per cent accuracy on average, only slightly above the 33.3 per cent expected from random guessing.
The report therefore warns policymakers and researchers against using AI models to develop climate policy.
AI accuracy falls among some languages
Performance also varied widely by language. Models answered 88.6 per cent of questions correctly in English, and did comparably well in Spanish, French and Portuguese.
Accuracy fell to 83.6 per cent in Hindi and Bengali, 81.4 per cent in Urdu and 78.3 per cent in Swahili. That’s because multilingual models don’t reason first and then translate, the report says. Their answers reflect the quantity and quality of the training data in each language.
Speakers of the lower-scoring languages live in regions disproportionately affected by climate change, the authors note.
Climate disinformation is growing more sophisticated
The report was commissioned as part of UNESCO’s contribution to the Global Initiative for Information Integrity on Climate Change, launched with the UN and Brazil in November 2024.
UNESCO says climate disinformation is becoming more sophisticated. Rather than denying climate change is real, those seeking to undermine climate change action increasingly suggest it isn’t human-caused, that technology alone will solve it, or that it's too late or costly to take action.
The researchers tested up to 33 leading models on nine datasets, across 13 languages and 656 climate-policy questions, which they checked against En-ROADS, a science-based simulation tool.

noticias.titulo: Belgian king grants PM De Wever more time to agree new budget
noticias.resumen: King Philippe had refused De Wever's resignation earlier this month and asked him to continue with budget talks, giving him until 16 November to solve the impasse.
noticias.texto:
King Philippe had refused De Wever's resignation earlier this month and asked him to continue with budget talks, giving him until 16 November to solve the impasse.
Belgium's King Philippe has given Prime Minister Bart De Wever more time to work out a new cost-cutting budget with his coalition partners after the latest round of talks failed to produce an agreement.
"The king has asked the prime minister to continue the negotiations with a view to reaching an agreement as soon as possible and thus avoiding a damaging political and budgetary crisis for the country," the Royal Palace said on Monday.
De Wever, a Flemish conservative, will report back to the king on 23 November, it added.
The prime minister had informed the monarch in an audience earlier on Monday that he had "not yet managed to reconcile the differing views within his coalition on the budget, but that there is still a willingness to seek solutions together," according to the Palace statement.
Philippe had refused De Wever's resignation earlier this month and asked him to continue with budget talks, giving him until 16 November to solve the impasse.
De Wever is seeking €10 billion by 2029 to plug a deficit gap, but coalition parties are at odds over how to find the funds.
Measures put forward have included spending cuts and a VAT increase.
Weekend talks had seen four of the five governing parties agree on the broad outlines of a deal.
But the leftist Vooruit party stood firm, arguing that high earners should have to contribute more to public finances to help offset some of the cuts.

noticias.titulo: Repsol sues Spanish power firms for €120m over 2025 blackout
noticias.resumen: The oil company has taken the electricity distributors of Iberdrola, Endesa and Naturgy, as well as grid operator Red Eléctrica, to court over damage to five industrial sites after the blackout that hit Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025.
noticias.texto:
The oil company has taken the electricity distributors of Iberdrola, Endesa and Naturgy, as well as grid operator Red Eléctrica, to court over damage to five industrial sites after the blackout that hit Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025.
Repsol has filed lawsuits against the electricity distributors of Iberdrola, Endesa and Naturgy, seeking around €120 million, according to Spanish media reports, for damage to its industrial sites following the blackout on 28 April 2025. Repsol is also seeking to hold Spain’s grid operator, Red Eléctrica, jointly liable in all five cases.
The lawsuits, filed in October, target the distributors that supply electricity to the affected sites. El Confidencial first reported the claims, and Repsol sources confirmed the filings to El País on Monday. Repsol is seeking compensation from Naturgy’s distributor for its site in A Coruña, from Iberdrola’s for its sites in Bilbao and Cartagena, and from Endesa’s for those in Tarragona and Puertollano.
Before going to court, Repsol tried to reach an out-of-court settlement, but the talks failed. Its chief executive, Josu Jon Imaz, said in February that Repsol was preparing legal action to seek compensation.
Spain’s regulator investigates possible breaches
A European expert panel concluded in March 2026 that several factors combined to trigger a rapid rise in voltage and a series of generator disconnections, cutting power across mainland Spain and Portugal.
In April 2026, Spain’s competition and energy regulator, the CNMC, opened an initial 20 cases over possible breaches of electricity rules and announced further cases the following week. The companies named in the first round included Red Eléctrica, Iberdrola, Endesa, Naturgy and Repsol itself.
The regulator said it had found signs of possible breaches. It said the blackout had several causes and that opening the cases did not establish which companies were responsible.

noticias.titulo: Shareholders sue Intel after its shares plunge nearly 29%
noticias.resumen: Shareholders have sued Intel after its shares fell nearly 29% in their biggest one-day drop in decades. A weaker-than-expected sales forecast exposed the impact of a deepening PC slump and Intel’s difficulty meeting demand for server chips.
noticias.texto:
Shareholders have sued Intel after its shares fell nearly 29% in their biggest one-day drop in decades. A weaker-than-expected sales forecast exposed the impact of a deepening PC slump and Intel’s difficulty meeting demand for server chips.
Shareholders have sued US chipmaker Intel, accusing it of hiding how badly a slump in personal computer sales was affecting its results.
Intel shares fell nearly 29% on 30 October, a day after the company issued a weaker-than-expected revenue forecast for the fourth quarter, citing a sluggish PC market and manufacturing bottlenecks.
The City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System, a Michigan pension fund for firefighters and police officers, filed the proposed class action on Friday, 13 November. Its law firm, Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd, announced the lawsuit that evening in the US and invited investors with substantial losses to apply to be lead plaintiff.
The complaint alleges that Intel and its executives made "materially false and/or misleading" statements about the company’s business and finances. It says Intel understated how badly weaker PC sales were affecting its Client Computing and Physical AI Group, the division that includes its laptop and desktop chip business.
What did Intel tell investors in July?
Intel had warned that the wider PC market was weakening. But on its July earnings call, Chief Financial Officer David Zinsner said he expected revenue from notebook and desktop chips to stay roughly flat in the third quarter and revenue in the broader division to rise slightly.
When Intel reported its third-quarter results on 29 October, revenue in the division had fallen 9% from the previous quarter, down about $800mn (€719mn) to $8.1bn (€7.3bn).
Intel’s quarterly filing showed that notebook and desktop revenue fell to $6.9bn (€6.2bn), down $424mn (€381mn) from a year earlier. The company said it sold 14% fewer units because of weaker demand and competition.
Laptop and desktop makers have been grappling with shortages of memory chips and rising component costs. PC shipments have fallen as manufacturers struggle to secure parts and higher prices put buyers off.
Intel said in October that customers were cutting back on orders to reduce stock. The lawsuit alleges that PC makers and distributors had been left with large stocks of unsold computers as higher component costs pushed up prices.
Intel also said it could not fully meet demand for server chips, limiting how much it could benefit from the expansion of AI data centres.
Intel expects the PC downturn to continue into 2027
Intel forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $15bn to $16bn (€13.5bn to €14.4bn). The midpoint was $1bn (€900mn) below its third-quarter revenue and, according to the complaint, about $1.5bn (€1.35bn) below the average analyst estimate.
The company expects the PC downturn to last through at least the first half of 2027. It expects the overall PC market to shrink by about 10% in 2027, measured in units, after a decline of about 12% in 2026.
Intel remains optimistic about longer-term demand for its products and is ordering more equipment to increase production.
By the close on 29 October, before Intel reported its results, its shares had more than doubled since the end of 2025, as investors bet the company would benefit from the AI boom. Intel says the growing use of AI is boosting demand for its general-purpose server chips.
Intel did not immediately respond to Euronews’ request for comment.

noticias.titulo: Europe must embrace AI's 'creative destruction', Nobel economist says
noticias.resumen: Nobel Prize-winning economist Philippe Aghion urged the EU to encourage new players in the AI market, ease restrictions on state aid and strengthen protections for workers facing technological disruption.
noticias.texto:
Nobel Prize-winning economist Philippe Aghion urged the EU to encourage new players in the AI market, ease restrictions on state aid and strengthen protections for workers facing technological disruption.
Artificial intelligence (AI) could drive economic growth in Europe, provided the EU’s competition rules allow new companies to enter the market, Nobel Prize-winning economist Philippe Aghion said on Monday.
His remarks come amid growing concerns over the dominance of a handful of US companies in the AI market and the technology’s impact on employment, with fears of widespread job losses in the coming years.
“With AI, more than ever, there is creative destruction because if you look at the rate of job destruction and job creation, it's being accelerated by the AI revolution – and that's where it's so important to let new firms come in,” Aghion said during an event in Brussels.
He added: “At the same time, it is important to have institutions like the flexicurity system that smooths out transition from old jobs to new jobs, because it helps manage the critical disruption.”
Aghion pointed to Denmark’s labour market model, which combines flexibility in hiring and firing with a generous safety net for unemployed workers.
A recent European Commission report shows that employment among highly skilled workers could grow by 20% by 2040 thanks to AI, while job losses among low-skilled workers could range from 20% to 60% across Europe.
Aghion shared the 2025 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for his work on “creative destruction”, the process by which new innovations continually displace older technologies, businesses and jobs.
Growth and job creation
Aghion said EU welfare systems are better equipped than the US system to manage AI-related employment changes: “We are ahead of the US when it comes to which labour market to accommodate AI revolution.”
However, he also said the EU should draw inspiration from the US in terms of industrial policy to ensure AI delivers growth and jobs.
“In the US, they have both competition policy and industrial policy. They have the DARPA - Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency - which is a competition-friendly way to do industrial policy.”
DARPA is a US agency responsible for developing emerging defence technologies. “In Europe so far we don't have the equivalent of the DARPA and I would very well imagine one to develop AI computing power and that would also encourage new firms to enter [the market].”
He added that the EU’s approach to competition policy was “precluding” the sector from receiving state aid, “which was a very anti-industrial policy.”
Aghion argued that EU competition rules should encourage new entrants and promote data sharing across the entire AI value chain, including cloud computing.
The dominance of US technology giants in the AI sector has already attracted scrutiny from EU regulators.
In December 2025, the European Commission launched an investigation into Google over concerns that the company could be distorting competition by imposing unfair terms on publishers and content creators or granting itself privileged access to their content.
The Commission, which enforces EU competition law, also opened an antitrust investigation into Meta to determine whether its policy restricting AI providers’ access to WhatsApp breached EU rules.

noticias.titulo: Albania's Rama slams Serbian nationalist song at EU conference
noticias.resumen: Albania's PM Rama criticised a band for playing a Serbian nationalist song claiming Kosovo as Serbian land at the European Commission’s enlargement conference. Marta Kos said it does not reflect the Commission’s position, while Pristina called it unacceptable.
noticias.texto:
Albania's PM Rama criticised a band for playing a Serbian nationalist song claiming Kosovo as Serbian land at the European Commission’s enlargement conference. Marta Kos said it does not reflect the Commission’s position, while Pristina called it unacceptable.
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama criticised the performance of a Serbian nationalist song that claims Kosovo as part of Serbia at the opening of the EU Enlargement Summit, prompting outrage in the region.
"I don't know if it was deliberate or because of ignorance. But a Serbian nationalistic song was performed here on the eve of this event," Rama said at the summit on Monday. "To add insult to injury, it was performed under the beautiful title Melodies of Unity."
"It's not that these words hurt the feeling of Albania or of the Albanian nation or of the Albanian citizens of the Republic of Kosovo, but it is about the need to let go of anything that brings us back in the past," he continued.
Slovenian band Marko Hatlak & Kapobanda played “Oj Kosovo, Kosovo” on Sunday evening at the concert opening the European Commission’s annual enlargement conference.
Playing such a politically charged song at a Commission-hosted conference outraged Kosovo, which saw it as a provocation.
“This is not cultural exchange. The song advances explicit political claims over the territory of the Republic of Kosova. Its inclusion in an official European Commission event dedicated to enlargement, unity and good-neighbourly relations is unacceptable,” Agron Bajrami, Kosovo’s ambassador to Belgium, said on X.
The band was meant to play a song from each candidate country, including Kosovo, which has no formal candidate status and is not recognised as a state by five EU countries. Yet the song chosen for Kosovo is Serbian in language and in sentiment.
“I regret the choice of the song by the musicians. It touches sensitive feelings. Particularly given the painful history and the different experiences of the communities in Kosovo which are coming from this area,” Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos told reporters on Monday.
“I want to stress that this song in no way reflects the position of the European Commission or myself with respect to Kosovo and its history. What is clear is that we cannot change our shared past, but we can choose our shared future,” Kos continued.
The song was written after Slobodan Milošević’s landmark 1989 Gazimestan speech, in which the then Serbian president cast Kosovo as the heart of Serbian national identity, on the eve of the Yugoslav wars.
"We all need to engage for transforming our neighbourhoods. This is what all this is about. Because at the end of the day, we are not seeking to come here. We are seeking to bring Europe in there," Rama added.

noticias.titulo: Move over Michelin: ‘Gold Key’ hospitality design awards crown best hotels for 2026
noticias.resumen: La Réserve Firenze, Six Senses London and 1 Hotel Copenhagen were among the European hotels recognised.
noticias.texto:
Move over Michelin: ‘Gold Key’ hospitality design awards crown best hotels for 2026
La Réserve Firenze, Six Senses London and 1 Hotel Copenhagen were among the European hotels recognised.
The winners have just been announced for the 46th Gold Key Awards for Excellence in Hospitality Design – and the top luxury hotel is in Europe.
La Réserve Firenze, which is made up of six apartments within a converted 15th-century palazzo, took the top gong.
With interiors by Gilles&Boissier, the property in Florence has “a soothing material palette, a subtly wabi-sabi atmosphere, and a meticulously curated selection of art”.
Writing about the interior design choices on the Gilles&Boissier website, Patrick Gilles said: “Our architectural approach was one of restraint, almost of silence.
“We opted for a deliberately understated design, while bringing as much light as possible into this long-dormant building on Via Santo Spirito, whose top floor overlooks the Arno and the city.”
The Gold Key Awards recognise interior designers across categories including lobbies, guestrooms, hotels and resorts among others.
This year, more than 425 entries were submitted for projects across the globe.
Other Gold Key winners and finalists
Six Senses London and Shangri-La Kunming in China, both of which were designed by AvroKO, were runners-up in the luxury hotel category.
The former is located within what was once the Whiteley’s department store, and has interiors that take inspiration from William Whiteley’s fascination with the Great Exhibition of 1851. The latter, meanwhile, is meant to feel like a tea merchant’s private residence, a nod to its location in Yunnan, which is known as the birthplace of tea.
As for resorts, the top gong went to Four Seasons Resort & Residences AMAALA at Triple Bay in Saudi Arabia.
According to design firm Goddard Littlefair, the design honours the “raw, elemental beauty of Triple Bay, its mineral geology, shifting desert light and vast horizons”.
Rosewood Mandarina in Mexico’s Riviera Nayarit, a runner-up in the resort category, was designed by Bando x Seidel Meersseman.
The team drew on the traditional art of the Indigenous Huichol and Cora peoples for the furnishings, with custom pieces including Barro Negro pottery and rope-assembly installations.
Another runner up from China was Zoland Resort Hotel on Emei Mountain in Sichuan Province. Designed by Studio J. Bridgland, the building is meant to blend into the surrounding forest, with local stone and timber throughout.
While the majority of the winners and runners up come from the Americas and Asia, Europe also had another runner-up in the eco-conscious/socially conscious hotel category: 1 Hotel Copenhagen.
Meant to “embrace biophilic design in a way that’s uniquely Nordic”, the property has handcrafted Danish furnishings and plenty of greenery.

noticias.titulo: The US has lost measles-free status. What does that mean and what’s next?
noticias.resumen: In countries where measles is endemic, the virus spreads in a continuous chain from person to person for a year or more.
noticias.texto:
In countries where measles is endemic, the virus spreads in a continuous chain from person to person for a year or more.
The United States has reportedly lost its measles-free status after 26 years, as an outbreak that began in Texas in early 2025 swept across the country.
The US has recorded 5,739 measles cases so far this year — up from 2,286 cases in 2025, according to a tracker from Johns Hopkins University. Almost all cases have been among unvaccinated people or those with unknown vaccination status. State health departments report 10 deaths linked to measles in 2026.
Last week, an expert group from the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) met to discuss the US’s status as a country that had eliminated measles. They determined that measles had established a foothold in the US for the first time since 2000, when it gained elimination status.
The loss of measles-free status means “decades of public health gains have been officially reversed,” said Wendy Armstrong, a doctor and president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America.
PAHO’s decision, which was widely expected by infectious disease experts, was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.
But what is measles-elimination status, how do countries lose it and what happens next?
How do countries lose measles-elimination status?
In countries where measles is endemic, the virus spreads in a continuous chain from person to person for a year or more.
In countries that have eliminated measles, the virus doesn’t spread continuously because enough people are vaccinated. Occasional outbreaks can still crop up, typically linked to international travel, but public health agencies can contain them quickly enough.
A country loses its elimination status if measles returns and continues to spread uninterrupted for at least a year, according to PAHO. The organisation tracks whether measles outbreaks are linked to the same viral strain, with the same genotype and lineage.
The US was declared measles-free in 2000, after it ran massive vaccination campaigns and created a programme to make the jabs free for millions of children.
But an outbreak in West Texas in early 2025 has since spread to other states, with closely related viruses infecting people in Utah as recently as May 2026, according to an analysis from ProPublica. That chain of spread is likely what cost the US its measles-free status, meaning measles is now considered endemic in the country.
Which other countries have lost measles-free status?
The US is not alone. Its northern neighbour Canada lost measles-free status in 2025, amid an outbreak that caused more than 6,400 cases across 10 provinces and territories.
In January, six countries in the World Health Organization’s European region — Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Spain, the United Kingdom and Uzbekistan — lost measles-free status after cases rose in 2024.
Measles was already considered endemic in France, Germany, Italy, Poland, Romania and a handful of other countries in Europe and Central Asia. There were nearly 34,000 measles cases across the region in 2025, according to the WHO.
Health officials say lagging vaccination rates give measles an opportunity to spread. The disease is so contagious that at least 95% of a community must be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks. Two doses of the measles vaccine provide up to 97% protection against measles.
How can countries get their measles-free status back?
The US and other countries can regain measles-free status if they interrupt the spread of the disease for at least one year.
It took Canada nearly two years to quell the outbreak that cost it its measles-free status; it began in October 2024 and was officially declared over in October 2026. To stop transmission, local health workers identified infected people and their contacts, did laboratory testing to track measles’ spread and promoted vaccination, Canada’s public health agency said.
European health officials have said countries should improve their disease surveillance, outbreak response and efforts to reach under-vaccinated communities.
In the US, Armstrong called on the government to fund state and local health departments, invest in the infectious disease workforce and promote measles vaccination.
“The reemergence of measles at dangerous levels has quickly become a threat to communities across the country,” she said.

noticias.titulo: US airports slowly return to normal after three days of disruption caused by take-off ban
noticias.resumen: Throughout the weekend, stranded passengers wandered through chaotic airports and sat on floors, waiting for updates or to be rebooked.
noticias.texto:
Throughout the weekend, stranded passengers wandered through chaotic airports and sat on floors, waiting for updates or to be rebooked.
US air travel was slowly returning to normal on Monday after three days of widespread disruption following an extraordinary take-off ban issued by US aviation authorities.
The ground stop issued on Friday afternoon was only the second time such a directive had been issued nationwide in the busy US airspace since planes were grounded following the 9/11 terrorist attacks and was blamed by the Trump administration on a faulty upgrade to communications equipment.
On Monday morning, more than 250 US-related flights, those traveling within, into or out of the United States, scheduled for the same day were cancelled, according to industry tracker FlightAware.
That marked a dramatic shift from the more than 2,300 flights that were cancelled on Sunday.
There were delays to more than 700 US-related flights scheduled for Monday, compared to more than 10,000 the previous day.
The Trump administration sought to reassure weary flyers as questions remained over how such chaos could unfold in the world's largest economy, a country that prides itself on its technological prowess.
Throughout the weekend, stranded passengers wandered through chaotic airports and sat on floors, waiting for updates or to be rebooked.
Officials blamed Friday's colossal disruption on faulty work to upgrade air traffic control communication cables.
President Donald Trump ended uncharacteristic days of silence on the ground stop on Sunday, but only to blame his predecessor Joe Biden for the debacle.
Trump insisted he inherited a mess from the Biden administration and said Congress, which his party has controlled for two years, must approve funds to upgrade America's outdated air traffic control system.
"The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster," Trump said, referring to the Federal Aviation Administration.
"Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began," Trump said.
FAA chief Bryan Bedford said on Saturday that air travel for millions of Americans stranded at airports would return to normal by the close of business on Sunday.
But Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday morning it will actually take longer to get planes, crews and travellers to where they need to be.
"We're going to see things come back to normal today, but probably fully normal tomorrow," Duffy said on ABC News.
"We had airplanes and crews out of position because of Friday, so it takes a little bit of time to do that."
Ageing infrastructure
Duffy also rejected calls for his resignation over the travel chaos, insisting he inherited woefully outdated air traffic control infrastructure such as radar equipment that dates back to the 1960s.
"So when we do work and things go wrong, of course I'm the secretary. But I also have to acknowledge what was delivered to me," Duffy said in an interview on CNN.
The ground stop not only plunged US air travel into chaos, but it also raised serious concerns about the country's ageing infrastructure.
Duffy has appealed for $50 billion (€45 billion) in funds to upgrade and modernise the air traffic control system, and called for Congress, which controls the purse strings of the US government, to "meet this moment."
But Democrats quickly pounced to say Congress under Trump's Republicans could already have done this.

noticias.titulo: Five things you need to know before Anthropic goes public
noticias.resumen: The maker of Claude wants investors to value it at more than $1 trillion (€909 billion), despite paper losses in the tens of billions and a set-up that leaves shareholders with little say.
noticias.texto:
The maker of Claude wants investors to value it at more than $1 trillion (€909 billion), despite paper losses in the tens of billions and a set-up that leaves shareholders with little say.
Anthropic is expected to set the final price of its shares on Wednesday 18 November and begin trading on the Nasdaq exchange in New York, United States, the following day under the symbol ANT.
The company has proposed a price of $70 to $78 (€64 to €71) a share, which would value it at about $1.2 trillion (€1.1trn) in the middle of that range. The listing will be the biggest test yet of whether investors believe artificial intelligence can make money over the long term.
Not everyone is convinced. At a briefing organised by the Interfaith Center on Corporate Responsibility, SOC Investment Group and Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund, governance and legal experts warned of “red flags” in the company’s filings.
“Anthropic is rushing toward an IPO without answering fundamental questions about its readiness to operate as a publicly traded company,” said New York City’s chief financial and accountability officer Mark Levine. He said the company had yet to show how it was tackling what it has itself called potential “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity” from AI.
Here are five things you need to know ahead of the launch.
1. The split with OpenAI
Anthropic was founded in early 2021 by a group of researchers who walked out of OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, where they had made their names working on AI safety.
Dario Amodei joined OpenAI in 2016, when it was still a nonprofit. He led its safety team and its research into “scaling laws”, the pattern by which AI models become more capable as they are trained on more data. His younger sister, Daniela Amodei, joined in 2018 and rose to vice president of safety and policy.
The siblings and several colleagues left in December 2020 after disagreeing with OpenAI’s leadership over how AI should be built. They set up Anthropic about four weeks later. The two companies, both based in San Francisco, have been bitter rivals ever since.
2. It has been backed by Big Tech
Anthropic’s filing shows Amazon and Google’s parent company Alphabet among its largest backers. Microsoft, Nvidia and Founders Fund, the investment firm started by Peter Thiel, have also invested. In May, Anthropic raised $65 billion (€59 billion) from investors who valued it at $965 billion (€877 billion). It was the first time a funding round had valued it above OpenAI.
Dario Amodei’s thinking was shaped by two overlapping movements. One is rationalism, associated with AI writer Eliezer Yudkowsky, who has long warned that advanced AI could pose a catastrophic risk to humanity. The other is effective altruism, which uses evidence to work out how money and time can do the most good.
Donors linked to effective altruism supplied much of Anthropic’s early funding. Facebook cofounder Dustin Moskovitz and Skype cofounder Jaan Tallinn backed its first round, alongside former Google chief executive Eric Schmidt.
3. Shareholders get a stake in the profits, not control
Anthropic is offering 825 million shares to the public at $70 to $78 (€64 to €71) each. Of those, about 801 million are new shares sold by the company and about 24 million are sold by existing shareholders. At the middle of the price range, that would raise roughly $61 billion (€55 billion), making it one of the largest stock market listings ever.
Separately, seven companies including Nvidia, Google and Microsoft have agreed to buy $26 billion (€24 billion) of shares without voting rights in a private deal alongside the listing.
What public buyers will not get is much influence. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, a type of US company legally required to pursue a stated purpose as well as profit. Its purpose is to “responsibly develop and maintain advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity”.
The founders hold 50.1% of shareholder votes, while an independent body, the Long-Term Benefit Trust, chooses four of the seven members of the company’s board.
The trust has five trustees, including former US Federal Reserve chair Ben Bernanke. None of them has a financial stake in the company.
Critics say the result leaves outside investors powerless. “Anthropic has built a governance structure that would leave shareholders with almost no voice,” said Josh Zinner, chief executive of the Interfaith Center on Corporate Responsibility. “Anthropic is shielding itself against outside accountability, while the decisions made inside the company will affect every person on earth.”
4. It is anchored to a vast infrastructure gamble
Anthropic has committed to spend at least $518 billion (€471 billion) with six suppliers over roughly a decade, to secure the chips, data centres and electricity its AI needs. About 80% of that cannot be cancelled and must be paid whether or not the capacity is used.
These commitments are not formally debt, but they work like it. Many of Anthropic’s biggest customers, by contrast, can cut or stop their spending at any time. The company is betting that demand for AI will keep outstripping the computing power available to run it.
Anthropic also depends heavily on a few partners. Nearly half its 2025 revenue came through Amazon and Google, which sell access to its AI through their cloud services. The same companies supply much of its computing power, and the filing says they would not provide all the capacity Anthropic asked for. It also warns that a catastrophic AI incident could cause damages too large to insure.
5. It faces rivals in Washington, San Francisco and China
In January, the US Department of Defense, under President Donald Trump, asked for unrestricted use of Claude. Anthropic refused to allow two uses: mass surveillance of Americans and fully autonomous lethal weapons.
In February, Trump ordered federal agencies to stop using Anthropic’s technology. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth then had the company labelled a supply-chain risk, a designation usually reserved for foreign adversaries.
Direct competitor OpenAI has pushed its own listing back to 2027 at the earliest and was recently valued at about $1.25 trillion (€1.14 trillion) in a private round, according to reports. That is close to Anthropic’s price tag.
OpenAI is private, so its figures have not been checked by independent auditors, and the two companies count sales made through cloud partners differently. The gap may therefore be smaller than it looks.
A price war could come from Chinese AI models such as DeepSeek, Alibaba’s Qwen, Moonshot’s Kimi and Z.ai’s GLM. Anyone can download them for free and they are much cheaper to run, and some US start-ups have moved routine work to them. Chinese open models accounted for about 30% of usage on the AI marketplace OpenRouter by early 2026.
Anthropic has accused several Chinese labs of using tens of thousands of fake accounts to copy Claude’s answers to train their own models. Analysts see the main danger as cheaper rivals forcing Anthropic to cut its prices and accept thinner profits, rather than overtaking it at the top end.

noticias.titulo: US and Iran slide closer to fresh all-out war as new exchange of fire increases
noticias.resumen: A sudden rise in Iranian attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz follows an increasing number of air strikes between the US and Iran, as both sides trade intensifying warning shots, bringing the region closer to a new all-out war. Meanwhile, a third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the region.
noticias.texto:
