A sudden rise in Iranian attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz follows an increasing number of air strikes between the US and Iran, as both sides trade intensifying warning shots, bringing the region closer to a new all-out war. Meanwhile, a third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the region.
The US and Iran have conducted widening airstrikes in a fast-moving cycle of violence since Sunday, while Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said two more oil tankers exploded in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, bringing the total number of tankers that caught fire in the waterway to six, since Sunday.
The US military launched new airstrikes on Iranian missile launchers across southern Iran on Sunday night after Iranian forces attacked a US base in Bahrain and fired missiles at tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. Amid this significant escalation across the region, the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier has now arrived to join two other carrier strike groups in US CENTCOM's operating region.
Iran targeted Bahrain twice over the last weekend, for the first time in months since the Iran war subsided, conducting a drone attack on the US helicopter compound at Al Riffa Air Base on Sunday, in response to previous US strikes. US CENTCOM denied any damage to US assets, as Iran appears to be ramping up its warnings and show force using attacks on Gulf states again.
Iran also attacked tankers in Hormuz which usually triggers immediate US strikes on Iran’s coastal military infrastructure.
The US military then struck Iranian launchers in Bandar Lengeh and Sirik in southern Iran on Sunday night, targetting a wider area than the previous strike cycles and with a higher rate of fire by both sides.
Flight tracking portals registered a much larger US Air Force presence over the Persian Gulf in the region than in the previous weeks, just as the US is continuing its military build-up.
More tankers struck in the Strait of Hormuz
The IRGC said on Sunday that two tankers were trying to cross the southern route of the Strait of Hormuz under direct US military guidance when they allegedly encountered naval mines that "lit up the skies for hours", Iran's Tasnim news agency reported.
The IRGC described the actions as a response to what it called the "illegal US blockade" and violation of Iranian regulations in the Strait of Hormuz, warning oil companies again that the southern route of the waterway was mined.
Then on Monday, Iran’s Navy announced that a "violator" oil tanker caught fire after colliding with a sea mine in the restricted area east of the Strait of Hormuz and was unable to move.
“Turning off tracking systems and unauthorised entry into prohibited and unsafe maritime areas exposes offending vessels to serious risks,” Iran’s Navy said in a statement.
It was not clear whether the tanker is one of six tankers reported by the IRGC to have caught fire, or if a separate incident occurred, and claims by the IRGC and the army about the number of tankers damaged and details of the explosions have not been independently confirmed.
However, the UK's Maritime Trade Operations Authority (UKMTO) issued a statement confirming that it had received reports of at least one incident in the early hours of Monday morning when an oil tanker was hit by "an unidentified projectile" while passing out of the Strait of Hormuz.
"The collision led to a fire in the engine room," the report said, adding that so far no casualties have been reported and all crew members are safe and that "the assessment of the damage and the extent of the environmental damage is currently unclear."
Oil prices rose on Monday following the large number of vessels incidents in the Strait of Hormuz.
Third US aircraft carrier arrives in the Middle East
The USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier arrived in the CENTCOM area of operations in the region, joining the USS George Washington and USS George H.W. Bush carrier strike groups, marking the first time since the Iraq war that the US has three carriers in the Middle East.
The US military is now completing a massive build-up of naval and air strike capabilities of approximately 19 US warships in the region, including the Red Sea, with guided missile destroyers and cruisers alongside other naval forces.
Meanwhile, the Wall Street Journal quoted US intelligence analysts who assess in a low confidence estimate that Iran now has between 1,500 and 2,500 new missiles in addition to new drones and short-range missiles, while Israeli military officials place Iran’s new capabilities at 1,500 ballistic missiles.
On 10 November, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) released a picture claiming to show the head of Iran’s armed forces and the IRGC Aerospace Force commander touring tunnels with missiles and launchers which they called a new underground “missile city.”
The Iranian regime has continued its threats against renewed US wide-scale attacks, with military officials telling Iranian Tabnak News on Sunday that "Iran's new offensive military doctrine means that the country will no longer be limited to calculated retaliation and will break the cycle of escalation," and threatening US bases in Europe too.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio lashed out at the “Shia clerics of Iran” on Sunday, stating that “every problem in the Middle East, every major problem in the Middle East – the Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia, the Shia militias that destabilize Iraq, the fighting elements that supported Assad and the destruction of Syria, Hizballah in Lebanon – everywhere you turn, there is one common denominator: the Shia clerics of Iran and their expansionist mentality.”
“This is an extraordinary historic danger and one that cannot be ignored,” Rubio warned.
As both sides appear to intensify their warning shots to build pressure and force concessions, the former head of Israel’s military intelligence research department Danny Citrinowicz said in a post on X that “the current situation in the Strait of Hormuz is inherently unstable and cannot be sustained indefinitely," and "that even if neither side wants a broader confrontation, the current dynamics are pushing both toward escalation.”
“As long as the United States maintains its naval blockade and attempts to push tankers in the southern shipping lane, Tehran will continue to regard these actions as acts of war," the Iran expert said, adding that "Iran is unlikely to accept this reality indefinitely. Instead, it will seek to raise the costs of the blockade through further attacks on tankers and potentially other targets, particularly if US military operations continue around Bandar Abbas," Citrinowicz said.
“There is a fundamental asymmetry between Washington and Tehran. The United States may believe it can maintain the blockade for an extended period, but Iran sees it as a direct threat to its economy, sovereignty, and national security. For the Iranian leadership, accepting the blockade without responding would amount to accepting a new strategic reality imposed by Washington. That is simply not how the regime in Tehran operates,” Citrinowicz concluded.

noticias.titulo: Sweden calls for new EU plan to unlock frozen Russian assets for Ukraine
noticias.resumen: Sweden urged the EU to use frozen Russian assets to supprt Ukraine, with Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard telling Euronews that the financial risks should be shared among member states.
noticias.texto:
Sweden urged the EU to use frozen Russian assets to supprt Ukraine, with Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard telling Euronews that the financial risks should be shared among member states.
Sweden has called on the European Commission to draw up a new proposal to use frozen Russian assets to help finance Ukraine, with Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard urging European countries to step up their military and financial support for Kyiv.
Speaking to Euronews, Stenergard said she hoped the Commission was working on a plan to move the assets out of Belgium and share the financial risks among EU member states.
She described the €90 billion loan agreed by the EU as an important step, but warned that bilateral support for Ukraine had since declined.
"We need more bilateral support. We need more loans, but we also need to use the frozen Russian assets," she said.
Stenergard also called for continued European military assistance, arguing that Russia was showing no interest in peace and that European countries should focus on increasing support for Kyiv while stepping up pressure on Moscow.
The foreign minister, who recently visited Abu Dhabi during negotiations aimed at ending the war, said she had seen nothing to make her optimistic about the prospects for a diplomatic breakthrough.
She insisted that Europe must have a seat at the negotiating table, arguing that any settlement would have far-reaching implications for European interests, including Ukraine's potential EU and NATO membership.
"We are not mediators," she said. "We should be at the table, but we should be on Ukraine's side."
Stenergard also warned that Russia was taking increasingly bold risks through hybrid attacks against European countries, particularly in the Baltic region.
She said Sweden had raised spending on civil defence to strengthen public preparedness and resilience, and called for greater European unity in the face of Russian attempts to sow division.
"What they basically want is to have us split up and also decrease support for Ukraine. So we should increase support for Ukraine. Stay united."

noticias.titulo: Concurrence : l’UEFA et une fédération de grands clubs de football européens visées par une plainte
noticias.resumen: L’Union des clubs européens estime que l’accord d’exclusivité conclu entre l’UEFA et une puissante organisation de clubs de football enfreint le droit européen de la concurrence.
noticias.texto: L’UEFA, l’instance dirigeante du football européen, et EFC, l’organisme représentant officiellement les clubs, ont fait l’objet lundi d’une plainte antitrust auprès de l’Union européenne déposée par une jeune organisation représentant des équipes qui ne sont pas dans l’élite. L’Union des clubs européens (UEC, en anglais) a contesté un accord stipulant que l’UEFA reconnaît l’association Clubs de football européens (EFC, en anglais) comme “ l’unique organisme ” représentant les clubs du continent. Elle souhaite que la Commission européenne examine si cet accord exclusif enfreint les règles de l’UE relatives aux accords anticoncurrentiels et aux abus de position dominante. L’UEC affirme que la représentation exclusive, combinée à ce qu’elle qualifie de “droits de vote inégaux” au sein d’EFC, permet aux clubs dominants d’influencer les règles qui s’appliquent à l’ensemble de la pyramide du football européen, aidant ainsi les grandes équipes, comme le Paris Saint-Germain ou le Bayern de Munich, à consolider leur avantage dans un secteur qui génère des dizaines de milliards d’euros de chiffre d’affaires annuel. “La question est simple : qui a son mot à dire sur les règles qui déterminent l’avenir de chaque club ? Aujourd’hui, une seule organisation détient ce pouvoir pour l’ensemble des clubs européens, alors que la plupart d’entre eux n’y ont aucune influence réelle”, a pointé Dennis Gudasic, directeur exécutif du Lokomotiva Zagreb en Croatie et secrétaire général de l’UEC. Reste qu’il sera difficile de convaincre Bruxelles d’ouvrir une enquête. La DG Concurrence, le puissant organe de la Commission chargé de l’application des règles de concurrence, s’est toujours montrée réticente à ouvrir des enquêtes dans les affaires liées au football, les considérant comme politiquement toxiques , selon des hauts responsables actuels et anciens de cette administration. L’UEFA entretient également de bonnes relations avec la Commission. Son président Aleksander Čeferin et le commissaire européen chargé des Sports, Glenn Micallef, ont renouvelé un accord de coopération lors d’une réunion qui s’est tenue à Nyon, en Suisse, la semaine dernière. En comparaison, les relations entre Bruxelles et la Fifa sont habituellement glaciales, selon trois responsables actuels et anciens de la Commission. Pourtant, Bruxelles s’est montré réticent à ouvrir une enquête officielle en matière de concurrence à l’encontre de l’instance dirigeante du football mondial au sujet de son calendrier des matchs internationaux, malgré la pression de députés européens. “La mission de l’UEFA est de veiller au football européen dans son ensemble”, a déclaré l’instance dans un communiqué. “Nous l’accomplissons grâce à un modèle de gouvernance inclusif, qui associe toutes les parties prenantes : les fédérations nationales, les ligues, les clubs, les joueurs et les supporters ont tous voix au chapitre, et les décisions sont prises par le dialogue et le compromis. Dans le cadre de ce modèle de gouvernance, le memorandum of understanding UEFA-EFC, publiquement accessible, offre depuis 2008 un cadre stable et transparent pour la coopération avec les clubs à l’échelle européenne. Il garantit que les clubs participants prennent véritablement part à toutes les décisions concernant les compétitions européennes de clubs.” Contactée par POLITICO, EFC n’a pas répondu à nos demandes de commentaire au moment de la parution de cet article. Miguel Maduro, ancien avocat général à la Cour de justice de l’Union européenne et ancien président de la commission de gouvernance de la Fifa, a conseillé l’UEC dans le cadre de sa plainte. Pour ce détracteur régulier de la gouvernance actuelle du football européen et mondial, cette affaire vise “à utiliser le droit européen de la concurrence pour protéger le modèle sportif européen, caractérisé par des compétitions véritablement ouvertes et équilibrées”. “Un système dans lequel un groupe restreint de clubs d’élite se voit conférer le pouvoir de décider qui peut participer aux compétitions européennes et comment les recettes sont réparties ne nuit pas seulement à la concurrence dans le football européen et national. Il détruit progressivement le modèle de compétition ouverte et équilibrée que l’UEFA elle-même prétend protéger”, a-t-il ajouté. Qui parle au nom des clubs ? L’UEC fonde en partie son argumentation sur l’arrêt rendu en 2023 par la Cour de justice de l’Union européenne concernant la Super Ligue . Elle fait valoir que les principes régissant la manière dont l’UEFA approuve les compétitions concurrentes devraient également s’appliquer à son accord avec EFC. “Quiconque contrôle l’accès au football européen doit le faire selon des critères transparents, objectifs et non discriminatoires. Un accord qui impose aux clubs d’être représentés exclusivement par une association au sein de laquelle la plupart d’entre eux n’ont pas leur mot à dire, et qui exclut de ses rangs les clubs qui adhèrent à une autre association, ne répond pas à ces critères”, a déclaré Miguel Maduro. Les règles d’EFC interdisent à ses membres d’adhérer à d’autres organisations transnationales représentant des clubs, à moins qu’elles ne soient reconnues par EFC ainsi que la Fifa ou l’UEFA. L’UEC fait valoir que les petits clubs n’ont pas d’influence significative au sein d’EFC, qui compte actuellement 920 membres dans le football masculin et féminin et est présidée par le puissant dirigeant qatari Nasser al-Khelaïfi . EFC indique sur son site web que tous ses membres peuvent élire des représentants au conseil d’administration et aux autres instances qui orientent ses travaux. Lors de son lancement en avril 2023, l’UEC avait reçu le soutien de Margaritis Schinas, alors vice-président de la Commission européenne. “Je ne considère pas cela comme un problème ni comme un facteur de fragmentation”, avait-il déclaré à POLITICO lors de l’événement . “C’est une bonne chose.” L’UEC affirme qu’un club a été averti en mai 2024 qu’il perdrait son statut de membre d’EFC s’il restait au sein de la nouvelle organisation. Et que 59 clubs auraient demandé que leur adhésion à l’UEC reste confidentielle, par crainte d’éventuelles pressions. Sa plainte conteste également l’influence d’EFC sur la manière dont sont gérées des compétitions de l’UEFA. Selon l’UEC, EFC désigne 16 des 20 membres de la commission des compétitions interclubs de l’UEFA, chargée d’examiner les modifications apportées aux formats des tournois, aux modalités de qualification et aux rétributions financières. Elle estime que cela confère à un groupe restreint de clubs un pouvoir sur les règles qui concernent l’ensemble des clubs européens. L’UEC fait valoir que les rétributions européennes renforcent l’avantage dont bénéficient déjà les clubs de haut niveau. Une étude citée dans son dossier d’information estime à 110 millions d’euros les recettes versées par l’UEFA à un club anglais au cours d’une seule saison, soit environ la moitié du chiffre d’affaires annuel total de certains de ses rivaux de la Premier League, selon les chiffres de 2023. Cette étude, pour laquelle l’UEC a pris en charge une partie du travail sur les données, a également révélé qu’une cinquantaine de clubs se sont partagé environ 80% des places attribuées depuis 2000 en Ligue des champions, la compétition phare de l’UEFA. L’UEC a estimé que les mécanismes de gouvernance et de répartition des recettes contribuent à perpétuer cette tendance. L’organisation souhaite que la Commission se procure et publie le memorandum of understanding actuel entre l’UEFA et EFC, et qu’elle ordonne la suppression de toute clause restrictive, ouvrant ainsi la voie à d’autres instances de clubs pour qu’elles soient reconnues et participent au processus décisionnel, tandis qu’EFC continue de représenter ses membres. “Nous respectons pleinement le rôle de l’UEFA”, a déclaré le président de l’UEC, Ovidiu Costeșin, directeur général du CS Universitatea Craiova, champion de Roumanie en titre. “Mais le respect, ça ne peut pas vouloir dire le silence.” Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

noticias.titulo: UK hands Palantir two-year reprieve on NHS contract
noticias.resumen: Health minister James Frith described the extension of Palantir's NHS contract as “a bridge, not the destination.”
noticias.texto: LONDON —The U.K. government has confirmed it plans to end Palantir’s contract to provide a data platform for the National Health Service in 2029. However it is not severing the contract immediately, as some MPs and campaigners had pushed it to do. The government will begin formal procurement for a “new” contract in the second half of 2027, with the process expected to take 18 months, health minister James Frith told MPs on Monday. He described the extension of Palantir’s contract until 2029 as “a bridge, not the destination.” In a bid to regain “public trust” and open up opportunities for “U.K. sovereign capabilities,” Frith said “interoperability, resilience and trusted common standards” will be “baked into” the new procurement round, though non-U.K. firms will also be encouraged to bid. Palantir’s contract has attracted considerable scrutiny from campaigners, health professionals and MPs over controversial views expressed by the company’s founders and concerns about vendor lock-in. Two parliamentary committees have called for its NHS contract to be ended in the last year. “We want to give the health and care system more choice, greater resilience and less dependence on any single supplier, as well as the ability to adapt and evolve as new technologies emerge in future, with better value for taxpayers through time,” Frith said. “These objectives require a new approach — an approach that will stimulate a more diverse and innovative supplier market, including greater use of sovereign AI as well as internationally developed capabilities,” he added. This approach will encompass investment in strategic technologies, changing how novel technologies are procured, and developing open standards, Frith said. “We must avoid over-dependence and our future capability should avoid being locked into any single technology,” he said. He didn’t say whether Palantir will be able to bid on the new contract in 2029. A Palantir spokesperson said the announcement was “good news for patients and for the NHS” and it was “proud” of its work. “We will now redouble our efforts over the next two years to continue and accelerate that support,” as well as “deepen our investment in the U.K.,” they said.

noticias.titulo: Le bras de fer entre Le Pen et les constitutionnalistes
noticias.resumen: L’initiative n’est pas habituelle : 110 professeurs de droit ont cosigné une tribune dans Le Monde, mercredi dernier, pour rappeler les règles prévues en matière révision de la Constitution. Leur message : modifier notre loi fondamentale via l’article 11, utilisé jadis par Charles de Gaulle, est irrégulier. Or, Marine Le Pen prévoit d’y recourir pour […]
noticias.texto:
Listen on
L’initiative n’est pas habituelle : 110 professeurs de droit ont cosigné une tribune dans Le Monde, mercredi dernier, pour rappeler les règles prévues en matière révision de la Constitution. Leur message : modifier notre loi fondamentale via l’article 11, utilisé jadis par Charles de Gaulle, est irrégulier. Or, Marine Le Pen prévoit d’y recourir pour faire adopter par référendum ce qui constitue le cœur de son programme : la préférence nationale, la prééminence du droit national, ou encore la suppression du droit du sol.
Anthony Lattier évoque les enjeux de cette dispute juridique et politique avec le constitutionnaliste Benjamin Morel, maître de conférence en droit public à l’université Paris-Panthéon-Assas, qui a interviewé, il y a quelques jours, la candidate du RN pour la revue Le Grand continent.

noticias.titulo: 5 countries announce plan to deport failed asylum-seekers to Rwanda
noticias.resumen: Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands plan to open the deportation hubs in 2027.
noticias.texto: VIENNA — Five European Union countries plan to open a deportation hub in Rwanda for rejected asylum seekers, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said Monday. “If people without the right of residence in the EU cannot be removed, our entire asylum system is made a mockery of. And we are not going to allow that,” Stocker said. Stocker, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and government ministers from those two countries plus the Netherlands, Germany and Greece announced the plan at a press conference. The ministers stopped short of confirming they had cemented a deal, but said the hub would become operational during 2027. There are still some “technical things” that have to be “sorted out,” Frederiksen said. “But the framework, the idea and the partnership is now in place.” A reform of EU legislation adopted earlier this year made it possible for countries to negotiate deals to set up such deportation centers — as long as they comply with fundamental rights obligations. The five countries plan to transfer people to Rwanda who have already gone through full asylum proceedings and were ordered to leave the EU. The countries said they intend to target adults without children, and specifically people who don’t cooperate — or whose home countries don’t collaborate — in the deportation process. “For me, today marks a crucial step towards a new migration system; a system that safeguards the cohesion of our societies and answers the concerns of our citizens. To put it very short, it needs to be a democratic decision who can enter and who can stay in our societies,” Frederiksen said. Staying in Rwanda The five countries want to set up a reception center with the capacity to register and process 100 people at a time. Rejected asylum seekers who decide to stay in Rwanda rather than return to their country of origin would be given a residence permit and support to find a job and learn the language. Rwanda’s Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said he expected few would opt to stay, but insisted that those who do “are not going to be kept in a camp … they’ll be integrated in our society.” “Those transferred to Rwanda will have the opportunity to settle, integrate into Rwandese society and build a new future,” said Dutch Foreign Affairs Minister Tom Berendsen. When sending migrants to Rwanda, their protection would remain a “key priority,” he said. The partnership would also have to meet the principle of non-refoulement, which forbids countries from forcing people to countries where they might be under threat, as well as other principles of international and European law, Berendsen added. Rwanda has “considerable experience in hosting refugees” and a “strong track record of working with international organizations, including the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees(UNHCR),” the Dutch minister said, adding that the five countries want to continue working with these organizations. It’s not yet clear whether the IOM will be involved. In a statement Monday, the U.N. organization confirmed it had received a request from Rwanda to support EU return hub arrangements. “IOM has indicated that it can support in principle, provided its mandate and international standards can be upheld,” the organization said. Civil society groups are not convinced. In a joint reaction , 47 human rights, civil society and trade union groups warned that European authorities had previously reported “torture in detention, arbitrary arrests and impunity within the security services” in Rwanda, as well as a “real risk” of refoulement. EU countries’ partnership “signals that Member States accept the risk of serious human rights violations against one of the most marginalized groups in society, in return for a deterrence goal that evidence clearly suggests they will not reach,” they wrote in a call on the EU to protect human rights. “I think we need to go beyond the existing cliché,” Biruta said on Monday. Rwanda is hosting more than 150,000 refugees “from as far as Afghanistan, from Sudan, Congolese, Burundians, and their rights were respected,” and it’s asking for a return hub system that meets “international law, European law and our national laws.” The country wants to bring on board international organizations and put an independent monitoring mechanism in place, he said: “Everyone will be welcome to witness and monitor what’s happening.” But civil society groups are worried return hubs would move vulnerable people far away from genuine oversight. “Looking at what we know from previous agreements with third countries, it has proven to be very difficult to guarantee any kind of human rights standard,” Meron Ameha Knikman, senior EU advocacy adviser at the International Rescue Committee, said ahead of the announcement. “It doesn’t matter what you put on paper — as long as it’s not under your jurisdiction, it’s extremely difficult if not impossible to enforce … any kind of guarantees.” More hubs to follow The ministers indicated that a deal with Rwanda could be the first in a string of return hub partnerships. “We are already exploring other partner countries, and I think other European countries will participate as well,” Frederiksen said. Return hubs aren’t just about ramping up deportations, but also about sending a signal, she argued, adding that if people don’t assume they’ll get to stay after entering the EU irregularly, many would rethink their decision to attempt it. Frederiksen also pushed back against human rights concerns in the partnership with Rwanda. “You have to remember that we are talking about people who don’t have a legal reason to be in Europe. It’s people who have entered illegally and that have no right to be protected in Europe or to stay,” Frederiksen said in a response to a question from POLITICO. “What is the alternative? Is it to continue the system we have today?” she asked. “Because if you believe in human rights, I don’t like the current system. It’s broken. I have been to refugee camps outside Europe and seen with my own eyes that some of those who are most fragile … will never come to Europe because it demands a lot of money and strength to travel.” “If the prospect of dying in the desert, being raped and tortured in Libya, or drowning at sea doesn’t deter people, it’s hard to see how the possibility of being sent to Rwanda would dissuade people,” Judith Sunderland, senior associate director in the refugee and migrant rights division of Human Rights Watch, told POLITICO. This article has been updated

noticias.titulo: Europeans court China’s help to keep climate action on track
noticias.resumen: Diplomats see China as key to breaking a deadlock holding up scientific reports.
noticias.texto: ANTALYA, Turkey — European governments will hold crunch talks with China this week, in a last-ditch bid to preserve the role of scientific advice in global climate summits. On the sidelines of the U.N. climate conference in Turkey’s Antalya, senior officials from several European delegations are meeting with their Chinese counterparts to get Beijing onside in a messy fight over scientific reports, five negotiators told POLITICO. “There’s a big diplomatic move,” said Francesco Corvaro, Italy’s climate envoy. “We’re working to create pressure.” The dispute ensnares the U.N.’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, a body which produces scientific assessments every five to seven years, and whose advice is considered the ultimate authority on the state of knowledge on global warming — and how to fight it. The IPCC’s scientists hope to release their next series of reports in 2028. But the timeline is set by consensus among world governments, and a small group of countries led by India and Saudi Arabia are seeking to postpone publication. As part of the dispute, they’re also blocking the body’s budget, throwing the IPCC into a funding crisis that could impede its work. Any delay to the next reports would deprive climate negotiators of fresh scientific input at the pivotal COP conference in 2028, when countries must assess their progress toward the Paris Agreement and take remedial action to fix shortfalls. (The exercise is known as the second global stocktake, or GST2). “We have this issue with the IPCC — the alliance of Saudi Arabia and India that wants to postpone the reports,” said Corvaro. “Without the reports of the IPCC, it’s tough to have a good global stocktake. We need to know the details of how far we’re falling short if we want to respond.” European countries see China as key to resolving the impasse. If they manage to pull Beijing onside, the diplomats said, the blocking countries may fold. Finding time The IPCC is due to publish three reports. The first will focus on the science, the second on how to prepare for the effects of climate change, and the third on how to ensure warming doesn’t get worse. The latter in particular is key for the global stocktake. Most countries want the body to deliver its reports in 2028, so that the stocktake at COP33 can draw on the latest scientific research. “It is essential that the IPCC continues its work and that the seventh assessment report can be delivered in good time to inform GST2,” EU chief negotiator Diana Acconcia told reporters last week. “Europe stands on the side of science.” But India and Saudi Arabia want more time, arguing this will allow authors and governments from developing countries to review and approve the reports. “You have to give adequate time” to developing countries’ scientists, said an official from a developing country opposing the 2028 timeline. “It’s more of a principled position … not to stonewall or delay any studies.” The official spoke on condition his country not be identified. Countries pushing for the 2028 timeline — which include not only European governments but many developing countries highly vulnerable to climate change — disagree. “We have seen efforts to undermine the IPCC and to block its reports informing the next global stocktake,” said Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine last week. “Our Pacific scientists tell us the work can and should be completed on time.” The leaders of Norway and Brazil also backed the IPCC’s role in their speeches in Antalya last week. A French official told reporters that the Indian and Saudi Arabian efforts are “absolutely unacceptable because, in a way, it’s questioning science.” India and Saudi Arabia have suggested an alternate timeline that would deliver the first, science-only report in time for the stocktake — but push the other two, which focus on actions for countries to take, out to 2029. The process is highly political. The last stocktake, in 2023, produced a hard-fought decision signed by all governments to transition away from fossil fuels — the first time the need to do so was acknowledged in a conference decision. Saudi Arabia has since sought to walk back that outcome. This time, the timeline debate has also dragged in questions about IPCC funding, which is already under pressure due to the exit of the United States. Without a budget, the body’s work cannot continue. The result is a diplomatic deadlock over what used to be a technical detail. For six consecutive meetings, the IPCC’s assembly has failed to reach an agreement. Last month’s gathering in Ethiopia was suspended without result. Countries are due to meet again on Dec. 1. — the final chance to settle on a budget for the coming year. “It’s not blocking,” the developing country official insisted. “A consensus has to be found. You can’t pass the budget in a non-transparent way.” India and Saudi Arabia also have the backing of Kenya and Russia, and diplomats say China has also objected to a fast publication timeline. But they believe that Beijing can be swayed. “China is in the middle — not completely aligned with Saudi Arabia and India,” said Corvaro. “We hope it’s possible to get a common understanding with them to underline the importance of science and data.” ‘Everything is polarized’ As the Antalya summit brings together ministers from across the world, countries are hopeful the dispute could be resolved this week. But the stakes are high. “We have an opportunity here to get consensus on the IPCC with ministers here,” said one European diplomat, who was not authorized to speak on the record. “If they manage that, I can’t see next month’s IPCC meeting fail. Otherwise, it might be doomed.” Countries are mindful about not dragging the IPCC into a political debate at the COP — the two bodies fall under separate U.N. procedures — but say finding a resolution is a matter of urgency. “We have to be careful here. We don’t want to make things more difficult for the IPCC,” said a second European diplomat. “But if they don’t agree on a budget in December, it will delay and disrupt work on the next reports. That’s unacceptable.” The governments of India and Saudi Arabia did not respond to requests for comment. The developing country official said his country would oppose any attempt to address the IPCC issue in the Antalya summit’s decision text. A first draft of the final conference decision , released Monday, suggests countries note the “importance of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change for the global stocktake.” The IPCC, for its part, has welcomed government talks in Antalya. “I think governments talking here in this space [at COP] is extremely helpful,” said IPCC Vice Chair Diana Ürge-Vorsatz. “It’s crucial that we have a decision very soon, because it’s very difficult for the scientists involved, it’s difficult for the institution. It’s very difficult for everyone to be in this uncertainty.” The fact that the IPCC’s bureaucratic procedures had become so political was “difficult to watch,” she added. “Why has it become polarized? Because, unfortunately, at the moment everything is polarized. And because there are some parties that are trying to undermine what science is telling us, because they don’t want to do what it takes to address climate change,” said Acconcia, the EU negotiator. The bloc would strive for a resolution in Antalya, she added. “We will fight for this outcome to be there.”

noticias.titulo: Google says Russian speakers pulled off first-ever fully automated AI cyberattack
noticias.resumen: The development could mark an inflection point in the use of AI for cyberattacks.
noticias.texto: Russian-speaking hackers built an AI agent that carried out what may be the first-ever fully-automated cyberattack, Google reported Monday. The tech giant’s cyber threat intelligence division said it had spotted hackers using artificial intelligence to “fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop for the first time.” The development could mark an inflection point in the use of AI for cyberattacks, which has dominated headlines and worried policymakers since AI firm Anthropic released its specialized model Mythos in April. Hackers, who used Russian in technical documentation identified by Google, set up a series of AI agents to “continuously compare pre- and post-patch code, identify vulnerabilities, and automatically develop exploits without human intervention,” Google said. That means the agents independently found software flaws and ways to use them. The attackers targeted French websites in the media, entertainment and education sectors, Google said. Until now, even the most advanced AI models could not carry out cyberattacks entirely independently; they often required skilled hackers to guide them or fix mistakes. The key change instead was that AI models allow hackers to accelerate attacks and make them more targeted. The development is likely to spook governments and critical infrastructure operators who are still reeling from this summer’s hack by an OpenAI agent into the Hugging Face platform. Though acting autonomously, that hack didn’t appear to be maliciously aimed at certain targets like the one being reported by Google. Fears are also running high after the recent discovery of major flaws in PHP , a programming language that underpins 70 percent of the web, and a series of hacks on supermarket fridges , which have been partially blamed on Iran. This article has been updated.

noticias.titulo: Entwurf des COP-Abkommens sieht „sofortigen“ Ausstieg aus fossilen Brennstoffen vor
noticias.resumen: Der Textentwurf sorgte für Irritationen bei europäischen Diplomaten.
noticias.texto: ANTALYA, Türkei — Australiens erster Entwurf für einen Abschlusstext der diesjährigen UN-Klimakonferenz soll als Gesprächsaufhänger dienen. Er sorgt jedenfalls dafür, dass die Diplomaten ins Gespräch kommen. Die Australier, die den Vorsitz bei den Verhandlungen auf dem COP31-Gipfel in Antalya innehaben, haben am Montag einen 18-seitigen Entwurf für einen Beschlusstext vorgelegt. Dieser enthält eine Vielzahl klarer Positionen, darunter die Forderung nach einem „sofortigen“ Ausstieg aus fossilen Brennstoffen im Energiesektor. Europäische Diplomaten, die sich bei POLITICO gemeldet haben, zeigen sich verwirrt über die Behauptung, der Text „erkenne“ die Forderung einiger Entwicklungsländer an, dass reiche Länder „bis 2030 Netto-Null-Emissionen erreichen“ sollten. Dieses Ziel liegt Jahrzehnte vor den Zielen der EU und des Vereinigten Königreichs zur Klimaneutralität im Jahr 2050. Eine Verdreifachung der Finanzmittel für Entwicklungsländer zur Vorbereitung auf Klimakatastrophen auf 120 Milliarden Dollar pro Jahr wird auch für die Industrieländer, die mit Haushaltsengpässen im eigenen Land zu kämpfen haben, schwer zu verkraften sein. Die Ölstaaten werden unterdessen aufgefordert, sich der Forderung nach einem schnelleren Ausstieg aus fossilen Brennstoffen anzuschließen, unter anderem „durch den sofortigen Umstieg weg von fossilen Brennstoffen in den Energiesystemen“. „Zweifellos werden die Menschen ein wenig Zeit brauchen, um das zu verarbeiten … Es ist sehr umfassend“, sagte Chris Bowen, Australiens Klimaminister, gegenüber Reportern. „Und die heftigen Reaktionen, die es gegeben hat, sind genau so beabsichtigt. Damit wird eine Diskussion darüber angestoßen, wie der endgültige Entwurf aussehen wird, den wir den Vertragsparteien im Laufe der Woche vorlegen werden.“ Der Vorschlag der türkischen Mitveranstalter, ein freiwilliges globales Elektrifizierungsziel festzulegen – das laut Ankara am Samstag von rund 30 Ländern unterstützt wird –, wurde ebenfalls in den Beschlussentwurf aufgenommen. Mehrere Länder haben Einwände gegen die Idee neuer Ziele erhoben . Jeder endgültige Beschluss der COP erfordert den Konsens aller Regierungen. „Dieser erste Entwurf wird sich vom endgültigen Entwurf unterscheiden – genau dafür ist der Prozess ja gedacht“, sagte Bowen. „Ich gehe also davon aus, dass es bis Ende der Woche noch mindestens einen weiteren Entwurf geben wird, aber wir werden so lange weiterarbeiten, bis wir ein Dokument haben, auf das sich alle einigen können.“ Dieser Text ist zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO erschienen.

noticias.titulo: SPONSORED EPISODE: Europe’s ambition to stop cancer
noticias.resumen: Europe is a leader in cancer research. But turning that science into treatments that reach patients is another matter. Every minute, five people in Europe are diagnosed with cancer, and the disease costs the European economy more than €100 billion a year. Five years after its launch, Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan has been scrutinized by […]
noticias.texto: Listen on Spotify Apple Music Amazon Music Europe is a leader in cancer research. But turning that science into treatments that reach patients is another matter. Every minute, five people in Europe are diagnosed with cancer, and the disease costs the European economy more than €100 billion a year. Five years after its launch, Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan has been scrutinized by the European Court of Auditors and the European Parliament. Both back its ambitions but find delivery falling short, with national cancer plans often lacking the resources to succeed and access to care varying widely among member countries. Meanwhile, Europe’s share of global commercial clinical trials has almost halved in a decade. With the EU’s proposed Biotech Act under negotiation and talks on the bloc’s next long-term budget under way, Europe has a chance to close the gap between innovation and access. In the second of two special podcast episodes produced by POLITICO Studio, experts in cancer policy explore what Europe must do to ensure every patient benefits from innovations in cancer care, from speeding up clinical trials to giving patients a real voice in policymaking. Hear from Elisabetta Zanon, chief executive of the European Cancer Organisation, which brings together cancer professionals and patients from across Europe; and Jennifer Young, VP and head of International Commercial Policy and Communications for Pfizer. noticias.titulo: Un brouillon de la COP31 préconise une sortie “immédiate” des énergies fossiles
noticias.resumen: Une version préliminaire de l'accord du sommet sur le climat a été publiée lundi.
noticias.texto: ANTALYA, Turquie — Censée lancer les négociations de la COP31, la première ébauche australienne du texte de couverture de la conférence des Nations unies sur le climat suscite déjà de vives discussions parmi les diplomates. Les Australiens, qui président les négociations lors du sommet de la COP31 à Antalya, ont présenté lundi un premier brouillon de 18 pages . Celui-ci contient un large éventail de positions fermes, notamment un appel à une sortie “immédiate” des énergies fossiles dans le secteur énergétique, qui serait une première. Les diplomates européens qui se sont exprimés auprès de POLITICO se sont dits perplexes face à l’idée selon laquelle le texte “reconnaîtrait” l’appel lancé par certains pays en développement, selon lequel les pays riches devraient “atteindre la neutralité carbone d’ici 2030”. Cet objectif devance de plusieurs décennies les objectifs de neutralité climatique de l’UE et du Royaume-Uni, fixés à 2050. Tripler le financement destiné aux pays en développement pour les aider à se préparer aux catastrophes climatiques, pour le porter à 120 milliards de dollars par an, sera également une pilule difficile à avaler pour les pays développés, qui sont eux-mêmes confrontés à des contraintes budgétaires au niveau national. Les pays producteurs de pétrole, quant à eux, sont invités à se rallier à l’appel en faveur d’une élimination plus rapide des combustibles fossiles, notamment “par le biais d’une transition immédiate vers des systèmes énergétiques sans combustibles fossiles”. “Il ne fait aucun doute que les gens auront besoin d’un peu de temps pour assimiler tout cela […] C’est un document très complet”, a déclaré Chris Bowen, ministre australien du Climat, lors d’un échange avec des journalistes. “Et les opinions tranchées qui ont été exprimées, c’est exactement ce que nous recherchions. Cela lance le débat sur ce à quoi ressemblera le projet final que nous soumettrons aux parties dans le courant de la semaine.” La proposition des co-organisateurs turcs visant à fixer un objectif mondial volontaire en matière d’électrification, qui, selon Ankara samedi, bénéficie du soutien d’une trentaine de pays, a également été intégrée au projet de décision. Plusieurs pays se sont opposés à cet objectif. Toute décision finale de la COP nécessite le consensus de tous les gouvernements. “Cette première version sera différente de la version finale ; c’est justement le but de ce processus”, a expliqué Chris Bowen. “Je m’attends donc à ce qu’il y ait au moins une autre version avant la fin de la semaine, mais nous continuerons à travailler jusqu’à ce que nous disposions d’un document faisant l’objet d’un consensus.” Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été traduit en français par Alexandre Léchenet.

noticias.titulo: European Parliament would back UK rejoining the EU, says senior lawmaker
noticias.resumen: Sandro Gozi, chair of the EU delegation to the U.K. parliament, says Brexit was a "disaster."
noticias.texto: LONDON — The European Parliament would give its backing to the U.K. reentering the EU, a senior MEP said Monday ahead of a major speech by Andy Burnham on Britain’s future relationship with Europe. Sandro Gozi, chair of the EU delegation to the U.K. parliament, told POLITICO that a majority of MEPs would be in favor, adding that the European Parliament “is the institution which is the most advanced in pushing for a new kind of relationship.” He said this is the case “across the political groups” because “even the extreme right must take stock of the fact that it [Brexit] was a bad decision.” Gozi, who is visiting London to attend an annual summit of British and EU lawmakers, welcomed Burnham’s decision to reopen the debate over Brexit, describing the U.K.’s departure from the bloc as a “disaster.” He said that if the U.K. were to rejoin the EU, it would be “a victory of the progressive forces against nationalism,” finding expression in National Rally in France and the AfD in Germany. It would show that “the future is not going back to nationalistic borders, but building up a future together,” he added. Marsha de Cordova, chair of the U.K. delegation to the European Parliament, hailed Friday’s EU-U.K. summit as “the first step” towards finding a way forward in Britain’s relationship with the EU. She shrugged off criticism that Burnham has opened up new splits in the Labour Party and the Cabinet, saying that while some Labour MPs have “sensitivities” about moving closer to the EU, “the prime minister and the foreign secretary are right to want to seek to have that conversation and that dialogue and debate.” “I welcome it because the evidence is there,” she added. “We didn’t have the evidence six years ago, or even 10 years ago. But now we do have the evidence. We’ve seen what happens.” Both politicians were skeptical of the value of the Labour Party’s “red lines”— which were introduced in the 2024 election manifesto and rule out rejoining the EU, the single market, the customs union or restoring freedom of movement — which Burnham has signaled he is not yet ready to tear up. “The red lines are being swept away by the debate,” said Gozi. “For me, they they are not there anymore.” De Cordova noted the red lines were drawn up “at a very, very different time… naturally, you need to revisit those at some point.” The prime minister, who fired the starting gun on a debate about the EU in his party conference speech in September, will give a speech Monday night where he is expected to argue the U.K. has “lost more than we gained” from leaving the European Union. At the same time, he will reiterate his commitment to Labour’s red lines for the time being, as a sign of a more gradual approach. His speech comes ahead of Friday’s meeting in Brussels, where the two sides are aiming to land a series of deals on agri-food, youth mobility and electricity trading.

noticias.titulo: ‘Emperor’s New Clothes’: Burnham breaks 10-year taboo on Brexit
noticias.resumen: Boris Johnson's 'oven ready' Brexit deal never tasted very good. That's part of the 'obvious truth' about Brexit, according to UK PM Andy Burnham.
noticias.texto:
“It’s like the emperor’s new clothes – where no one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on.”
That’s the main salvo from UK premier Andy Burnham at a speech on EU-UK relations on Monday night (16 November) ahead of a summit in Brussels with EU leaders this Friday where he is expected to unveil a series of agreements ranging from food and carbon emissions, to youth mobility and industrial policy.
“The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we have gained,” he adds.
It might seem remarkably uncontroversial from most Europeans on this side of the Channel, but saying it breaks a 10-year taboo among leaders of the UK’s main parties.
Though the summit and accompanying deals are, in part, a PR exercise, they do mark the biggest step by far towards closer EU-UK ties since the 2016 referendum that took the Britain out of the bloc.

noticias.resumen: While Europe crafts its role in the Ukraine peace talks, Vladimir Putin’s renewed offensive raises the cost of every EU decision.
noticias.texto:
Europe still doesn’t know how its so-called ‘Big 5’ will negotiate with Ukraine, the US, and Russia in practice, as Moscow escalates aggression on all fronts, while making “absurd” demands on Nato.
Foreign ministers discussed the composition and mandate of the Big 5 format in Brussels on Monday (16 November).
They spoke after the US and Russia invited Europe to join the peace process and EU leaders decided informally in Dublin last Friday that they should be represented by France, Germany, Italy, Poland, the UK, plus the EU institutions.
And foreign ministers broadly endorsed the model.
“The Europeans are determined to take charge of their own security and not let anyone write their history … for them,” said French foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot on Monday.
Germany’s Johann Wadephul said: “It is now clear who speaks [for Europe] … so let’s get to work”.
“Poland will represent our entire region, the entire eastern flank … this means that we are in the game,” said Polish foreign minister Radek Sikorski.
Danish foreign minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen also said: “I feel completely safe with this format”.
But the Dublin accord still left open questions of the Big 5's internal structure and who should represent the EU institutions.

noticias.titulo: Five EU countries tout Rwanda deportation partnership, but no formal deal as key details remain secret
noticias.resumen: Rwanda is set to host a so-called EU return hub. No formal deal has been announced as technical details still need to be sorted out in negotiations. The hope is to start deporting people next year.
noticias.texto: Rejected asylum seekers with deportation orders from possibly even as far away as Afghanistan may end up in Rwanda, following the announcement of talks spearheaded by five European countries with Kigali on Monday (16 November). No formal deal has been signed, posing questions on why Austria’s chancellor Christian Stocker and Denmark’s prime minister Mette Frederiksen, along ministers from Austria, Germany, Greece, the Netherlands and Rwanda’s interior minister Vincent Biruta, would announce anything. Instead, they gathered in Vienna, held a press conference and told journalists that a “partnership” had been agreed with Rwanda amid outstanding technical issues that still need to be sorted in the hopes of signing a formal deal in the coming months. Read more Rwanda revealed as EU’s first migrant return hub, but what’s in it for Kigali? The plan is to start deportations next year, said Austria’s Stocker despite Rwanda’s checkered human rights spanning political repression to its support of the M23 armed group operating in the eastern DR Congo. Even so Stocker described it as a “truly historic paradigm”, noting that Austria had deported more people than it has had asylum applications. His comments were largely echoed by Frederiksen, who said they now have a broad majority of European countries for a more sustainable migration policy. “We are now ready to move into more concrete steps,” said Frederiksen, who claimed they intend to remove incentives for “illegal migration” by sending a global signal that they are not welcomed in Europe. Little detail Nobody would cite potential costs when pressed on specifics. Rwanda’s Biruta said those received in Rwanda would have the opportunity to voluntarily continue home, go somewhere else, or integrate with legal residence and get jobs. He cited Rwanda’s experience of working with the International Organisation for Migration (IOM), a UN offshoot that flies in refugees stranded in Libya to a Rwandan hosted transit centre before being resettled elsewhere. “We are sensitive to people who are seeking asylum. This is our main motivation,” he said. “We are not looking at really getting money,” he said amid promises that people would not be put in camps. noticias.titulo: More EU sanctions on Russian propagandists and hackers, as thousands of fake accounts target voters
noticias.resumen: The EU agreed on Monday (16 November) to sanction 30 people and two organisations over Russian cyberattacks and disinformation campaigns targeting Europe, as researchers uncovered thousands of fake accounts used to target election campaigns.
noticias.texto: The EU agreed on Monday (16 November) to sanction 30 people and two organisations over Russian cyberattacks and disinformation campaigns aimed at Europe, as researchers uncovered thousands of fake accounts used to target election campaigns. “We all care about human rights and freedom of expression, but human rights and freedoms of expression are not designed for robots,” French liberal MEP Nathalie Loiseau, chair of the parliament’s committee dealing with foreign interference, said during a hearing on the topic on Monday. Also on Monday, a report by Alliance4Europe revealed at least 8,505 Russian fake accounts were used ahead of the Swedish general elections in September. They also found that public authorities tend to respond to disinformation targeting specific posts and campaigns, rather than account networks and systems spreading false narratives for months. Read more Swedish election ‘not a priority’ for Moscow interference but still a target for troll farms and disinformation “[But] taking down single channels or posts achieves little while the infrastructure, the platform weaknesses and the payouts that sustain it stay in place,” reads the report. Russian propaganda networks switched from one country to another, changing profile names and photos to pose as local citizens. The researchers found that the same 550 fake accounts exposed ahead of the Dutch parliamentary elections in October 2025 then spread disinformation ahead of Hungary’s vote in April. While some spread false claims, often branded as coming from trusted news sources, many of them focus on following thousands of social media accounts with controversial and polarising lines, tricking the platform’s algorithm into boosting their reach, researchers said. Read more EU sanctions needed against Russian bot and troll factories, MEPs say Though the impact of fakes is often not spectacular in size, electoral campaigns are “a moment of sensitivity” in which uncertainty plays a key role, Omri Preiss, from Alliance4Europe and one of the report authors, told EUobserver. noticias.titulo: [Interview] ‘Georgia has reached final stage of autocratic consolidation,’ warns former deputy foreign minister
noticias.resumen: Georgia’s fall from EU frontrunner to near-total state capture is not just a regional tragedy but a case study in how Russia exploits European complacency to pull an entire country back into its orbit, explains former minister.
noticias.texto: Georgia was once the frontrunner among countries aspiring to European Union integration. Twenty years ago, it was the only country in the region officially announcing its pro-European foreign policy course, declaring that Georgia wanted to become part of the EU and Nato, not only because of security guarantees, but because Europe had always been part of Georgia’s national identity and cultural belonging. This was demonstrated at length through those years with specific democratic reforms and the transformation of the country after the Rose Revolution in 2003. But since then, Georgia is now on a different path — one of illiberal democracy and pro-Russian sentiment. On 9 November, Guillaume Mercier, a European Commission spokesperson, announced that Georgia would not be invited to the Enlargement Forum happening this week (15-16 November). In an exclusive interview with the country’s former deputy foreign affairs minister Nino Kalandadze, we return to the biggest pivotal moments, as well as to how Georgia can be taken as a cautionary tale for the EU and its member states. “Georgia had previously been a failed state, but it was transformed almost overnight into a beacon of democracy,” Kalandadze told EUobserver. “There was a common understanding that democracy was a self-sustainable and self-sufficient project, and that all countries would eventually understand that democracy was what they needed to develop and thrive,” she says. Back in 2012, in the Transparency International ranking of its Corruption Perception Index, Georgia ranked ahead of several EU member states, including the Czech Republic, Latvia, Slovakia, Romania and Bulgaria. “We worked hard to eliminating organised crime and widespread corruption, topping international rankings, and becoming the number one reformer,” says Kalandadze. But in 2026, Georgia illustrates how unsustainable democratic achievements can become and how easily European integration can be reversed. Read more When the state turns on its own: Georgia’s civil society under siege Compared to where the country was 14 years ago, now “we have a ruling system that has remained in power for four consecutive years without majority support,” says Kalandadze. That is problematic, as it has banned international funding and civil society organisations, thereby “eliminating critical media and critical voices, establishing a system of political prisoners, with leaders and activists in prison or exile, and essentially cleared the way for itself by eliminating political competition,” Kalandadze says. And now, “we have essentially reached the final stage of autocratic consolidation,” says the former deputy foreign affair minister. “There is no way for us to maintain the instruments we need to move closer to European integration.” The soul is intact, the body is changing In 2024, some 20,000 Georgian citizens took to the streets to defend European integration, their freedom, and the choice they made about the foreign policy direction Tbilisi should follow. The demonstrators back then called it “March for Europe”. “This is still a freedom-loving and civilised society,” says Kalandadze. Indeed, “society made the effort to transform Georgia into a country that could obtain EU candidate status,” she also says. But the political system failed. “It is a combination of what many would call democratic naivety, but also perhaps convenience and ignorance on the part of international partners,” she says. The “blind eye” over Russia that the EU followed are one of the reasons for Kalandadze to explain Georgia’s U-turn. noticias.titulo: What Marine Le Pen and Alice Weidel are planning for Brussels
noticias.resumen: The AfD's Alice Weidel envisages reducing EU powers under existing rules within three years, pursuing treaty reform within seven, and using Germany's budgetary leverage along the way. Hot on her heels, Marine Le Pen is looking towards national elections across Europe to build a coalition of like-minded governments.
noticias.texto: It’s been an early Christmas for Europe’s centre-left, watching even the most unshakeable populists stumble. Viktor Orbán’s defeat in April sent shockwaves through Europe after 16 years of entrenched cronyism , while Serbia followed hot on the heels of this October, reminding leaders that clinging to power is not the same as keeping the vote . And just when the drama seemed to subside, American voters, fed up with soaring prices , showed that the fury that lifts politicians to power can just as swiftly sweep them away. Should Brussels’ centre-left pop the champagne? Not so fast. The trouble with celebrating populists’ downfall is that the grievances that put them in office are still simmering. Alice Weidel in Germany and Marine Le Pen in France, for one, seem to have read the room. ‘Frexit’ and the single currency Putting reform before withdrawal is no small thing. Le Pen has already ditched Frexit , while Weidel’s AfD is reconsidering its longstanding hostility to the euro . These are not merely plans to trim ‘ Brussels bureaucracy’ ; they strike at the question of who gets the final say in Europe. For Germany’s export-dependent economy, leaving Europe’s single market and common currency could carry an uncomfortable price tag (€690bn). Rather, Weidel has baked into her proposed major reform of Germany’s role in the EU a shift from, in her words, its current paymaster role to one which reinforces German sovereignty. Weidel has even put a timetable on the ambition. Her party’s roadmap envisages reducing EU powers under existing rules within three years, pursuing treaty reform within seven, and using Germany’s budgetary leverage along the way. Hot on her heels, Le Pen is looking towards national elections across Europe to build a coalition of like-minded governments . Both appear to recognise that power in Brussels can begin with power at home. And with populist parties gaining influence across the continent , changing the EU from within may offer more political leverage than another Brexit season. Who holds the purse strings? The timing of Le Pen and Weidel’s rise could hardly be more uncomfortable. As the EU hammers out its nearly €2 trillion 2028–2034 budget , it is juggling the costly business of backing Ukraine, beefing up defence, and answering demands to spend more at home. For Le Pen and Weidel, Brussels’ budgetary nightmare could be the ideal stage to show who should really control the purse strings. Enter Le Pen, stage right. If in power following the 2027 French elections, Le Pen wants to slash France’s EU contributions while simultaneously demanding the return of €2.2 bn annually in customs duties collected at French borders. Yet France is also a major beneficiary of EU agricultural funding. Cutting Brussels’ contributions could therefore raise awkward questions about who picks up the bill for French farmers. A September 2026 German Council on Foreign Relations study warns that a future French government could exploit the national ratification process to obstruct the EU’s revenue arrangements, even after a painstaking budget agreement. Even if Brussels manages to hammer out a deal before French voters have their say, the squabble over who foots the bill is unlikely to vanish. The EU’s revenue rules still demand a chorus of unanimous approval and a round of national rubber-stamping, which could hand a future French government a fresh bargaining chip long after the ink dries on any spending pact. Brussels still faces the headache of actually securing the cash, with nationalist parties like AfD threatening to, if in power, block decisions until their demands are met. Crowded calendar for 2027 And Brussels has already spotted the storm. Emmanuel Macron has urged EU leaders to reach a budget agreement before the year is out, warning that Europe’s crowded 2027 election calendar could make negotiations considerably harder. But rushing through a deal does not guarantee it will put the matter to bed. Even after governments agree on spending, a future French administration could still challenge the arrangements for financing it. And while Weidel’s AfD remains outside Germany’s government, its proposed roadmap offers a glimpse of how the country’s financial weight might be used to demand wider institutional changes. The warning for Brussels is clear: the next Eurosceptic challenge may not come from those threatening to storm out, but from those determined to stay and rewrite the rulebook.

noticias.titulo: ‘Prague doesn’t want Nazis’: Activists block Slovak far-right MEP from conference about deporting immigrants
noticias.resumen: In a heavily guarded Prague hotel, anti-migrant ideologues from Germany, Hungary and Czech Republic rallied together in support of a petition to deport foreigners that was rejected by the EU on rights grounds. MEP Milan Mazurek, previously convicted of inciting hatred towards Roma, was stopped from going inside by antifascist protesters.
noticias.texto: In a heavily guarded hotel on a drizzly Friday evening, anti-migrant ideologues from Germany, Hungary and the Czech Republic rallied together in Prague to discuss how to deport foreigners at a conference titled “What Comes After the EU? Migration or Remigration?”. Outside, hundreds of protesters blocked each entrance to the Hotel Step Wellness, a towering complex in an industrial neighbourhood of the Czech capital, where the conference was held. Demonstrators held banners that read slogans such as “Stop Islamophobia and antisemitism” while chanting “Prague doesn’t want Nazis”. The protest was announced online by Prague is Feminist ( Praha je feministická ), an antifascist protest group. Activists were determined to block entry to the conference on the Save Europe Act , a petition proposing an EU law on remigrating people who are not deemed ancestral Europeans. The initiative was rejected by the EU commission in July for violating fundamental rights, but organisers have pushed on, challenging the decision before the EU General Court and organising a series of events to push their campaign. At the event in Prague on Friday (13 November), protesters managed to keep some speakers out. Read more By rejecting a racist ‘remigration’ petition, the EU may have finally awakened its sleeping democracy experiment Despite a heavy riot police presence, protesters surrounded Slovak MEP Milan Mazurek of the far-right Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN) group as he arrived at the venue. Police were unable to get him inside, and he was eventually forced to turn back. This article continues, but the full version is available only to EUobserver.com subscribers. noticias.titulo: EU Commission clears UniCredit’s Commerzbank takeover, tells Berlin not to stand in the way
noticias.resumen: The European Commission has waved through Europe’s biggest cross-border bank takeover since the financial crisis, and warned it would “react accordingly” to any national government trying to block it.
noticias.texto:
The European Commission has approved Italian lender UniCredit’s takeover of Germany’s Commerzbank without any conditions.
That removes one of the last regulatory hurdles to what EU competition commissioner Theresa Ribera called “the biggest cross-border banking deal since the financial crisis” on Monday (16 November).
But competition was never the main obstacle. The German government, which still holds a 13 percent stake in Commerzbank following a 2009 bailout, opposed the deal from the moment UniCredit built a nine percent stake in September 2024.
About half of that was bought from the German government itself, which sold part of its holdings at the time.
Shortly after, Berlin said that it would not sell any more of its shares, and the finance ministry has since repeatedly described UniCredit’s bid as “aggressive and hostile”, most recently in July and September this year.

noticias.titulo: Ghost of Yalta returns, amid fears that Trump, Xi, and Putin will carve up Ukraine and Europe
noticias.resumen: History’s warning from Yalta hangs over today’s secretive talks, as European leaders answer an existential carve‑up threat with a clumsy committee instead of a single hard‑nosed envoy who knows the Kremlin’s playbook.
noticias.texto: On Thursday (19 November), the US, Russian, and Chinese leaders will meet in Shenzhen, China, with no Europeans present. Europeans were also kept out of the main negotiating table at the US-mediated Russian-Ukrainian talks in Abu Dhabi last week, though their officials held separate meetings on the sidelines Europeans will however be at the next round of Ukraine peace talks: a seeming concession by the Russians to an American request. The Europeans should beware. If the agenda is already set, they and their security will be there as an item for discussion, not as participants. In 2021 the Kremlin demanded the de facto demilitarisation of countries that joined Nato after 1997. Former US president Joe Biden’s administration rightly rejected that. Now US president Donald Trump’s envoys appear to be considering a much tougher set of Russian demands as part of a deal to end the Ukraine war. The Europeans have responded to this looming threat of a new Yalta with dithering and disunity. At the Dublin summit in Dublin last week , EU leaders of 500 million-plus people, with a combined economic weight of €28 trillion, nearly a quarter of global GDP, faced this existential question by nominating a committee: national security advisers from Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland; plus officials (still unspecified) from the European Union. It is good to have Poland on board. But a better choice would have featured, or at least explicitly included, the EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas. EU treaties give her, not an ad hoc committee, the foreign-policy job. Read more EU leaders hand Ukraine peace talks to France, Germany, UK, Italy, Poland plus Brussels – instead of a single envoy The former Estonian prime minister has an unparalleled understanding of Kremlin negotiating tactics. And the Trump administration loathes her – another reason to insist on her presence Diluting her role confirmed east Europeans’ feelings that “our knowledge and understanding about Russia and its erstwhile victims remain suspect when set against the fantasies and prejudices of Western Europeans,” noted Estonia’s former president Toomas Hendrik Ilves. But in truth all Europeans are being sidelined. No lessons learned from Yalta This article continues, but the full version is available only to EUobserver.com subscribers.
